By distributivity \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}} \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} = \big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\big(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\big)\), and each sum of the lengths of the pieces is a telescoping sum equal to the length of the edge (section 3.5.2). The right side of the inequality in step 5 is therefore \(\eta\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).

2. All orders give the same number.

  1. Let \(I\) and \(I'\) be iterated integrals of \(f\) in two orders. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take the band \(\delta\) that the first part gives for the error \(\eta/(2V_{\mathrm{K}})\). The band depends only on the uniform continuity of \(f\), not on the order, so it works for both integrals.
  2. A grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\) exists. By the Archimedean property 1.33 there is a natural number \(N\) such that \(N\delta\) is larger than the length of each of the three edges, and we divide each edge into \(N\) equal pieces. We choose points \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) in the cells, and let \(S\) be the Riemann sum.
  3. By the first part \(|I - S| \le \eta/2\) and \(|I' - S| \le \eta/2\). By the triangle inequality for numbers \(|I - I'| \le |I - S| + |S - I'| \le \eta\).
  4. We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so by lemma 1.32 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers \(|I - I'| = 0\).

3. A rectangle.

  1. The steps are the same, with two partitions and two integrals in place of three. The cells are rectangles with the areas \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\), and in step 2 of the first part \(|PQ|^2 < 2 \cdot \delta'^2/4 < \delta'^2\).

Source: LEBL2 Thms. 10.2.2 and 10.2.3 (PDF pp. 104-106) for integrable functions, the corollary for continuous functions with any number of coordinates and in any order on PDF p. 106. The source uses lower and upper sums. The proof with Riemann sums is not from the source.

The theorem says two things. The first is that the integral over a box is the limit of the sums of values of the function times the volumes of small pieces, like the sum of the forces on the rectangles of the wall. This is how we computed forces and moments on the faces of a small cube in section 2.8.4, with equal rectangles and points at their centres. Item 1 says that such sums approach the integral for a continuous force per unit area as the rectangles get smaller. The second is that we may choose the order of integration as it suits us. We saw this on the wall: horizontal and vertical strips gave the same force of 9810 N.

How fast the sums approach the integral is shown by the wall of figure 4.12. Let us cut it into \(l\) equal horizontal strips and into any number of vertical ones, and choose in each rectangle a point on its upper edge, at the depth \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} = (i - 1)\,H/l\). The sum over the vertical strips gives the factor \(b\) as in section 4.2.1. We compute the sum over \(i\) with the formula \(0 + 1 + \dots + (l - 1) = (l - 1)\,l/2\), which we derived for the work of a force in section 3.5.1:

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{l} \rho g\,b\,\frac{(i - 1)\,H}{l}\,\frac{H}{l} = \frac{\rho g\,b\,H^2}{l^2}\,\frac{(l - 1)\,l}{2} = 9810\ \text{N} \cdot \Big(1 - \frac1l\Big) .\]

For \(l = 4\) this is 7357,5 N, for \(l = 16\) it is 9196,9 N. The error is \(9810\ \text{N}/l\). Item 1 of the theorem bounds it from above. On a strip of height \(H/l\) the force per unit area changes by at most \(\rho g H/l = 9810\ \text{Pa}/l\). Steps 3 and 5 of the proof, with this number in place of \(\eta\), therefore give the bound \(9810\ \text{Pa}/l \cdot 2\ \text{m}^2 = 19\,620\ \text{N}/l\), where \(2\ \text{m}^2\) is the area of the wall. This is twice the true error. The bound is rough, but it is enough to make the error go to zero.

Why does the theorem require continuity? For a function that is not continuous, the inner integral may not exist at all. In example 10.2.1 (PDF pp. 103-104) LEBL2 takes the function on the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) that equals \(1\) when \(x = \tfrac12\) and \(y\) is a fraction, and \(0\) elsewhere. The iterated integral in which we integrate first in \(x\) is zero. At \(x = \tfrac12\), however, the function \(y \mapsto f(\tfrac12, y)\) is the function of section 3.5.3 that is \(1\) at fractions and \(0\) elsewhere and is not integrable, so the iterated integral in the other order makes no sense. Such functions do not occur in mechanics, but they show that the claim is not self-evident.

For computing we need a few more rules, which we get for the integral over a box from the properties of the integral over an interval.

Lemma 4.10 Properties of the integral over a box (lastnosti integrala po kvadru)

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be continuous functions on the box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) with the volume \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\), and \(\alpha\) a number.

  1. Linearity: \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \alpha f\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. Constant function: \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \alpha\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).
  3. Additivity: if the plane \(x = c\) with \(a_1 < c < b_1\) divides \(K\) into the boxes \(K' = [a_1, c] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) and \(K'' = [c, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}'} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{K}''} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The same holds for the planes \(y = c\) and \(z = c\).
  4. Monotonicity: if \(f(P) \le g(P)\) for every point \(P \in K\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\). In particular, the integral of a non-negative function is non-negative.

The same holds for the integral over a rectangle, with the area in place of the volume.

Proof

We must show four items. All follow from the properties of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.38), used on each of the three iterated integrals.

1. Linearity.

  1. The function \(f + g\) is continuous on \(K\) by corollary 1.67, item 1, so its integral exists.
  2. For fixed \(x\) and \(y\), by linearity of the integral over an interval, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}z = \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f\,\mathrm{d}z + \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} g\,\mathrm{d}z\).
  3. Both functions on the right are continuous in \(y\) by lemma 4.7, so by the same linearity the middle integral of the sum splits into the sum of the middle integrals. These are continuous functions of \(x\), and the outer integral splits in the same way.
  4. For \(\alpha f\) the computation is the same, with the rule \(\int \alpha\,h = \alpha \int h\) at each of the three steps.

2. Constant function.

  1. By item 3 of lemma 3.38, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} \alpha\,\mathrm{d}z = \alpha\,(b_3 - a_3)\), which is again a constant number. By the same item the middle integral equals \(\alpha\,(b_3 - a_3)(b_2 - a_2)\), and the outer one \(\alpha\,(b_3 - a_3)(b_2 - a_2)(b_1 - a_1) = \alpha\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).

3. Additivity.

  1. For the plane \(x = c\) we use the additivity of the integral over an interval (item 2 of lemma 3.38) on the outer integral in \(x\), whose integrand is continuous on \([a_1, b_1]\) by lemma 4.7. The two inner integrals are the same for \(K\), \(K'\) and \(K''\) at every \(x\).
  2. For the plane \(y = c\), by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, we write all three integrals as iterated integrals in which the outer integral is in \(y\), and repeat step 1. We proceed in the same way for the plane \(z = c\).

4. Monotonicity.

  1. For fixed \(x\) and \(y\), \(f(x, y, z) \le g(x, y, z)\) for every \(z\), so by monotonicity of the integral over an interval (item 4 of lemma 3.38) \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f\,\mathrm{d}z \le \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} g\,\mathrm{d}z\).
  2. Both sides are continuous functions of \(y\) by lemma 4.7, so by the same item the inequality survives the middle integral, and in the same way the outer one.
  3. For a non-negative function \(g\) we take \(f = 0\), whose integral is zero by item 2.

Source: LEBL2 Props. 10.1.10 and 10.1.11 (PDF p. 96) for linearity and monotonicity, and example 10.1.9 (PDF p. 95) for the constant function, for integrable functions. Item 3 and the proofs with iterated integrals are not from the source.

Let us use the rules on the weight of a part of the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a round cross section of diameter 10 mm hangs under its own weight. It is held in the idealized way: only the centre \(O\) of the top face is fixed, and a force that carries the weight pulls the top face up evenly (section 1.7.1). The axis \(x\) points vertically down from \(O\), the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are horizontal. In our minds we cut out of the bar the box \(K = [3, 6] \times [-c, c] \times [-c, c]\), with coordinates in metres and with \(c = 0{,}003\) m. It lies inside the bar, because each of its points is at most \(\sqrt{c^2 + c^2} = 4{,}243\) mm from the axis, less than the radius of 5 mm. The body force on the material is the weight, \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(\rho g = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{N/m}^3 = 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3\) (definition 2.25). A small piece of volume \(\Delta V\) has a weight of approximately \(\rho g\,\Delta V\). The sum of the weights of the cells of a grid is a Riemann sum of the function \(\rho g\), which approaches the integral by theorem 4.9, item 1. The weight of the box is therefore

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \rho g\,\mathrm{d}V = \rho g\,V_{\mathrm{K}} = 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3 \cdot 3\ \text{m} \cdot (0{,}006\ \text{m})^2 = 8{,}264\ \text{N} ,\]

by item 2 of lemma 4.10. So we write the total body force on a part of a body as the integral of the body force, as SADD (3.7.1) (PDF p. 77) does. Since \(\vek b\) is a vector, we agree that the integral of a vector function is the vector of the integrals of its components:

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = \Big( \int_{\mathrm{K}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V,\ \int_{\mathrm{K}} b_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}V,\ \int_{\mathrm{K}} b_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}V \Big) .\]

For our box this is \(8{,}264\ \text{N} \cdot \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), a force of \(8{,}264\) N vertically down. The same agreement holds for the integral of a vector function over a rectangle.

4.2.4 Bodies made of boxes and the integral over the surface

A box is a simple body. Many machine parts, beams with a rectangular cross section, plates and brackets, are made up of several boxes, just as the letter L is made up of two rectangles (figure 4.15). The integral over such a body is the sum of the integrals over the boxes it is made of. That this sum does not depend on how we cut the body is easiest to show when all boxes are cells of a single grid.

Definition 4.11 Body made of boxes (telo iz kvadrov)

Let \(K\) be a box and a grid that cuts it into cells \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) (section 4.2.3). A set of points \(V\) is a body made of boxes (telo iz kvadrov) if it is the union of some cells of this grid, at least one. These cells are the cells of the body \(V\).

  1. The integral of a continuous function \(f\) over the body \(V\) is the sum of the integrals over its cells, \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{V}} \int_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. A face of a cell of the body \(V\) is an outer face if the cell on the other side of the face is not a cell of the body \(V\) or if the face lies on the surface of the box \(K\). The surface (površina) \(S\) of the body \(V\) is the union of its outer faces. The outward normal \(\vek n\) on an outer face is the outward normal of the cell the face belongs to, so one of the vectors \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  3. Let \(f\) be a function that is continuous on every outer face. The surface integral (ploskovni integral) of \(f\) over the surface \(S\) is the sum of the integrals over the outer faces, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 478) defines the integral over a body in space as the limit of sums over the boxes of a grid that lie in the body. The definition for bodies made of boxes is not from the source.

A body made of boxes is thus a set of points made up of finitely many cells of one grid. The integral over it and the surface integral are sums of integrals over cells and over rectangles, so linearity and monotonicity of lemma 4.10, items 1 and 4, hold for them. Figure 4.15 shows a section of an L-shaped body made of four cells. The faces on which two cells of the body touch are not outer faces and do not belong to the surface, which agrees with the picture: from outside we do not see them. The function under a surface integral may have two values on an edge where two outer faces meet, one for each face. This is so for the normal, which on one face is, for example, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and on the other \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The surface integral allows this, because each face is integrated separately. The simplest body made of boxes is a box itself, with a grid of one single cell. Its surface is its six faces.

Lemma 4.12 The integral does not depend on the grid (integral ni odvisen od mreže)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes. The integral of a continuous function over \(V\), the surface \(S\), the outward normals and the surface integral over \(S\) do not depend on the grid with which we cut \(V\) into cells. For the surface integral we assume that the function is continuous on every outer face of both grids that we compare. This holds for instance for the function \(g\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(g\) continuous on \(V\).

Proof

We must show that two grids that both cut \(V\) into cells give the same. First we compare a grid with a grid that has one more plane, then any two grids.

  1. Let the second grid have one more plane, for example \(x = c\) with \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} < c < x_{\mathrm{i}}\) (figure 4.15, right). The plane cuts each cell between the planes \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}}\) into two, and the other cells remain. The body \(V\) is the union of the halves of its cut cells and of its uncut cells, so these are the cells of the body \(V\) in the new grid. Half of a cell that is not a cell of the body \(V\) is not in \(V\) either. Its points that lie on no plane of the grid lie in no other cell of the old grid, and so not in \(V\).
  2. By lemma 4.10, item 3, the integral over a cut cell is the sum of the integrals over its halves. The integral over \(V\) is therefore the same in both grids.
  3. The faces of cells that are perpendicular to the axis \(y\) or \(z\) and lie between the planes \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}}\) are cut in two by the plane \(x = c\). A half is an outer face exactly when the whole face was, because the cell on the other side is cut in the same way and is a cell of the body exactly when it was before. The new faces in the plane \(x = c\) separate the two halves of the same old cell, which are both in \(V\) or both outside, so no new face is an outer face. The faces perpendicular to the axis \(x\) remain. The surface \(S\) and the normals are therefore the same, and by lemma 4.10, item 3, for a rectangle, so is the surface integral.
  4. Let two arbitrary grids for \(V\) be given. First we extend both to a common box that contains both original boxes, by adding new end points to the partitions. The new cells lie outside \(V\), so nothing changes. The grid that has all the planes of both grids is obtained from each of them by adding planes one after another. By steps 1 to 3, each of the two grids gives the same integrals, surface and normals as this common grid.

Source: The lemma is not from the source. LEBL2 Prop. 10.1.5 (PDF p. 93) uses the same idea of a common refinement for sums on a rectangle.

The lemma lets us cut a body made of boxes into cells as it suits us. Whenever we need a finer grid, for example so that some face or some smaller cube is made of whole cells, we may take it without changing the integrals.

4.2.5 The divergence theorem

Let us return to the fundamental theorem of calculus. For a function \(G\) with a continuous derivative on \([a, b]\),

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b G'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(b) - G(a) .\]

We can read the right side as a sum over the boundary of the interval. The boundary of the interval is the two end points \(a\) and \(b\). At the end point \(b\) the direction out of the interval points toward larger numbers, which we write as the number \(+1\), at the end point \(a\) toward smaller ones, which we write as \(-1\). The right side is \(G(b) \cdot (+1) + G(a) \cdot (-1)\), the value times the outward direction, summed over the boundary. For a box we expect the same. The role of the function \(G\) is taken by a function of three variables \(f\), the role of the derivative by the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\), and the role of the end points by the faces of the box (figure 4.16). The two faces perpendicular to the axis \(x\) have the outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), whose component \(x\) is \(\pm 1\). On the other four faces the component \(x\) of the normal is zero.

For a vector field we add up three such terms, one for each component. The sum of the three partial derivatives has its own name.

Definition 4.13 Divergence of a field (divergenca polja)

Let \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) be a vector field, that is, a rule that assigns a vector to every point of some set, and let its components have partial derivatives at the point \(P\) (definition 1.23). The divergence (divergenca) of the field \(\vek v\) at the point \(P\) is the number

\[\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P) + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(P) + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(P) .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §9.8 (1) (PDF p. 428), where it is written \(\operatorname{div}\vek v\), CM (2.4.34) (PDF p. 76), where it is written \(\nabla\cdot\vek A\).

What the divergence measures we will see after the theorem. Let us state it.

Theorem 4.14 Divergence theorem (izrek o divergenci)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes with the surface \(S\) and the outward normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) (definition 4.11), \(D\) an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(f\), \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) functions that are continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.88).

  1. We have
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.8}\]
    and the same with \(y\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and with \(z\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\) in place of \(x\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  2. For the field \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.9}\]
Proof

We must show both items. We prove item 1 first for one box, with the fundamental theorem of calculus and the theorem on the order of integration, then for a body made of boxes, where the contributions of the inner faces cancel. Item 2 is the sum of three cases of item 1.

1. One box.

  1. Let \(V = K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) be a box with a grid of one cell. The function \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), so it is also continuous on \(D\) (lemma 1.89), and all integrals over the faces of the box exist. On the face \(x = b_1\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\), on the face \(x = a_1\) we have \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\), and on the other four faces \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) (figure 4.16). The integral of the zero function is zero (lemma 4.10, item 2, for a rectangle), so by definition 4.11, item 3, and by linearity
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(b_1, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y - \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(a_1, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  2. The function \(\partial f/\partial x\) is continuous on \(D\), hence also on \(K\). By theorem 4.9 on the order of integration we may write the integral over \(K\) as an iterated integral in which the inner integral is in \(x\):
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}x \bigg) \mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  3. Let \(y\) and \(z\) be fixed and \(G(x) = f(x, y, z)\) for \(x \in [a_1, b_1]\). The points \((x, y, z)\) lie in \(K\) and hence in \(D\), where \(f\) has a partial derivative in \(x\). By the definition of the partial derivative 1.23, \(G\) is differentiable at every point of \([a_1, b_1]\) and \(G'(x) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\). A differentiable function is continuous (lemma 1.77). The derivative \(G'\) is continuous on \([a_1, b_1]\), because \(\partial f/\partial x\) is continuous on \(K\) and the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x', y, z)\) is \(|x' - x|\).
  4. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, item 1, therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(b_1) - G(a_1) = f(b_1, y, z) - f(a_1, y, z) .\]
  5. We put this into step 2 and use linearity of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.38, item 1) on the middle and on the outer integral. We get the right side of step 1. This proves (4.8) for a box.
  6. For \(y\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\) we repeat steps 1 to 5, only now the inner integral is in \(y\) and the faces \(y = a_2\) and \(y = b_2\) appear. The same for \(z\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\).

2. A body made of boxes.

  1. By definition 4.11 and by the first part, used on each cell of the body,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{V}} \int_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{V}} \int_{\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{ijk}}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    where \(S_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) is the surface of the cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\), its six faces, with the outward normals of this cell.
  2. The sum on the right is the sum of the integrals over all faces of all cells of the body. A face that is not an outer face is shared by two cells of the body that lie on its opposite sides (figure 4.17). For one cell its outward normal is \(\vek n\), for the other \(-\vek n\). The functions under the two integrals, \(f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(f\,(-n_{\mathrm{x}})\), are therefore opposite, and by linearity (lemma 4.10, item 1, for a rectangle) the two integrals cancel.
  3. What remains are the integrals over the outer faces, each once and with the outward normal of the body. Their sum is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) by definition 4.11, item 3.

3. A field.

  1. We use item 1 three times, with the function \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the coordinate \(x\), with the function \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and the coordinate \(y\) and with the function \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) and the coordinate \(z\), and add the equations. By linearity of the integral over each cell and over each face (lemma 4.10, item 1), the sum of the left sides is the left side of (4.9), and the sum of the right sides is the right side.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, equations (2) and (2*) (PDF p. 479), with the proof on PDF pp. 480-482, CM (2.4.45) and (2.4.46) (PDF p. 82), SADD (1.8.6) (PDF p. 28), all for bodies bounded by a piecewise smooth surface. The proof for bodies made of boxes is a simplification of KREYSZIG's proof.

The proof shows where the theorem comes from (figure 4.17). On one box it is the fundamental theorem of calculus, used on every segment in the box parallel to the axis \(x\). The integral of the derivative along the segment is the difference of the values at the point where the segment leaves the box and at the point where it enters. The theorem on the order of integration stacks these segments into the box. In a body made of boxes the contributions of the inner faces cancel, because the shared face of two cells has opposite outward normals for the two of them. Only the surface remains. The sum on the right side of (4.9) is the scalar product \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\) (definition 2.8), so the right side adds up the part of the field that points out of the body. The theorem is also called Gauss's theorem. It needs a field that is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the whole body. In a body made of two glued materials the displacement field has no continuous derivatives at the interface (section 1.15.6). We then use the theorem on each material separately, provided the field in each material can be written by a formula that stays continuously differentiable a little beyond the interface, for example by a polynomial. The interface then contributes one surface integral for each side.

What does the theorem say for a displacement field? Let \(\vek v = \vek u\) be the displacement field of a body. On a patch of the surface with the area \(\Delta A\), \(\vek u\cdot\vek n\) is the part of the displacement in the direction of the outward normal, that is, how far the patch moves outward. For small displacements, \(\vek u\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\) is approximately the volume the patch sweeps as it moves, positive when it moves outward and negative when it moves inward. The right side of (4.9) is therefore approximately the change of volume of the body. On the left side is the integral of the sum \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), which by section 1.17.4 is, for small strains, the relative change of volume of a small piece. The theorem thus says that the changes of volume of small pieces add up to the change of volume of the body, which we can compute from the displacements of the surface alone. Hence the name: divergence means moving apart. Where the divergence of the displacements is positive, neighbouring points move apart and small pieces grow.

Let us test the theorem on the hanging bar of section 4.2.3. The steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m and diameter 10 mm hangs under its own weight and is held in the idealized way. The axis \(x\) points down from the centre \(O\) of the top face. Its displacement field is (1.18),

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). Where the numbers \(0{,}3\) and \(0{,}6\) come from we explained in section 1.7.1. This time we take the box along the whole length of the bar, \(K = [0, L] \times [-c, c] \times [-c, c]\) with \(c = 0{,}003\) m. The components of the field are polynomials, so their partial derivatives, again polynomials, are continuous at every point of space (corollary 1.67), and we may take the whole space for \(D\).

The left side. The partial derivatives are \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2a\,(L - x)\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), so the divergence is \(2a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). It does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), so by definition 4.8 and by lemma 3.38, item 3, the inner integral in \(z\) equals \(2c \cdot 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\), and the middle one in \(y\) equals \(4c^2 \cdot 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). The function \(Lx - x^2/2\) has the derivative \(L - x\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus \(\int_0^L (L - x)\,\mathrm{d}x = L^2/2\), and

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \Big( \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = 4c^2 \cdot 0{,}8\,a \cdot \frac{L^2}{2} = 1{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2 = 0{,}2811\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

The right side. The box has six faces (figure 4.18).

  1. The bottom face \(x = L\) with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, y, z) = a L^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). The inner integral in \(z\) is \(\int_{-\mathrm{c}}^{c} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z = 2c\,y^2 + \tfrac23 c^3\), the outer one in \(y\) is \(2c \cdot \tfrac23 c^3 + \tfrac23 c^3 \cdot 2c = \tfrac83 c^4\). The integral over the face is therefore \(4c^2\,a L^2 - 0{,}3\,a \cdot \tfrac83 c^4 = 4\,a\,c^2 L^2 - 0{,}8\,a\,c^4\).
  2. The top face \(x = 0\) with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{x}}(0, y, z) = 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the integral over the face \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4\).
  3. The face \(y = c\) with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand is \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, c, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,c\). The integral in \(z\) gives the factor \(2c\), the integral in \(x\) the factor \(L^2/2\), together \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).
  4. The face \(y = -c\) with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, -c, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,c\), the same as in item 3, and the integral is again \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).
  5. The faces \(z = \pm c\) with the normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) give the same as the faces \(y = \pm c\), each \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).

The sum is \(4\,a\,c^2 L^2 - 0{,}8\,a\,c^4 + 0{,}8\,a\,c^4 - 4 \cdot 0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2 = 1{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\), the same as the left side.

What do the numbers mean (figure 4.18)? The bottom face, of area \(4c^2 = 36\ \text{mm}^2\), moves down by \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, 0, 0) = a L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm and sweeps \(36\ \text{mm}^2 \cdot 0{,}01952\ \text{mm} = 0{,}7027\ \text{mm}^3\), when we neglect the very small term \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4\). The four side faces move toward the axis, because the bar gets thinner, and each sweeps \(0{,}1054\ \text{mm}^3\) inward, together \(0{,}4216\ \text{mm}^3\). The top face stays in place at its centre, while its rim rises by a very small amount, and it sweeps only \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4 = 1{,}3 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\). The volume of the box grows by \(0{,}7027 - 0{,}4216 = 0{,}2811\ \text{mm}^3\). The box has the volume \(36\ \text{mm}^2 \cdot 10\,000\ \text{mm} = 360\,000\ \text{mm}^3\), so the relative change is \(0{,}2811/360\,000 = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\). This is exactly the sum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) at the point \(P\) at the depth of 5 m, which we computed in section 1.17.4. Why exactly at \(P\)? The sum \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) is a linear function of the depth, so its average over the bar equals the value at the middle, at \(x = L/2 = 5\) m, where \(P\) lies.

4.2.6 Bodies with a curved surface

The round hanging bar is not a body made of boxes. Its side face, the mantle of a cylinder, is curved, and the outward normal on it changes from point to point. At the point \((x, y, z)\) of the mantle, where \(y^2 + z^2 = r^2\) and \(r = 5\) mm is the radius of the cross section, the outward normal is \(\vek n = (0, y/r, z/r)\) (figure 4.19). This vector is a unit vector, because \((y/r)^2 + (z/r)^2 = 1\), it has no component along the axis of the bar, and it points away from the axis. On the top face the outward normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), on the bottom face \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The top and bottom faces are not rectangles either, but discs.

The divergence theorem holds for such bodies too. Precisely: let \(V\) be a closed and bounded set of points bounded by a surface made of finitely many smooth pieces, and let the components of the field \(\vek v\) be continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(V\). Then (4.9) holds, where \(\vek n\) is the outward normal of the surface (KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, PDF p. 479, CM (2.4.46), PDF p. 82, SADD (1.8.6), PDF p. 28). KREYSZIG proves the theorem first for a body bounded above and below by the graph of a function, and then for a body that can be cut into finitely many such pieces, so that the contributions of the inner cuts cancel as with our cells (PDF pp. 480-482). For the most general bodies he says that a limit process is still needed (PDF p. 482). We will take the same route, for a class of bodies that includes the round hanging bar.

The route is as follows. In this subsection we define a body bounded above and below by a graph, and show how to cut the round bar into three such bodies. The integral over such a body will again be an iterated integral, except that the limits of the inner integral will not be constant but will depend on the outer variables. So in section 4.2.7 we show that such an integral changes continuously, and how to differentiate it with respect to a variable on which the limits depend. Then we define the integral over such a body (section 4.2.8) and over its curved surface (section 4.2.9). Finally we prove the theorem and test it on the round bar (section 4.2.10). Only the bodies that we cannot cut into such pieces remain cited, together with two questions about the independence of the integral, which we will name when they come up.

Let us start with a body that is a box with a curved top and bottom lid (figure 4.20). Below it, in the plane \(z = 0\), lies the rectangle \([a, b] \times [c, d]\), which we call the shadow of the body. Above every point \((x, y)\) of the shadow the body occupies a vertical segment that starts at the height \(g(x, y)\) and ends at the height \(h(x, y)\). The bottom lid of the body is the graph of the function \(g\), the top lid the graph of the function \(h\), and the four side faces are flat, in the planes \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) and \(y = d\). In this section the letter \(g\) is not the gravitational acceleration but a function.

Definition 4.15 Body between two graphs (telo med dvema grafoma)

Let \(a < b\) and \(c < d\) be numbers and \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) a rectangle in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), that is, the set of points \((x, y)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(c \le y \le d\). Let \(U\) be an open set of points of the plane that contains \(R\), that is, a set that contains, together with each of its points, a disc of some radius \(r > 0\) around it. Let \(g\) and \(h\) be functions whose input is a point \((x, y)\) of \(U\) and whose output is a number, and which are continuously differentiable on \(U\): at every point of \(U\) they have the partial derivatives with respect to \(x\) and to \(y\) (definition 1.23), which are continuous at every point of \(U\). Let \(g(x, y) \le h(x, y)\) for every point \((x, y) \in R\). The set of points of space

\[V = \{ (x, y, z) : (x, y) \in R,\ g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y) \} \tag{4.10}\]

is a body between two graphs (telo med dvema grafoma), of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R\). The graph of the function \(h\) over \(R\) is its top lid, the graph of the function \(g\) its bottom lid. We use the same name for the set obtained when the roles of the coordinates are exchanged, for example the set of points with \(a \le x \le b\), \(c \le z \le d\) and \(g(x, z) \le y \le h(x, z)\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, (6) (PDF p. 480), where the shadow of the body is a more general region, not only a rectangle. The restriction to a rectangle is not from the source.

The definition says what goes in. The rectangle \(R\) is the shadow of the body. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) take a point of the shadow as input, and their output is the height of the bottom and of the top lid above it. Why must they be continuously differentiable, and on an open set containing \(R\)? From their partial derivatives we will compute the normal of a lid in section 4.2.9, and in the proof of the theorem we will need them also on the edge of the shadow. A partial derivative at a point needs values of the function on both sides of the point (definition 1.23), so the functions must be defined a little beyond the edge. The inequality \(g \le h\) says that the bottom lid is not above the top lid. Equality is allowed: for the bar, the lids will meet at the edge of the shadow. The simplest body between graphs is the box \([a, b] \times [c, d] \times [g_0, h_0]\), for which \(g\) and \(h\) are constant functions with the values \(g_0 < h_0\), with zero partial derivatives.

A body over a rectangle is a special case. KREYSZIG allows the shadow, the set of points \((x, y)\) below the body, to be a more general region of the plane (KREYSZIG §10.7, (6), PDF p. 480). We will need the rectangle in the proof of the theorem, where we will exchange the order of integration in \(x\) and in \(y\). On a rectangle we may do so by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration. On more general regions we do not have this theorem. KREYSZIG avoids it by requiring the body to have this shape in the direction of all three axes, and obtains the terms with \(x\) and \(y\) from the term with \(z\) by renaming the axes (PDF pp. 480-481). How severe is our restriction? Less than it seems, because we may exchange the roles of the coordinates and cut a body into several pieces. Let us show this on the round bar.

The round hanging bar of length \(L = 10\) m, with a cross section of radius \(r = 5\) mm and the axis \(x\) down from the centre \(O\) of the top face, is the set of points with \(0 \le x \le L\) and \(y^2 + z^2 \le r^2\). Let

\[q(t) = \sqrt{r^2 - t^2} , \qquad -r \le t \le r ,\]

be the upper half of the circle of radius \(r\). At every \(y\) between \(-r\) and \(r\) the cross section of the bar occupies a vertical chord from \(z = -q(y)\) to \(z = q(y)\). Is the bar a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-r, r]\)? It is not, because \(q\) has no derivative at \(t = r\). For \(k > 0\) we have \(q(r - k) = \sqrt{2rk - k^2}\), so the slope of the segment from the point of the graph above \(r - k\) to the point above \(r\) is

\[\frac{q(r) - q(r - k)}{k} = -\frac{\sqrt{2rk - k^2}}{k} = -\sqrt{\frac{2r}{k} - 1} .\]

For \(r = 5\) mm it is \(-31{,}61\) at \(k = 0{,}01\) mm and \(-316{,}2\) at \(k = 0{,}0001\) mm. As \(k\) goes to zero, \(2r/k\) grows beyond every bound, and with it the absolute value of the slope, so there is no limit. The tangent at the point \((r, 0)\) is vertical (figure 4.21, left). For \(t > r\) the function \(q\) is not even defined, because \(r^2 - t^2 < 0\).

So we cut the bar with the planes \(y = 3\) mm and \(y = -3\) mm into three pieces (figure 4.21, right). We chose the number \(3\) because \(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\). The points \((y, z) = (\pm 3, \pm 4)\) in millimetres therefore lie on the circle, and \(q(\pm 3) = 4\) and \(q(\pm 4) = 3\). Let us write the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres.

  1. The middle piece \(C\) consists of the points of the bar with \(-3 \le y \le 3\). For such \(y\), \(z\) lies between \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\), so \(C\) is a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(y\).
  2. The right piece \(D\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \ge 3\). For such a point \(z^2 \le 25 - y^2 \le 16\), so \(-4 \le z \le 4\) (lemma 1.26, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square). From \(y^2 \le 25 - z^2 = q(z)^2\) it follows by the same lemma that \(y \le q(z)\). Conversely, every point with \(-4 \le z \le 4\) and \(3 \le y \le q(z)\) satisfies \(y^2 + z^2 \le q(z)^2 + z^2 = 25\). The piece \(D\) is therefore a body between the graphs of the constant function \(3\) and the function \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\). Here \(y\) is the coordinate that runs between the graphs. The condition \(3 \le q(z)\) holds because \(q(z)^2 = 25 - z^2 \ge 9\).
  3. The left piece \(E\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \le -3\). Like \(D\), it is a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(z)\) and \(-3\) over the same rectangle.

For the pieces to be bodies between graphs, we still have to show that \(q\) is continuously differentiable on an open interval containing \([-4, 4]\). We get rid of the root by writing the difference of two roots through the difference of their squares.

Lemma 4.16 Derivative of the upper half of a circle (odvod zgornje polovice krožnice)

Let \(r > 0\) and \(q(t) = \sqrt{r^2 - t^2}\) for \(-r < t < r\). Then \(q(t) > 0\), the function \(q\) is differentiable at every point of the open interval \((-r, r)\),

\[q'(t) = -\frac{t}{q(t)} , \tag{4.11}\]

and \(q'\) is continuous at every point of \((-r, r)\). The function \(q\) is thus continuously differentiable on \((-r, r)\).

Proof

We must show that the difference quotient of the function \(q\) converges to \(-t/q(t)\) and that this number changes continuously with \(t\).

  1. Let \(-r < t < r\). Then \(|t| < r\) and by lemma 1.26 \(t^2 < r^2\), so \(r^2 - t^2 > 0\). The square root of a positive number is positive, because its square is positive, while the square of the number \(0\) is \(0\) (theorem 1.34). Thus \(q(t) > 0\).
  2. Let \(s, t \in (-r, r)\). We have \(\big(q(s) - q(t)\big)\big(q(s) + q(t)\big) = q(s)^2 - q(t)^2 = (r^2 - s^2) - (r^2 - t^2) = t^2 - s^2\). Since \(q(s) + q(t) > 0\), we may divide by it:
    \[q(s) - q(t) = -\frac{(s - t)(s + t)}{q(s) + q(t)} .\]
  3. Continuity. The denominator in step 2 is not smaller than \(q(t)\), because \(q(s) \ge 0\). The numerator is at most \(2r\,|s - t|\) in absolute value, because \(|s + t| \le |s| + |t| < 2r\). Hence
    \[|q(s) - q(t)| \le \frac{2r}{q(t)}\,|s - t| ,\]
    which is less than \(\eta\) when \(|s - t| < \eta\,q(t)/(2r)\). The function \(q\) is thus continuous at \(t\) (definition 1.56).
  4. The difference quotient. Let \(k \neq 0\) and \(|k| < r - |t|\), so that \(t + k\) lies in \((-r, r)\). By step 2 with \(s = t + k\),
    \[\frac{q(t + k) - q(t)}{k} = -\frac{2t + k}{q(t + k) + q(t)} .\]
  5. We compare the quotient with the number \(-t/q(t)\). We write the two fractions with a common denominator and simplify the numerator:
    \[-\frac{2t + k}{q(t + k) + q(t)} + \frac{t}{q(t)} = \frac{t\,\big(q(t + k) - q(t)\big) - k\,q(t)}{\big(q(t + k) + q(t)\big)\,q(t)} .\]
    In the numerator, \(-(2t + k)\,q(t) + t\,\big(q(t + k) + q(t)\big) = t\,q(t + k) - t\,q(t) - k\,q(t)\).
  6. The denominator is not smaller than \(q(t)^2\), because \(q(t + k) \ge 0\). By step 3, \(|q(t + k) - q(t)| \le 2r\,|k|/q(t)\), and \(|t| < r\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (step 6 of the proof of lemma 1.6) the absolute value of the difference in step 5 is therefore at most
    \[\frac{r \cdot 2r\,|k|/q(t) + |k|\,q(t)}{q(t)^2} = C_{\mathrm{t}}\,|k| , \qquad C_{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{2r^2 + q(t)^2}{q(t)^3} .\]
  7. For \(\eta > 0\) we take as the band \(\delta\) the smaller of the numbers \(\eta/C_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(r - |t|\). For every \(k\) with \(0 < |k| < \delta\) the difference in step 5 is less than \(\eta\). By the definition of the derivative 1.8 and of the limit 1.5, \(q'(t) = -t/q(t)\).
  8. Continuity of the derivative. For \(s \in (-r, r)\), as in step 5,
    \[-\frac{s}{q(s)} + \frac{t}{q(t)} = \frac{t\,\big(q(s) - q(t)\big) - (s - t)\,q(t)}{q(s)\,q(t)} .\]
    By step 3, \(|q(s) - q(t)| < q(t)/2\) when \(|s - t| < q(t)^2/(4r)\), and then \(q(s) > q(t)/2\) and the denominator is greater than \(q(t)^2/2\). As in step 6, the numerator is at most \((2r^2/q(t) + q(t))\,|s - t|\). The difference is therefore at most \(2C_{\mathrm{t}}\,|s - t|\), which is less than \(\eta\) when \(|s - t|\) is smaller than \(\eta/(2C_{\mathrm{t}})\) and than \(q(t)^2/(4r)\). The derivative is continuous at \(t\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 4.1.4 (PDF p. 156) computes the derivative of the function \(\sqrt x\) with the same device of a difference of squares, and Proposition 4.1.10 (PDF p. 159) is the chain rule, from which the formula would follow. The proof is not from the sources.

For the bar \(r = 5\) mm, and the interval \([-4, 4]\) lies in \((-5, 5)\). The function \(q(y)\), taken as a function of the point \((x, y)\) on the open set of points of the plane with \(-5 < y < 5\), has the partial derivative zero with respect to \(x\) and the partial derivative \(q'(y)\) with respect to \(y\). Both are continuous, because two points of the plane differ in the coordinate \(y\) by at most their distance. The same holds for \(-q(y)\), for \(\pm q(z)\) and for the constant functions \(\pm 3\). All three pieces are therefore bodies between graphs. The cut at \(y = \pm 3\) makes sure that each piece uses the function \(q\) only on the interval \([-4, 4]\), where its derivative is at most \(4/3\) in absolute value, at \(t = \pm 4\). In the piece \(D\) the lids \(y = 3\) and \(y = q(z)\) meet at \(z = \pm 4\), because \(q(\pm 4) = 3\), which the definition allows.

The pieces touch only at the cuts. A point that lies in \(C\) and in \(D\) has \(y \le 3\) and \(y \ge 3\), so \(y = 3\), and lies on the rectangle \(0 \le x \le L\), \(-4 \le z \le 4\) in the plane \(y = 3\). An interior point of the piece \(C\), however, has \(y < 3\). A ball around it lies in \(C\), where \(y \le 3\) (section 1.15.6), and if the point had \(y = 3\), the ball would contain points with \(y > 3\). So no interior point of the piece \(C\) lies in \(D\), and likewise no interior point of the piece \(D\) lies in \(C\). The same holds for the pieces \(C\) and \(E\), while the pieces \(D\) and \(E\) have no common points.

Finally let us show that a body between graphs is closed and bounded. We will need this, because we will use the theorem on uniform continuity 4.6 on it.

Lemma 4.17 A body between two graphs is closed and bounded (telo med grafoma je zaprto in omejeno)

The body between graphs \(V\) of definition 4.15 is a closed and bounded set of points (definition 1.72).

Proof

We must show that the limit of a convergent sequence of points of \(V\) lies in \(V\) and that all points of \(V\) are at most some number away from the origin.

  1. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous at every point of \(U\) by lemma 1.89, that a continuously differentiable function is continuous. The lemma speaks of functions of three variables, but its proof with theorem 1.86 on the change of a field over a short step holds likewise for functions of two variables.
  2. Let the sequence of points \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = (x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}, z_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(V\) converge to the point \(P = (x, y, z)\). By lemma 1.64 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \to x\), \(y_{\mathrm{n}} \to y\) and \(z_{\mathrm{n}} \to z\).
  3. From \(a \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\) and \(c \le y_{\mathrm{n}} \le d\), by lemma 1.46 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 2, it follows that \(a \le x \le b\) and \(c \le y \le d\). The point \((x, y)\) lies in \(R\).
  4. The points \((x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to \((x, y)\), and \(g\) is continuous at \((x, y)\). By lemma 1.66 on continuity through sequences of points, therefore, \(g(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \to g(x, y)\). Likewise \(h(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \to h(x, y)\).
  5. From \(g(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \le z_{\mathrm{n}} \le h(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}})\), by lemma 1.46, item 1, it follows that \(g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y)\). The point \(P\) lies in \(V\), which is therefore closed.
  6. Boundedness. The rectangle \(R\), seen as the set of points \((x, y, 0)\) of space, is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous on it, so by theorem 1.76, the extreme value theorem in space, there are numbers \(m\) and \(M\) with \(m \le g\) and \(h \le M\) on \(R\). For every point of \(V\) we therefore have \(|z| \le |m| + |M|\), and also \(|x| \le |a| + |b|\) and \(|y| \le |c| + |d|\). As for the box in section 1.13.4, \(|\overrightarrow{OP}|\) is at most the root of the sum of the squares of these three bounds.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. The proof follows the examples of the box and the bar in section 1.13.4.

4.2.7 Differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter

Let us recall the proof of the divergence theorem for a box (theorem 4.14). We wrote the integral of the term \(\partial f/\partial x\) as an iterated integral whose inner integral is over \(x\), which we were allowed to do by theorem 4.9. The fundamental theorem of calculus then turned the integral along every segment parallel to the axis \(x\) into the difference of the values on the faces \(x = a_1\) and \(x = b_1\). For a body between graphs we can treat the term \(\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) in this way, because the segments parallel to the axis \(z\) are exactly the chords from the bottom to the top lid. The terms \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\) and \(\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\), however, are inside the inner integral over \(z\), whose limits \(g(x, y)\) and \(h(x, y)\) depend on \(x\) and \(y\). So we must bring the derivative with respect to \(y\) out of the integral. In doing so both the integrand and the limits change, and the motion of the limits will give terms on the lids. This section says how such an integral changes: first, that it changes continuously, which we need for the iterated integral to exist at all, and then how to differentiate it.

The inner integral of a body between graphs is the function

\[F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z ,\]

whose input is a point \((x, y)\) of the shadow and whose output is a number. When the point moves a little, the integrand changes a little, and the two limits move a little. The uniform continuity of the function \(f\) bounds the change of the integrand, as in lemma 4.7. The motion of the limits adds or removes a short piece of the interval, on which \(f\) is bounded, so its contribution is small too.

Lemma 4.18 Continuity of an integral with variable limits (zveznost integrala s spremenljivima mejama)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(V\). Then for every point \((x, y) \in R\) the integral

\[F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\]

exists, and for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|F(x', y') - F(x, y)| < \eta\) for all points \((x, y), (x', y') \in R\) with \((x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2 < \delta^2\).

Proof

We must show that the integral exists and that it changes little when the point moves a little. We split the intervals of integration at two nearby points into a common part and pieces at the ends.

  1. Existence. For fixed \(x\) and \(y\) the function \(z \mapsto f(x, y, z)\) is continuous on \([g(x, y), h(x, y)]\), because the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y, z')\) is \(|z - z'|\). By theorem 3.37 it is integrable. If \(g(x, y) = h(x, y)\), the integral is zero by the convention of definition 3.33.
  2. Bounds. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded by lemma 4.17, so by theorem 1.76 there is a number \(M > 0\) with \(|f| \le M\) on \(V\). By the same theorem, applied to the continuous function \(h - g\) on \(R\), there is a number \(H > 0\) with \(h - g \le H\) on \(R\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|f(Q) - f(Q')| < \eta/(2H)\) for any two points \(Q, Q' \in V\) with \(|QQ'| < \delta_1\). By the same theorem on \(R\) there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|g(P') - g(P)| < \eta/(4M)\) and \(|h(P') - h(P)| < \eta/(4M)\) for any two points \(P, P' \in R\) with \(|PP'| < \delta_2\). For \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\).
  4. Let \(P = (x, y)\) and \(P' = (x', y')\) be points of \(R\) with \(|PP'| < \delta\). We write \(g = g(P)\), \(h = h(P)\), \(g' = g(P')\) and \(h' = h(P')\), and \(z_1 = \max\{g, g'\}\) and \(z_2 = \min\{h, h'\}\). For short we also write \(f(P, z)\) for \(f(x, y, z)\).
  5. The case \(z_1 \le z_2\), when the intervals \([g, h]\) and \([g', h']\) overlap. The interval \([g, h]\) splits into \([g, z_1]\), \([z_1, z_2]\) and \([z_2, h]\), and by additivity (lemma 3.38, item 2, with the convention for pieces of length zero) \(F(P)\) is the sum of the integrals over these three pieces. Likewise \(F(P')\) splits over \([g', z_1]\), \([z_1, z_2]\) and \([z_2, h']\). Hence
    \[\begin{aligned} F(P') - F(P) = {} & \int_{\mathrm{z}_1}^{z_2} \big(f(P', z) - f(P, z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{g}'}^{z_1} f(P', z)\,\mathrm{d}z + \int_{\mathrm{z}_2}^{h'} f(P', z)\,\mathrm{d}z \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{z_1} f(P, z)\,\mathrm{d}z - \int_{\mathrm{z}_2}^{h} f(P, z)\,\mathrm{d}z . \end{aligned}\]
  6. The points \((P, z)\) and \((P', z)\) with \(z_1 \le z \le z_2\) lie in \(V\) and are a distance \(|PP'| < \delta_1\) apart, so the first integrand is less than \(\eta/(2H)\) in absolute value. By the bound (lemma 3.38, item 3) the first integral is at most \(\eta\,(z_2 - z_1)/(2H) \le \eta/2\) in absolute value, because \(z_2 - z_1 \le h - g \le H\).
  7. By the bound, the other four integrals are at most \(M\) times the length of the interval in absolute value. Of the lengths \(z_1 - g\) and \(z_1 - g'\) one is zero and the other \(|g' - g|\), because \(z_1\) is the larger of the numbers \(g\) and \(g'\). Likewise, of the lengths \(h - z_2\) and \(h' - z_2\) one is zero and the other \(|h' - h|\). The sum of the four is therefore at most \(M\,(|g' - g| + |h' - h|) < M \cdot 2\eta/(4M) = \eta/2\).
  8. The case \(z_1 > z_2\), when the intervals do not overlap. Since \(g \le h\) and \(g' \le h'\), then \(g' > h\) or \(g > h'\). Let \(g' > h\), the other case is the same with the two points exchanged. Then \(h - g < g' - g\) and \(h' - g' < h' - h\). By the bound \(|F(P)| \le M\,(h - g)\) and \(|F(P')| \le M\,(h' - g')\), so \(|F(P') - F(P)| \le |F(P')| + |F(P)| < M\,(|g' - g| + |h' - h|) < \eta/2\).
  9. In both cases, by the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|F(P') - F(P)| < \eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. For constant limits it is LEBL1 Proposition 7.5.12 (PDF p. 292), as lemma 4.7.

The lemma has extended item 1 of lemma 4.7 to variable limits. The function \(F\) thus has the property of that item, so by its item 2 the middle integral \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d F(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\) exists and is a continuous function of \(x\). The iterated integral of the function \(f\) in the order \(z\), \(y\), \(x\) therefore exists. Two devices were the key: uniform continuity, which bounded the change of the integrand for all \(z\) at once, and the boundedness of the function \(f\), which bounded the contribution of the pieces at the ends.

Now the derivative. Take a function of two variables \(f(t, s)\) and its integral over \(t\) whose limits depend on \(s\):

\[G(s) = \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s})}^{\psi(s)} f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

We chose the letters \(t\) and \(s\) so that they do not get mixed up with the coordinates. In the proof of the theorem, \(t\) will be the coordinate \(z\), and \(s\) will be \(y\) or \(x\). When \(s\) increases by \(k\), \(G\) changes for three reasons (figure 4.22, left). The integrand changes over the whole interval, by about \(k\,\partial f/\partial s\). The upper limit moves by about \(\psi'(s)\,k\), and the interval gains a piece of this length, on which the integrand is about \(f(\psi(s), s)\). The lower limit moves by about \(\varphi'(s)\,k\), and the interval loses a piece with the integrand about \(f(\varphi(s), s)\). Divided by \(k\), this gives the three terms of the derivative.

Lemma 4.19 Differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter (odvod integrala po parametru)

Let \(\alpha < \beta\) and \(c < d\) be numbers, and let the function \(f\), whose input is two numbers \(t\) and \(s\) and whose output is a number \(f(t, s)\), have the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial s\) at every point of the rectangle \([\alpha, \beta] \times [c, d]\). Let the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) be continuous on this rectangle.

  1. The function
    \[G(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\]
    is differentiable at every point \(s \in (c, d)\), its derivative is
    \[G'(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{4.12}\]
    and \(G'\) is continuous on \((c, d)\).
  2. Let \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) be functions on \([c, d]\) with \(\alpha \le \varphi(s) \le \psi(s) \le \beta\) for every \(s \in [c, d]\), which are differentiable at the point \(s_0 \in (c, d)\). Then the function
    \[G(s) = \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s})}^{\psi(s)} f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\]
    is differentiable at \(s_0\), and
    \[\begin{aligned} G'(s_0) = {} & \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s}_0)}^{\psi(s_0)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s_0)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & + f\big(\psi(s_0), s_0\big)\,\psi'(s_0) - f\big(\varphi(s_0), s_0\big)\,\varphi'(s_0) . \end{aligned} \tag{4.13}\]
Proof

We must show both items. For the first we write the change of the integrand with the mean value theorem and bound it uniformly for all \(t\). For the second we split the change of the function \(G\) into the change of the integrand, which the first item handles, and the pieces at the ends.

1. Constant limits.

  1. For every \(s \in [c, d]\) the functions \(t \mapsto f(t, s)\) and \(t \mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\) are continuous on \([\alpha, \beta]\), because the distance between the points \((t, s)\) and \((t', s)\) is \(|t - t'|\). By theorem 3.37 they are integrable, so the numbers \(G(s)\) and \(I(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\) exist.
  2. The rectangle is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(\big|\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t', s') - \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\big| < \eta/(2(\beta - \alpha))\) for any two points of the rectangle less than \(\delta_1\) apart.
  3. Let \(s \in (c, d)\) and let \(\delta\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_1\), \(s - c\) and \(d - s\). Let \(0 < |k| < \delta\), so that \(s + k\) lies in \((c, d)\).
  4. Let \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\). The function \(\sigma \mapsto f(t, \sigma)\) is differentiable at every point of \([c, d]\), because \(\partial f/\partial s\) exists there, so by lemma 1.77 it is continuous on the closed interval between \(s\) and \(s + k\). By the mean value theorem 1.82 there is a number \(\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}\) between \(s\) and \(s + k\) such that
    \[f(t, s + k) - f(t, s) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}})\,k .\]
  5. The point \((t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}})\) is less than \(|k| < \delta_1\) away from \((t, s)\), so by step 2
    \[\begin{aligned} & \Big| f(t, s + k) - f(t, s) - k\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) \Big| \\ & \quad = |k|\,\Big| \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}}) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) \Big| \le \frac{\eta\,|k|}{2(\beta - \alpha)} \end{aligned}\]
    for every \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\).
  6. The function inside the absolute value on the left is a continuous function of \(t\) (step 1 and corollary 1.62). By linearity (lemma 3.38, item 1) its integral is \(G(s + k) - G(s) - k\,I(s)\), and by the bound (item 3 of the same lemma) this is at most \(\eta\,|k|/2\) in absolute value. We divide by \(|k|\):
    \[\Big| \frac{G(s + k) - G(s)}{k} - I(s) \Big| \le \frac{\eta}{2} < \eta .\]
  7. The error \(\eta\) was arbitrary, so by the definition of the derivative 1.8 and of the limit 1.5, \(G'(s) = I(s)\).
  8. Continuity of the derivative. For \(s, s' \in (c, d)\) with \(|s' - s| < \delta_1\), by step 2 and the bound, \(|I(s') - I(s)| \le (\beta - \alpha) \cdot \eta/(2(\beta - \alpha)) < \eta\). The function \(G' = I\) is therefore continuous at every point of \((c, d)\).

2. Variable limits.

  1. For \(w \in [\alpha, \beta]\) and \(\sigma \in [c, d]\) let \(K(w, \sigma) = \int_\alpha^w f(t, \sigma)\,\mathrm{d}t\), which for \(w = \alpha\) is zero by the convention of definition 3.33. By additivity (lemma 3.38, item 2, with the same convention for pieces of length zero), for every \(\sigma \in [c, d]\)
    \[G(\sigma) = K\big(\psi(\sigma), \sigma\big) - K\big(\varphi(\sigma), \sigma\big) .\]
  2. We write \(s = s_0\) and let \(0 < |k|\), where \(|k|\) is smaller than the numbers \(s - c\) and \(d - s\). We also write \(\varphi = \varphi(s)\), \(\psi = \psi(s)\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{k}} = \varphi(s + k)\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = \psi(s + k)\). By step 1, adding and subtracting \(K(\psi, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k)\),
    \[\begin{aligned} G(s + k) - G(s) = {} & \big[K(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(\psi, s + k)\big] \\ & - \big[K(\varphi_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k)\big] \\ & + \int_{\varphi}^{\psi} \big(f(t, s + k) - f(t, s)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t . \end{aligned}\]
    By additivity and linearity the last term equals \(K(\psi, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k) - K(\psi, s) + K(\varphi, s)\).
  3. The last term divided by \(k\) approaches \(\int_\varphi^\psi \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\). If \(\varphi < \psi\), this is the first item, applied on the rectangle \([\varphi, \psi] \times [c, d]\), which lies in \([\alpha, \beta] \times [c, d]\). If \(\varphi = \psi\), both sides are zero.
  4. The pieces at the ends. Let \(\chi\) be one of the functions \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\), \(w = \chi(s)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \chi(s + k)\). We must show that \(\big(K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k)\big)/k\) approaches \(f(w, s)\,\chi'(s)\). We choose an error \(\eta\) with \(0 < \eta \le 1\). Larger errors need not be considered, because the band that fits the error \(1\) fits them. Let \(\eta' = \eta/\big(|\chi'(s)| + 1 + |f(w, s)|\big)\), which is not larger than \(1\). The function \(f\) is continuous at the point \((w, s)\), so there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|f(t, \sigma) - f(w, s)| < \eta'\) for the points \((t, \sigma)\) of the rectangle less than \(\delta_2\) away from \((w, s)\). The function \(\chi\) is differentiable at \(s\), hence continuous there (lemma 1.77), and there is a \(\delta_3 > 0\) such that \(|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w| < \delta_2/2\) for \(|k| < \delta_3\).
  5. Let \(|k|\) also be smaller than \(\delta_3\) and than \(\delta_2/2\). For every \(t\) between \(w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) the distance between the points \((t, s + k)\) and \((w, s)\) is \(\sqrt{(t - w)^2 + k^2}\). It is not larger than \(|t - w| + |k|\), because the square of this sum is \((t - w)^2 + 2\,|t - w|\,|k| + k^2\) (lemma 1.26), so it is smaller than \(\delta_2/2 + \delta_2/2 = \delta_2\). Hence \(f(w, s) - \eta' < f(t, s + k) < f(w, s) + \eta'\).
  6. If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} > w\), then by additivity \(K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k) = \int_{\mathrm{w}}^{w_{\mathrm{k}}} f(t, s + k)\,\mathrm{d}t\). By the bound and step 5 this number lies between \((f(w, s) - \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\) and \((f(w, s) + \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\). If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} < w\), the difference is \(-\int_{\mathrm{w}_\mathrm{k}}^{w} f(t, s + k)\,\mathrm{d}t\) and lies between \((f(w, s) + \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\) and \((f(w, s) - \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\). If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = w\), it is zero. In all three cases
    \[\big| K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k) - f(w, s)\,(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w) \big| \le \eta'\,|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w| .\]
  7. The difference quotient \((w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)/k\) of the function \(\chi\) at \(s\) converges to \(\chi'(s)\). By the definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(\eta'\), for small enough \(|k|\) the difference \(|(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)/k - \chi'(s)|\) is therefore smaller than \(\eta'\), and since \(\eta' \le 1\), \(|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w|/|k| < |\chi'(s)| + 1\). We divide the inequality of step 6 by \(|k|\) and use the triangle inequality for numbers:
    \[\begin{aligned} \Big| \frac{K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k)}{k} - f(w, s)\,\chi'(s) \Big| &< \eta'\,\big(|\chi'(s)| + 1\big) \\ &\quad + |f(w, s)|\,\eta' . \end{aligned}\]
    By the choice of the number \(\eta'\) in step 4 the right side equals \(\eta\). The quotient therefore approaches \(f(w, s)\,\chi'(s)\).
  8. By step 2, \((G(s + k) - G(s))/k\) is a sum of three quotients. By step 7 the first approaches \(f(\psi, s)\,\psi'(s)\), the second with the minus sign \(-f(\varphi, s)\,\varphi'(s)\), and by step 3 the third \(\int_\varphi^\psi \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\,\mathrm{d}t\). For the error \(\eta\) we take \(|k|\) so small that each of the three quotients is less than \(\eta/3\) away from its limit. By the triangle inequality, \((G(s + k) - G(s))/k\) is then less than \(\eta\) away from the sum of the limits, which is the right side of (4.13).

Source: LEBL2 Theorem 9.1.1 (PDF pp. 65-66) for item 1, where \(f\) is given only on the rectangle. The source does not have item 2, and its proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says what the figure predicted. The first item says that with constant limits we may differentiate under the integral sign. The second adds two terms contributed by the moving limits: the value of the integrand at the limit, times the speed at which the limit moves. The proof used devices we know: the mean value theorem, as in the first item of the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, uniform continuity, as in theorem 3.37, and the bound of the integral over a short piece, as in the second item of the fundamental theorem of calculus. The derivative in this second item even follows from the second item of the lemma. With the integrand \(f(t, s) = f(t)\), which does not depend on \(s\), the constant lower limit \(\varphi(s) = \alpha\) and the upper limit \(\psi(s) = s\), the second item gives \(G'(s) = f(s) \cdot 1\).

Let us test the second item on the cross section of the round bar (figure 4.22, right). The square of the distance of the point \((y, z)\) of the cross section from the axis of the bar is \(y^2 + z^2\). At every \(y\) we integrate it along the chord from \(z = -q(y)\) to \(z = q(y)\):

\[\Theta(y) = \int_{-\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{y})}^{q(y)} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z .\]

We will meet such an integral in section 4.2.10, because the downward displacement of the hanging bar has the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). Here \(t = z\), \(s = y\), \(f(z, y) = y^2 + z^2\), \(\varphi = -q\) and \(\psi = q\). For the rectangle we take \([-5, 5] \times [2, 4]\) in millimetres. On it \(f\) is a polynomial with the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y = 2y\), and the limits \(\pm q(y)\) lie in \([-5, 5]\). At \(y = 3\) mm we have \(q(3) = 4\) mm and by (4.11) \(q'(3) = -3/4\), so \(\varphi'(3) = 3/4\). By (4.13)

\[\begin{aligned} \Theta'(3) &= \int_{-4}^{4} 2 \cdot 3\,\mathrm{d}z + (9 + 16) \cdot \Big(-\frac34\Big) - (9 + 16) \cdot \frac34 \\ &= 48 - 18{,}75 - 18{,}75 = 10{,}5\ \text{mm}^2 . \end{aligned}\]

The first term says that the integrand grows, because \(y^2\) grows with \(y\). The other two say that the chord gets shorter. When \(y\) increases by a small step, say \(0{,}01\) mm, each end of the chord moves toward the axis \(y\) by about \(0{,}75\) times as much, \(0{,}0075\) mm, at a place where the integrand is \(y^2 + q(y)^2 = r^2 = 25\ \text{mm}^2\). Let us check without the lemma. By the fundamental theorem of calculus with the function \(y^2 z + z^3/3\), whose derivative with respect to \(z\) is \(y^2 + z^2\), we get \(\Theta(y) = 2\,q(y)\,y^2 + \tfrac23\,q(y)^3\), and \(\Theta(3) = 72 + 42{,}667 = 114{,}667\ \text{mm}^3\). With SymPy we computed \(\Theta(3{,}01) = 114{,}771\ \text{mm}^3\) and the difference quotient \((\Theta(3{,}01) - \Theta(3))/0{,}01 = 10{,}44\) mm², and with the step \(0{,}001\) mm \(10{,}49\) mm². The quotients approach \(10{,}5\) mm².

4.2.8 Integral over a body between two graphs

Now we can define the integral of a function over a body between graphs as the integral over a box, with iterated integrals in the order \(z\), \(y\), \(x\). The inner integral over \(z\) exists by lemma 4.18 and has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7. By item 2 of that lemma the middle integral over \(y\) therefore exists and is a continuous function of \(x\), and the outer integral exists by theorem 3.37.

Definition 4.20 Integral over a body between two graphs (integral po telesu med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(V\). The integral of the function \(f\) over the body \(V\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z \bigg) \mathrm{d}y \bigg) \mathrm{d}x . \tag{4.14}\]

For a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates the inner integral is over the coordinate that runs between the graphs, and the middle and the outer one are over the coordinates of the rectangle, in the order given by the description of the body.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.3, (3) (PDF p. 453), for the double integral over a region between two curves, and §10.7 (PDF pp. 478-479), where the triple integral is defined by a subdivision into small boxes and computed by three successive integrations. LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.8 (PDF p. 126) states that the integral of the general theory over a region between two graphs in the plane equals the iterated integral, and leaves the proof to the reader. The definition by the iterated integral is not from the sources.

The round bar is not described by a single body between graphs but by three pieces. We define the integral over it as the sum of the integrals over the pieces.

Definition 4.21 Body cut into pieces (telo, razrezano na kose)

Let \(V\) be a set of points that is the union of the bodies between graphs \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\) (definition 4.15), each with its own naming of the axes, and let no interior point of any of them lie in another one. We then say that \(V\) is cut into pieces (razrezano na kose) \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\). The integral of a continuous function \(f\) over a body cut in this way is the sum of the integrals over the pieces (definition 4.20),

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{V}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482) cuts a body by auxiliary surfaces into pieces, for which it proves the divergence theorem separately. The definition of the integral as a sum over the pieces is not from the sources.

The definition agrees with the ones we already have. A box is a body between the graphs of constant functions, and then (4.14) is equation (4.7). A body made of boxes is cut into pieces that are its cells, and definition 4.21 gives the sum of definition 4.11, item 1. Two things remain open, however. Would another order of integration give the same number, and would another cut of the same body give the same sum? For a box and for a body made of boxes we proved both (theorem 4.9 and lemma 4.12). In general this is told by the theory of the integral over bounded sets, which defines the integral without iterated integrals (LEBL2 §10.3-10.5, PDF pp. 108-127), and which we do not develop in the book. For the divergence theorem we do not need it, because the proof uses only one order and only the given cut. Whenever we compute the integral over a body cut into pieces, we will say which cut we use.

For computing we need linearity and monotonicity.

Lemma 4.22 Properties of the integral over a body between two graphs (lastnosti integrala po telesu med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between graphs or a body cut into pieces (definition 4.21), \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) continuous functions on \(V\) and \(\alpha\) a number.

  1. Linearity: \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} (f_1 + f_2)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_2\,\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \alpha f_1\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. Monotonicity: if \(f_1(P) \le f_2(P)\) for every point \(P \in V\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_2\,\mathrm{d}V\).
Proof

We must show both items. The proof is the proof of lemma 4.10, items 1 and 4.

  1. For a body between graphs we use, on each of the three iterated integrals, the linearity or the monotonicity of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.38, items 1 and 4), first on the inner one, then on the middle and on the outer one. We may do so because by lemma 4.18 and by lemma 4.7, item 2, all the intermediate integrals are continuous functions.
  2. For a body cut into pieces we add the equalities or inequalities of step 1 over the pieces.

Source: LEBL2 Propositions 10.1.10 and 10.1.11 (PDF p. 96) for integrable functions on a rectangle. The proof by iterated integrals is not from the sources.

The integral of the constant function \(1\) over a body is its volume. For a box this is the school volume by lemma 4.10, item 2. Let us compute the volume of the round bar with the cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\) of section 4.2.6 (figure 4.21, right), with the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres.

  1. The piece \(C\). The inner integral is \(\int_{-\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{y})}^{q(y)} 1\,\mathrm{d}z = 2\,q(y)\), the middle one \(A_{\mathrm{C}} = \int_{-3}^{3} 2\,q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\), and the outer one \(\int_0^L A_{\mathrm{C}}\,\mathrm{d}x = L\,A_{\mathrm{C}}\).
  2. The piece \(D\). The inner integral, now over \(y\), is \(\int_3^{q(z)} 1\,\mathrm{d}y = q(z) - 3\), the middle one \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = \int_{-4}^{4} \big(q(z) - 3\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\), the outer one \(L\,A_{\mathrm{D}}\).
  3. The piece \(E\). The inner integral is \(-3 - (-q(z)) = q(z) - 3\), so the middle one is again \(A_{\mathrm{D}}\).

The numbers \(A_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{D}}\) are the areas of the cross sections of the pieces. We cannot compute them with the tools of the book, because the function whose derivative is \(\sqrt{25 - t^2}\) needs the inverse sine function, which we have not defined. SymPy gives \(A_{\mathrm{C}} = 56{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\) and \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\). The area of the cross section is therefore \(A = A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}} = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), which is the area of a disc \(\pi r^2\) of radius \(5\) mm from school geometry. The volume of the bar is

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} 1\,\mathrm{d}V = L\,(A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}}) = L\,A = 10\,000\ \text{mm} \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 785\,400\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

For a constant function \(\alpha\), by linearity \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \alpha\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha\,L\,A\). The same holds for a function that depends only on \(x\). Its inner integrals over the pieces give its value times the area of the cross section of the piece, and the areas add up to \(A\). We will use this for the equilibrium of the whole bar in section 4.2.11.

4.2.9 Integral over a curved surface

The surface of a body between graphs has six pieces (figure 4.20). The four side pieces are flat, in the planes \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) and \(y = d\), with the outward normals \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). Each is a region between graphs in its own plane. The piece in the plane \(x = a\) consists of the points \((a, y, z)\) with \(c \le y \le d\) and \(g(a, y) \le z \le h(a, y)\), and we will write the integral over it as an iterated integral, with the inner integral over \(z\). The two lids are new, and they are curved. How do we compute the area of a small patch on a curved lid, and where does the normal to it point?

Take the top lid, the graph of the function \(h\), and on it the patch above a small rectangle of the shadow with sides \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) (figure 4.23). When we move from the point \((x, y)\) by \(\Delta x\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), the height of the lid changes by about \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\), by theorem 1.86 on the change of a field over a short step, written for two variables. The side of the patch above the side \(\Delta x\) is therefore about the vector \(\vek a\), and the side above the side \(\Delta y\) about the vector \(\vek b\), where

\[\vek a = \Big(\Delta x,\ 0,\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\Big) , \qquad \vek b = \Big(0,\ \Delta y,\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y\Big) .\]

The patch is approximately the parallelogram spanned by \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\). By definition 2.29

\[\begin{aligned} \vek a\times\vek b &= \Big( 0 - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y,\ \ 0 - \Delta x\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y,\ \ \Delta x\,\Delta y - 0 \Big) \\ &= \Big( -\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1 \Big)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y . \end{aligned}\]

By item 4 of lemma 2.30 this vector is perpendicular to both sides, hence to the patch, and its length is the area of the parallelogram (section 2.8). We write

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \Big( -\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1 \Big) .\]

The area of the patch is about \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\), and the unit normal to it is \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}/|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\) (definition 2.16). The component \(z\) of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) is \(1\), so the normal points up, out of the body, which lies below the top lid. For the bottom lid we take the opposite vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (\partial g/\partial x,\ \partial g/\partial y,\ -1)\), which points down, out of the body.

The divergence theorem will add up the products \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\) over the patches. In each of them the length of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), which has a root, cancels:

\[\vek v\cdot\frac{\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}}{|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|}\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y = \Big( v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y .\]

This is what the divergence theorem will need. For the integral of a function that is not of the form \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\), however, the root remains.

The integrand on the lid is the value of a function at the point \((x, y, h(x, y))\), which depends on the point \((x, y)\) of the shadow through the function \(h\). The following lemma says that it is continuous.

Lemma 4.23 Continuity of a composite function (zveznost sestavljene funkcije)

Let \(f\) be a function that is continuous on a set of points of space \(W\). Let \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions defined on a set \(M\), which is an interval or a set of points of the plane, such that the point \(p(Q) = \big(p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q), p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q), p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q)\big)\) lies in \(W\) for every \(Q \in M\). If \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous at the point \(Q_0 \in M\), the function \(Q \mapsto f(p(Q))\) is continuous at \(Q_0\).

Proof
