We must show that the values \(f(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}}))\) converge to \(f(p(Q_0))\) for every sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(M\) that converges to \(Q_0\). We use the lemma on continuity through sequences twice.

  1. Let the sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(M\) converge to \(Q_0\). The function \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous at \(Q_0\), so by lemma 1.66 on continuity through sequences of points (on an interval by lemma 1.59) \(p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q_0)\). Likewise \(p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q_0)\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q_0)\).
  2. By lemma 1.64 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, the points \(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) therefore converge to \(p(Q_0)\). They all lie in \(W\), and \(f\) is continuous at \(p(Q_0)\), so by lemma 1.66 \(f(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}})) \to f(p(Q_0))\).
  3. The sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) was arbitrary, so by the same lemma, in the other direction, the function \(Q \mapsto f(p(Q))\) is continuous at \(Q_0\).

Source: LEBL1 Proposition 3.2.7 (PDF p. 125) for functions of one variable. The proof with sequences for points is not from the sources.

Now we can write down how we integrate over the surface of a body between graphs.

Definition 4.24 Flux and integral over the surface of a body between two graphs (pretok in integral po površini telesa med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15). Its surface (površina) \(S\) consists of six pieces:

  • the top lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\), the points \((x, y, h(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), with the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \big(-\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1\big)\),
  • the bottom lid \(S_{\mathrm{g}}\), the points \((x, y, g(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), with the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = \big(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y},\ -1\big)\),
  • the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\), the points \((a, y, z)\) and \((b, y, z)\) with \(c \le y \le d\) and \(z\) between \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((a, y)\) or \((b, y)\), with the vectors \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\),
  • the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\), the points \((x, c, z)\) and \((x, d, z)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(z\) between \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((x, c)\) or \((x, d)\), with the vectors \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\).

On every piece with the vector \(\vek N\) the outward unit normal (zunanja enotska normala) is \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\). The surface integral of a function \(f\) over the top lid is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d f\big(x, y, h(x, y)\big)\,\big|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}(x, y)\big|\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{4.15}\]

and over the bottom lid likewise, with \(g\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). Over the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) it is the number \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} f(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\), over \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) the same with \(b\), over \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) the number \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{c})}^{h(x, c)} f(x, c, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\), over \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) the same with \(d\). The integral over the surface \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\) is the sum of these six numbers, when all the integrals exist. For a field \(\vek v\) the flux (pretok) of the field through the surface is the integral over the surface of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\). For a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates we rename the coordinates in these formulas, so that the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) has the component \(1\) in the direction of the coordinate that runs between the graphs.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, (2) and (3) (PDF p. 469): \(\vek N = \vek r_{\mathrm{u}}\times\vek r_{\mathrm{v}}\), \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\) and \(\mathrm{d}A = |\vek N|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v\), and §10.5, Problem 13 (PDF p. 469), \(\vek N = (-f_{\mathrm{u}}, -f_{\mathrm{v}}, 1)\) for the surface \(z = f(x, y)\). The definition with the pieces of the surface of a body between graphs is not from the sources.

Lemma 4.25 Flux through the surface of a body between two graphs (pretok skozi površino telesa med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between graphs with the surface \(S\) of definition 4.24.

  1. If the function \(f\) is continuous on \(S\), the integrals over all six pieces of the surface exist.
  2. If \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous on \(V\), then
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = {} & \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big[ v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big]_{\mathrm{h}} \mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big[ v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big]_{\mathrm{g}} \mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(b, y)} v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} v_{\mathrm{x}}(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{d})}^{h(x, d)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, d, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{c})}^{h(x, c)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, c, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x , \end{aligned} \tag{4.16}\]
    where the bracket with the index \(h\) means that \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) are taken at the point \((x, y, h(x, y))\) and the partial derivatives at the point \((x, y)\), and likewise with the index \(g\).
Proof

We must show that the integrands are continuous and that on the lids the root cancels.

1. Existence.

  1. The top lid. The function \((x, y) \mapsto f(x, y, h(x, y))\) is continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.23, with the functions \(p_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y) = x\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y) = y\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}} = h\), which are continuous.
  2. The square of the length \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 1 + (\partial h/\partial x)^2 + (\partial h/\partial y)^2\) is a sum of products of continuous functions, hence continuous by corollary 1.67, item 1. For numbers \(A, B \ge 1\) we have \(|A - B| = |A^2 - B^2|/(A + B) \le |A^2 - B^2|/2\), and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| \ge 1\). The difference of the lengths at two points is therefore at most half the difference of the squares, and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\) is continuous.
  3. The integrand in (4.15) is a product of continuous functions and is continuous on \(R\). Since \(R\) is closed and bounded, it is uniformly continuous by theorem 4.6, so it has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7, and by its item 2 the iterated integral exists. For the bottom lid it is the same.
  4. The side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) is the intersection of the closed set \(V\) (lemma 4.17) with the plane \(x = a\), which is closed (lemma 1.73, item 1), so by item 2 of the same lemma it is closed, and it is bounded. The proof of lemma 4.18, in which the numbers \(y\) of the interval \([c, d]\) take the place of the points \((x, y)\) of the rectangle, shows that the function \(y \mapsto \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} f(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\) is continuous on \([c, d]\), hence integrable. For the other three side pieces it is the same.

2. Flux.

  1. On the top lid \(\vek n = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}/|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\), so at every point \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand in (4.15) with \(f = \vek v\cdot\vek n\) is thus the first bracket in (4.16). It is continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.23 and corollary 1.67, so the integral exists as in step 3 of the first part.
  2. On the bottom lid likewise \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}| = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = -\big(v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}}\big)\), and by linearity (lemma 3.38, item 1), applied to both iterated integrals, we take the minus sign out.
  3. On \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = v_{\mathrm{x}}\), on \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = -v_{\mathrm{x}}\), and likewise on \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) with \(\pm v_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrals exist by lemma 4.18, because \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) are continuous on \(V\).
  4. The sum of the six integrals is the right side of (4.16).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, (3) and (3*) (PDF p. 469), \(\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek N\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v\), and (5″) (PDF p. 470) for the lid \(z = h(x, y)\). The proof is not from the sources.

The definition describes every piece of the surface in a single way, with the two variables given by the description of the body. The same surface can be described in other ways too. The part of the plane \(y = 3\) between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round bar is, for the piece \(C\), a side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) above the edge \(y = 3\) of its shadow, and for the piece \(D\) the bottom lid. That the surface integral does not depend on the description follows from the rule for the change of variables in a double integral (LEBL2 Theorem 10.7.2, PDF p. 134), which we do not prove in the book. We do not need it for the divergence theorem, and for the bar we will check the agreement of the two descriptions directly.

Let us test the definition on the mantle of the round bar. The top lid of the piece \(C\) is the graph of the function \(h(x, y) = q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\). By lemma 4.16 \(\partial h/\partial y = q'(y) = -y/q(y)\), and the partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is zero. Hence

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \Big(0,\ \frac{y}{q(y)},\ 1\Big) , \qquad |\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 1 + \frac{y^2}{q(y)^2} = \frac{q(y)^2 + y^2}{q(y)^2} = \frac{r^2}{q(y)^2} ,\]

and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = r/q(y)\). The outward unit normal is \(\vek n = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\,q(y)/r = (0,\ y/r,\ q(y)/r)\). On the lid \(z = q(y)\), so \(\vek n = (0, y/r, z/r)\), the normal of the mantle that we wrote at the beginning of section 4.2.6 (figure 4.19, right). The area of the lid is the integral of the function \(1\):

\[\int_0^L \int_{-3}^{3} \frac{r}{q(y)}\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = L \cdot 6{,}435\ \text{mm} ,\]

where \(\int_{-3}^{3} 5/q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = 6{,}435\) mm was computed by SymPy, because it again needs the inverse sine. This is the length of the arc of the circle above the chord from \(y = -3\) to \(y = 3\). The bottom lid of the piece \(C\) has the same area. For the piece \(D\) the top lid is the graph of the function \(q(z)\) over \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\), with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = (0,\ 1,\ z/q(z))\) and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = r/q(z)\), and its area is \(L \cdot 9{,}273\) mm. The same holds for the bottom lid of the piece \(E\). The mantle of the bar consists of these four lids, with the total area

\[L \cdot (2 \cdot 6{,}435 + 2 \cdot 9{,}273)\ \text{mm} = L \cdot 31{,}42\ \text{mm} ,\]

which is the length of the bar times the circumference of the circle \(2\pi r = 31{,}42\) mm, the area of the mantle of a cylinder from school geometry. The integral of a constant function over a flat side piece is its value times the area of the region between graphs in its plane. The top face of the bar, \(x = 0\), consists of the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) of all three pieces, with the total area \(A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}} = A\).

4.2.10 Divergence theorem for curved bodies

Now we have all the parts. The proof will follow the proof for a box. The term with the derivative with respect to \(z\) is handled by the fundamental theorem of calculus along the chords from the bottom to the top lid. The terms with the derivatives with respect to \(y\) and to \(x\) are brought out of the inner integral over \(z\) by lemma 4.19, item 2, at the price of terms on the lids, and then the fundamental theorem of calculus does its work along \(y\) or \(x\). Before that we must settle one more technical question. The lemma on differentiating an integral needs the function on a rectangle around the chord, while we know the field \(\vek v\) only on an open set \(D\) containing the body. Near the edge of the body the rectangle reaches a little out of the body. The following lemma says that it stays in \(D\) if it is narrow enough.

Lemma 4.26 Neighbourhood of a closed bounded set (okolica zaprte omejene množice)

Let \(K\) be a closed and bounded set of points of space (definition 1.72) and \(D\) an open set of points that contains \(K\). Then there is a number \(\delta > 0\) such that every point that is less than \(\delta\) away from some point of the set \(K\) lies in \(D\).

Proof

We must show that a single radius suffices for all points of \(K\). We argue by contradiction, with the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, as in the proof of theorem 4.6.

  1. Suppose that no such \(\delta\) exists. Then for every natural number \(n\) there are a point \(P_{\mathrm{n}} \in K\) and a point \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) that does not lie in \(D\), with \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}| < 1/n\).
  2. The set \(K\) is bounded, so by lemma 1.75 the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(C\). The set \(K\) is closed, so \(C\) lies in \(K\) and therefore in \(D\).
  3. The sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) also converges to \(C\). The proof is the same as in steps 5 and 6 of the proof of theorem 4.6.
  4. The set \(D\) is open, so there is an \(r > 0\) such that all points less than \(r\) away from \(C\) lie in \(D\). Since \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(C\), for large enough \(k\) the distance \(|C Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}|\) is smaller than \(r\) (definition 1.63), and \(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(D\). This contradicts step 1, so the assumption is false.

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 7.4.10 (the Lebesgue covering lemma, PDF p. 282), with open covers instead of a single open set. The proof with sequences is not from the sources.

Theorem 4.27 Divergence theorem for a body between two graphs (izrek o divergenci za telo med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15), with the surface \(S\) and the outward unit normal \(\vek n\) (definition 4.24). Let \(D\) be an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.88). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.17}\]

The same holds for a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates.

Proof

We must show that the integral of each of the three partial derivatives equals the part of the right side of (4.16) in which the same component of the field appears.

1. Preparation.

  1. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded (lemma 4.17). By lemma 4.26 there is a \(\delta_0 > 0\) such that every point that is less than \(\delta_0\) away from some point of \(V\) lies in \(D\).
  2. The partial derivatives of the components of the field are continuous on \(D\) by definition 1.88, and the components themselves by lemma 1.89, that a continuously differentiable function is continuous. All of them are therefore continuous on \(V\). The integrals of the partial derivatives over \(V\) therefore exist (definition 4.20), and by linearity (lemma 4.22) the left side of (4.17) is the sum \(I_{\mathrm{x}} + I_{\mathrm{y}} + I_{\mathrm{z}}\) of the integrals of the functions \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\), \(\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\) and \(\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) over \(V\).
  3. For a function \(w\) that is continuous on \(V\), the functions \((x, y) \mapsto w(x, y, h(x, y))\) and \((x, y) \mapsto w(x, y, g(x, y))\) are continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.23, and so are their products with the partial derivatives of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) by corollary 1.67, item 1. Since \(R\) is closed and bounded, these functions are uniformly continuous by theorem 4.6, and by lemma 4.7 their iterated integrals over \(R\) in both orders exist.

2. The derivative with respect to \(z\).

  1. Let \((x, y) \in R\) and \(g(x, y) < h(x, y)\). The points \((x, y, z)\) with \(g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y)\) lie in \(V\) and therefore in \(D\), where \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) has a continuous partial derivative with respect to \(z\). The function \(z \mapsto v_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z)\) is therefore differentiable at every point of this interval, continuous by lemma 1.77, and its derivative is continuous. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, item 1,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z = v_{\mathrm{z}}\big(x, y, h(x, y)\big) - v_{\mathrm{z}}\big(x, y, g(x, y)\big) .\]
    If \(g(x, y) = h(x, y)\), both sides are zero.
  2. Both functions on the right are continuous on \(R\) by step 3 of the preparation. We integrate the equality over \(y\) and over \(x\) and use linearity (lemma 3.38, item 1). The integral \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) therefore equals the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the first two lines of (4.16).

3. The derivative with respect to \(y\).

  1. Let \(x \in [a, b]\) be fixed. For \(y \in [c, d]\) let
    \[\begin{aligned} F(y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z , \\ E(y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z + v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} , \end{aligned}\]
    where \(g\), \(h\) and their derivatives are taken at the point \((x, y)\). By lemma 4.18 and step 3 of the preparation, \(F\) and \(E\) are continuous on \([c, d]\).
  2. Let \(y_0 \in (c, d)\). Let us show that \(F'(y_0) = E(y_0)\). Let \(\alpha = g(x, y_0) - \delta_0/2\) and \(\beta = h(x, y_0) + \delta_0/2\). The functions \(y \mapsto g(x, y)\) and \(y \mapsto h(x, y)\) are continuous at \(y_0\), so there is a \(\delta_1\) with \(0 < \delta_1 \le \delta_0/2\) such that the interval \([y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) lies in \((c, d)\) and \(\alpha \le g(x, y) \le h(x, y) \le \beta\) for every \(y\) with \(|y - y_0| \le \delta_1\).
  3. Every point \((x, y, z)\) with \(|y - y_0| \le \delta_1\) and \(\alpha \le z \le \beta\) lies in \(D\). Let \(z^*\) be the number of the interval \([g(x, y_0), h(x, y_0)]\) closest to \(z\): \(z\) itself if it lies in the interval, otherwise the nearer end. Then \(|z - z^*| \le \delta_0/2\), the point \((x, y_0, z^*)\) lies in \(V\), and the distance between the two points is \(\sqrt{(y - y_0)^2 + (z - z^*)^2} \le \sqrt{\delta_0^2/4 + \delta_0^2/4} < \delta_0\). By step 1 of the preparation the point lies in \(D\).
  4. On the rectangle \([\alpha, \beta] \times [y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) with the variables \(t = z\) and \(s = y\) let \(f(z, y) = v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z)\). By step 3 the rectangle lies in \(D\), which is open, so \(f\) has the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y = \partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\) at every point of it. Both functions are continuous on the rectangle, because the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y', z')\) equals the distance between \((z, y)\) and \((z', y')\). The functions \(\varphi(y) = g(x, y)\) and \(\psi(y) = h(x, y)\) have values in \([\alpha, \beta]\) and are differentiable at \(y_0\), with the derivatives \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}(x, y_0)\) and \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}(x, y_0)\) (definition 1.23). By lemma 4.19, item 2, \(F'(y_0) = E(y_0)\).
  5. The function \(F\) is thus continuous on \([c, d]\) and differentiable at every point of \((c, d)\), and its derivative \(E\) is continuous on \([c, d]\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, item 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d E(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = F(d) - F(c)\). By the definition of the function \(E\) and by linearity, therefore,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y = F(d) - F(c) - \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big( v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  6. All three terms on the right are continuous functions of \(x\). For \(F(d) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{d})}^{h(x, d)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, d, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\) and \(F(c)\) this is lemma 4.18, for the last integral lemma 4.7, item 2, with step 3 of the preparation. We integrate the equality over \(x\) and use linearity. The integral \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) therefore equals the last two lines of (4.16), together with the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) in the first two lines.

4. The derivative with respect to \(x\).

  1. For \((x, y) \in R\) let
    \[\begin{aligned} \tilde F(x, y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z , \\ \tilde E(x, y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z + v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} - v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} . \end{aligned}\]
    As in steps 2 to 5 of the third part, only with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged, for fixed \(y\) the function \(x \mapsto \tilde F(x, y)\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and differentiable at every point of \((a, b)\) with the derivative \(\tilde E(x, y)\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \tilde E(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tilde F(b, y) - \tilde F(a, y)\).
  2. The function \(\tilde E\) is continuous on the rectangle \(R\) by lemma 4.18 and step 3 of the preparation. By theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, for a rectangle,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y = \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \big(\tilde F(b, y) - \tilde F(a, y)\big)\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  3. By the definition of the function \(\tilde E\) and by linearity
    \[I_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big( v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} - v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
    By step 2 this equals the third and the fourth line of (4.16), together with the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) in the first two lines.

5. The sum.

  1. We add \(I_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) from the fourth, third and second part. We obtain the right side of (4.16), which by lemma 4.25, item 2, is the flux \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, (2*) (PDF p. 479), with a proof for bodies that lie between graphs in the direction of all three axes (PDF pp. 480-482). It treats the term with the derivative with respect to \(z\) as we do. The proof of the terms with the derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) by lemma 4.19 is not from the sources.

The proof has shown where the terms on the lids with the derivatives of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) come from. When we bring the derivative with respect to \(y\) out of the integral over \(z\), the limits move, and the lemma on differentiating an integral adds the values of the field on the lids, multiplied by the slope of the lid in the direction \(y\). These are exactly the components \(-\partial h/\partial y\) and \(\partial g/\partial y\) of the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). The normal to the lid, which we obtained geometrically in section 4.2.9, from the vector product of the sides of a patch, has thus also come out of the computation. The fundamental theorem of calculus appeared three times in the proof, once for each coordinate, as for the box. We needed the rectangle \(R\) only in step 2 of the fourth part, where we exchanged the order of integration in \(x\) and in \(y\).

Let us test the theorem on the right piece \(D\) of the round hanging bar, with the displacement field of the hanging bar (1.18),

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), the length \(L = 10\) m and the radius of the cross section \(r = 5\) mm. The bar hangs under its own weight and is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1. The piece \(D\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \ge 3\) mm, a body between the graphs of the constant function \(3\) mm and the function \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\) (section 4.2.6, figure 4.21, right). The components of the field are polynomials, so they are continuously differentiable in all of space, which we take as the open set of the theorem.

The left side. In section 4.2.5 we computed the divergence \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). It does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), so the inner and the middle integral give \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\,A_{\mathrm{D}}\), with the area of the cross section of the piece \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\) from section 4.2.8, and the outer one

\[0{,}8\,a\,\frac{L^2}{2}\,A_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}4\,a L^2 A_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}01952\ \text{mm} \cdot 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2 = 0{,}08731\ \text{mm}^3 ,\]

where \(a L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm \(= 0{,}01952\) mm is the displacement of the lower end of the bar.

The right side. The flux through the six pieces of the surface of the piece \(D\), by lemma 4.25 with \(y\) as the coordinate that runs between the graphs:

  1. The side piece \(x = L\), part of the bottom face of the bar, with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integral of the function \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, y, z) = aL^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) over the cross section of the piece is \(aL^2 A_{\mathrm{D}} - 0{,}3\,a\,\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}2183\ \text{mm}^3\), where \(\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} = \int_{-4}^{4}\int_3^{q(z)} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z = 203{,}8\ \text{mm}^4\). The second term is very small, \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\).
  2. The side piece \(x = 0\), part of the top face of the bar, with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{x}}(0, y, z) = 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the flux \(0{,}3\,a\,\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} = 1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\).
  3. The top lid \(y = q(z)\), part of the mantle, with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = (0,\ 1,\ z/q(z))\). At a point of the lid \(\vek u\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = u_{\mathrm{y}} + u_{\mathrm{z}}\,z/q(z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\big(q(z) + z^2/q(z)\big) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,r^2/q(z)\). The integral over \(z\) is \(r\) times the arc length \(9{,}273\) mm from section 4.2.9, and the integral over \(x\) gives \(L^2/2\). The flux is \(-0{,}6\,a\,\tfrac{L^2}{2} \cdot 5\ \text{mm} \cdot 9{,}273\ \text{mm} = -0{,}2715\ \text{mm}^3\).
  4. The bottom lid \(y = 3\), the cut toward the piece \(C\), with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (0, -1, 0)\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z) = 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) \cdot 3\ \text{mm}\). The integral over \(z\) from \(-4\) to \(4\) gives the factor \(8\) mm, the one over \(x\) the factor \(L^2/2\), together \(0{,}6\,a\,\tfrac{L^2}{2} \cdot 24\ \text{mm}^2 = 0{,}1405\ \text{mm}^3\).
  5. The side pieces \(z = \pm 4\). There \(q(\pm 4) = 3\), so \(y\) runs from \(3\) to \(3\), and the integrals are zero by the convention of definition 3.33. The pieces are segments on the mantle that have no area.

The sum is \(0{,}2183 + 0{,}0000 - 0{,}2715 + 0{,}1405 = 0{,}0873\ \text{mm}^3\), the same as the left side. We computed all the integrals with SymPy. What do they say? The lower end of the piece moves down and sweeps \(0{,}2183\ \text{mm}^3\) outward. The mantle moves toward the axis of the bar, because the bar gets thinner, and sweeps \(0{,}2715\ \text{mm}^3\) inward. The cut \(y = 3\) also moves toward the axis, in the direction \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), which for the piece \(D\) is the outward direction, so it contributes \(0{,}1405\ \text{mm}^3\). The piece \(D\) follows the thinning of the bar toward its axis.

The round bar itself is not one body between graphs but is cut into three pieces. We apply the theorem to each piece and add the equalities. On the left we get the integral over the bar (definition 4.21). On the right, however, we get the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces of all three bodies, also through the cuts \(y = \pm 3\), which are not part of the surface of the bar. As with the cells of a body made of boxes, the contributions of each cut cancel, because the cut has the normal \(\vek n\) for the piece on one side and \(-\vek n\) for the piece on the other side (figure 4.24).

Corollary 4.28 Divergence theorem for a body cut into pieces (izrek o divergenci za telo, razrezano na kose)

Let \(V\) be cut into the pieces \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\), which are bodies between graphs (definition 4.21). Let the pieces of the surfaces of these bodies (definition 4.24) be divided into outer and inner ones, and the inner ones into pairs, so that each pair consists of pieces of the surfaces of two different bodies and the flux of every continuous field through one piece is the negative of the flux through the other. Let \(S\) be the union of the outer pieces, the surface of the body \(V\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\) the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces. Let \(D\) be an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.18}\]
Proof

We must show that the fluxes through the inner pieces cancel.

  1. Every body \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(V\), hence in \(D\). By theorem 4.27 the integral of the divergence of the field \(\vek v\) over \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals the flux through its surface, that is, the sum of the fluxes through its six pieces.
  2. We add the equalities over \(k\) from \(1\) to \(m\). The sum of the left sides is, by definition 4.21, the integral of the divergence over \(V\).
  3. The sum of the right sides is the sum of the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces of all bodies \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\). The inner pieces come in pairs, and the two fluxes of each pair are opposite numbers that cancel. What remains is the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces, which is \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482): for a body that auxiliary surfaces cut into finitely many pieces, the integrals over the auxiliary surfaces cancel in pairs. The proof follows the source.

The condition on the pairs has to be checked for every cut. For two flat pieces in the same plane that both descriptions give by the same iterated integral and with opposite normals, it holds by itself. So it is for the bar. The cut \(y = 3\) is, for the piece \(C\), the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) with the flux \(\int_0^L \int_{-\mathrm{q}(3)}^{q(3)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\), and for the piece \(D\) the bottom lid with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (0, -1, 0)\) and with the flux \(\int_0^L \int_{-4}^{4} \big(-v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\). Since \(q(3) = 4\), these are the same iterated integral with opposite signs, for every continuous field \(\vek v\). The same holds for the cut \(y = -3\) between the pieces \(C\) and \(E\). For pieces that the two descriptions give differently, the agreement would need the rule for the change of variables (LEBL2 Theorem 10.7.2, PDF p. 134).

Let us check the corollary on the whole bar, with the same displacement field. The fluxes through the pieces of the surfaces and the integrals of the divergence are in cubic millimetres, computed with SymPy:

\(C\) \(D\) \(E\) bar
bottom face \(x = L\) \(1{,}0965\) \(0{,}2183\) \(0{,}2183\) \(1{,}5331\)
top face \(x = 0\) \(3{,}4 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-8}\)
mantle \(-0{,}3768\) \(-0{,}2715\) \(-0{,}2715\) \(-0{,}9199\)
cut \(y = 3\) \(-0{,}1405\) \(0{,}1405\) \(0\)
cut \(y = -3\) \(-0{,}1405\) \(0{,}1405\) \(0\)
sum of the fluxes \(0{,}4386\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}6132\)
integral of the divergence \(0{,}4386\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}6132\)

For each piece the last two rows are equal, as theorem 4.27 says. In the column of the bar the cuts cancel, as the corollary says. What remains is the bottom face, which moves down by \(aL^2 = 19{,}52\) µm and sweeps \(aL^2 A = 1{,}5331\ \text{mm}^3\), the mantle, which moves toward the axis and sweeps \(0{,}6\,aL^2 A = 0{,}9199\ \text{mm}^3\) inward, and a very small contribution of the top face, which rises a little at the rim. The volume of the bar increases by \(0{,}4\,aL^2 A = 0{,}6132\ \text{mm}^3\). The relative change is \(0{,}6132/785\,400 = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\), the same as for the box in section 4.2.5. Why the same? The divergence \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) depends only on the depth. For every part of the bar that spans its whole length, the relative change of volume is therefore the mean of this linear function, which is its value at the middle, \(0{,}4\,aL\), whatever the shape of the cross section.

With this we have proved the divergence theorem for all bodies that can be cut into finitely many bodies between graphs so that the inner pieces of the surfaces pair up. Such are the box, the body made of boxes and the round bar, that is, all the bodies of our examples. Three things remain cited. The first are the bodies that we cannot cut in this way. For them KREYSZIG states the theorem (§10.7, Theorem 1, PDF p. 479), and his proof only mentions that they would need a further limit process (PDF p. 482). The second is the independence of the integral of the order of integration and of the cut (LEBL2 §10.3-10.5, PDF pp. 108-127). The third is the independence of the surface integral of the description of the surface (LEBL2 Theorem 10.7.2, PDF p. 134). Whenever we use the theorem for a body that we cannot cut into pieces between graphs, we will say that we rely on the cited theorem of section 4.2.6.

4.2.11 Equilibrium of a part of a body

Now we can keep the promise of section 2.7.6. We derived the equilibrium equations (2.31) from the equilibrium of small cubes. Do they also imply the equilibrium of every finite part of the body? Two kinds of forces act on such a part. The rest of the body acts on it across its surface \(S\), with the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) per unit area, where \(\vek n\) is the outward normal of the part (definition 2.19). On all its material acts the body force \(\vek b\) per unit volume. The total force across the surface is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\), the total body force the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V\), both by components, as we agreed in section 4.2.3.

Corollary 4.29 Equilibrium of a part of a body (ravnovesje dela telesa)

Let a body be in equilibrium and let \(V\) be a part of it that is a body made of boxes with the surface \(S\) and the outward normal \(\vek n\), and let every point of \(V\) be an interior point of the body. Let the stress components be continuously differentiable on an open set \(D\) that contains \(V\) (definition 1.88), let the body force \(\vek b\) be continuous on \(V\), let the equilibrium equations (2.31) hold at every point of \(V\), and let the assumption of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.23) hold at every point of \(V\), that the average force per unit area on a plane face approaches the traction vector at the point when we shrink the face towards this point. Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t(\vek n)\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = \vek 0 , \tag{4.19}\]

where \(\vek t(\vek n)\) is the traction vector at a point of the surface \(S\) for the outward normal \(\vek n\) of the part \(V\).

Proof

We must show that each component of the left side is zero. We integrate the equilibrium equations over \(V\) and use the divergence theorem and Cauchy's formula.

  1. At every point of \(V\) the first equation (2.31) holds, \(\dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). All four terms are continuous on \(V\).
  2. The integral of the zero function is zero (lemma 4.10, item 2, on each cell). By linearity (same lemma, item 1) therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
  3. By the divergence theorem 4.14, item 2, with the field \((v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}})\), which is continuously differentiable on \(D\), the first integral equals
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  4. Every point of the surface \(S\) is an interior point of the body at which the assumption of Cauchy's formula holds, so Cauchy's formula holds there (theorem 2.23). By (2.24) the integrand of step 3 is the component \(t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n)\) of the traction vector. From step 2 we get \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} t_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).
  5. For the component \(y\) we repeat steps 1 to 4 with the second equation (2.31) and the field \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}})\), for the component \(z\) with the third equation and the field \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\). By (2.24) the integrands on the surface are \(t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n)\) and \(t_{\mathrm{z}}(\vek n)\).

Source: SADD (3.7.1)-(3.7.3) (PDF pp. 77-78), where the argument runs the other way: the equilibrium equations follow from the equilibrium of every part.

The proof wrote out exactly the picture of a wall of bricks from section 2.7.6. In the proof of the divergence theorem for a body made of boxes the contributions of the inner faces cancelled, because the outward normal of a shared face is \(\vek n\) for one cell and \(-\vek n\) for the other. By lemma 2.20 the two forces across the shared face are therefore opposite too. What remains are the forces on the surface of the part and the body forces. For a body that moves with an acceleration, the right side of (4.19) would hold, instead of the zero vector, the integral of the density times the acceleration, as in the equations of motion of section 2.7.6. We did not use the symmetry of stress (theorem 2.35). We need it for the second condition of equilibrium of a part, that the sum of the moments of the forces across the surface and of the body forces is zero. That follows in the same way from the equilibrium equations, the divergence theorem and the symmetry of stress (SADD (3.7.6) onward, PDF pp. 78-79), which we do not write out here.

Let us test the corollary on the box \(K = [x_1, x_2] \times [-c, c] \times [-c, c]\) in the hanging bar, with \(x_1 = 3\) m, \(x_2 = 6\) m and \(c = 0{,}003\) m, as in section 4.2.3 (figure 4.25). The bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, is held in the idealized way, and has the axis \(x\) pointing down. The only stress component that is not zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) (section 2.7.6), a polynomial that is continuously differentiable in the whole space. All points of the box are interior points of the bar. Each is at most 4,243 mm from the axis, so at least \(5 - 4{,}243 = 0{,}757\) mm from the mantle of the bar, at least 3 m from the top face and at least 4 m from the bottom face. By (2.24), \(\vek t(\vek n) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\).

  1. On the top face \(x = x_1\) we have \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek t = (-\rho g\,(L - x_1), 0, 0)\). The integrand is constant, so the integral over the face of area \(4c^2\) is \((-4c^2\rho g\,(L - x_1), 0, 0)\). The part of the bar above the box pulls it up with the force \(36 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3 \cdot 7\ \text{m} = 19{,}28\) N.
  2. On the bottom face \(x = x_2\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek t = (\rho g\,(L - x_2), 0, 0)\). The part of the bar below the box pulls it down with the force \(4c^2\rho g\,(L - x_2) = 11{,}02\) N.
  3. On the four side faces \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), so \(\vek t = \vek 0\). The neighbouring material does not act on the side faces.
  4. The weight of the box is \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = (4c^2\rho g\,(x_2 - x_1), 0, 0)\), that is \(8{,}264\) N down, as we computed in section 4.2.3.

The component \(x\) of the left side of (4.19) is \(4c^2\rho g\,\big({-(L - x_1)} + (L - x_2) + (x_2 - x_1)\big) = 0\), with the numbers rounded to hundredths of a newton \(-19{,}28 + 11{,}02 + 8{,}26 = 0\). The weight of the box is thus exactly the difference between the forces on its top and bottom faces. This is the same reasoning as in section 2.1, where we got the axial force from the equilibrium of the part of the bar below a cross section, only the box does not reach the bottom.

What about the whole bar (figure 4.25, left)? It is a cylinder, not a body made of boxes, and its surface is not in the interior of the body. On the surface of a body the traction vector is the force of the surroundings per unit area. SADD requires on the surface that this force be related to the stresses at the points of the surface by Cauchy's formula (§5.2, PDF pp. 104-106). For the hanging bar this is so: the top face is pulled up by the force \(\rho g L\) per unit area, which is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(0)\), while the bottom face and the mantle are free, \(\vek t = \vek 0\), which agrees with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(L) = 0\) and with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) on the mantle. The integrands are constant on each face, so we compute the integrals with the cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and the volume \(AL\), which we computed with the cut of the bar into three pieces in sections 4.2.8 and 4.2.9. The force on the surface is \((-\rho g L A, 0, 0)\), a force of \(60{,}10\) N up, and the body force is \((\rho g A L, 0, 0)\), the weight of \(60{,}10\) N down. The sum is the zero vector, as (4.19) requires. The divergence theorem for a body cut into pieces (corollary 4.28) tells us that the test is no accident. With it corollary 4.29 holds, with the same proof, also for a part of a body that is cut into pieces between graphs, if in step 2 we use the linearity of lemma 4.22, and in step 3 corollary 4.28 in place of theorem 4.14. So it holds for round parts of the bar in its interior, which are not made of boxes. It holds also for the whole bar, although the points of its surface are not interior points. At the points of the surface step 4 needs only Cauchy's formula, which holds on the surface of the bar by the requirement of SADD. The equilibrium equations, which step 1 needs, hold at all points of the bar for the polynomial stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\).

SADD takes this road in the opposite direction. From the equilibrium of every part of the body it obtains, with the divergence theorem, that the integral of the left side of the equilibrium equations is zero over every part, and concludes from this that the integrand is zero at every point (SADD (3.7.3) and (3.7.4) with (1.8.12), PDF pp. 28-29 and 78). We will need a similar conclusion in the next sections: a continuous function is zero if every integral of it of a certain kind is zero.

With this we have what we need for a body in space: the integral over a body and over its surface, and the theorem that connects them. The next section writes equilibrium in a new form, which does not speak about the forces on individual pieces, but about the work of the forces in small displacements that the supports allow, first for a rigid body, then for a bar and a truss. For a body in space we will derive this form in section 4.4, and there the divergence theorem will play the role that integration by parts plays for the bar.

4.3 Virtual displacements of a bar

So far we have always written equilibrium with forces. For a whole body these are the conditions that the resultant of the forces is the zero vector and that the sum of the moments is the zero vector (equations (2.2) and (2.35)), and for every small box in the body the equilibrium equations (2.31). This is how in section 4.1 we computed the axial forces in both bars of the bracket fixed to the wall, from the equilibrium of the pin at joint \(C\). In this section we write the same equilibrium in another way, with work. The idea is simple. In our minds we move a body in equilibrium a little, but only in the way its supports allow, and we leave the forces as they are. Then we compute the work the forces would do on this imagined displacement. We will show that the body is in equilibrium exactly when this work is zero for every such displacement.

Why write equilibrium once more when we already know it? For three reasons. First, the support forces, which we often do not know, drop out, because the points held by the supports do not move. Second, for a bar we will get an equation in which an integral stands in place of the derivative of the axial force. The finite element method, which we will meet in chapters 6 and 7, rests on this form of equilibrium. Third, with a cleverly chosen imagined displacement we get one unknown force at a time, without solving a system of equations.

The goal of the section is to state this claim precisely and to prove it for three kinds of bodies, starting with the simplest. First for a rigid body, a lever on a pin, on which the idea is clearest. Then for a straight bar loaded along its axis by forces distributed over its length, as weight loads the hanging bar. There we will need integration by parts from section 3.5.8 and a new lemma from mathematics. At the end for the bracket of two bars from section 4.1. The general body follows in the next section.

What do we assume? In section 4.1 we assumed four things for the whole chapter: a linear elastic material, small displacements, slow loading and loads that keep their direction. The principle we are going to derive needs less, so we list the assumptions separately.

  1. The displacements are small. We therefore write equilibrium on the shape of the body before loading, as in chapter 2.
  2. The supports are ideal, without friction. An ideal support acts only in the directions in which it prevents motion, so its force does no work in a displacement the support allows. A support with friction would act also in the direction in which it allows sliding, its force would do work and would stay in the equations (EP §3.4.1, p. 128, GR §1.1.2, PDF p. 34).
  3. We assume nothing about the material. We will use only equilibrium, not the relation between stress and strain. The principle therefore holds for steel, rubber or any other material. We will need a linear elastic material only at the end of the section, when we compute the displacement of the joint from the changes of the lengths of the bars.

We do not need slow loading, because we will not load the body, we will test its equilibrium position.

4.3.1 The lever

We start with a body whose equilibrium we already know how to write. A rigid lever (vzvod) lies horizontally on a support and can turn about a pin (zatič) at the point \(O\) (figure 4.26). The pin is frictionless. We lay the axis \(x\) along the lever to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up and the axis \(z\) toward the viewer, so that the coordinate system is right-handed (definition 2.28), with the origin at \(O\). We measure lengths in centimetres, so that the coordinates are whole numbers. The left end of the lever is \(A = (-40, 0, 0)\), the right end \(B = (120, 0, 0)\). At the left end a load with a weight of 300 N acts, so the force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}} = (0, -300, 0)\) N. We push the right end down with the force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}} = (0, -P, 0)\) N, where \(P\) is the number we are looking for. The pin acts on the lever at the point \(O\) with a force \(\vek R\) that we do not know. We neglect the weight of the lever. That the lever is rigid is an idealization. A steel lever bends a little under the load, but its points move by much less than its lengths, so the moments of the forces hardly change (assumption 1).

How large must \(P\) be for the lever to be in equilibrium? As in section 2.8.3 we write the sum of the moments about \(O\). The force \(\vek R\) acts at \(O\), the vector from \(O\) to \(O\) is the zero vector, so its moment is zero. By (2.32) the moments of the other two forces are

\[\begin{aligned} (-40, 0, 0)\times(0, -300, 0) &= (0, 0, 12\,000)\ \text{N cm} , \\ (120, 0, 0)\times(0, -P, 0) &= (0, 0, -120\,P)\ \text{N cm} . \end{aligned}\]

The sum of the moments \((0, 0, 12\,000 - 120\,P)\) N cm is the zero vector for \(P = 100\). From the equilibrium of the forces, \(\vek R + \vek F_{\mathrm{A}} + \vek F_{\mathrm{B}} = \vek 0\), we then get \(\vek R = (0, 400, 0)\) N. The pin carries the load and the push.

Now we approach the same question with work. Imagine that we turn the lever about the pin a little and leave the forces as they are.

We will denote imagined displacements and the quantities that describe them by the letter \(\delta\) in front of the symbol of the quantity: \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{A}}\) will be the imagined displacement of the point \(A\). The notation \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{A}}\) is a single name of a new quantity, not the product of a number \(\delta\) and a vector \(\vek u_{\mathrm{A}}\). The letter \(\delta\) alone, without a symbol after it, has another meaning in the book. In the definition of the limit 1.5 and of continuity 1.56 it is a positive number that bounds how far the argument is from the chosen point. The notation \(\delta\) for imagined displacements is used by EP (§3.4.1, pp. 126-128) and GR (§1.1.1, PDF pp. 32-33).

The pin allows only turning about the axis \(z\) through \(O\). How do the points of the lever move then? Let the point at a distance of 1 cm from \(O\) move perpendicular to the lever by \(\delta\varphi\) centimetres. The number \(\delta\varphi\) is a ratio of two lengths, a number without a unit, like the ratio \(s/h\) for the sheared cube in section 1.6.2. The point at a distance of 40 cm moves 40 times as much, the point at 120 cm 120 times as much. For positive \(\delta\varphi\) the lever turns counterclockwise, seen from the tip of the axis \(z\): the right end goes up, the left end down. These displacements come from the vector product. Let \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = (0, 0, \delta\varphi)\) be a vector in the direction of the axis of turning. For a point \(\vek r = (x, 0, 0)\) on the lever, by (2.32)

\[\begin{aligned} \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r &= (0, 0, \delta\varphi)\times(x, 0, 0) \\ &= (0 \cdot 0 - \delta\varphi \cdot 0,\ \ \delta\varphi\,x - 0 \cdot 0,\ \ 0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot x) = (0,\ x\,\delta\varphi,\ 0) . \end{aligned}\]

The ends therefore move by \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{A}} = (0, -40\,\delta\varphi, 0)\) cm and \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{B}} = (0, 120\,\delta\varphi, 0)\) cm, and the point \(O\) does not move (figure 4.26). The work the forces would do on these displacements we compute as if they were constant, with the scalar product of force and displacement:

  1. Load: \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{A}} = (-300)(-40\,\delta\varphi) = 12\,000\,\delta\varphi\) N cm. The load moves down, in the direction of its force, so the work is positive.
  2. Push: \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{B}} = (-P)(120\,\delta\varphi) = -120\,P\,\delta\varphi\) N cm. The end \(B\) moves up, against the force, so the work is negative.
  3. Pin: \(\vek R\cdot\vek 0 = 0\), because \(O\) does not move.
  4. The sum is \((12\,000 - 120\,P)\,\delta\varphi\) N cm. It is zero for every \(\delta\varphi\) exactly when \(P = 100\).

We got the same equation as from the moments, and the force of the pin did not enter the computation at all. The meaning is plain. When the lever turns, the push moves three times as far as the load, 120 against 40. For the two parts of the work to cancel, the push must be three times smaller than the load. This is the law of the lever we know from school, told with work. The number \(12\,000 - 120\,P\) is moreover exactly the \(z\) component of the sum of the moments. This is no coincidence, and we will show it in general.

Is the displacement \((0, x\,\delta\varphi, 0)\) really a turn? In a true turn the point \(B\) would move along a circle about \(O\), while our displacement moves it along the tangent, to the point \((120, 120\,\delta\varphi, 0)\). Its distance from \(O\) is then \(120\sqrt{1 + \delta\varphi^2}\) cm, a little more than 120 cm. For \(\delta\varphi = 0{,}001\) the point \(B\) moves by \(0{,}12\) cm, while the distance grows by \(6 \cdot 10^{-5}\) cm, 2000 times less. This is the same effect as with the vertical edge \(AD\) of the sheared cube, which only leaned and became longer by a term with the square of the shift. Our imagined displacement therefore keeps the distances only up to terms with the square of the number \(\delta\varphi\). This is why we think of imagined displacements as small: they must respect rigidity and the supports at least to first order.

4.3.2 Virtual displacement and virtual work

Three things mattered for the lever. The displacement was imagined, the forces did not cause it. Only a displacement allowed by the pin and by the rigidity of the lever was permitted. During the displacement the forces stayed as they are in equilibrium. Conditions that restrict how the points of a body can move are called constraints (vezi) (GR §1.2.2, PDF p. 36). The pin is a constraint that holds the point \(O\) in place. Rigidity is a constraint that keeps the distances between the points of the lever. Now we state all this precisely.

Definition 4.30 Virtual displacement (virtualni pomik)

Let given forces act on a body in a given position. A virtual displacement (virtualni pomik) of the body is an imagined displacement of its points that its supports and other constraints allow, that is, all the conditions that restrict how its points can move. A virtual displacement must satisfy the conditions of the constraints exactly or at least up to terms with the squares of the virtual displacement. During a virtual displacement all forces on the body stay as they are in the given position.

Source: EP §3.4.1 (pp. 126-128), EP §4.2.1 (p. 167), GR §1.1-1.2 (PDF pp. 32-36). EP takes the virtual displacement from the equilibrium position. The book also uses it in converse statements, in which equilibrium is only being checked, so it defines it for every given position.

Definition 4.31 Virtual work (virtualno delo)

Let a force \(\vek F\) act at a point of a body that has the virtual displacement \(\delta\vek u\). The virtual work (virtualno delo) of the force \(\vek F\) is the number \(\vek F\cdot\delta\vek u\). The virtual work of several forces is the sum of the virtual works of the individual forces.

Source: EP §3.4.1 (p. 127), EP (4.2.1) (p. 167), GR (1.5) (PDF p. 33).

Virtual work is therefore the work a constant force would do on a straight displacement (definition 4.1), except that the displacement is not real. Why do we not change the forces during a virtual displacement? Because with a virtual displacement we test the equilibrium position. We ask whether the forces acting in this position are in equilibrium, and so we compute with exactly these forces (EP, p. 126). A virtual displacement has nothing to do with the real displacement that would occur if we changed the loading (EP, p. 126). Virtual work is proportional to the virtual displacement: if we double the displacement, the work doubles as well. Whether the virtual work is zero therefore does not depend on the size of the displacement. Smallness matters only because of the constraints, which, as we saw with the lever, a virtual displacement keeps only to first order.

Quantities determined by a virtual displacement are called virtual quantities. We denote them by the letter \(\delta\) in front of the symbol, as for the lever: \(\delta\vek u\) is the virtual displacement of a point, \(\delta u(x)\) the virtual displacement of the point of a bar at the place \(x\), \(\delta e\) the virtual elongation (virtualni podaljšek) of a bar.

4.3.3 The rigid body

Which virtual displacements are available to a free rigid body, held by no support? Its only constraint is rigidity: the distance between no two points may change (definition 1.10). For the lever the role was played by a turn about the axis \(z\). In general a small displacement of a rigid body has two parts (figure 4.27). The first part is a displacement of all points by the same vector \(\delta\vek a\). The second part is a small turn about an axis through a chosen point \(O\), which we describe by a vector \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\) in the direction of the axis. The point \(P\) with the vector \(\vek r = \overrightarrow{OP}\) moves in the turn by \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r\). By item 4 of lemma 2.30 on the properties of the vector product this displacement is perpendicular to the axis and to \(\vek r\). How long is it? Let \(\vek e = \delta\boldsymbol\varphi/|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|\) be the unit vector in the direction of the axis. By item 1 of lemma 2.32 on the lever arm and the magnitude of the moment, applied to the line through \(O\) in the direction \(\vek e\) and to the point \(P\), the distance of the point \(P\) from the axis of the turn is \(\ell = \sqrt{|\vek r|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2}\). In the lemma the vector from the point to the line appears, here \(-\vek r\), which gives the same squares. By item 5 of the lemma on the properties of the vector product, and because \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|\,\vek e\), we have \(|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r|^2 = |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\,|\vek r|^2 - (\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\cdot\vek r)^2 = |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\,\big(|\vek r|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2\big) = |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\,\ell^2\). The point therefore moves by \(|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|\) times its distance from the axis. The number \(|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|\) is a ratio of lengths, like \(\delta\varphi\) for the lever. For the lever \(\delta\vek a = \vek 0\), because the pin holds the point \(O\).

For the lever we saw that such a displacement keeps the distances only approximately. The next lemma says how closely.

Lemma 4.32 Small rigid displacement (majhen togi premik)

Let \(O\) be a point and let \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\) be vectors. Let every point \(P\) of a body move by

\[\delta\vek u(P) = \delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\overrightarrow{OP} .\]

Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be points of the body with the distance \(L = |\overrightarrow{PQ}| > 0\) before the displacement and the distance \(L_1\) after it. Then

\[L \le L_1 \le L\,\big(1 + \tfrac12\,|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\big) .\]
Proof

We must show that the distance does not decrease in the displacement and that it grows by at most \(\tfrac12 L\,|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\). We compute the square of the new distance.

  1. Let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{PQ}\). The points after the displacement are \(P + \delta\vek u(P)\) and \(Q + \delta\vek u(Q)\), and the vector between them is \(\vek d + \delta\vek u(Q) - \delta\vek u(P)\), because coordinates are subtracted component by component ((1.8)).
  2. The vector \(\delta\vek a\) cancels in the difference \(\delta\vek u(Q) - \delta\vek u(P)\). By item 2 of lemma 2.30 on the properties of the vector product, \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\overrightarrow{OQ} - \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\overrightarrow{OP} = \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times(\overrightarrow{OQ} - \overrightarrow{OP}) = \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d\), because \(\overrightarrow{OQ} - \overrightarrow{OP} = \overrightarrow{PQ}\). The vector between the points after the displacement is therefore \(\vek d + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d\).
  3. By the formula for the square of the length of a sum (lemma 2.9)
    \[L_1^2 = |\vek d + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d|^2 = |\vek d|^2 + 2\,\vek d\cdot(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d) + |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d|^2 .\]
  4. By item 4 of the lemma on the properties of the vector product, the vector product is perpendicular to its second factor, \(\vek d\cdot(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d) = 0\). Hence \(L_1^2 = L^2 + |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d|^2\).
  5. By item 5 of the same lemma, \(|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek d|^2 = |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\,L^2 - (\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\cdot\vek d)^2\), which lies between \(0\) and \(|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\,L^2\). Hence \(L^2 \le L_1^2 \le L^2\,(1 + |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2)\).
  6. The expanded square \(\big(1 + \tfrac12\,|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\big)^2 = 1 + |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2 + \tfrac14\,|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^4\) is not smaller than \(1 + |\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\). Hence \(L^2 \le L_1^2 \le \big(L\,(1 + \tfrac12\,|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2)\big)^2\).
  7. The numbers \(L\), \(L_1\) and \(L\,(1 + \tfrac12\,|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2)\) are nonnegative. By lemma 1.26, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, the inequalities between the squares carry over to the numbers themselves.

Source: CM, PDF p. 143, shows that the displacement \(\delta\vek u = \boldsymbol\omega\times\delta\vek x\) is a small rigid turn, and SADD (2.2.10) (PDF p. 45) writes the displacement \(\delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r\) in components as the most general small rigid displacement. The bound and its proof are not from the sources.

The lemma says that the distance between two points changes by at most \(\tfrac12 L\,|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi|^2\), a term with the square of a small number. For the lever, with \(L = 160\) cm from \(A\) to \(B\) and \(\delta\varphi = 0{,}001\), this is at most \(8 \cdot 10^{-5}\) cm, while \(B\) moves by \(0{,}12\) cm. A displacement of the form \(\delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r\) therefore respects rigidity to first order and is, by definition 4.30, a virtual displacement of a free rigid body. The converse also holds, if we read "to first order" as saying that the displacement has a zero small strain tensor at every point of the body, that is, that no short fibre gets longer by a first-order term (SADD (2.2.10), PDF p. 45). For a body in one piece, whose interior points form a connected open set (definition 1.126), and a continuously differentiable displacement, such a displacement is at the interior points of the body, by theorem 1.130 on a displacement field without strain, of the form \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) with a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\). By (2.32), \(\mat W\,\vek r = \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r\) for \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = (W_{\mathrm{zy}}, W_{\mathrm{xz}}, W_{\mathrm{yx}})\), because \(W_{\mathrm{ij}} = -W_{\mathrm{ji}}\) and the diagonal entries of the matrix \(\mat W\) are zero (lemma 1.101, item 3).

Now let us show why the virtual work for the lever was the moment of the forces times \(\delta\varphi\).

Theorem 4.33 Principle of virtual displacements for a rigid body (načelo virtualnih pomikov za togo telo)

Let the forces \(\vek F_1, \dots, \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) act on a rigid body at the points \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\), the forces of the supports among them. Let \(O\) be a point and \(\vek r_{\mathrm{i}} = \overrightarrow{OA_{\mathrm{i}}}\). For arbitrary vectors \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\) let the point \(A_{\mathrm{i}}\) move by \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = \delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r_{\mathrm{i}}\). Then the virtual work of the forces is

\[\begin{aligned} \vek F_1\cdot\delta\vek u_1 + \dots + \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{k}} &= \delta\vek a\cdot(\vek F_1 + \dots + \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}) \\ &\quad + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\cdot(\vek r_1\times\vek F_1 + \dots + \vek r_{\mathrm{k}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}) . \end{aligned} \tag{4.20}\]

The body is in equilibrium exactly when the virtual work of the forces is zero for all vectors \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\).

Proof

We first rearrange the virtual work of each force separately, then we check both directions of the claim about equilibrium.

  1. By item 2 of lemma 2.12 on the properties of the scalar product, \(\vek F_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\delta\vek a + \vek F_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r_{\mathrm{i}})\).
  2. The second term is a scalar triple product. By definition 2.48 it is the determinant of the matrix with the columns \(\vek F_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\) and \(\vek r_{\mathrm{i}}\), and by the cyclic exchange of the columns (lemma 2.49 on the properties of the determinant, item 1)
    \[\vek F_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r_{\mathrm{i}}) = \det(\vek F_{\mathrm{i}}, \delta\boldsymbol\varphi, \vek r_{\mathrm{i}}) = \det(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi, \vek r_{\mathrm{i}}, \vek F_{\mathrm{i}}) = \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\cdot(\vek r_{\mathrm{i}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{i}}) .\]
  3. We sum over \(i\) from \(1\) to \(k\). By the symmetry and the distributivity of the scalar product (the lemma on the properties of the scalar product, items 1 and 2) we get (4.20).
  4. Let the body be in equilibrium. By definition 2.3 and by equation (2.35) the resultant \(\vek F_1 + \dots + \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the sum of the moments about \(O\) are zero vectors. If the moment condition was written about some other point, the sum of the moments about \(O\) equals the sum about that point, so it is the zero vector. This is what lemma 2.33 says, that the moment does not depend on the point, and we may use it because the resultant is zero. Both terms on the right side of (4.20) are therefore zero for all \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\).
  5. Conversely, let the virtual work be zero for all \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\). For \(\delta\vek a = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = \vek 0\) the right side of (4.20) is the \(x\) component of the resultant, which is therefore zero. In the same way, with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), the other two components are zero. The resultant is the zero vector.
  6. With \(\delta\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) we get in the same way that the sum of the moments about \(O\) is the zero vector. By definition 2.3 and equation (2.35) the body is in equilibrium.

Source: EP §4.2.1 (pp. 167-168) for forces acting at one point and with the displacement \(\delta\vek u\) only, GR §1.2.1 (PDF pp. 35-36) for a system of particles. The form with \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\) is not from the sources.

The proof showed where the connection between work and moments comes from. The displacement \(\delta\vek a\) multiplies the resultant of the forces, the turn \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\) the sum of the moments. Because the vectors \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\) are arbitrary, zero virtual work means six equations, three for the forces and three for the moments, which is exactly equilibrium.

And a body held by supports? For the lever the pin does not allow all \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\), only \(\delta\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = (0, 0, \delta\varphi)\). The force of the pin acts at a point that does not move, so its virtual work is zero, and only the load and the push remain in the equation. The right side of (4.20) is then \(\delta\varphi\) times the \(z\) component of the sum of the moments, and zero virtual work gives exactly the equation \(12\,000 - 120\,P = 0\), in which the force of the pin does not appear. In general: when a body is held by ideal supports, the virtual work of the forces other than the support forces is zero for every virtual displacement the supports allow exactly when those equilibrium equations hold in which the support forces do not appear (GR §1.2.1, PDF pp. 35-36). The support forces then follow from the remaining equations.

A support force can also be found with virtual work. We remove the support in our minds and keep its force as a known force on the body. Then we move the body exactly in the direction the support prevented. For the lever, let us move the whole lever vertically by \(\delta\vek a = (0, \delta v, 0)\), with \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = \vek 0\). The virtual work of all three forces is

\[(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}} + \vek F_{\mathrm{B}} + \vek R)\cdot\delta\vek a = (-300 - 100 + R_{\mathrm{y}})\,\delta v ,\]

and because it must be zero for every \(\delta v\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}} = 400\) N. Such a displacement picks out a single unknown force. On this idea rests the unit dummy-displacement method (metoda enotskega virtualnega pomika). In a structure that can deform, we choose a virtual displacement that is a unit vector in the direction of the sought force at the point where we look for the force, and zero at the other points where forces act. For the rigid lever we moved the whole lever, so the known forces \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}}\) also stayed in the equation. The word dummy is an old word for virtual (EP §4.2.3, p. 172). We will use it for the bracket at the end of the section.

4.3.4 A bar under a distributed load

For the rigid body a virtual displacement was described by six numbers, the components of the vectors \(\delta\vek a\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi\). A bar, however, can stretch, and every piece of it can move differently. A virtual displacement of a bar will therefore be a function. First we set up the model precisely.

A straight bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = L\) and is fixed at the end \(x = 0\), so that this end does not move, \(u(0) = 0\). All forces act along the axis of the bar, so the bar only stretches or shortens, and the internal force in every cross section is the axial force \(N(x)\) (definition 2.5). As in chapter 1 we describe the bar by the displacement \(u(x)\): the whole cross section at the place \(x\) moves along the axis by \(u(x)\). The thinning of the bar, which the field of section 1.7.1 describes, is left out of this model. At the free end \(x = L\) a force \(F\) acts in the direction of the axis \(x\), positive when it pulls toward increasing \(x\). Along the length of the bar forces are distributed that act on every piece of it, like weight in the hanging bar (figure 4.28). We describe them by the force per unit length.

Definition 4.34 Distributed axial load (porazdeljena osna obtežba)

Let a bar lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\). A distributed axial load (porazdeljena osna obtežba) is a continuous function \(q\) on the interval \([0, L]\) whose input is the place \(x\) on the bar and whose output is the force per unit length of the bar in the direction of the axis \(x\) at that place. The force in the direction of the axis \(x\) on the part of the bar between the cross sections \(x_1 < x_2\) is

\[\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

Source: ONATE1 §2.2 (PDF pp. 66-67), where it is written \(t_{\mathrm{x}}\), EP example 3.5.3 (p. 148), where it is written \(f\).

Why is the force on a part of the bar an integral? The function \(q\) gives the force per unit length at every place. On a short piece \([t_{\mathrm{i}-1}, t_{\mathrm{i}}]\) a force therefore acts that lies between \(m_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \(m_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{i}}\) are the smallest and the largest value of the function \(q\) on the piece. The forces of the pieces add up, so the force on a part of the bar lies between the lower and the upper sum of the function \(q\) for every partition, and by lemma 3.34, item 2, it is the integral. The same reasoning gave us in section 3.5.6 the weight of the part of the hanging bar below a cross section. For the hanging bar \(q(x) = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m at every place. Why do we require continuity? So that the integral exists (theorem 3.37) and so that we may use the fundamental theorem of calculus. A force acting at a single place inside the bar, for example the weight at the middle of the hanging bar from section 1.12.2, is not of this form. There the axial force jumps, and such loads are excluded in this section.

From the equilibrium of the parts of the bar we now get the axial force, as we got it for the hanging bar in section 2.1.

Lemma 4.35 Equilibrium of an axially loaded bar (ravnovesje palice pod osno obtežbo)

Let a bar lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\). Let a distributed axial load \(q\) act on it, and at the end \(x = L\) a force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(x\). Let every part of the bar between the cross section \(x\) and the end \(L\) be in equilibrium. Then the axial force in the cross section \(x\) is

\[N(x) = F + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{4.21}\]

where for \(x = L\) the integral is zero. The function \(N\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, L)\), and

\[N'(x) + q(x) = 0 \quad \text{for every } x \in (0, L) , \qquad N(L) = F . \tag{4.22}\]
Proof

We first get \(N(x)\) from the equilibrium of a part of the bar, then the derivative from the fundamental theorem of calculus.

  1. Let \(0 \le x < L\). Three forces along the axis \(x\) act on the part of the bar from the cross section \(x\) to the end \(L\). By definition 2.5, \(N(x)\) is the \(x\) component of the force with which the part on the side of larger \(x\) acts on the part on the side of smaller \(x\). By the law of action and reaction (section 2.1) the left part acts on our right part with the opposite force, whose \(x\) component is \(-N(x)\). The distributed load acts on it, by definition 4.34, with the force \(\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), and the end with the force \(F\).
  2. All forces point along the axis \(x\), so the equilibrium of forces (2.2) is a single equation for the \(x\) components: \(-N(x) + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t + F = 0\). This gives (4.21).
  3. At \(x = L\) no part of the bar is left, only the end cross section. The force across it is the force at the end, \(N(L) = F\), which is (4.21) with the integral zero.
  4. Let \(G(x) = \int_0^x q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for \(x \in [0, L]\), with \(G(0) = 0\) by the convention of definition 3.33. For \(0 < x < L\), by additivity (lemma 3.38 on the properties of the integral, item 2), \(\int_0^L q = G(x) + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q\), so \(N(x) = F + G(L) - G(x)\). The same equality holds at \(x = 0\), where \(G(0) = 0\), and at \(x = L\), where it gives \(N(L) = F\).
  5. The function \(q\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, item 2, the function \(G\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, L)\), and \(G'(x) = q(x)\).
  6. The number \(F + G(L)\) is constant. By step 4, \(N\) is therefore continuous on \([0, L]\), and by the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.79, items 1, 2 and 4) \(N\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, L)\) with the derivative \(N'(x) = 0 - G'(x) = -q(x)\). This is the first equation of (4.22), the second is step 3.

Source: EP example 3.5.3, equations (4) and (5) (pp. 148-149), derived from minimum energy for a linear elastic bar that also has a spring at its end, ONATE1 §2.2 (PDF pp. 66-67). The proof from the equilibrium of parts is not from the sources.

Let us test the lemma on the hanging bar. There \(q = \rho g A\) and \(F = 0\), because the lower end is free. By (4.21) \(N(x) = \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L \rho g A\,\mathrm{d}t = \rho g A\,(L - x)\), which is (2.3), and \(N'(x) = -\rho g A = -q(x)\). The equation \(N' + q = 0\) says that the axial force drops over every metre of the bar by exactly the load on that metre. It is the equation \(\sigma' + \rho g = 0\) from section 2.7.1, multiplied by the cross-section area \(A\).

4.3.5 The principle for a bar

What does a virtual displacement of a bar look like? The fixed end must not move, this is the constraint the support imposes, so \(\delta u(0) = 0\). There are no other constraints. The bar is not rigid, so every piece of it may stretch, and \(\delta u\) may be an almost arbitrary function of the place \(x\). We will require only that it is differentiable and that its derivative is continuous. Physically this means that there are no cracks in the bar, since at a crack the displacement would change abruptly, and that the stretching changes from piece to piece without jumps. Mathematically we need it for the integrals and for the fundamental theorem of calculus.

How large is the virtual work of the external forces? On a short piece \([x, x + \Delta x]\) the load acts with a force of about \(q(x)\,\Delta x\), and the piece moves by about \(\delta u(x)\). The virtual work is about \(q(x)\,\delta u(x)\,\Delta x\), and by the same reasoning as above the sum over the pieces approaches an integral. The force at the end contributes \(F\,\delta u(L)\), the support nothing, because \(\delta u(0) = 0\). The virtual work of the external forces is therefore

\[\int_0^L q(x)\,\delta u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L) .\]

For a rigid body in equilibrium the virtual work was zero. For a bar it is not. Take the hanging bar and the virtual displacement \(\delta u(x) = c\,x\), in which every piece stretches by the same fraction \(c\). The virtual work of the weight is \(\int_0^L \rho g A\,c\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = c\,\rho g A\,L^2/2\), which is not zero for \(c \neq 0\), although the bar is in equilibrium. Where is the difference? In a bar the internal forces also do work when the pieces stretch.

Look at one piece of the bar between the cross sections \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) (figure 4.29). The left part of the bar acts on it with the force \(-N(x_1)\), the right part with the force \(N(x_2)\), and the load acts on it, and all these forces are in equilibrium.
