In the virtual displacement the left face of the piece moves by \(\delta u(x_1)\), the right one by \(\delta u(x_2)\). We split the displacement into two parts. First the whole piece moves by \(\delta u(x_1)\), as a rigid body. In this part the virtual work of the forces on the piece is the resultant of the forces times \(\delta u(x_1)\), and this is zero, because the piece is in equilibrium, just as for the rigid body. Then the piece stretches: the right face moves by a further \(\delta u(x_2) - \delta u(x_1)\). In this part the work is done mainly by the force \(N(x_2)\) on the right face, \(N(x_2)\,(\delta u(x_2) - \delta u(x_1))\). The load adds a part that is negligible for a short piece, because it is proportional to the product of the length of the piece and its stretching. For a short piece of length \(\Delta x\) the stretching is about \(\delta u'(x)\,\Delta x\), so the virtual work of all forces on the piece is about \(N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\,\Delta x\). The number \(\delta u'(x)\) is the virtual strain (virtualna deformacija) close to the place \(x\), the virtual stretching per unit length. Now we add up the virtual works of all the pieces. At every inner cross section, equal and opposite forces act on the two neighbouring pieces, and the faces of both pieces move by the same \(\delta u\), so their parts of the work cancel. Nothing remains of the internal forces, and the sum is the virtual work of the external forces. On the other side are the sums of \(N\,\delta u'\,\Delta x\), which approach an integral. We therefore expect

\[\int_0^L N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q(x)\,\delta u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L) .\]

Books call the left side the internal virtual work (notranje virtualno delo) and the right side the external virtual work (zunanje virtualno delo) (EP §3.4.1, p. 128, ONATE1 (2.4), PDF p. 67). The internal virtual work has the same form as the work of the stresses on a small box in section 3.6.2. There the stress was multiplied by the change of the strain, here the axial force is multiplied by the virtual strain. The reasoning with pieces was only approximate. Now we prove the equality exactly.

Theorem 4.36 Principle of virtual displacements for a bar (načelo virtualnih pomikov za palico)

Let a bar lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and be fixed at \(x = 0\). Let a distributed axial load \(q\), continuous on \([0, L]\), act on it, and at the end \(x = L\) a force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(x\). Let the function \(N\) be continuous on \([0, L]\), differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, L)\), and satisfy \(N'(x) + q(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in (0, L)\) and \(N(L) = F\). Let a virtual displacement of the bar be any function \(\delta u\) that is differentiable at every point of some open interval containing \([0, L]\), has a derivative \(\delta u'\) continuous on \([0, L]\), and satisfies \(\delta u(0) = 0\). Then for every virtual displacement of the bar

\[\int_0^L N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q(x)\,\delta u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L) . \tag{4.23}\]
Proof

We must show that the two integrals differ by exactly \(F\,\delta u(L)\). The proof is an integration by parts. We cannot use corollary 3.40 on integration by parts literally, because it requires the derivative of the function \(N\) also at the end points of the interval, so we repeat its proof with item 1 of the fundamental theorem of calculus.

  1. Let \(G(x) = N(x)\,\delta u(x)\) for \(x \in [0, L]\). The function \(\delta u\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \([0, L]\), so it is continuous there (lemma 1.77). The function \(N\) is continuous by assumption. Hence \(G\) is continuous on \([0, L]\) as a product of continuous functions (corollary 1.62).
  2. Let \(0 < x < L\). The functions \(N\) and \(\delta u\) are differentiable at \(x\). By the product rule (lemma 1.79, item 3) and by the assumption \(N'(x) = -q(x)\),
    \[G'(x) = N'(x)\,\delta u(x) + N(x)\,\delta u'(x) = -q(x)\,\delta u(x) + N(x)\,\delta u'(x) .\]
  3. The function \(f(x) = -q(x)\,\delta u(x) + N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), because \(q\), \(\delta u\), \(N\) and \(\delta u'\) are continuous there, and sums and products of continuous functions are continuous (corollary 1.62). By step 2, \(G'(x) = f(x)\) for every \(x \in (0, L)\).
  4. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, item 1, with the functions \(G\) and \(f\),
    \[\int_0^L \big(-q(x)\,\delta u(x) + N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\big)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(L) - G(0) = N(L)\,\delta u(L) - N(0)\,\delta u(0) .\]
  5. Because \(\delta u(0) = 0\) and \(N(L) = F\), the right side is \(F\,\delta u(L)\).
  6. By linearity (lemma 3.38 on the properties of the integral, item 1) the left side is \(\int_0^L N\,\delta u' - \int_0^L q\,\delta u\). We add \(\int_0^L q\,\delta u\) to both sides and get (4.23).

Source: EP §3.4.1, example 3.4.2 (pp. 129-131) for a cantilever beam with an axial load, ONATE1 (2.3), (2.4) (PDF p. 67), EP example 3.5.3 (p. 148), where the integration by parts is done in the opposite direction.

What did the proof show? Equation (4.23) is the equilibrium of the bar, multiplied by the virtual displacement and integrated over the length of the bar. Integration by parts moved the derivative from the axial force to the virtual displacement. In doing so two terms at the end points appeared. The term at the fixed end dropped out, because \(\delta u(0) = 0\), and the term at the free end gave \(F\,\delta u(L)\), because \(N(L) = F\). This is the exact form of the reasoning with pieces. The end-point term is the virtual work of the forces acting at the ends, while the internal forces between the pieces cancelled.

Three things are worth remembering. First, the theorem holds for every material, since we used only the equilibrium (4.22). Second, the force of the support at \(x = 0\) does not appear in the equation, because \(\delta u(0) = 0\), just as the force of the pin for the lever. Third, the axial force in the equation is not differentiated, only multiplied by \(\delta u'\). For a linear elastic bar with Young's modulus \(E\) the axial force is \(N = A\,\sigma = E A\,u'\), because the stress is \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\) ((3.1)) and the strain \(\varepsilon = u'\) (definition 1.9). The equation then reads

\[\begin{aligned} \int_0^L E A\,u'(x)\,\delta u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &= \int_0^L q(x)\,\delta u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L) \\ &\quad \text{for every virtual displacement of the bar } \delta u , \end{aligned}\]

and only the displacement \(u\) with its first derivative appears in it. The finite element method for bars builds on this form (ONATE1 (2.4), PDF p. 67), and we will meet it in chapter 7.

The equality we checked at the end of section 3.5.8 is exactly this theorem. There we computed for the hanging bar that \(\int_0^L N\,u'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\int_0^L \rho g A\,u\,\mathrm{d}x\) are both \(7{,}821 \cdot 10^{-4}\) J. This is equation (4.23) with \(q = \rho g A\), \(F = 0\) and the real displacement \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) in the role of the virtual displacement. The real displacement is also a virtual displacement of the bar, since it is a polynomial and satisfies \(u(0) = 0\).

4.3.6 Mathematics: the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations

Does the converse hold? If some axial force \(N\) satisfies equation (4.23) for every virtual displacement of the bar, is the bar then in equilibrium, that is, do \(N' + q = 0\) and \(N(L) = F\) hold? Only a yes tells us that the equation with virtual work fully replaces equilibrium. The idea is this. We do the integration by parts in the opposite direction and get \(\int_0^L (N' + q)\,\delta u\,\mathrm{d}x + (F - N(L))\,\delta u(L) = 0\) for every virtual displacement. If the function \(N' + q\) were positive somewhere, we would choose a virtual displacement that is nonzero and positive only there, and the integral would be positive. For this we need a lemma that books name after the calculus of variations (variacijski račun), the branch of mathematics that looks for the functions for which some integral is smallest (EP §3.5, pp. 134 and 142).

Lemma 4.37 Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (osnovna lema variacijskega računa)

Let \(g\) be a function continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\), and let

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g(x)\,\psi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\]

for every function \(\psi\) that is differentiable at every point of some open interval containing \([a, b]\), has a derivative continuous on \([a, b]\), and satisfies \(\psi(a) = \psi(b) = 0\). Then \(g(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\).

Proof

The proof is by contradiction. If \(g\) were positive at some point, it would be positive on a small interval around it because of continuity, and with a function \(\psi\) that is positive only there the integral would be positive.

  1. Suppose that \(g(c) \neq 0\) for some \(c \in [a, b]\). If \(g(c) < 0\), we take \(-g\) instead of \(g\). This function is continuous, it satisfies the same assumption, because \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (-g)\,\psi = -\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g\,\psi = 0\) by linearity (lemma 3.38 on the properties of the integral, item 1), and it is positive at \(c\). We may therefore assume \(g(c) > 0\).
  2. The function \(g\) is continuous at \(c\). By definition 1.56 with \(\eta = g(c)/2\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(x) - g(c)| < g(c)/2\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\) with \(|x - c| < \delta\). For these \(x\), \(g(x) > g(c) - g(c)/2 = g(c)/2\).
  3. Let \(a'\) be the larger of the numbers \(a\) and \(c - \delta\), and \(b'\) the smaller of the numbers \(b\) and \(c + \delta\). Each of the numbers \(a\) and \(c - \delta\) is smaller than each of the numbers \(b\) and \(c + \delta\), because \(a < b\), \(a \le c < c + \delta\), \(c - \delta < c \le b\) and \(c - \delta < c + \delta\). Hence \(a' < b'\). We take \(\alpha = a' + (b' - a')/3\) and \(\beta = b' - (b' - a')/3\). Then \(a < \alpha < \beta < b\), and every \(x \in [\alpha, \beta]\) satisfies \(c - \delta < x < c + \delta\). By step 2, therefore, \(g(x) > g(c)/2\) for every \(x \in [\alpha, \beta]\).
  4. For every real number \(x\) let \(\psi(x) = (x - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - x)^2\) when \(\alpha \le x \le \beta\), and \(\psi(x) = 0\) otherwise (figure 4.30). The function \(\psi\) is nowhere negative. Because \(a < \alpha\) and \(\beta < b\), \(\psi(a) = \psi(b) = 0\).
  5. The function \(\psi\) is differentiable at every point \(x < \alpha\) and \(x > \beta\) with the derivative \(0\), because it is constant on an open interval around such a point. On the interval \((\alpha, \beta)\) it equals the polynomial \(p(x) = (x - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - x)^2\). The expanded squares \((x - \alpha)^2 = x^2 - 2\alpha x + \alpha^2\) and \((\beta - x)^2 = \beta^2 - 2\beta x + x^2\) have, by the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.79), the derivatives \(2\,(x - \alpha)\) and \(-2\,(\beta - x)\), so by the product rule
    \[p'(x) = 2\,(x - \alpha)\,(\beta - x)^2 - 2\,(x - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - x) = 2\,(x - \alpha)\,(\beta - x)\,(\alpha + \beta - 2x) .\]
  6. At the point \(\alpha\), \(\psi(\alpha) = 0\). For \(0 < h < \beta - \alpha\) the difference quotient is \((\psi(\alpha + h) - \psi(\alpha))/h = h^2\,(\beta - \alpha - h)^2/h = h\,(\beta - \alpha - h)^2\), and for \(h < 0\) it is \(0\), because there \(\psi(\alpha + h) = 0\). In both cases its absolute value is at most \(|h|\,(\beta - \alpha)^2\). For \(\eta > 0\) we take \(\delta\) the smaller of the numbers \(\beta - \alpha\) and \(\eta/(\beta - \alpha)^2\), and for \(0 < |h| < \delta\) the absolute value of the quotient is smaller than \(\eta\). By definitions 1.5 and 1.8, therefore, \(\psi'(\alpha) = 0\). In the same way \(\psi'(\beta) = 0\).
  7. The derivative \(\psi'\) is continuous at every point. Outside the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\) it is constantly zero on an open interval around the point. On \((\alpha, \beta)\) it equals the polynomial \(p'\), which is continuous (corollary 1.62). At the point \(\alpha\), \(p'(\alpha) = 0 = \psi'(\alpha)\). For a given \(\eta > 0\) the continuity of the polynomial \(p'\) at \(\alpha\) therefore gives \(\delta > 0\), which we take at most \(\beta - \alpha\), such that \(|\psi'(x)| = |p'(x)| < \eta\) for \(\alpha \le x < \alpha + \delta\), while to the left of \(\alpha\), \(\psi'(x) = 0\). The same at the point \(\beta\).
  8. The function \(\psi\) therefore meets all the requirements of the lemma, since it is differentiable everywhere, its derivative is continuous and \(\psi(a) = \psi(b) = 0\). By assumption \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g\,\psi = 0\).
  9. The function \(g\,\psi\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) as a product of continuous functions. By additivity (lemma 3.38, item 2), \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g\,\psi = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^\alpha g\,\psi + \int_\alpha^\beta g\,\psi + \int_\beta^b g\,\psi\). On \([a, \alpha]\) and on \([\beta, b]\), \(\psi = 0\), so the first and the third integral are zero by the bound (the same lemma, item 3, with \(m = M = 0\)).
  10. Let \(h = \beta - \alpha\). On the middle part \([\alpha + h/4, \beta - h/4]\) both \(x - \alpha\) and \(\beta - x\) are at least \(h/4\), so \(\psi(x) \ge (h/4)^4 = h^4/256\) and \(g(x)\,\psi(x) \ge g(c)\,h^4/512\). On the remaining two parts of the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\), \(g\,\psi \ge 0\). By additivity and the bound, therefore,
    \[\int_\alpha^\beta g\,\psi \ge 0 + \frac{g(c)\,h^4}{512} \cdot \frac{h}{2} + 0 = \frac{g(c)\,h^5}{1024} > 0 .\]
  11. By steps 9 and 10, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g\,\psi > 0\), which contradicts step 8. Hence \(g(c) = 0\) for every \(c \in [a, b]\).

Source: CHK lemma 8.1 (PDF p. 157), for functions \(\psi\) with a continuous second derivative, without proof. EP lemma 3.1 (pp. 140-141) states it for arbitrary continuous functions and proves it with \(\psi = g\). The proof with the function \((x - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - x)^2\) is not from the sources.

Why not simply \(\psi = g\), as EP does (figure 4.30)? Because \(\psi\) must be zero at the end points and differentiable with a continuous derivative, and \(g\) need be neither. EP allows any continuous function, which is why \(\psi = g\) works there. A virtual displacement of the bar must be zero at least at the fixed end, and its derivative appears in the internal virtual work. The bump (grbina) \((x - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - x)^2\) is zero outside a small interval where \(g\) is positive, and the squares make it join the zero function smoothly, with zero derivative, at the end points of that interval. Without the squares, with the function \((x - \alpha)(\beta - x)\), it would have a corner at \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and would not be differentiable.

4.3.7 Equilibrium from virtual work

With the fundamental lemma we can prove the converse of the principle for a bar.

Theorem 4.38 Equilibrium of a bar from virtual displacements (ravnovesje palice iz virtualnih pomikov)

Let a bar lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and be fixed at \(x = 0\). Let a distributed axial load \(q\), continuous on \([0, L]\), act on it, and at the end \(x = L\) a force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(x\). Let the function \(N\) be continuous on \([0, L]\) and differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, L)\), and let there be a function \(p\), continuous on \([0, L]\), with \(N'(x) = p(x)\) for every \(x \in (0, L)\). If equation (4.23) holds for every function \(\delta u\) that is differentiable at every point of some open interval containing \([0, L]\), has a derivative continuous on \([0, L]\), and satisfies \(\delta u(0) = 0\), then

\[N'(x) + q(x) = 0 \quad \text{for every } x \in (0, L) \qquad \text{and} \qquad N(L) = F .\]
Proof

We do the integration by parts in the opposite direction. The fundamental lemma then gives the equation inside the bar, and one chosen virtual displacement the condition at the end.

  1. Let \(\delta u\) be a virtual displacement of the bar as described in the theorem, and \(G(x) = N(x)\,\delta u(x)\) on \([0, L]\). As in steps 1 to 3 of the proof of theorem 4.36, \(G\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), at every point \(x \in (0, L)\) we have \(G'(x) = p(x)\,\delta u(x) + N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\), and this function is continuous on \([0, L]\).
  2. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, item 1, and because \(\delta u(0) = 0\),
    \[\int_0^L \big(p(x)\,\delta u(x) + N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\big)\,\mathrm{d}x = N(L)\,\delta u(L) .\]
  3. By the linearity of the integral, therefore, \(\int_0^L N\,\delta u' = N(L)\,\delta u(L) - \int_0^L p\,\delta u\). We insert this into (4.23), which holds by assumption, and move all terms to the left side:
    \[\int_0^L \big(p(x) + q(x)\big)\,\delta u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + \big(F - N(L)\big)\,\delta u(L) = 0 .\]
  4. Take a function \(\psi\) that is differentiable at every point of some open interval containing \([0, L]\), has a derivative continuous on \([0, L]\), and satisfies \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\). Such a function is a virtual displacement of the bar. For \(\delta u = \psi\) the end-point term drops out, and by step 3, \(\int_0^L (p + q)\,\psi = 0\).
  5. The function \(p + q\) is continuous on \([0, L]\). By step 4 it satisfies the assumption of the fundamental lemma 4.37 on the interval \([0, L]\), so \(p(x) + q(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in [0, L]\). For \(x \in (0, L)\), \(p(x) = N'(x)\), so \(N'(x) + q(x) = 0\).
  6. The integral in step 3 is now zero for every virtual displacement, so \((F - N(L))\,\delta u(L) = 0\) for every virtual displacement of the bar. Take \(\delta u(x) = x\). This function is a polynomial, differentiable everywhere with derivative \(1\), and \(\delta u(0) = 0\). We get \((F - N(L))\,L = 0\), and because \(L > 0\), \(N(L) = F\).

Source: EP example 3.5.3, equations (3) to (5) (pp. 148-149), for a bar with a spring at its end, EP §4.2.2 (p. 169) for a body, ONATE1 §1.7 (PDF p. 47), which states that the principle is a necessary and sufficient condition for equilibrium.

Theorems 4.36 and 4.38 together say that equation (4.23) for all virtual displacements of the bar is equivalent to the equilibrium of the bar. Two conditions came out of it. The equation \(N' + q = 0\) holds inside the bar, the condition \(N(L) = F\) at the free end. Conditions at the ends of a body that a solution must satisfy are called boundary conditions (robni pogoji). The condition at the fixed end, \(u(0) = 0\), does not appear in the equation, it is built into the choice of the virtual displacements, which must be zero there. EP calls the first kind of boundary conditions, which prescribe a displacement, essential or geometric boundary conditions (bistveni ali geometrijski robni pogoji), and the second kind, which prescribe a force and which the equation itself delivers, natural or force boundary conditions (naravni ali silni robni pogoji) (EP §3.5.7, pp. 146-147).

4.3.8 The hanging bar

Let us test the principle on the hanging bar and see with numbers what the equation says. Recall the setting. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a round cross section of diameter 10 mm, of area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), and of density \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ hangs under its own weight. The axis \(x\) points vertically down from the centre of the top face. Only the centre \(O\) of the top face is fixed, and the top face is pulled up evenly by a force that carries the weight of the bar (section 1.7.1). For the displacement along the axis only \(u(0) = 0\) matters. The load is the weight, \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m, the lower end is free, \(F = 0\), and by lemma 4.35 the axial force is \(N(x) = \rho g A\,(L - x)\) (figure 4.31).

Uniform virtual stretching. Let \(\delta u(x) = c\,x\), where \(c\) is a small number without a unit, for example \(c = 10^{-6}\), for which the lower end moves by 10 µm. The virtual strain is \(\delta u' = c\) everywhere, every piece stretches by the same fraction. The function is a polynomial and \(\delta u(0) = 0\), so it is a virtual displacement of the bar.

  1. Internal virtual work. The function \(L x - x^2/2\) has the derivative \(L - x\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus
    \[\int_0^L \rho g A\,(L - x)\,c\,\mathrm{d}x = c\,\rho g A\,\Big(L^2 - \frac{L^2}{2}\Big) = c\,\frac{\rho g A\,L^2}{2} .\]
  2. External virtual work. The function \(x^2/2\) has the derivative \(x\), so
    \[\int_0^L \rho g A\,c\,x\,\mathrm{d}x + 0 \cdot \delta u(L) = c\,\frac{\rho g A\,L^2}{2} .\]
  3. Both sides are equal, \(c \cdot 300{,}5\) N m, so for \(c = 10^{-6}\) they are \(3{,}005 \cdot 10^{-4}\) J.

What do the two sides mean? The left side is \(c\) times the area under the graph of the axial force in figure 4.31, a triangle with base \(L\) and height \(\rho g A L\). The right side adds up the weights of the pieces, each multiplied by the depth of the piece, since the piece at depth \(x\) moves by \(c\,x\). The principle says that these two numbers are equal. This is so because the axial force at depth \(x'\) is the weight of everything below it. The weight of the piece at depth \(x\) is therefore contained in the axial force at every depth \(x'\) between \(0\) and \(x\), and when we integrate the axial forces over depth, this weight contributes over a length \(x\). The integral of the axial forces is therefore the sum of the weights of the pieces, each multiplied by its depth.

Nonuniform virtual stretching. Let \(\delta u(x) = c\,x^2/L\). The virtual strain \(\delta u'(x) = 2c\,x/L\) grows from zero at the top to \(2c\) at the bottom.

  1. Internal virtual work. The function \(L x^2/2 - x^3/3\) has the derivative \(L x - x^2\), so
    \[\int_0^L \rho g A\,(L - x)\,\frac{2c\,x}{L}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{2c\,\rho g A}{L}\,\Big(\frac{L^3}{2} - \frac{L^3}{3}\Big) = c\,\frac{\rho g A\,L^2}{3} .\]
  2. External virtual work. The function \(x^3/3\) has the derivative \(x^2\), so
    \[\int_0^L \rho g A\,\frac{c\,x^2}{L}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{c\,\rho g A}{L} \cdot \frac{L^3}{3} = c\,\frac{\rho g A\,L^2}{3} .\]
  3. Both sides are equal, \(c \cdot 200{,}3\) N m, so for \(c = 10^{-6}\) they are \(2{,}003 \cdot 10^{-4}\) J.

A wrong axial force. Does the principle notice a mistake? Suppose we wrongly thought that every cross section carries the weight of the whole bar, \(N(x) = \rho g A\,L\). With the virtual displacement \(\delta u = c\,x\) the left side is \(\int_0^L \rho g A\,L\,c\,\mathrm{d}x = c\,\rho g A\,L^2 = c \cdot 601{,}0\) N m, while the right side stays \(c \cdot 300{,}5\) N m. The equation does not hold, and by theorem 4.36 such an axial force is not in equilibrium. Indeed, for it \(N' + q = \rho g A \neq 0\) and \(N(L) = \rho g A\,L \neq 0 = F\).

The force that holds the bar. The displacement \(\delta u(x) = c\), in which all points move by the same \(c\), is not a virtual displacement of this bar, because the top must not move. As for the lever, however, we may remove the constraint in our minds and keep the force with which the bar is held at the top as a force on the bar. We denote its \(x\) component by \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\). Step 4 of the proof of theorem 4.36 holds also for such a displacement, only the term \(-N(0)\,\delta u(0)\) no longer drops out. By definition 2.5 and by the law of action and reaction at the top cross section, \(R_{\mathrm{x}} = -N(0)\), so this term is the virtual work of the force that holds the bar, and the equation reads

\[\int_0^L N(x)\,\delta u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q(x)\,\delta u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L) + R_{\mathrm{x}}\,\delta u(0) .\]

For \(\delta u = c\) the virtual strain is zero, so the left side is zero, and the right side is \(\int_0^L \rho g A\,c\,\mathrm{d}x + 0 + R_{\mathrm{x}}\,c = (\rho g A\,L + R_{\mathrm{x}})\,c\). Because it must be zero for every \(c\), \(R_{\mathrm{x}} = -\rho g A\,L = -60{,}10\) N. The bar is held at the top by a force of the size of its weight, pointing up, against the axis \(x\).

4.3.9 The bracket of two bars

Finally we apply virtual displacements to the bracket of two bars from section 4.1.4 and restate its setting. The bracket is a truss (definition 4.4) in a vertical plane. The axis \(x\) points horizontally to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up, the axis \(z\) toward the viewer, and all points have the coordinate \(z\) equal to zero. The joint \(C\) is at the origin, \(C = (0, 0, 0)\). The bar \(AC\) is horizontal, with the pin \(A = (-4, 0, 0)\) m on the wall, the bar \(BC\) is inclined, with the pin \(B = (-4, 3, 0)\) m on the wall, and its length is \(\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2}\ \text{m} = 5\ \text{m}\). At the joint \(C\) hangs a load that acts on it with the force \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\), \(F = 10\) kN. Each bar carries only an axial force, \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) respectively (lemma 4.5). As in section 4.1.4 we do not treat buckling of the compressed bar \(AC\). For the principle we will not need Young's modulus or the cross-section areas, since it does not use the relation between stress and strain. We will need them only at the end, for the displacement of the joint.

The unit vectors along the bars, from the pin on the wall toward the joint \(C\), are (figure 4.32)

\[\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0, 0) , \qquad \vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) .\]

A bar acts on the pin \(C\) with the force \(-N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\) or \(-N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\): a bar in tension pulls it toward the wall, a compressed bar pushes it away from the wall. The equilibrium of the pin \(C\) is therefore

\[-N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} + \vek F = \vek 0 .\]

From it we got in section 4.1.4 \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN. The forces of the bars on the pin are then \(-N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac{F}{3}\,(4, 0, 0)\) and \(-N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac{F}{3}\,(-4, 3, 0)\), and their sum with \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\) is the zero vector.

What does a virtual displacement of the bracket look like? The pins on the wall do not move. The joint \(C\), however, can move by any small vector \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (\delta u, \delta v, 0)\) in the plane of the bracket, and the bars follow it, each turning about its pin and stretching a little. By how much does a bar stretch? Take a bar of length \(L\) from the pin on the wall to the joint, pointing in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n\) (figure 4.33). Before the displacement the vector of the bar is \(L\,\vek n\), after the displacement of the joint \(L\,\vek n + \delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\).

  1. By the formula for the square of the length of a sum (lemma 2.9), and because \(\vek n\) is a unit vector, the square of the new length is \(L_1^2 = L^2 + 2L\,\vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + |\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2\).
  2. As for the sheared cube in equation (1.17), \(L_1 - L = (L_1^2 - L^2)/(L_1 + L)\). By step 1 the numerator is \(2L\,\vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + |\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2\), and the denominator is \(L_1 + L = 2L + (L_1 - L)\). We multiply the equation by the denominator and multiply out the bracket: \(2L\,(L_1 - L) + (L_1 - L)^2 = 2L\,\vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + |\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2\).
  3. We subtract \(2L\,\vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + (L_1 - L)^2\) from both sides, divide by \(2L\) and add \(\vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). We get the exact equation \(L_1 - L = \vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \big(|\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2 - (L_1 - L)^2\big)/(2L)\). The second term is a difference of the squares of two small numbers, divided by the length of the bar. Since \(L_1 - L\) is almost \(\vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), this term is almost \(\big(|\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2 - (\vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})^2\big)/(2L)\). By lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, item 3, its numerator is the square of the length of the part of the displacement perpendicular to the bar. We leave the second term out, as we left out the term \(s^2\) next to the term \(2hs\) for the sheared cube.

The virtual elongation of the bar is therefore

\[\delta e = \vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} , \tag{4.24}\]

the projection of the virtual displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar. The part of the displacement perpendicular to the bar only turns the bar, as the vertical edge \(AD\) of the sheared cube only leaned. Let us check with numbers. Let \(C\) move vertically down by 1 mm, \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (0, -1, 0)\) mm. By (4.24) the bar \(BC\) becomes longer by \(\tfrac15\,\big(4 \cdot 0 + (-3)(-1\ \text{mm})\big) = 0{,}6\) mm, while the exact computation with the lengths gives \(0{,}600064\) mm. The difference \(0{,}000064\) mm is the term left out in step 3, \(\big(1\ \text{mm}^2 - (0{,}6\ \text{mm})^2\big)/(2 \cdot 5000\ \text{mm})\). By (4.24) the bar \(AC\) does not become longer, while exactly it becomes longer by \(0{,}000125\) mm, which is the term left out for \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), \(|\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2/(2 \cdot 4\ \text{m})\).

Now we multiply the equilibrium of the pin \(C\) by the virtual displacement \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) with the scalar product, just as for the rigid body we multiplied forces by displacements.

  1. By the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12, items 2 and 3) the equilibrium of the pin gives \(-N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek F\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\).
  2. By (4.24) the scalar products with \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\) are the virtual elongations of the bars. We move the first two terms to the right side:
    \[N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\delta e_{\mathrm{AC}} + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\delta e_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek F\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} . \tag{4.25}\]

On the left is the internal virtual work: the axial force of each bar times its virtual elongation. It is the internal virtual work of a bar from theorem 4.36. Bar \(i\) has no load along its length, so its axial force \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant. The component of the virtual displacement of its cross sections along the bar is zero at the pin on the wall and \(\delta e_{\mathrm{i}}\) at the joint. By the theorem with \(q = 0\) and the force \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) at the end, therefore, \(\int_0^{L_{\mathrm{i}}} N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\delta w_{\mathrm{i}}'(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\delta e_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \(\delta w_{\mathrm{i}}(s)\) is this component and \(s\) the distance from the pin on the wall. We use new letters because in this section \(\delta u\) and \(x\) already are the horizontal component of the virtual displacement of the joint and the horizontal coordinate. On the right is the external virtual work of the load. The pins on the wall do not move, so the forces of the wall do not appear. The converse also holds. If equation (4.25) holds for every \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) in the plane of the bracket, we read it back as \((\vek F - N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}})\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), and with \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\) we get the \(x\) and \(y\) components of the equilibrium of the pin. The \(z\) component is zero by itself for forces in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane.

Let us compute the axial forces. For \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (\delta u, \delta v, 0)\), by (4.24) \(\delta e_{\mathrm{AC}} = \delta u\) and \(\delta e_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0{,}8\,\delta u - 0{,}6\,\delta v\), and the work of the load is \(\vek F\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -F\,\delta v\). Equation (4.25) reads

\[N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\delta u + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,(0{,}8\,\delta u - 0{,}6\,\delta v) = -F\,\delta v \quad \text{for all } \delta u, \delta v .\]

For \(\delta v = 0\) we get \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} + 0{,}8\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), and for \(\delta u = 0\), \(-0{,}6\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -F\). Hence \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F/0{,}6 = 16{,}67\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -0{,}8\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -13{,}33\) kN, the same as in section 4.1.4.

It is even better to choose the virtual displacement so that only one bar becomes longer (figure 4.34).

  1. Let \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \tfrac{c}{5}\,(3, 4, 0)\), where \(c\) is a small length. This displacement is perpendicular to the bar \(BC\), since \((3, 4, 0)\cdot(4, -3, 0) = 12 - 12 = 0\). The bar \(BC\) only turns about \(B\), \(\delta e_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), while the bar \(AC\) becomes longer by \(\delta e_{\mathrm{AC}} = 0{,}6\,c\). The work of the load is \(\vek F\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -0{,}8\,F\,c\). Equation (4.25) gives \(0{,}6\,c\,N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -0{,}8\,F\,c\), so \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN, without knowing \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}\).
  2. Let \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (0, c, 0)\), perpendicular to the bar \(AC\). Then \(\delta e_{\mathrm{AC}} = 0\), \(\delta e_{\mathrm{BC}} = -0{,}6\,c\) and the work of the load is \(-F\,c\). The equation gives \(-0{,}6\,c\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -F\,c\), so \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN.

Each choice gave one axial force, because only one bar became longer. This is how the unit dummy-displacement method works (EP §4.2.3, p. 172), which we mentioned for the lever. EP uses it on a similar truss of two bars in example 4.2.2 (pp. 173-174). Take the unit virtual displacement in the direction of the load, \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (0, -1, 0)\). Then \(\delta e_{\mathrm{AC}} = 0\), \(\delta e_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0{,}6\) and \(\vek F\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = F\), so equation (4.25) says \(F = 0{,}6\,N_{\mathrm{BC}}\). The load equals the internal virtual work for the unit virtual displacement in its direction.

Now we can also answer the question of section 4.1.4, where the joint \(C\) moves. By section 4.1.4 the bars changed their lengths by \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = -2{,}721\) mm and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 4{,}252\) mm. The real displacement of the joint \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\), written by its components as in section 4.1.4, is small, so the same computation holds for it as for the virtual displacement: the change of the length of a bar is, to first order, the projection of the displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar, \(\Delta L = \vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). This gives two equations for two unknowns:

  1. Bar \(AC\): \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = u\), so \(u = -2{,}721\) mm.
  2. Bar \(BC\): \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\), so \(v = (0{,}8\,u - \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}})/0{,}6 = \big(0{,}8 \cdot (-2{,}721\ \text{mm}) - 4{,}252\ \text{mm}\big)/0{,}6 = -10{,}71\ \text{mm}\).

The joint \(C\) therefore moves by \(2{,}721\) mm toward the wall and by \(10{,}71\) mm down. The component \(v = -10{,}71\) mm agrees with the number that we got in section 4.1.4 from the equality of the work of the load and the stored energy, and now we have the horizontal part as well. Here we used that the material is linear elastic (assumption 1 of section 4.1), since the changes of the lengths were computed from the axial forces with Young's modulus. EP does the same in example 4.2.2 (pp. 173-174), except that it first writes the axial forces with the displacement of the joint and inserts them into the virtual work equation. How to get the displacement of the joint from energy without computing the axial forces we will see in section 4.5.

The position of the joint \(C\) in the plane was described by two numbers, and two independent choices of the virtual displacement gave two equations. The joint has two degrees of freedom, and the two numbers that describe its position are generalized coordinates, which we mentioned in section 1.5.1. Virtual displacements written with generalized coordinates are the starting point of analytical mechanics in chapter 8 (GR §1.2.3, PDF pp. 38-39).

Let us sum up how we arrived at the principle. For the rigid body we multiplied the forces by the virtual displacements of their points with the scalar product and added. The displacement of all points by the same vector picked out the resultant, the turn the sum of the moments, so zero virtual work was equivalent to equilibrium, and the support forces dropped out. For the bar we multiplied the equilibrium \(N' + q = 0\) by the virtual displacement, integrated over the length and moved the derivative to the virtual displacement with integration by parts. This produced the internal virtual work \(\int N\,\delta u'\,\mathrm{d}x\), which equals the external one. We proved the converse with the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations. For the bracket of two bars we multiplied the equilibrium of the pin at the joint by the virtual displacement of the joint, and the virtual elongations of the bars were the projections of this displacement. The same projection rule also gave the real displacement of the joint. In the next section we do the same for a general body. The stress components will take the place of the axial force, and the divergence theorem the place of integration by parts.

4.4 The principle of virtual displacements for a body

In section 4.3 we wrote the equilibrium of a bar in a new form. The bar was fixed at the end \(x = 0\), a force \(q(x)\) per unit length acted along it in the direction of the axis, and a force \(F\) acted at the free end \(x = L\). Instead of the equation \(N' + q = 0\) at every point and the condition \(N(L) = F\) at the end we wrote a single equation,

\[\int_0^L N\,\delta u'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,\delta u\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L) ,\]

which holds for every virtual displacement of the bar \(\delta u\), that is, for every function with a continuous derivative and with \(\delta u(0) = 0\) (theorem 4.36 on the principle of virtual displacements for a bar). On the left is the work of the axial forces on the virtual elongations of the pieces of the bar, on the right the work of the external forces on the virtual displacements. The converse holds too: if the equation holds for every such \(\delta u\), the bar is in equilibrium (theorem 4.38).

The goal of this section is the same for a body of any shape in space. In chapter 2 we described the equilibrium of a body by the three equilibrium equations (2.31) at every interior point, by the symmetry of stress (2.37) and by the condition that on the loaded part of the surface the traction vector equals the force per unit area with which the surroundings act on the body. We will replace all of this by a single equation that must hold for every virtual displacement the supports allow. Why would we want that? For three reasons. The new equation contains no derivative of the stresses, only first partial derivatives of the virtual displacement, and the finite element method of chapters 6 and 7 stands on it. Its derivation needs no property of the material, so the equation holds for every material. And from it we will derive the theorems on energy in the next sections.

The route is as follows. First we set up the model precisely: the body, its supports and loads, and the assumptions. Then we say which virtual displacements are admissible. With a picture of a body built from small boxes we explain why the work of the stresses on the virtual strains must equal the work of the external forces on the virtual displacements. Then we prove it with the divergence theorem, which plays the role of integration by parts in space. The converse follows: if the equation holds for all virtual displacements the supports allow, the equilibrium equations and the condition on the surface hold. At the end we test the principle on the cube in pure shear and on the hanging bar.

4.4.1 The body, its supports and its loads

Take a body that before loading occupies the set of points \(V\), with surface \(S\), and a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with axes \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) (figure 4.35). We must say how the body is held and what acts on it. We distinguish three kinds of forces.

  1. Supports. On a part of the surface, which we denote by \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the displacement is prescribed. Such a part is for example the bottom face of a cube glued to a table, like the sheared cube in section 1.6.2. There the displacement is zero. In general a displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) is prescribed on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), which need not be zero, for example at a support that settles by a known distance. The forces with which the supports act on the body are not known in advance. They are exactly what is needed for the points of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) to move by the prescribed displacement.
  2. Prescribed surface forces. On the rest of the surface, which we denote by \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), we know the force per unit area with which the surroundings act on the body. We denote it by \(\bar{\vek t}\). Examples are the pressure of water on a wall or the even pull on the top face of the hanging bar. Where nothing acts on the surface, \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\), and this too is a prescribed force. The bar over the letter says here that the quantity is prescribed (predpisan), and has nothing to do with the bar for turned axes in section 2.9.
  3. Body force. A force with density \(\vek b\) acts on every bit of the material (definition 2.25), for example the weight with density \(\rho g\).

The parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) do not overlap and together make up the whole surface (SADD §5.2, PDF p. 104, EP §4.2.2, p. 168). At every point of the surface we therefore know either the displacement or the force per unit area, not both. This is a simplification. For a body that slides along a smooth rigid wall, at the same point the component of the displacement perpendicular to the wall is prescribed, and so is the component of the force along the wall, which is zero (SADD §5.2, PDF p. 104). We do not treat such supports in this section.

The model makes four more assumptions. For each we say why it is justified and where we will use it.

  1. Small deformations. The body deforms so little that we do not distinguish its shape before and after loading. We therefore write all integrals over the body \(V\) and the surface \(S\) before loading, with the outward normal of the surface before loading. In steel structures the dimensions change by less than a thousandth (section 1.17), and we already proceeded this way for the equilibrium equations in section 2.7. For large deformations the forces act on the body in its deformed shape, and we would have to write the integrals over the deformed body or use the stresses referred to the original shape from section 2.13 (BOWER §2.4.5, PDF pp. 88-89).
  2. Equilibrium. The body is at rest. At every interior point the stress satisfies the equilibrium equations (2.31), at every point it is symmetric (theorem 2.35 on the symmetry of stress), and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the traction vector given by Cauchy's formula equals the prescribed force, \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) (equation (2.42)), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal. These are the conditions we will rewrite as one equation.
  3. No jumps. The stress components are continuously differentiable (definition 1.88) on an open set that contains the body together with its surface. So the stress never changes with a jump, not even right next to the surface. The body force density \(\vek b\) is continuous on the body, the prescribed force \(\bar{\vek t}\) on each outer face of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) separately. On an edge where two faces with different normals meet it may have two values, as on the edge between the top face of the cube in pure shear, which we push to the right, and its right face, which we pull up (section 2.6.6). We need this so that the integrals exist and so that we may use the divergence theorem. Point forces and the contact of two materials are thereby left out (section 1.15). The assumption excludes two more things. First, a load that acts on part of a flat face only and drops to zero at the edge of that part. The normal is the same on both sides of such an edge, so a continuous stress gives the same traction \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) on both sides, and \(\bar{\vek t}\) cannot jump there. Second, a re-entrant corner (vbočeno oglišče), where two faces meet at an angle larger than \(180^\circ\), measured through the body. There the stress of the true solution may be unbounded (BARBER §11.2.3, PDF p. 175). In the figures of this chapter we draw loads on part of a face as an idealization. An exact treatment would replace them by loads that fall continuously to zero at the edge of the patch.
  4. Shape. For the proof that we write out in full, let the body consist of cells of one grid, that is, let it be a body made of boxes (definition 4.11), and let \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) consist of whole outer faces of these cells. A box is the simplest such body. For bodies made of boxes we have proved the divergence theorem (theorem 4.14). For bodies cut into pieces between graphs, like the round hanging bar, we proved it in section 4.2.10, and at the end of section 4.4.4 we say what changes in the proofs for them. For other bodies with a curved surface we only stated it with a source (section 4.2.6), and the same goes for everything we derive from it.

We have assumed nothing about the material. We will nowhere need the relation between stresses and strains from chapter 3, nor that the stresses come from the displacements of the body.

Two bodies we already know will accompany the section. The first is the steel cube with edge \(h = 10\) mm in pure shear from section 2.6.6, glued to a table with its bottom face, as in section 3.2.5. The origin is at the bottom front left corner \(A\), the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) into the depth and the axis \(z\) up. The bottom face is \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the displacement is zero there. We push the top face to the right, pull the right face up and the left face down, all with the force \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa per unit area. The front and back faces are free. These five faces are \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). The stress is the same at all points, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\), the other components are zero, and we neglect the weight, because it changes the stress by only \(765\) Pa, as we saw in section 2.7. On the top face with normal \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) Cauchy's formula gives \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}) = \tau_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is indeed the prescribed force pushing to the right. On the bottom face with normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) it gives \(-\tau_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). This is the force of the glue, which pulls to the left. In this example we know it because we know the stress, but in general we do not know the force of a support in advance.

The second body is the steel hanging bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a round cross section of diameter 10 mm, with the axis \(x\) vertically down from the centre \(O\) of the top face. It is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1: a force spread evenly over the top face pulls it up, and the point \(O\) is fixed, with the material right next to it not turning, only so that the bar cannot move or turn as a whole (CM, PDF p. 306). The weight is carried by the pull on the top face, so in this model there is no force at the point \(O\). The whole surface is therefore \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\): on the top face \(\bar{\vek t} = -\rho g L\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the lateral surface and the bottom face are free, \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). The part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty. The body force is the weight, \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the only stress component that is not zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305). On the top face with normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) Cauchy's formula gives \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(0) \cdot (-1), 0, 0) = -\rho g L\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the prescribed upward pull.

4.4.2 Admissible virtual displacements

In section 4.3 a virtual displacement was an imagined small displacement that the supports allow, during which the forces stay as they are (definition 4.30). The sign \(\delta\) in front of a quantity means a virtual quantity, as we agreed in section 4.3.1. For a body a virtual displacement is a field. Its input is the three coordinates of a point of the body before loading, its output three numbers \(\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\delta u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\delta u_{\mathrm{z}}\), the components of the vector by which we imagine the point to move. Which fields do we allow?

Definition 4.39 Kinematically admissible virtual displacement (kinematično dopusten virtualni pomik)

Let a body occupy the set of points \(V\) before loading, and let the displacement be prescribed on the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of its surface. A kinematically admissible virtual displacement (kinematično dopusten virtualni pomik) is a vector field \(\delta\vek u = (\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}, \delta u_{\mathrm{y}}, \delta u_{\mathrm{z}})\) that is continuously differentiable (definition 1.88) on an open set containing the body together with its surface, and equal to the zero vector at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). Its virtual strain (virtualna deformacija) at a point of the body is the symmetric matrix \(\delta\ten\varepsilon\) with entries

\[\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) ,\]

where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the coordinate named \(j\): \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\).

Source: SADD §6.5 (PDF p. 137), EP §4.2.2 (pp. 168-169), BOWER §2.4.4 (PDF p. 85) and §2.4.6 (PDF pp. 89-90).

The word kinematically says that the condition is about displacements only, not about forces. BOWER writes that kinematically admissible is just a complicated way of saying that the field is continuous, differentiable and zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (BOWER, PDF p. 85). Why exactly these two conditions? We explain each by what we will use it for.

Why must the virtual displacement be zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\)? We do not know the forces of the supports. If the points of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) do not move during the virtual displacement, these forces do no work, and they do not appear in the equation we will derive. We will get an equation that contains only known forces. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), on the other hand, the virtual displacement can be anything. What if a displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) that is not zero is prescribed on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\)? The virtual displacement is zero there all the same. A virtual displacement is an imagined change from the true state, and on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the support allows no change of the displacement.

Why must it be continuously differentiable? From its partial derivatives we compute the virtual strain, which we need at every point of the body, and the continuity of the partial derivatives is needed by the divergence theorem, which we will use in the proof. Physically the condition says that the material does not tear anywhere during the imagined displacement.

The virtual strain is the small strain tensor (equation (1.51)) computed from the field \(\delta\vek u\) instead of from the displacement field \(\vek u\). If \(\delta\mat H\) is the displacement gradient of the field \(\delta\vek u\) (definition 1.107), with entries \(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), then \(\delta\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,(\delta\mat H + \delta\mat H^\T)\). Since we think of the virtual displacement as small, by section 1.17 this is the strain that the imagined displacement would cause, up to negligible terms.

Must the virtual displacement be small? The definition does not require it. In the equation we will derive, every term contains a component of the field \(\delta\vek u\) or its partial derivative exactly once. If we multiply the field by a number, both sides are therefore multiplied by the same number. The size does not matter. We need smallness only for the mental picture: during a small imagined displacement the shape of the body and the forces on it do not change noticeably.

Let us test the definition on the glued cube (figure 4.36). The part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the bottom face, where \(z = 0\).

  • The field \(\delta\vek u = (\gamma z, 0, 0)\), where \(\gamma\) is a number, is continuously differentiable, because its components are polynomials, and it is zero at \(z = 0\). It is therefore kinematically admissible. The only partial derivative that is not zero is \(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = \gamma\), so \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tfrac12\,(\gamma + 0) = \gamma/2\), and all other virtual strains are zero. For \(\gamma = 0{,}001\) this field has the same shape as the true field of the sheared cube (1.16), only here we merely imagine it.
  • The field \(\delta\vek u = (\delta a, 0, 0)\) moves the whole cube by \(\delta a\) in the direction of the axis \(x\). It is continuously differentiable, all its partial derivatives are zero, so the virtual strain is zero. But it is not kinematically admissible, because it also moves the glued bottom face.
  • A field that moves the upper half of the cube by \(\delta a\) and the lower half not at all is not continuous, because it has a jump on the plane \(z = h/2\). It is not kinematically admissible, because the material would tear there.

For the hanging bar \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty, so every continuously differentiable virtual displacement is admissible. Moving the whole bar down by \(\delta a\) is admissible too. The point \(O\) is fixed only against a motion of the bar as a whole and carries no force in the model, so moving the point \(O\) adds no work.

Among the admissible fields, those that only move or turn the body as if it were rigid are especially simple. For a move by a constant vector all partial derivatives are zero. For a small rotation about the axis \(y\), for example \(\delta\vek u = \theta\,(z, 0, -x)\) with a number \(\theta\), we have \(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = \theta\) and \(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x = -\theta\), so \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\,(\theta - \theta) = 0\), and all other virtual strains are zero too. These fields do not deform the body. For the cube they are not admissible, because they move the bottom face, for the hanging bar they are.

4.4.3 Why the internal work equals the external work

When the body moves by an admissible virtual displacement, the forces on it do virtual work. A force \(\vek F\) whose point of application has the virtual displacement \(\delta\vek u\) does the virtual work \(\vek F\cdot\delta\vek u\) (definition 4.31). The body force on a small piece of volume \(\Delta V\) is approximately \(\vek b\,\Delta V\), and when the piece moves by \(\delta\vek u\), it does work of approximately \(\vek b\cdot\delta\vek u\,\Delta V\). The prescribed force on a small patch of area \(\Delta A\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) does work of approximately \(\bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u\,\Delta A\). The forces of the supports do no work, because on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the virtual displacement is zero. When we add up over all pieces and patches and make them smaller, we get integrals. The stresses, in turn, do work on the virtual strain. In section 3.6 we computed that the forces on the faces of a small box of volume \(\Delta V\) do the work \(\Delta V \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) when the strain of the box changes slightly by \(\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) while the stress stays nearly the same. A move and a rotation of the box as a whole did no work. Here the change of strain is the virtual strain \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). For the bar we called the work of the axial forces on the virtual elongations the internal virtual work and the work of the loads the external virtual work (section 4.3). For a body we define them as follows.

Definition 4.40 Internal and external virtual work of a body (notranje in zunanje virtualno delo telesa)

Let a body occupy the set of points \(V\), let there be supports on the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of its surface, let a force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) be prescribed on the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), let a body force with density \(\vek b\) act on the material, and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the stresses in the body. Let \(\delta\vek u\) be a kinematically admissible virtual displacement with virtual strain \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 4.39). The internal virtual work (notranje virtualno delo) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V ,\]

and the external virtual work (zunanje virtualno delo) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

The indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

Source: SADD (6.5.1), (6.5.3) (PDF pp. 137-138), EP (4.2.2), (4.2.3) (p. 169).

The double sum has nine terms. Since the stress and the virtual strain are symmetric matrices, the terms with swapped indices are equal, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\), and the sum has six different terms:

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} .\]

SADD writes it with engineering shear strains, where the factor two hides in \(\delta\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (SADD (6.5.3), PDF p. 138). The internal virtual work has the unit J, like every work: a stress in Pa times a virtual strain without a unit times a volume in m³ gives N·m.

Why is there no factor one half, as in the strain energy density \(w = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\) of the steel bar in section 3.6? There the stress grew from zero to its final value during loading, together with the strain, and the average stress was half the final one. During a virtual displacement, however, the stresses do not change. They are the true stresses in equilibrium, and the virtual strain is added to them without changing them. So the work is simply the stress times the virtual strain (SADD, PDF p. 138).

Now the question the whole section answers. Why should the internal virtual work equal the external one? The answer is shown by a picture of a body built from small boxes like a wall from bricks (figure 4.37). Every box is in equilibrium. Let us add up the virtual work of all forces on all boxes, and do it in two ways.

First, face by face. Take the shared face of two neighbouring boxes. The force with which the right box acts on the left one across this face is, by lemma 2.20 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut, opposite to the force with which the left box acts on the right one. But during the virtual displacement the face moves in the same way for both boxes, because the field \(\delta\vek u\) is continuous. The works of the two forces are therefore opposite numbers and cancel in the sum. What remains are only the forces on faces that lie on the surface of the body, and the body forces. Their work is the external virtual work, since the forces of the supports do no work.

Second, box by box. The virtual displacement of a small box is close to a sum of four simple parts (figure 4.38): a move of the box as a whole, a rotation of the box as a whole, an elongation along an axis, and a shear. In the move all points of the box move in the same way, and the work of all forces on the box is the scalar product of their resultant with this move. The resultant is zero, because the box is in equilibrium. In the rotation the work of all forces is the scalar product of the sum of their moments with the rotation vector, by theorem 4.33 on the principle of virtual displacements for a rigid body, and the sum of the moments is zero, because the box is in equilibrium. What remains is the work on the deformation of the box, which by section 3.6 is approximately \(\Delta V \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The sum over the boxes is the internal virtual work.

Both ways add up the same work, so the two sums are equal: the external virtual work equals the internal one. In this argument we used both conditions of equilibrium of every box, zero resultant and zero sum of moments, and the fact that two neighbouring boxes move in the same way on their shared face. This is the idea, not a proof. It contains too many approximations: the boxes have a finite size, the virtual displacement on a box is only approximately made of four parts, the stress is not the same everywhere in a box. The exact route is given by the divergence theorem. In it the integral takes over the role of the sum over boxes, and the cancelling of the forces on inner faces is exactly what we saw in the proof of the divergence theorem for a body made of boxes in section 4.2.

4.4.4 The principle of virtual displacements

First let us prove an equality that we will need twice, for the principle and for its converse. For the bar, integration by parts (corollary 3.40),

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,g'\,\mathrm{d}x = f(b)\,g(b) - f(a)\,g(a) - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f'\,g\,\mathrm{d}x ,\]

was the tool that moved the derivative from the function \(g\) to the function \(f\) and gave terms at the end points in exchange. In space the stress plays the role of the function \(f\), the virtual displacement the role of the function \(g\), and the surface of the body replaces the end points of the interval.

Lemma 4.41 Internal virtual work through the surface (notranje virtualno delo prek površine)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes (definition 4.11) with surface \(S\) and outward unit normal \(\vek n\). Let the stress components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the components of the field \(\delta\vek u\) be continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface, and let the stress be symmetric at every point, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\). Let \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}V , \tag{4.26}\]

where \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) is the traction vector at the points of the surface, and the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\).

Proof

We must show that the internal virtual work splits into the work of the traction vector on the surface and a volume integral with derivatives of the stresses. Using the symmetry of stress and the product rule, we first write the integrand on the left as a sum of partial derivatives of some field plus a remainder, then we apply the divergence theorem to the sum of partial derivatives.

  1. By the definition of the numbers \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and by multiplying out the product with the sum, at every point
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\frac{\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\frac{\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
  2. In the first double sum we swap the names of the indices, writing \(i\) instead of \(j\) and \(j\) instead of \(i\). The sum runs over the same nine pairs, so it does not change, and it equals \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\,\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\). By symmetry \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so the first double sum equals the second one, and
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\frac{\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
    For the pair of indices \(x\), \(y\) this means \(2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\big(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\big) = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\), which are the terms of the right-hand sum with the pairs \((i, j) = (y, x)\) and \((x, y)\).
  3. For every pair of indices \(i\), \(j\) the expression \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\) is at every point a product of two functions. If we hold fixed the coordinates other than \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), it is a function of one variable, and by the product rule (lemma 1.79, item 3)
    \[\frac{\partial\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}})}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\frac{\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
  4. For \(i = x, y, z\) let \(v_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\). So for example \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\cdot\delta\vek u\) by (2.23). We sum the equation of step 3 over \(j\) and over \(i\). The partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.79, item 1), so from steps 2 and 3 we get at every point
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} - \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}} .\]
  5. The field \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable on the open set of the hypothesis. A continuously differentiable function is continuous (lemma 1.89). By step 3 the partial derivatives of the components of \(\vek v\) are sums of products of continuous functions, so they are continuous by corollary 1.67 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space, item 1. For the same reason all functions in step 4 are continuous.
  6. We integrate the equality of step 4 over \(V\). The integral over a body made of boxes is the sum of the integrals over the cells (definition 4.11), and on every cell the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals (lemma 4.10 on the properties of the integral over a box, item 1). We get
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big(\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  7. By the divergence theorem 4.14, which we may use because by step 5 \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big(\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} (v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  8. At every point of the surface
    \[v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\Big)\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}} .\]
    By Cauchy's formula in components (2.24), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the component \(j\) of the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\), for example \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). Therefore \(v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\delta\vek u\), and because of the symmetry \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) (equation (2.42)).
  9. Inserting steps 7 and 8 into step 6 we get (4.26).

Source: SADD (6.5.2) (PDF p. 137), EP (4.2.3) (p. 169), BOWER §2.4.4.1 (PDF p. 86). The sources do these steps for a general body and do not separate them into a lemma.

The lemma is integration by parts in space. On the left the components of the virtual displacement are differentiated, on the right the components of the stress, and the surface integral plays the role of the terms at the end points. We used the symmetry of stress only in step 2. Without it, the left side would contain the partial derivatives \(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) instead of the virtual strain. The field \(\vek v\) has a simple meaning: \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the work of the force per unit area on the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the virtual displacement, \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\cdot\delta\vek u\), and likewise \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Now the principle itself follows. We get it from the lemma with the equilibrium equations and the two conditions on the surface.

Theorem 4.42 Principle of virtual displacements (načelo virtualnih pomikov)

Let the body before loading occupy a set of points \(V\) that is a body made of boxes (definition 4.11), and let its surface \(S\) be divided into parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) that do not overlap and consist of whole outer faces of cells. Let the displacement be prescribed on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), a force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) that is continuous on each outer face of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and let a body force with density \(\vek b\), continuous on \(V\), act on the material. Assume:

  1. the stress components are continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface,
  2. at every interior point of the body the equilibrium equations (2.31) hold,
  3. at every point of the body the stress is symmetric, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\),
  4. at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal.

Then for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement \(\delta\vek u\) with virtual strain \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 4.39) the internal virtual work equals the external one (definition 4.40):

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.27}\]
Proof

We must show that in the equality (4.26) the volume integral on the right turns into the work of the body force and the surface integral into the work of the prescribed force.

  1. By assumption 1 the stress components are continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface, by definition 4.39 so are the components of the field \(\delta\vek u\), and by assumption 3 the stress is symmetric. By lemma 4.41 on the internal virtual work through the surface, (4.26) therefore holds.
  2. With indices the equilibrium equations (2.31) read \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} + b_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for \(j = x, y, z\). For \(j = x\) this is the first equation, \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial y + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}/\partial z + b_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). By assumption 2, at every interior point
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} b_{\mathrm{j}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}} = -\vek b\cdot\delta\vek u .\]
  3. The equality also holds at the points of the surface. Let \(Q\) be a point of the surface and \(C\) the centre of a cell of the body that contains \(Q\). The points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}} = Q + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{QC}\) for \(n = 2, 3, \dots\) lie in the interior of this cell, because each of their coordinates is strictly between the bounds of the cell, and they converge to \(Q\), because \(|Q_{\mathrm{n}} Q| = |QC|/n\) (definition 1.63). Both sides of the equality of step 2 are continuous functions of the point, the first by step 5 of the proof of the lemma, the second because \(\vek b\) is continuous. By lemma 1.66 on continuity through sequences of points, the values of both sides at the points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) converge to the values at \(Q\). The values are equal at every point \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\), so by the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence (lemma 1.39) they are equal at \(Q\) too.
  4. The function under the second volume integral in (4.26) and \(-\vek b\cdot\delta\vek u\) are therefore equal at every point of the body, so their integrals are equal too:
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}V = -\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  5. The surface integral is the sum of the integrals over the outer faces (definition 4.11, item 3). Every outer face belongs to \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) or to \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), so the surface integral is the sum of the integrals over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(\delta\vek u = \vek 0\) by definition 4.39, so there \(\vek t(\vek n)\cdot\delta\vek u = 0\), and the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is zero. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) by assumption 4. Therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  6. We insert steps 4 and 5 into (4.26). The minus in front of the volume integral and the minus of step 4 give a plus, and we get (4.27).

Source: SADD (6.5.1), (6.5.2) (PDF p. 137), EP (4.2.2), (4.2.3) (p. 169), BOWER §2.4.4.1 (PDF p. 86) and §2.4.6 (PDF pp. 89-90). The sources prove the theorem for a general body with the divergence theorem. Step 3 is not from the sources.

This is the central result of the chapter, so let us remember it. The proof showed how equilibrium turns into an equality of works. The lemma moved the derivative from the virtual displacement to the stress. The equilibrium equations turned the volume integral with derivatives of the stress into the work of the body force. On the surface two conditions acted: on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the virtual displacement is zero, so the forces of the supports do no work, and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the traction vector equals the prescribed force. The second condition of equilibrium, the symmetry of stress, entered in step 2 of the lemma, where it allowed us to write the virtual strain instead of the partial derivatives of the virtual displacement. This is the exact form of the argument with boxes: a rotation of a box does no work, because the sum of the moments is zero.

What is not in the theorem? There is no true displacement field \(\vek u\) and no relation between stresses and strains. The stress need only be in equilibrium, and the virtual displacement is an arbitrary admissible field that has no connection with the stress. That is why the principle holds for every material, linear elastic, nonlinear elastic or one that deforms permanently. EP stresses this by saying that the principle is independent of any constitutive law, that is, of any relation between stresses and strains (EP §4.2.2, p. 169).

What about a body with a curved surface, for example the round hanging bar? The proof of the lemma used the divergence theorem in step 7 and the linearity of the integral over the body in step 6, while all other steps hold at every point separately. For a body cut into pieces between graphs (definition 4.21) we have both: the linearity by lemma 4.22 and the divergence theorem by corollary 4.28. The lemma therefore holds for it too, with steps 1 to 9 unchanged. The surface integral in it is then the sum of the integrals over the outer pieces of the surface (definition 4.24). The proof of the principle used the cells of the body in two more places. In step 3 it reached every point of the surface by a sequence of interior points, and in step 5 it split the surface into whole outer faces. For a body cut into pieces we therefore also require that \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) consist of whole outer pieces and that every point of the body is the limit of a sequence of its interior points. With these the principle holds too.

For the round bar we check the second requirement as follows. Let \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{Q}}, y_{\mathrm{Q}}, z_{\mathrm{Q}})\) be a point of the bar and \(M = (L/2, 0, 0)\) a point on its axis. The point \(Q_{\mathrm{n}} = Q + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{QM}\) has the coordinates \(\big((1 - \tfrac1n)\,x_{\mathrm{Q}} + \tfrac{L}{2n},\ (1 - \tfrac1n)\,y_{\mathrm{Q}},\ (1 - \tfrac1n)\,z_{\mathrm{Q}}\big)\). Its coordinate \(x\) lies between \(L/(2n)\) and \(L - L/(2n)\), so strictly between \(0\) and \(L\), and the sum \(y^2 + z^2\) is \((1 - \tfrac1n)^2\,(y_{\mathrm{Q}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{Q}}^2) < r^2\). The functions \(x\) and \(y^2 + z^2\) are continuous functions of the point (corollary 1.67). Continuity at the point \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) (definition 1.65), written with an error smaller than the distance to the bound, gives a band around \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) in which the strict inequalities still hold. The points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) are thus interior points of the bar, and they converge to \(Q\), because \(|Q_{\mathrm{n}} Q| = |QM|/n\). For the bar \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the whole surface. The lemma and the principle of virtual displacements therefore hold also for the round hanging bar, cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\) of section 4.2.6. For bodies that we cannot cut into pieces between graphs we rely on the cited theorem of section 4.2.6, and that is how we will use the lemma and the principle for them too.

4.4.5 The converse of the principle
