In the finite element method we do not know the stresses. We look for them by requiring the equation (4.27) for many virtual displacements. Is the body then really in equilibrium? For the bar we showed in section 4.3 that it is, with the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (lemma 4.37). It says that a continuous function whose integral with every admissible function is zero is itself zero. In space we need the same, only with a bump in a box instead of on an interval. The idea is simple. If a continuous function \(g\) is positive at some point \(P\), it is positive in a small box around \(P\) too. Take a function that is positive in this box and zero outside it. The integral of the product with \(g\) is then positive, not zero.

We build the bump from three bumps of the kind we used in the proof of the fundamental lemma 4.37. For numbers \(\alpha < \beta\) let

\[p_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (t - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - t)^2 \quad \text{for } \alpha \le t \le \beta , \qquad p_{\alpha\beta}(t) = 0 \quad \text{for other } t .\]

Between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both factors are positive, so \(p_{\alpha\beta}\) is positive there, and at the end points and outside it is zero (figure 4.39, left). The squares in the factors make the graph touch the axis without a kink, with zero derivative. The box \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) is the set of points with \(\alpha_1 \le x \le \beta_1\), \(\alpha_2 \le y \le \beta_2\) and \(\alpha_3 \le z \le \beta_3\). The product \(p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,p_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\) is positive in the interior of the box \(K\) and zero outside it (figure 4.39, right).

Lemma 4.43 Fundamental lemma for boxes and rectangles (osnovna lema za kvadre in pravokotnike)

For numbers \(\alpha < \beta\) let \(p_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (t - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - t)^2\) for \(\alpha \le t \le \beta\) and \(p_{\alpha\beta}(t) = 0\) for other \(t\).

  1. The function \(p_{\alpha\beta}\) is differentiable at every real number and its derivative is continuous. Therefore, for every box \([\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\), the function \(\varphi(x, y, z) = p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,p_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\) is continuously differentiable in all of space.
  2. Let \(g\) be a function of three variables, continuous on an open set \(D\). If for every box \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) that lies in \(D\)
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g(x, y, z)\,p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,p_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 ,\]
    then \(g = 0\) at every point of \(D\).
  3. Let \(R\) be the rectangle \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2]\) in the plane \(z = c\) and \(f\) a function of the point, continuous on \(R\). If for all numbers \(a_1 < \alpha_1 < \beta_1 < b_1\) and \(a_2 < \alpha_2 < \beta_2 < b_2\)
    \[\int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} \int_{\alpha_2}^{\beta_2} f(x, y, c)\,p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 ,\]
    then \(f = 0\) at every point of \(R\).
Proof

We must show three items. In the first we rely on the proof of the fundamental lemma, in the other two we derive a contradiction from a point where the function is not zero, with a bump around this point.

1. Derivative of the bump.

  1. The function \(p_{\alpha\beta}\) is the function \(\psi\) of step 4 of the proof of the fundamental lemma 4.37. In steps 5 to 7 of that proof we showed that it is differentiable at every real number and that its derivative is continuous. On the interval \((\alpha, \beta)\) the derivative equals \(2\,(t - \alpha)\,(\beta - t)\,(\alpha + \beta - 2t)\), at the points \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and outside the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\) it is zero.
  2. The partial derivative of the function \(\varphi\) with respect to \(x\) is \(p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}'(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,p_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\), because in differentiating with respect to \(x\) the other two factors are constant (lemma 1.79, item 2). Each of the three factors is a continuous function of one coordinate and therefore a continuous function of the point, since a coordinate of the point \(Q\) differs from the coordinate of the point \(P\) by at most the distance \(|PQ|\). By corollary 1.67, item 1, the partial derivative is therefore a continuous function of the point. The same holds for the partial derivatives with respect to \(y\) and \(z\). The function \(\varphi\) is therefore continuously differentiable in all of space (definition 1.88).

2. Box.

  1. Suppose that \(g(P) \ne 0\) at some point \(P\) of the set \(D\), say \(g(P) > 0\). If \(g(P) < 0\), we proceed in the same way with the function \(-g\), which satisfies the hypothesis too, because the integral is multiplied by \(-1\) when the function is multiplied by \(-1\).
  2. The function \(g\) is continuous at \(P\). By definition 1.65 with the error \(\eta = g(P)/2\) there is \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|g(Q) - g(P)| < g(P)/2\), so \(g(Q) > g(P)/2\), for every point \(Q\) of the set \(D\) with \(|PQ| < \delta_1\). Since \(D\) is open, there is \(r_1 > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(r_1\) from \(P\) are in \(D\). Let \(r\) be smaller than the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(r_1\).
  3. Let \(K\) be the box with centre \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) and edge \(r\), so \(\alpha_1 = x_{\mathrm{P}} - r/2\), \(\beta_1 = x_{\mathrm{P}} + r/2\) and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\). Every point \(Q\) of the box \(K\) is at a distance of at most \(\sqrt{3\,(r/2)^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,r < r\) from \(P\) by (1.10). The box therefore lies in \(D\), and at every one of its points \(g(Q) > g(P)/2\).
  4. Let \(\varphi\) be the product of the three bumps of the box \(K\), as in item 1. In \(K\), \(\varphi \ge 0\), so \(g\,\varphi \ge \tfrac12\,g(P)\,\varphi\) at every point of \(K\).
  5. The integral over a box is an iterated integral (definition 4.8), and each of the three iterated integrals is monotone (lemma 3.38, item 4), so
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V \ge \frac{g(P)}{2} \int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  6. We integrate a product of three functions, each depending on a single coordinate, step by step. In integrating over \(x\) the factors depending on \(y\) and \(z\) are constant and we take them out (lemma 3.38, item 1), and likewise for \(y\). Therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \cdot \int_{\alpha_2}^{\beta_2} p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y \cdot \int_{\alpha_3}^{\beta_3} p_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\,\mathrm{d}z .\]
  7. Each of the three integrals is positive. Let \(\ell = \beta - \alpha\). On the middle half of the interval, from \(\alpha + \ell/4\) to \(\beta - \ell/4\), both factors \(t - \alpha\) and \(\beta - t\) are at least \(\ell/4\), so there \(p_{\alpha\beta}(t) \ge (\ell/4)^4\). Elsewhere on \([\alpha, \beta]\), \(p_{\alpha\beta} \ge 0\). By additivity and the bound of the integral (lemma 3.38, items 2 and 3) we therefore have \(\int_\alpha^\beta p_{\alpha\beta}\,\mathrm{d}t \ge \tfrac{\ell}{2}\,(\ell/4)^4 > 0\). The exact value is \(\ell^5/30\).
  8. By steps 5 to 7, \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V > 0\). The box \(K\) lies in \(D\), so by the hypothesis this integral is zero. This is a contradiction, so \(g(P) = 0\).

3. Rectangle.

  1. Let \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, c)\) be a point of the rectangle \(R\) that does not lie on its edge, so \(a_1 < x_{\mathrm{P}} < b_1\) and \(a_2 < y_{\mathrm{P}} < b_2\), and suppose that \(f(P) > 0\). As in steps 2 and 3 of item 2 we find a square with centre \(P\) and side \(r\) that lies in \(R\) and does not reach its edge, and on which \(f > f(P)/2\). Here the distance of the corners from \(P\) is \(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\,r < r\).
  2. As in steps 4 to 8 of item 2, only with two factors instead of three, the integral of the hypothesis for this square is positive, which is a contradiction. Therefore \(f = 0\) at every point of \(R\) that does not lie on the edge.
  3. Let \(Q\) be a point on the edge of \(R\) and \(C\) the centre of the rectangle. The points \(Q + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{QC}\) for \(n = 2, 3, \dots\) do not lie on the edge and converge to \(Q\). At them \(f = 0\) by step 2, so by lemma 1.66 on continuity through sequences of points \(f(Q) = 0\) too.

Source: EP Lemma 3.1 and (3.5.22), (3.5.23) (pp. 140-141) for functions of one variable, with a different proof. The bump in a box and the proof are not from the sources.

For each box the lemma needed only a single bump, the product of three functions \(p_{\alpha\beta}\). A single one was enough, because we chose the box so small that the function \(g\) was positive everywhere in it, while the bump was zero outside it. Item 1 will ensure that a virtual displacement made from the bump is continuously differentiable, and so kinematically admissible.

Theorem 4.44 Converse of the principle of virtual displacements (obrat načela virtualnih pomikov)

Let the body \(V\), the parts of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the prescribed force \(\bar{\vek t}\) and the body force \(\vek b\) be as in theorem 4.42. Let the stress components be continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface, and let the stress be symmetric at every point. If the equation (4.27) holds for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement, then

  1. the equilibrium equations (2.31) hold at every interior point of the body,
  2. on every outer face that belongs to the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of that face.
Proof

We must show two items. We compare the equation (4.27) with lemma 4.41 and get an integral that is zero for every admissible virtual displacement. Then we choose virtual displacements that are not zero only in a small box, first in the interior of the body and then next to the surface.

1. Equilibrium equations.

  1. For \(j = x, y, z\) let \(g_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} + b_{\mathrm{j}}\). These are the left-hand sides of the equilibrium equations (2.31), and the functions \(g_{\mathrm{j}}\) are continuous on the body, because the partial derivatives of the stress are continuous and \(\vek b\) is continuous.
  2. Let \(\delta\vek u\) be a kinematically admissible virtual displacement. By lemma 4.41 on the internal virtual work through the surface, (4.26) holds, and by the hypothesis (4.27) holds. The left side is the same in both equations, so the right sides are equal. We split the surface integral into the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), which is zero because \(\delta\vek u = \vek 0\) there, and the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). Moving all terms to one side we get
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} g_{\mathrm{j}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \big(\bar{\vek t} - \ten\sigma\,\vek n\big)\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 .\]
    This holds for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement.
  3. Let \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) be a box that lies in the set of interior points of the body, and \(\varphi\) the product of its three bumps from lemma 4.43. Take \(\delta\vek u = (\varphi, 0, 0)\). By item 1 of the lemma this field is continuously differentiable in all of space. Outside \(K\) it is zero, and the points of \(K\) are interior points of the body, so \(\delta\vek u\) is zero at every point of the surface, in particular on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). It is therefore a kinematically admissible virtual displacement, and the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) of step 2 is zero for it.
  4. We add the planes \(x = \alpha_1\), \(x = \beta_1\), \(y = \alpha_2\), \(y = \beta_2\), \(z = \alpha_3\) and \(z = \beta_3\) to the grid of the body. By lemma 4.12 the integral over the body does not change, and in the new grid the box \(K\) is a union of cells. On the cells outside \(K\), \(\varphi = 0\), so the integrals over them are zero, and by lemma 4.10, item 3, the integrals over the cells in \(K\) add up to the integral over \(K\). Step 2 therefore reads \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} g_{\mathrm{x}}\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).
  5. The set of interior points of the body is open (section 1.15), and \(g_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous on it. Step 4 holds for every box in it, so by lemma 4.43, item 2, \(g_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) at every interior point of the body.
  6. In the same way, with \(\delta\vek u = (0, \varphi, 0)\) and \(\delta\vek u = (0, 0, \varphi)\), we get \(g_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(g_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The equations \(g_{\mathrm{x}} = g_{\mathrm{y}} = g_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) are the equilibrium equations (2.31).

2. The condition on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\).

  1. By item 1, \(g_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) at every interior point, and, as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 4.42, by continuity also at every point of the surface. The volume integral of step 2 of item 1 is therefore zero for every admissible virtual displacement, and what remains is
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \big(\bar{\vek t} - \ten\sigma\,\vek n\big)\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 .\]
  2. Let \(R = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2]\) in the plane \(z = c\) be one of the outer faces that belong to the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and let its outward normal be \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), so the body lies below it. For faces with another normal we proceed in the same way, only with the roles of the coordinates swapped or with a sign. Choose numbers \(a_1 < \alpha_1 < \beta_1 < b_1\) and \(a_2 < \alpha_2 < \beta_2 < b_2\). Since the body consists of finitely many boxes and there is no material above \(R\), there is \(d > 0\) such that the box \([\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [c - d, c]\) lies in the body, while the box \([\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [c, c + d]\) lies outside the body except for its bottom face (figure 4.40).
  3. For a chosen \(j\) let \(\delta u_{\mathrm{j}} = p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,\chi(z)\), where \(\chi(z) = p_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{d},\,\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{d}}(z)/d^4\), and let the other two components be zero. By item 1 of lemma 4.43 this field is continuously differentiable in all of space. It is different from zero only in the interior of the box \([\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [c - d, c + d]\). This box meets the surface of the body only in the rectangle \([\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2]\) in the plane \(z = c\), which lies in \(R\), so in \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). The field is therefore zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement.
  4. On all other outer faces of the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the virtual displacement is zero by step 3, and on the face \(R\) it is different from zero only inside the rectangle \([\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2]\). When we cut \(R\) with the lines \(x = \alpha_1\), \(x = \beta_1\), \(y = \alpha_2\) and \(y = \beta_2\), the integral of step 1 therefore equals, by lemma 4.10, item 3, for a rectangle, the integral over this rectangle. In the plane \(z = c\), \(\chi(c) = d^2 \cdot d^2/d^4 = 1\), so
    \[\int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} \int_{\alpha_2}^{\beta_2} \big(\bar t_{\mathrm{j}} - (\ten\sigma\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\,p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 .\]
  5. The function \(\bar t_{\mathrm{j}} - (\ten\sigma\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{j}}\) is continuous on \(R\), because \(\bar{\vek t}\) and the stress are continuous. Step 4 holds for all numbers of step 2, so by lemma 4.43, item 3, \(\bar t_{\mathrm{j}} = (\ten\sigma\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{j}}\) at every point of \(R\). This holds for \(j = x, y, z\), so \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on all of \(R\).

Source: SADD (6.5.7)-(6.5.9) (PDF pp. 138-139), EP (4.2.4)-(4.2.6) (p. 169), BOWER §2.4.4.2 (PDF pp. 86-88) and §2.4.6 (PDF p. 90). The sources conclude that the expressions under the integrals are zero because the virtual displacement is arbitrary. The proof with bumps is not from the sources.

The converse does not give the symmetry of stress, it assumes it. Only the virtual strain, which is symmetric, appears in the internal virtual work, so the equation does not see the antisymmetric part of the stress at all. BOWER too assumes the symmetry before writing the principle (BOWER, PDF p. 85). The second condition of equilibrium is thus built into the principle through the fact that the virtual strain stands in it, while the first condition follows from the equation. For a body with a curved surface the sources prove the converse differently. BOWER, for example, chooses a virtual displacement that inside the body is proportional to the left-hand sides of the equilibrium equations and zero on the surface, which also needs second derivatives of the stress (BOWER, PDF pp. 87-88).

4.4.6 Two tests

The cube in pure shear. Let us restate the setting. A steel cube with edge \(h = 10\) mm is glued to a table with its bottom face. The origin is at the corner \(A\) at the bottom front left, the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) into the depth, the axis \(z\) up. We push the top face to the right, pull the right face up and the left face down, all with the force \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa per unit area, and the front and back faces are free. The stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\) everywhere, the other components are zero, and we do not take the weight into account (figure 4.41, left). As the virtual displacement take the admissible field \(\delta\vek u = (\gamma z, 0, 0)\), which moves the top face by \(\gamma h\) to the right and the bottom face not at all.

  1. The virtual strain is \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \gamma/2\), the others are zero, as we computed in section 4.4.2. In the double sum only the terms with the pair \(x\), \(z\) remain:
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = 2\,\tau_0\,\frac{\gamma}{2} = \tau_0\,\gamma .\]
  2. This number is the same at all points of the cube, so the internal virtual work equals this number times the volume of the cube, \(\tau_0\,\gamma\,h^3\) (lemma 4.10 on the properties of the integral over a box, item 2).
  3. There is no body force, so the external virtual work is done only by the prescribed forces on the five faces of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). On the top face, where \(z = h\), \(\bar{\vek t} = \tau_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\delta\vek u = (\gamma h, 0, 0)\), so \(\bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u = \tau_0\,\gamma h\) at every point of the face, and the integral over the face of area \(h^2\) is \(\tau_0\,\gamma\,h^3\).
  4. On the right face \(\bar{\vek t} = \tau_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), on the left one \(-\tau_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The virtual displacement, however, has only an \(x\) component, so \(\bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u = 0\) on both. On the front and back faces \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\).
  5. The external virtual work is therefore \(\tau_0\,\gamma\,h^3\), equal to the internal one.

With numbers, for \(\gamma = 0{,}001\): the force on the top face is \(\tau_0\,h^2 = 50 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 5000\) N, the face moves by \(\gamma h = 10\) µm, and the work is \(5000\ \text{N} \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{m} = 0{,}05\) J. That is also \(\tau_0\,\gamma\,h^3 = 50 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 0{,}001 \cdot 10^{-6}\) J. The work of the force pushing the top face goes into the work of the stresses on the virtual shear of every piece of the cube. We notice one more thing. This field has the shape of the true field of the sheared cube, but the stress of \(50\) MPa is not the stress that would cause such a displacement. By section 3.2.5 that would be \(75{,}38\) MPa. The principle does not care, because in it the stress and the virtual displacement are not connected.

What goes wrong with a field that is not admissible? Take the move of the whole cube, \(\delta\vek u = (\delta a, 0, 0)\) (figure 4.41, right). The virtual strain is zero, so the internal virtual work is zero. The external virtual work over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), however, is the work of the force on the top face, \(\tau_0\,h^2\,\delta a\), and on the right and left faces the work is zero. For \(\delta a = 1\) µm this is \(5000\ \text{N} \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m} = 0{,}005\) J, not zero, and the equation (4.27) does not hold. Missing is the work of the force of the glue, which pulls the bottom face to the left with the force \(\tau_0\,h^2\) and does \(-\tau_0\,h^2\,\delta a = -0{,}005\) J. With it the sum would be zero, which is the first condition of equilibrium of the whole cube in the direction of the axis \(x\). Since in general we do not know the forces of the supports, we remove them by not allowing virtual displacements to move anything on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\).

The hanging bar. Let us restate the setting. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a round cross section of area \(A = 78{,}54\) mm² hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points down from the centre \(O\) of the top face. A force spread evenly over the top face, \(\rho g L\) per unit area, pulls it up, which is an idealization, the point \(O\) is fixed only against a motion of the bar as a whole, and the lateral surface and the bottom face are free. The only stress component that is not zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\), the body force is \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and \(\rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m, while the weight of the bar is \(W = \rho g A L = 60{,}10\) N. As the virtual displacement take

\[\delta\vek u = (\delta_0 + \kappa x^2,\ 0,\ 0) , \qquad \delta_0 = 1\ \text{µm} , \qquad \kappa = 10^{-8}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

The top face moves down by \(\delta_0 = 1\) µm, the bottom face by \(\delta_0 + \kappa L^2 = 2\) µm (figure 4.42). Since \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty, the field is admissible.

  1. The only partial derivative that is not zero is \(\partial\,\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2\kappa x\), so \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2\kappa x\), and the other virtual strains are zero. Of the nine terms of the double sum a single one remains: \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2\rho g\kappa\,x\,(L - x)\).
  2. This function depends only on \(x\). The integral over the bar is therefore the area of the cross section times the integral over \(x\). For a bar with a rectangular cross section, as treated by CM (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305), the bar is a box, and this follows from theorem 4.9, because integrating a constant function over \(y\) and \(z\) gives the area of the cross section. For the round bar we compute the integral with the cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\) of section 4.2.6 (definition 4.21). In every piece \(x\) is the outer variable, so the two inner integrals of a function that depends only on \(x\) give this function times the area of the cross section of the piece, and the areas of the pieces add up to \(A\) (section 4.2.8).
  3. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, with the function \(L x^2/2 - x^3/3\), whose derivative is \(L x - x^2\), the internal virtual work is therefore
    \[\begin{aligned} A \int_0^L 2\rho g\kappa\,(L x - x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x &= 2\rho g\kappa A \Big(\frac{L^3}{2} - \frac{L^3}{3}\Big) = \frac{\rho g\kappa A L^3}{3} \\ &= \frac{6{,}010 \cdot 10^{-8} \cdot 1000}{3}\ \text{J} = 2{,}003 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{J} . \end{aligned}\]
  4. The work of the body force is
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho g\,(\delta_0 + \kappa x^2)\,\mathrm{d}V &= \rho g A \Big(\delta_0 L + \frac{\kappa L^3}{3}\Big) \\ &= 6{,}010 \cdot \big(10^{-5} + 3{,}333 \cdot 10^{-6}\big)\ \text{J} = 8{,}013 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{J} . \end{aligned}\]
  5. On the top face, where \(x = 0\), \(\bar{\vek t} = -\rho g L\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\delta\vek u = (\delta_0, 0, 0)\), so \(\bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u = -\rho g L\,\delta_0\) at every point of the face. The integral over the face of area \(A\) is \(-\rho g A L\,\delta_0 = -W\,\delta_0 = -6{,}010 \cdot 10^{-5}\) J. On the lateral surface and on the bottom face \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\).
  6. The external virtual work is \(8{,}013 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{J} - 6{,}010 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{J} = 2{,}003 \cdot 10^{-5}\) J, equal to the internal one.

The pattern in the numbers deserves an explanation. The virtual displacement has two parts. The part \(\delta_0\) moves the whole bar in the same way. For it the virtual strain is zero, and the work of the weight, \(W\,\delta_0\), exactly cancels the work of the pull on the top face, \(-W\,\delta_0\). This is the first condition of equilibrium of the whole bar: the upward pull equals the weight. The part \(\kappa x^2\) does not move the top face, so the pull does no work there, and the work of the weight on this part, \(\rho g\kappa A L^3/3\), is exactly the internal virtual work. Why is the function in the figure largest in the middle? The stress \(\rho g\,(L - x)\) is largest at the top, where it carries the whole bar, and the virtual strain \(2\kappa x\) at the bottom, where the stretching of the imagined field is largest. Their product is zero at both ends and largest in between, at \(x = L/2\).

What is three-dimensional about the bar? Of the nine products in the internal virtual work only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) remained, because the other stress components are zero. If we added components \(\delta u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\delta u_{\mathrm{z}}\) to the virtual displacement, nothing would change. In the internal work no stress sees them, the body force has no \(y\) and \(z\) components, and the lateral surface is free. When \(\delta u_{\mathrm{x}}\) depends only on \(x\), the integral over the cross section, \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \rho g A\,(L - x)\), is the axial force \(N(x)\), and the internal virtual work is \(\int_0^L N\,\delta u'\,\mathrm{d}x\), exactly the left side of the principle for the bar from section 4.3. The principle for the bar is thus a special case of the principle for a body.

4.4.7 What the principle says

We now have the equilibrium of a body written in two equivalent ways, which theorems 4.42 and 4.44 connect. The first way is the equations at every point: the equilibrium equations in the interior and \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). The second way is one equation for all admissible virtual displacements, the equality of internal and external virtual work. Books call the second the weak form (šibka oblika) of equilibrium (BOWER §8.1.2, PDF p. 496). The word weak says that it asks less differentiability of the solution: there are no derivatives of the stress in the equation, only first partial derivatives of the virtual displacement (EP §6.3.6.2, p. 323). BOWER adds that for a computer this is exactly what matters, because derivatives are hard to compute accurately while integrals are easy (BOWER, PDF p. 87). The finite element method requires the virtual work equation only for finitely many chosen virtual displacements and gets from it a system of equations for the unknown displacements. We will see this in chapters 6 and 7.

Where does the principle in this form not hold? Where one of the assumptions from the beginning of the section fails.

  • For large deformations we may not identify the shapes before and after loading. BOWER writes the principle with stresses referred to the original shape, of the kind we met in section 2.13, and with integrals over the body before loading, where the virtual strain is replaced by a virtual change of the deformation gradient or of the Green-Lagrange tensor (BOWER §2.4.5, PDF pp. 88-89).
  • For a body that accelerates, the equilibrium equations are no longer satisfied. The right side of the equilibrium equations then holds the density times the acceleration (section 2.7), and the virtual work equation gets the additional term \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho\,\vek a\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V\), where \(\vek a\) is the acceleration (BOWER, PDF p. 86). We can think of the force \(-\rho\,\vek a\) per unit volume as one more body force, which is d'Alembert's form of dynamics (GR (1.1), PDF p. 32). We will use this in chapter 8.
  • Where the stress is not continuously differentiable, for example at a point force or at the contact of two materials, we may not use the divergence theorem in our form on the whole body.
  • The stress must be symmetric. Bodies with distributed moments that are not moments of forces were already excluded in section 2.8.

The principle holds for every material, because we took the stress as given. How, then, do we find the stresses and displacements? Only when we express the stresses by the displacements, with the relation between stresses and strains from chapter 3, does the virtual work equation become an equation for the unknown displacement field. For the ideal elastic material of section 3.6, in the next section we will take as the virtual displacement the difference of two displacement fields that respect the supports and get from the principle a number that is smallest for the true displacement field.

4.5 Minimum total potential energy

In section 4.4 we wrote the equilibrium of a body as one single equation, the principle of virtual displacements. In the derivation we used no relation between stress and strain, so it holds for every material. In section 3.6, however, we met materials that store the work needed for a deformation and return all of it on unloading. What does the principle of virtual displacements say for a body made of such a material? It says something that fits into one sentence: among all shapes that the supports allow, the body comes to rest in the one for which a certain number, the sum of the stored energy and the potential energy of the loads, is smallest. So we can also find the equilibrium by looking for a smallest value.

The goal of the section is to state this claim precisely, to prove it, and to show what it is good for. It is good for three things. First, it gives a new way of computing displacements. Instead of writing the equilibrium for every part of a structure separately, we look for the smallest value of one single function. For the bracket of two bars from section 4.1 this will be a function of two numbers, the horizontal and the vertical displacement of the joint, and its smallest value will give the displacement of the joint without knowing the bar forces first. Second, it gives approximate solutions. When we cannot compute the true displacement field, we try a family of simple fields and choose the one with the smallest energy. The Ritz method and the finite element method, which we will meet in chapters 6 and 7, rest on this idea. Third, it tells how force is related to energy. The force on a structure is the derivative of the strain energy with respect to the displacement of the point it acts on. This relation bears Castigliano's name.

The physical model is the same as in section 4.4, with additions about the material and the loads. Let us list all assumptions and say for each where we use it.

  1. The body is at rest, the strains are small, and we compute all quantities on the shape of the body before loading, the strain with the small strain tensor (definition 1.113). This is how the principle of virtual displacements is written, and all proofs of the section stand on it.
  2. The material is ideal elastic (definition 3.42) and linear elastic. So the stress components are linear functions of the strain components, and the material stiffness matrix is symmetric (theorem 3.46). The strain energy density is therefore half the sum of the products of stresses and strains, \(w = \tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (theorem 3.46, item 2). We use this when we express the energy of a body in equilibrium by the work of the loads, and in the proof of the principle.
  3. The strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero. This is the assumption about a stable material from section 3.6, which for an isotropic material is equivalent to a positive bulk modulus and a positive shear modulus (theorem 3.47). We use it in the proof that the energy of the true field is smallest.
  4. The loads do not change with the deformation, neither in size nor in direction. Weight is such a load. What this means and why it is needed we say in subsection 4.5.3, where we use the assumption.
  5. Supports prescribe the displacements on a part of the surface. In the first theorem of the section we assume that these displacements are zero, as for a face that is glued or welded to an immovable wall.
  6. The displacement fields are continuously differentiable (definition 1.88), and the stresses of the true field have continuous partial derivatives, as the principle of virtual displacements requires.

The route is this. First, on a vertical bar with a load, where everything depends on one number, we show what potential energy is and why it is smallest in equilibrium. Then we derive from the principle of virtual displacements a theorem which says that the energy a body stores in equilibrium is half the work the loads would do if they were at full value all the time. The precise definition of the number we compare and the proof of the principle follow. We test the principle on the bracket of two bars, show how it is related to the principle of virtual displacements, and derive from it that a force is the derivative of the energy with respect to a displacement. At the end we test on the hanging bar what the energy of simple trial fields gives, fields that are not the true field.

4.5.1 A bar with a load

Let us start with the simplest body we know. We stand the steel bar from section 4.1 upright, with length \(L = 10\) m and a round cross section of diameter 10 mm and area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\). Its upper end is fixed to the ceiling so that it does not move. On its lower end we hang a load that weighs \(F = 10\) kN (figure 4.43). We neglect the weight of the bar, 60,10 N, because it is only 0,6 % of the weight of the load. The stress in the bar is then \(F/A = 127{,}3\) MPa, below the yield stress 220 MPa, so the force with which the bar pulls the load up is proportional to the elongation \(e\). This force is \(k\,e\), where \(k = EA/L = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, as in section 4.1, and \(E = 196\) GPa is Young's modulus of steel. The upper end is at rest, so the elongation \(e\) is also the downward displacement of the lower end. The bar acts as a spring whose state is described by one single number, \(e\).

Where does the load come to rest? The load is in equilibrium when the bar pulls it up with a force as large as the weight pulls it down, \(k\,e = F\), so at the elongation

\[\Delta L = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{10\,000\ \text{N}}{1{,}539 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m}} = 6{,}496\ \text{mm} .\]

We got there with forces. Now let us answer the same question with energy. Imagine that we hold the lower end with the load by hand at some elongation \(e\), not necessarily \(\Delta L\) (figure 4.43). The bar pulls the load up with the force \(k\,e\), the weight pulls it down with the force \(F\), and the hand must add the difference \(F - k\,e\) upward. At \(e = 0\) the hand carries the whole load, at \(e = \Delta L/2\) half of it, since \(k\,\Delta L/2 = F/2\), and at \(e = \Delta L\) nothing. All these states are possible, since in all of them the bar is fixed to the ceiling, but without the hand only the last one is in equilibrium. In each state the bar is stretched evenly, because only the two forces at its ends act on it. To each state we assign two energies.

The first is the strain energy of the bar. In section 4.1 we showed that the force that stretches the bar slowly to the elongation \(\Delta L\) does the work \(\tfrac12 k\,\Delta L^2\), and that the bar stores it as strain energy (theorem 4.3). The same statement holds for every final elongation, so at the elongation \(e\) the strain energy of the bar is \(U(e) = \tfrac12 k\,e^2\).

The second is the energy of the load. When the load is lowered by \(e\), the weight does the work \(F\,e\) on it, because it is a constant force pointing along the path, and its work is the product of force and path (definition 4.1). The load could pass this work on, for example by lifting another body over a pulley. When we lift the load back, however, we have to put the same work in ourselves. So the load holds a store of work that lowering uses up and lifting restores. This store is called the potential energy (potencialna energija) of the load. Only its change matters, so we choose it to be zero at \(e = 0\). At the elongation \(e\) the load is lower by \(e\), the weight has done the work \(F\,e\), and the potential energy of the load is \(-F\,e\). This is the school rule that the potential energy of a body equals its weight times its height, except that here the height is measured from the starting position and is therefore negative. EP uses the same example, a spring with a weight, to show that the work of the constant force of the load is not equal to the work of the internal force of the spring (EP §3.1.2, pp. 99-100).

The sum of the two energies is

\[\Pi(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2 - F\,e . \tag{4.28}\]

The table shows it for five states. The energies are in joules, computed with \(k\) and \(F\) above.

elongation \(e\) \(U(e) = \tfrac12 k\,e^2\) \(-F\,e\) \(\Pi(e)\)
\(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)
\(\Delta L/2 = 3{,}248\) mm \(8{,}120\) \(-32{,}48\) \(-24{,}36\)
\(\Delta L = 6{,}496\) mm \(32{,}48\) \(-64{,}96\) \(-32{,}48\)
\(3\Delta L/2 = 9{,}744\) mm \(73{,}08\) \(-97{,}44\) \(-24{,}36\)
\(2\Delta L = 12{,}99\) mm \(129{,}9\) \(-129{,}9\) \(0\)

The table shows three patterns (figure 4.44). The sum \(\Pi\) is smallest at \(e = \Delta L\), exactly at equilibrium. The values at elongations equally far to the left and to the right of \(\Delta L\) are equal, at \(\Delta L/2\) and at \(3\Delta L/2\) it is \(-24{,}36\) J. At \(2\Delta L\) the sum is zero again, as at the start. Where does all this come from? Let us rewrite the sum so that it shows how it depends on the distance from \(\Delta L\).

  1. We expand the square of the difference as the product \((e - \Delta L)(e - \Delta L)\): we multiply every term of the first bracket by every term of the second and get \(e^2 - 2\,e\,\Delta L + \Delta L^2\). Therefore
    \[\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2 = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2 - k\,\Delta L\,e + \tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2 .\]
  2. The equilibrium elongation satisfies \(k\,\Delta L = F\). So the middle term is \(k\,\Delta L\,e = F\,e\), and the last one is \(\tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2 = \tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\).
  3. From step 1 we express \(\tfrac12\,k\,e^2 - F\,e\) and insert step 2:
    \[\Pi(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2 - \tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L . \tag{4.29}\]

The first term is half the positive number \(k\) times a square, so it is never negative and is zero only at \(e = \Delta L\). The second term does not depend on \(e\). The sum is therefore smallest at \(e = \Delta L\), where \(\Pi(\Delta L) = -\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L = -32{,}48\) J. The first term depends only on the distance \(|e - \Delta L|\), so the values at \(\Delta L/2\) and \(3\Delta L/2\) are equal. At \(e = 2\Delta L\) the distance is again \(\Delta L\), the first term is \(\tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2 = \tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\) and cancels the second to zero. But the first term is one more thing: the strain energy the bar would have if it were stretched by the difference \(e - \Delta L\). By how much the energy of a state exceeds the energy of equilibrium is thus told by the strain energy of the difference of the two elongations. This will be the core of the proof for every body.

Why is the smallest value exactly at equilibrium? By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.79) the derivative of \(\Pi\) with respect to \(e\) is \(k\,e - F\), the force with which the bar pulls the load up, minus the weight of the load. This is the negative of the force \(F - k\,e\) that the hand has to add. For \(e < \Delta L\) the derivative is negative. The weight overcomes the bar, and a load that the hand lets go starts to move down, toward smaller energy. For \(e > \Delta L\) the derivative is positive, the bar overcomes the weight, and the load starts to move up, again toward smaller energy. Without the hand the load is in equilibrium only where the derivative is zero, and that is at \(e = \Delta L\), where \(\Pi\) has its smallest value.

And what does the smallest value itself, \(-\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\), mean? In equilibrium the load is lower by \(\Delta L\) than at the start, the weight has done the work \(F\,\Delta L = 64{,}96\) J, but the bar stores only \(\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L = 32{,}48\) J (figure 4.45). Where did the other half go? It depends on how we lower the load. If we lower it slowly by hand, the hand pushes up with the force \(F - k\,e\) all the time, while the load moves down. The force of the hand and the displacement point in opposite directions, so the hand does negative work. The function \(F\,e - \tfrac12\,k\,e^2\) has the derivative \(F - k\,e\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39 the work of the hand is

\[-\int_0^{\Delta L} (F - k\,e)\,\mathrm{d}e = -\Big(F\,\Delta L - \tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2\Big) = -\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L ,\]

where we used \(k\,\Delta L = F\). So the hand receives exactly the other half, the grey triangle in figure 4.45. If instead we let the load go suddenly at \(e = 0\), the hand receives nothing, and the difference goes into motion. In section 4.1 we saw that the load then slides past \(\Delta L\), stops only at \(2\,\Delta L\) when there is no damping, and oscillates about \(\Delta L\) (CK §5.1, PDF p. 137). At \(2\,\Delta L\) the energy \(\Pi\) is zero again, as at the start, so the zero in the last row of the table is no coincidence: there the strain energy of the bar uses up exactly the work of the weight.

The bar with a load has shown the idea that we now carry over to a body. We compare all states that the supports allow, not only the equilibrium one. To each state we assign the sum of the strain energy and the potential energy of the loads. The equilibrium state has the smallest sum, and the difference to every other state is the strain energy of the difference of the displacements, \(\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2\). We also saw that the strain energy in equilibrium is half the work the weight would do over the whole displacement. Let us start with this observation.

4.5.2 Clapeyron's theorem

Let us return to the body from section 4.4 and repeat the setting. Before loading the body occupies the set of points \(V\) with surface \(S\). On the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface there are supports that prescribe the displacements. On the rest of the surface, \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) with which the surroundings act on the body is prescribed. On the free parts of the surface \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). A body force with density \(\vek b\) (definition 2.25) acts on the material, for example the weight. The stresses in the body are continuously differentiable, symmetric, satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.31) in the interior and Cauchy's formula \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal. The principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.42) then says that

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\]

for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement \(\delta\vek u\), that is for every continuously differentiable field that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (definition 4.39). Here \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the components of its virtual strain, and the indices \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

In section 4.1 we got the strain energy of a bar by multiplying the energy density \(w\) by the area of the cross section and integrating along the length. In a body that is not a bar the energy density changes in all three directions. A small piece of the body with volume \(\Delta V\) at the point \(P\) stores approximately \(w(P)\,\Delta V\). The energy of the body is the sum of the energies of its pieces, and when we shrink the pieces, the sum becomes an integral over the body (section 4.2).

Definition 4.45 Strain energy of a body (deformacijska energija telesa)

Let a body occupy the set of points \(V\), and let the material be ideal elastic at every point, with a strain energy density \(w\) (definition 3.43) that is a continuous function of the point on \(V\). The strain energy (deformacijska energija) of the body is the number

\[U = \int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

Source: EP (3.2.8) (p. 106) and (4.3.4) (p. 180), SADD §6.1 (PDF pp. 128-131), CM (7.6.11) (PDF p. 345).

Let us test the definition on the bar pulled at its end with the force 10 kN. The energy density is the same in the whole bar, \(w = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon = 4{,}136 \cdot 10^4\ \text{J/m}^3\) (section 4.1), the volume of the bar is \(A L = 7{,}854 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3\), and by the rule for the integral of a constant function over the round bar (section 4.2.8) \(U = 4{,}136 \cdot 10^4\ \text{J/m}^3 \cdot 7{,}854 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3 = 32{,}48\) J, as it should be.

For the bar with a load the strain energy in equilibrium was half the product of the weight of the load and the displacement, \(\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\). Does this hold for every body? It does, and the proof is short, because the principle of virtual displacements does all the work.

Theorem 4.46 Clapeyron's theorem (Clapeyronov izrek)

Let the body be as in theorem 4.42 on the principle of virtual displacements, made of an ideal elastic and linear elastic material. Let \(\vek u\) be the displacement field of the body in equilibrium, continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface and equal to zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and let its stresses satisfy assumptions 1 to 4 of theorem 4.42. Then the strain energy of the body is half the work that the body force and the prescribed force on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) would do on the displacements \(\vek u\) if they were at full value all the time:

\[2\,U = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.30}\]
Proof

We have to show that the two sides of the principle of virtual displacements become the two sides of equation (4.30) when we take the true displacement field as the virtual displacement.

  1. The field \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body with its surface, and it is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so it is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.39). In the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.42) we may therefore take \(\delta\vek u = \vek u\).
  2. The virtual strain of the field \(\delta\vek u = \vek u\) is the small strain tensor of the body in equilibrium, because both are computed from the same partial derivatives, \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The left side of the principle is therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  3. The material is ideal elastic and linear elastic, so by theorem 3.46 on the symmetry of the elastic constants, item 2, at every point \(\sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\,w\).
  4. By the linearity of the integral over a body (section 4.2) the integral of the function \(2\,w\) is twice the integral of \(w\). The left side is therefore \(2\int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,\mathrm{d}V = 2\,U\) (definition 4.45).
  5. The right side of the principle at \(\delta\vek u = \vek u\) is \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\). The two sides are equal, which is (4.30).

Source: EP Theorem 4.6.1, (4.6.10) (pp. 220-221), SADD (6.4.1) (PDF p. 135), CM §7.4 (PDF pp. 314-321). EP and SADD prove the theorem directly with the divergence theorem. We got it from the principle of virtual displacements, which had already taken that step.

In the proof we took the true displacement as the virtual one. In section 4.3 a virtual displacement meant an imagined displacement with the forces unchanged, while the true displacement is the one the forces really cause. May we do this? We may, because as a mathematical statement the principle of virtual displacements asks only two things of the field \(\delta\vek u\): that it is continuously differentiable and that it is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The true field meets both, the first by assumption 6 at the start of the section, the second because the supports do not move. The principle does not ask the displacement to be small, because both sides are multiplied by the same number when the field is multiplied by a number (section 4.4).

Why half? The right side of equation (4.30) is the work the loads would do if they were as large during the whole motion as at its end, like the load on the bar. For the bar with a load this was \(F\,\Delta L = 64{,}96\) J, and the bar stored half of it. In slow loading, however, the loads grow from zero, and each does only half the product of final force and final displacement, like the force at the end of the bar in section 4.1. Clapeyron's theorem says that for every linear elastic body this work is stored completely. In section 4.1 we checked this for the bar and for the hanging bar and promised a proof for every body. Let us write it down.

Corollary 4.47 Work of the loads and strain energy (delo obremenitev in deformacijska energija)

Let the body, its material and the displacement field \(\vek u\) be as in theorem 4.46. Let the loads grow slowly from zero to their final values, all in the same proportion: at a number \(\lambda\) between \(0\) and \(1\) the body force is \(\lambda\,\vek b\) and the prescribed force on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is \(\lambda\,\bar{\vek t}\). Let the body take the state with displacements \(\lambda\,\vek u\) at every \(\lambda\). Then the work of the loads in this loading equals the strain energy of the body in the final state,

\[W_{\mathrm{zun}} = \tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A = U .\]
Proof

We have to show that every bit of the load does half the product of final force and final displacement, then write the sum as an integral and use Clapeyron's theorem.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of the body with \(\vek u(P) \ne \vek 0\). At the number \(\lambda\) its displacement is \(\lambda\,\vek u(P)\), so the point moves along a straight segment from its position before loading to its position after loading, in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek d = \vek u(P)/|\vek u(P)|\). When it has travelled the distance \(s\), \(\lambda = s/|\vek u(P)|\).
  2. A small piece with volume \(\Delta V\) at \(P\) is then acted on by the force approximately \(\lambda\,\vek b(P)\,\Delta V\). Its projection onto the direction of motion is \((s/|\vek u(P)|)\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek d\,\Delta V\). The function \(s^2/2\) has the derivative \(s\), so by item 2 of definition 4.1 and the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39 the work of this force is
    \[\int_0^{|\vek u(P)|} \frac{s}{|\vek u(P)|}\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek d\,\Delta V\,\mathrm{d}s = \tfrac12\,|\vek u(P)|\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek d\,\Delta V = \tfrac12\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek u(P)\,\Delta V .\]
    At \(\vek u(P) = \vek 0\) the piece does not move, the work is zero, and the formula gives the same.
  3. In the same way the prescribed force on a small patch with area \(\Delta A\) at a point \(P\) of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) does the work \(\tfrac12\,\bar{\vek t}(P)\cdot\vek u(P)\,\Delta A\). The forces of the supports on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) do no work, because \(\vek u = \vek 0\) there.
  4. We add up the works of the pieces and patches. The sums are Riemann sums of the functions \(\tfrac12\,\vek b\cdot\vek u\) and \(\tfrac12\,\bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\), which are continuous, and when we shrink the pieces they approach the integrals by theorem 4.9, item 1 (section 4.2). The work of the loads is therefore \(\tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  5. By Clapeyron's theorem 4.46 this is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 2\,U = U\).

Source: CM (7.4.4) (PDF p. 315), SADD §6.1 (PDF p. 128), EP p. 100. The step-by-step proof is not from the sources.

The corollary assumes that the body takes the state \(\lambda\,\vek u\) at every \(\lambda\). Why is this reasonable? Under the loads \(\lambda\,\vek b\) and \(\lambda\,\bar{\vek t}\) the field \(\lambda\,\vek u\) meets all the requirements of equilibrium. The stresses are linear functions of the strains, so the stresses of the field \(\lambda\,\vek u\) are \(\lambda\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The equilibrium equations and Cauchy's formula are linear, so \(\lambda\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) satisfy them with the loads \(\lambda\,\vek b\) and \(\lambda\,\bar{\vek t}\) when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) satisfy them with \(\vek b\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\). That the body takes exactly this state and not some other follows from item 2 of theorem 4.51, proved below, when the supports prevent every displacement without strain. We used the same argument for the hanging bar in section 4.1.

Let us test the theorem on the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m and cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points down from the top cross section. We describe it with the bar model from section 4.1, in which every cross section moves only down, by \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), while the top cross section does not move. The weight per unit length is \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m. In section 4.1 we computed \(U = 391{,}03\) µJ. The work of the weight over the whole displacement, if the weight were at full value all the time, is

\[\int_0^L q\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \rho g A\,a \int_0^L (2Lx - x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac23\,\rho g A\,a\,L^3 = 782{,}06\ \text{µJ} ,\]

where we computed the integral by the fundamental theorem of calculus with the function \(Lx^2 - x^3/3\), whose derivative is \(2Lx - x^2\). This is exactly \(2\,U\), as Clapeyron's theorem says. We saw the same equality, \(\int_0^L N\,u'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,u\,\mathrm{d}x\), for the hanging bar already in section 4.3, but there we did not connect it with energy. The bar model is not the body of the theorem, since it is described by one single function \(u(x)\). For it we get the theorem from the principle of virtual displacements for a bar (theorem 4.36), taking \(\delta u = u\) and the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\), with the same steps as above.

When does the theorem fail? First, when the supports prescribe displacements that are not zero, for example when we move one end of a bar by a chosen distance. Then the forces of the supports do work too, and the theorem holds if on the right we take, instead of the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the integral of the force per unit area \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) times the displacement over the whole surface \(S\) (EP (4.6.10), p. 221). Our proof does not cover this case, because the true field is then not zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and is not a kinematically admissible virtual displacement. Second, for a material that is not linear elastic, for example rubber, the energy density is not half the sum of the products of stresses and strains (section 3.6), and step 3 of the proof fails. Third, for large deformations, where the principle of virtual displacements does not hold in this form (section 4.4).

4.5.3 Total potential energy

For the bar with a load we compared the states that the supports allow. For a body we need the same: displacement fields that agree with the prescribed displacements at the supports and are arbitrary elsewhere. They need not be true, and the body need not be in equilibrium in them. For the bar such a state was every elongation \(e\) at which the hand held the load (figure 4.43).

Definition 4.48 Kinematically admissible displacement field (kinematično dopustno polje pomikov)

Let a body occupy the set of points \(V\) before loading, and let the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) be prescribed on the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of its surface. A displacement field \(\vek u\) is kinematically admissible (kinematično dopustno) if it is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface and equals the prescribed displacement at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\).

Source: EP (4.3.13) (p. 181), where the admissible fields satisfy \(\vek u = \hat{\vek u}\) on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{u}}\), CM (PDF p. 346), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139).

The word kinematically says here too that only displacements are involved, not forces. The requirement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) means that the field respects the supports. Continuous differentiability makes sure that the field has a small strain tensor at every point and with it a strain energy density. The difference of two kinematically admissible fields is continuously differentiable and equals \(\bar{\vek u} - \bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so it is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.39). We will need this in the proof.

Now we still need the potential energy of the loads. For the load on the bar we got it from the work of the weight, \(-F\,e\). There we used that the weight is the same at every elongation, so its work was the product of a constant force and the path. The same holds for every load that does not change with the deformation, neither in size nor in direction. Such a load is called a dead load (obremenitev, neodvisna od deformacije), and weight is the most important example. A constant force \(\vek F\) whose point of application moves by \(\vek u\) does the work \(\vek F\cdot\vek u\) on the straight path (definition 4.1), and the potential energy of such a force is \(-\vek F\cdot\vek u\). For the body force and for the prescribed force on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we add up the contributions of the pieces and patches and shrink them, as for the strain energy. The potential energy of the loads is therefore

\[-\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\]

(EP §3.3.1, p. 124).

Which loads are not like this? Water presses perpendicular to the surface it touches (section 2.6.6). When a wall under water tilts, the force of the water on it tilts too, so the direction of the load changes with the deformation. Similarly the force of a rope fastened to a point of the body and to a fixed point in the surroundings changes when the point of the body moves sideways. For small deformations these changes are small, and we treat the load as independent of the deformation. For large ones, however, such loads have no potential energy of this form. EP defines the potential energy of the loads only for forces that are independent of the deformation (EP §3.3.1, p. 124).

Definition 4.49 Total potential energy (celotna potencialna energija)

Let a body be made of an ideal elastic material with strain energy density \(w\), with the displacement prescribed on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), a body force with density \(\vek b\) and a prescribed force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where \(\vek b\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\) are independent of the deformation. The total potential energy (celotna potencialna energija) of the body at a kinematically admissible displacement field \(\vek u\) is the number

\[\Pi(\vek u) = U(\vek u) - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad U(\vek u) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,\mathrm{d}V , \tag{4.31}\]

where \(w\) at every point is computed from the components of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\) at that point.

Source: EP (3.3.1) (p. 124) and (4.3.7) (p. 180), CM (7.6.11)-(7.6.13) (PDF p. 345), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139), where \(\Pi = U_{\mathrm{T}} - W\).

What kind of object is \(\Pi\)? A function whose input is a whole displacement field and whose output is one number in joules. The function \(\Pi(e)\) of the bar with a load had one number as its input, because one number described the whole state. Here the input is a field that assigns a displacement to every point of the body. Books call such functions functionals (funkcionali) (CM, PDF p. 343). The first term is the strain energy of the body at the field \(\vek u\). The notation \(U(\vek u)\) says that the energy is computed from this field, which need not be the true one. The other two terms are the potential energy of the loads. For the bar with a load \(U(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2\) and the potential energy of the load is \(-F\,e\), so the definition gives \(\Pi(e)\) from equation (4.28).

4.5.4 The principle of minimum total potential energy

For the bar with a load the difference between the energy of a state and that of equilibrium was the strain energy of the difference, \(\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2\). For a body we will show the same. First we need a rule for how the strain energy density behaves for a sum of two strains. For the bar it was the expanded square \((e - \Delta L)^2\). For a body \(w\) is a sum of products of strain components, and we get the rule by expanding the products in the same way. We write the strain as the Voigt column of six components, as in section 3.6,

\[\{\varepsilon\} = (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}},\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}) ,\]

where \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are the engineering shear strains, and \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\ix{p}}\) is the entry of the column in place \(\ix{p}\), which runs from \(1\) to \(6\). We stack the stresses into the column \(\{\sigma\} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) without factors of two. For a symmetric stress with components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and another symmetric strain with components \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), whose column \(\{\eta\}\) we stack in the same way as \(\{\varepsilon\}\),

\[\begin{aligned} \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{zz}} \\ &\quad + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{yz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} , \end{aligned} \tag{4.32}\]

because in the double sum of nine terms every shear pair appears twice, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{yx}} = 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xy}}\), while in the column the factor two hides in the engineering shear strain.

Lemma 4.50 Energy density of a sum of strains (gostota energije vsote deformacij)

Let the material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic and linear elastic, with entries \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\) of the material stiffness matrix, and let \(\{\varepsilon\}\) and \(\{\eta\}\) be columns of six strain components that need not be small strains. For every such column \(\{\zeta\}\) let \(w(\{\zeta\}) = \tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}}\sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\zeta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\zeta\}_{\mathrm{q}}\), and let the stress that belongs to it be the column with the entries \(\sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\zeta\}_{\mathrm{q}}\). For a small strain these are the strain energy density (theorem 3.46, item 2) and the stress given by the material law. Then

\[w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = w(\{\varepsilon\}) + \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\eta\}) , \tag{4.33}\]

where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the stress components that belong to the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the components of the strain \(\{\eta\}\).

Proof

We have to show that the expanded energy density of the sum falls into three parts. We use the formula for the energy density and the symmetry of the stiffness matrix.

  1. By the definition of the polynomial \(w\) in the hypothesis of the lemma
    \[w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\big(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}} + \{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\big)\big(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}}\big) ,\]
    where \(\ix{p}\) and \(\ix{q}\) run from \(1\) to \(6\).
  2. We expand every term as the product of two brackets and get four double sums:
    \[\frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}} .\]
  3. By the same definition the first sum is \(w(\{\varepsilon\})\) and the last one \(w(\{\eta\})\).
  4. In the third sum we take out \(\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) and get \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\). The inner sum is the entry \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) of the stress that belongs to the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\), so the third sum is \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\).
  5. In the second sum we rename the indices, \(\ix{p}\) to \(\ix{q}\) and \(\ix{q}\) to \(\ix{p}\). The sum runs over all pairs, so it does not change, and it equals \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{q}} \sum_{\ix{p}} C_{\mathrm{qp}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). By item 1 of the theorem on the symmetry of the elastic constants \(C_{\mathrm{qp}} = C_{\mathrm{pq}}\), so this is the third sum from step 4, \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\).
  6. The second and the third sum together give \(\sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), which by equation (4.32) equals \(\sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Together with step 3 this is (4.33).

Source: The squares are expanded in the proof of EP (4.3.19) (p. 183), where this is written for an isotropic material. The lemma as a separate statement and the step-by-step proof are not from the sources.

The lemma is the expansion of the square \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\) for a function of six variables. It does not ask for small strains, because it only expands a polynomial. We shall need this, since the difference of two small strains need not be small: the components \(-0{,}0009\) and \(0{,}0009\) are below the bound \(0{,}001\) in absolute value, but their difference \(0{,}0018\) is not. The middle term is expressed here with the stress and has a physical meaning: the energy density of a sum is the sum of the densities, corrected by the work of the stress of the first strain on the second strain. The symmetry of the stiffness matrix is needed in step 5. Without it the second and the third sum would differ, and we could not write the mixed term with the stress. For an isotropic material we check the lemma directly. Its energy density is \(w = \tfrac12\,\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + \mu \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\) (section 3.6), where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the volumetric strain. Expanding the squares gives the mixed term \(\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(\eta_{\mathrm{v}} = \eta_{\mathrm{xx}} + \eta_{\mathrm{yy}} + \eta_{\mathrm{zz}}\). Hooke's law (3.13) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for equal indices and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for different ones, so \(\sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the same.

Now we can state the main theorem of the section. Figure 4.46 shows the two fields the theorem speaks about: the true displacement field and any other field that respects the supports.

Theorem 4.51 Principle of minimum total potential energy (načelo najmanjše celotne potencialne energije)

Let the body be as in theorem 4.42 on the principle of virtual displacements, made of an ideal elastic and linear elastic material whose strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero. Let the loads \(\vek b\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\) be independent of the deformation. Let \(\vek u\) be a kinematically admissible displacement field whose stresses satisfy assumptions 1 to 4 of theorem 4.42: they are continuously differentiable, symmetric, satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.31) in the interior, and \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). Then for every kinematically admissible displacement field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) with small strains:

  1. the difference of the total potential energies is the strain energy of the difference of the fields,
    \[\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) - \Pi(\vek u) = U(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u) \ge 0 , \tag{4.34}\]
  2. the equality \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u)\) holds only if the small strain tensor of the field \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is zero at every point of the body.

The strain of the field \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) need not be small, so we compute \(U(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u)\) with the density \(w\) as the polynomial from lemma 4.50.

Proof

We have to show that the difference of the energies falls into an expression from the principle of virtual displacements, which is zero, and the strain energy of the difference of the fields, which is not negative. We follow the computation for the bar with a load.

1. Difference of the energies.

  1. Let \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\). The difference of two kinematically admissible fields is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.48 and the paragraph after it).
  2. We denote the components of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek v\) by \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial v_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\), where \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). The partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.79, applied to one variable with the other two fixed), so the field \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u + \vek v\) has at every point the strain with components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the strain components of the field \(\vek u\).
  3. By lemma 4.50 on the energy density of a sum of strains, at every point \(w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = w(\{\varepsilon\}) + \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\eta\})\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the stresses of the field \(\vek u\).
  4. We integrate over the body and use the linearity of the integral over a body (section 4.2):
    \[U(\tilde{\vek u}) = U(\vek u) + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V + U(\vek v) .\]
  5. The scalar product is distributive (lemma 2.12), so \(\vek b\cdot\tilde{\vek u} = \vek b\cdot\vek u + \vek b\cdot\vek v\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\cdot\tilde{\vek u} = \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u + \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek v\). By the linearity of the integral the integrals of the potential energy of the loads split in the same way.
  6. We insert steps 4 and 5 into equation (4.31), which defines the total potential energy, and arrange the terms:
    \[\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u) + \Big[ \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}A \Big] + U(\vek v) .\]
  7. The stresses of the field \(\vek u\) satisfy the assumptions of the principle of virtual displacements, and by step 1 \(\vek v\) is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement with virtual strain \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By theorem 4.42 the expression in square brackets is therefore zero, and \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) - \Pi(\vek u) = U(\vek v)\).
  8. The polynomial \(w\) is zero at the zero column. At every column \(\{\eta\} \ne 0\) it is positive, also when \(\{\eta\}\) is not a small strain. Indeed, choose a number \(\lambda > 0\) so small that \(\lambda\{\eta\}\) is a small strain. Every term of the polynomial \(w\) has two strain factors, so \(w(\lambda\{\eta\}) = \lambda^2\,w(\{\eta\})\). At the small strain \(\lambda\{\eta\} \ne 0\) the polynomial \(w\) is the strain energy density, which is positive by assumption, so \(w(\{\eta\}) = w(\lambda\{\eta\})/\lambda^2 > 0\). Hence \(w(\{\eta\}) \ge 0\) at every point. The integral over a box is an iterated integral (definition 4.8), and each of the three iterated integrals of a nonnegative function is nonnegative (lemma 3.38, item 4). The integral over the body is the sum of the integrals over its boxes (section 4.2), so \(U(\vek v) \ge 0\).

2. Equality.

  1. Let \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u)\). By item 1, \(U(\vek v) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), where \(g = w(\{\eta\})\) at every point of the body.
  2. The function \(g\) is continuous. The field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable, so the components \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuous functions of the point, and \(g\) is a sum of products of two of them with constant numbers, which is continuous by corollary 1.67 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space. By step 8 of item 1, \(g \ge 0\).
  3. Suppose that \(g(P) > 0\) at some interior point \(P\) of the body. By the definition of continuity 1.65 with the allowed error \(g(P)/2\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(g > g(P)/2\) at all points of the body closer to \(P\) than \(\delta\).
  4. Since \(P\) is an interior point, a small cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) with centre \(P\) and edge \(d > 0\) lies in the body around it, with its corners closer to \(P\) than \(\delta\). On it \(g > g(P)/2\).
  5. To the grid that cuts the body into cells we add the six planes in which the faces of the cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) lie. The integral over the body does not change, because it does not depend on the grid (section 4.2), and the cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) is now a union of cells. The integral over the body is the sum of the integrals over the cells. By step 8 of item 1, applied to each cell, none of them is negative, so the sum is not smaller than the sum of the integrals over the cells of the cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\), that is than the integral over \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\).
  6. On \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) we have \(g > g(P)/2\), so by monotonicity and the rule for a constant function, applied to the three iterated integrals (lemma 3.38, items 3 and 4), the integral over \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) is not smaller than \(\tfrac12\,g(P)\,d^3\). Hence \(U(\vek v) \ge \tfrac12\,g(P)\,d^3 > 0\), which contradicts step 1. So \(g = 0\) at every interior point.
  7. Every point on the surface of the body is the limit of a sequence of interior points, as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 4.42, and \(g\) is continuous, so by lemma 1.66 on continuity through sequences of points \(g = 0\) on the surface too.
  8. By step 8 of item 1 the polynomial \(w\) is positive at every column that is not zero. Since \(g = w(\{\eta\}) = 0\) at every point, \(\{\eta\}\) is the zero strain at every point.

Source: EP §4.3.1, (4.3.6), (4.3.19)-(4.3.20) (pp. 179-183), CM (7.6.14) (PDF p. 346), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139), which states the principle and leaves the proof to other books. EP proves the minimum only for an isotropic material, by expanding the squares in the Navier equations. The proof with lemma 4.50 and item 2 are not from the sources. For a body cut into pieces between graphs, such as the round bar, item 1 holds, because the principle of virtual displacements holds for it (end of section 4.4.4) and so does the monotonicity of the integral (lemma 4.22). Item 2 holds for it and for other bodies with a curved surface as far as the rules of step 5 hold for the integral over such a body, which LEBL2 §10.3-10.5 (PDF pp. 108-127) gives.

What does the theorem say? The true displacement field has the smallest total potential energy among all fields that respect the supports. Every other field has a larger one, larger by exactly the strain energy the body would have if it were deformed by the difference of the two fields. For a body this is the same as the term \(\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2\) in equation (4.29) was for the bar with a load. The proof has shown where this comes from. The mixed term of the expanded energy, the work of the stress of the true field on the strain of the difference, cancels against the potential energy of the loads on the difference, because the true field is in equilibrium and the difference is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement. Only the energy of the difference remains, which is not negative because the material is stable.

Item 2 tells when another field has the same energy as the true one. The difference must be free of strain. For a body held by its supports so that it can neither move nor turn as a rigid body, such a difference can only be zero, and the true field is the only one with this energy. That a field without strain is a small rigid displacement we will use in section 4.7.

Where does the theorem stop holding? Each of the assumptions was needed. Without loads independent of the deformation, the potential energy of the loads of the form \(-\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\) does not exist. Without linearity and the symmetry of the stiffness matrix, lemma 4.50 does not hold. Without a positive energy density, step 8 fails, and the true field may only be a point where the derivative of the energy in every direction is zero, not the smallest value, as we will see in subsection 4.5.6. For large displacements, finally, a compressed bar may bend sideways, and the straight shape is no longer the shape with the smallest energy.
