EP shows that for a beam in which the term due to large rotations is kept, the minimum cannot be guaranteed when the axial force is compressive (EP Example 4.3.1, pp. 184-187). We do not treat buckling in this chapter.

4.5.5 The bracket of two bars

Let us test the principle on the bracket from section 4.1 and repeat its setting (figure 4.47, left). The bracket lies in a vertical plane. The axis \(x\) points horizontally to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up, and the origin is at the joint \(C = (0, 0, 0)\). The horizontal bar \(AC\) has length \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m, and its end \(A = (-4, 0, 0)\) m is pinned to the wall. The inclined bar \(BC\) has length \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m, and its end \(B = (-4, 3, 0)\) m is also pinned to the wall. At the joint \(C\) a load acts with the force \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\), \(F = 10\) kN, which is independent of the deformation. Both bars are steel, with \(E = 196\) GPa and cross-section area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\), so \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}} = E A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N. The truss model (definition 4.4) assumes that the bars carry only axial forces. We do not check the compressed bar \(AC\) for buckling. In section 4.1 we got from the equilibrium of the pin \(C\) the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN and the energy \(U = 53{,}57\) J. There we estimated the component \(v\) of the displacement of the joint from the equality of work and energy as \(v = -10{,}71\) mm.

The state of the bracket is described by two numbers. The pins \(A\) and \(B\) do not move and the bars are straight, so everything is fixed by the displacement of the joint \(C\). As in sections 4.1 and 4.3 we write it as \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\). The number \(u\) is the horizontal displacement, positive to the right, the number \(v\) the vertical displacement, positive upward. In section 4.3 we got the displacement of the joint from the elongations of the bars, and these from the axial forces, which we knew from the equilibrium of the pin. Now let us find it with energy, without knowing the axial forces in advance. Every pair of numbers \(u\), \(v\) is an admissible state, since it respects both pins. For every such state let us compute the total potential energy.

  1. For a small displacement of the joint a bar lengthens by the projection of the displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar, as we saw for virtual displacements in section 4.3. With the unit vectors from the pin toward the joint, \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\), the elongations are
    \[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = u , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v .\]
  2. A bar with elongation \(\Delta L\) carries the axial force \(N = EA\,\Delta L/L\) and stores the energy \(N^2 L/(2EA)\) (theorem 4.3). Inserting the force, the energy is \(EA\,\Delta L^2/(2L)\). The energy of the bracket is the sum of the energies of the two bars:
    \[U(u, v) = \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,u^2 + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\big(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\big)^2 .\]
  3. The load is independent of the deformation, so its potential energy is \(-\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -\big(0 \cdot u + (-F)\,v\big) = F\,v\). A load that goes down has \(v < 0\), and its potential energy is negative, as for the bar with a load.
  4. The total potential energy is the sum. With numbers, \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}/(2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}) = 2{,}45 \cdot 10^6\) N/m and \(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}/(2 L_{\mathrm{BC}}) = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, and expanding the square,
    \[\begin{aligned} \Pi(u, v) &= 3{,}7044 \cdot 10^6\,u^2 - 1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\,u\,v \\ &\quad + 0{,}7056 \cdot 10^6\,v^2 + 10^4\,v , \end{aligned} \tag{4.35}\]
    with displacements in metres and energy in joules. The numbers in front of the squares and the product are \(3{,}7044 \cdot 10^6 = 2{,}45 \cdot 10^6 + 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 0{,}8^2\), \(0{,}7056 \cdot 10^6 = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 0{,}6^2\) and \(1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6 = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 2 \cdot 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6\), the last one with a minus, because the bracket contains \(-0{,}6\,v\). The number \(10^4\) is the load \(F = 10\,000\) N.

Theorem 4.51 is about a body, while we described the bracket with the truss model, in which every bar is only an elongation and an axial force. So we repeat the computation of the proof for the bracket, where it is simpler. Let \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) be the true displacement of the joint from section 4.3, at which the bars carry the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) from section 4.1, and let \(\vek w = (w_{\mathrm{x}}, w_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) be any vector.

  1. The elongation of a bar for the displacement \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek w\) is \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w\), by the distributivity of the scalar product, and the same for \(BC\).
  2. We expand the square of the sum, \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\). The energy of the bar \(AC\) is therefore
    \[\frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})^2 + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w) + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w)^2 ,\]
    and the same for \(BC\). The first term is the energy of the bar in the true state.
  3. In the middle term \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})/L_{\mathrm{AC}} = E A_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}/L_{\mathrm{AC}} = N_{\mathrm{AC}}\), the axial force of the true state. The middle term is therefore \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w)\).
  4. The potential energy of the load changes by \(-\vek F\cdot\vek w\). All together:
    \[\begin{aligned} \Pi(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek w) - \Pi(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}) &= \big[ N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek w - \vek F\cdot\vek w \big] \\ &\quad + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w)^2 + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek w)^2 . \end{aligned}\]
  5. The expression in square brackets is \((N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} - \vek F)\cdot\vek w\). The equilibrium of the pin \(C\) from section 4.1, \(\vek F - N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek 0\), says that the vector in the bracket is the zero vector. This is also the principle of virtual displacements for the truss from section 4.3 with the virtual displacement \(\vek w\). Let us check with numbers: \(-13\,333\ \text{N} \cdot (1, 0, 0) + \tfrac15 \cdot 16\,667\ \text{N} \cdot (4, -3, 0) = (0, -10\,000, 0)\ \text{N} = \vek F\).
  6. Two squares remain, which are not negative. Both are zero only if \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w = w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek w = 0{,}8\,w_{\mathrm{x}} - 0{,}6\,w_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), so \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = w_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). Every other displacement of the joint therefore has a larger energy than the true one, and there is only one true displacement.

Now let us find the true displacement. Where \(\Pi\) has its smallest value, the function of one variable that we get by holding one component fixed has its smallest value too. Its derivative is zero there (lemma 1.80), and this derivative is a partial derivative of \(\Pi\) (definition 1.23). From steps 2 and 3 of the energy computation, with \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}/L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4{,}9 \cdot 10^6\) N/m and \(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}/L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 3{,}92 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, we get

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial u} &= \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,u + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\big(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\big) \cdot 0{,}8 = 0 , \\ \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial v} &= \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\big(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\big) \cdot (-0{,}6) + F = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

What do the two equations say? The expression \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}\,u/L_{\mathrm{AC}}\) is the axial force of the bar \(AC\), and the expression \(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}\,(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v)/L_{\mathrm{BC}}\) the axial force of the bar \(BC\). So the equations are \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} + 0{,}8\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) and \(-0{,}6\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} + F = 0\), the \(x\) and \(y\) components of the equilibrium of the pin \(C\) with the sign changed. The derivatives of the total potential energy are exactly the equilibrium equations of the joint. The second gives \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F/0{,}6 = 16{,}67\) kN, the first \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -0{,}8\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -13{,}33\) kN, as in section 4.1. The elongations are \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = N_{\mathrm{BC}} L_{\mathrm{BC}}/(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}) = 4{,}252\) mm and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = -2{,}721\) mm. From \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u\) and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\) it follows that

\[u = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} , \qquad v = \frac{0{,}8\,u - \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}}{0{,}6} = \frac{-2{,}177 - 4{,}252}{0{,}6}\ \text{mm} = -10{,}71\ \text{mm} .\]

We checked with SymPy that the smallest value of the function (4.35) lies at \(u = -2/735\) m and \(v = -3/280\) m, which is the same, and that \(\Pi = -53{,}57\) J there.

The joint moves 2,721 mm to the left and 10,71 mm down (figure 4.47, right). To the left because the compressed bar \(AC\) shortens and the joint stays at its end. Down almost four times as much. Why? A vertical motion of the joint does not lengthen the bar \(AC\) to first order, since it is perpendicular to it, and it lengthens the bar \(BC\) by only \(0{,}6\) of the motion. The bracket is therefore much more flexible vertically than horizontally. This shows in equation (4.35) too, where the number in front of \(v^2\) is more than five times smaller than the number in front of \(u^2\).

Let us also confirm the observation from section 4.1. There we got the component \(v\) of the displacement of the joint from the equality of the work of the load and the energy as \(v = -2U/F\) and promised a proof. For the bracket Clapeyron's theorem reads \(2U = \vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). We prove it like theorem 4.46, except that in the principle of virtual displacements for the truss from section 4.3 we take the true displacement of the joint instead of a virtual one. The left side of the principle is then \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}\), and each term is twice the energy of the bar, \(N\,\Delta L = 2 \cdot \tfrac12\,N\,\Delta L\) (theorem 4.3). The right side is \(\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). With numbers the left side is \((-13\,333\ \text{N})(-2{,}721\ \text{mm}) + 16\,667\ \text{N} \cdot 4{,}252\ \text{mm} = 36{,}28\ \text{J} + 70{,}86\ \text{J} = 107{,}14\) J, and the right side \((-10\,000\ \text{N})(-10{,}71\ \text{mm}) = 107{,}14\) J. Since \(\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -F\,v\), we get \(v = -2U/F = -10{,}71\) mm, as estimated. The smallest value of the energy is \(\Pi = U - \vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = U - 2U = -U = -53{,}57\) J, as for the bar with a load, where it was \(-\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\).

Figure 4.48 shows the function (4.35) with contour lines. A contour line (plastnica) is a line along which the function has a constant value, as a contour line on a map connects points of the same height above sea level. The contour lines are ellipses with a common centre at the lowest point. They are ellipses because \(\Pi\) is a polynomial of degree two in two variables with a smallest value, and the difference from the smallest value is, by step 4 of the computation above, a sum of two squares. The ellipses are strongly elongated and almost vertical, because the energy changes slowly in an almost vertical direction and quickly in the horizontal one. The state before loading, \(u = v = 0\), lies on the contour line \(\Pi = 0\).

Let us also test equation (4.34). Take the state in which the joint goes down by the true 10,71 mm but does not move horizontally, \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek w\) with \(\vek w = (2721, 0, 0)\) µm. The function (4.35) gives \(\Pi = -26{,}14\) J, which is \(27{,}43\) J more than the smallest value. By step 4 of the computation above, the energy of the difference \(\vek w\) is \(2{,}45 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot (2{,}721 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2 + 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot (0{,}8 \cdot 2{,}721 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2 = 18{,}14\ \text{J} + 9{,}29\ \text{J} = 27{,}43\) J, exactly that much.

4.5.6 The derivative in every direction is zero

For the bracket the partial derivatives of the total potential energy were zero in the true state. This is not special to the bracket. What happens to the energy of a body if we move from some admissible field \(\vek u\) in the direction of an admissible virtual displacement \(\vek v\), by a multiple \(\alpha\,\vek v\)? This time the field \(\vek u\) need not be the true one.

  1. The field \(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v\) has the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \alpha\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the strain components of the field \(\vek v\), because the partial derivative of the field \(\alpha\,\vek v\) is \(\alpha\) times the partial derivative of the field \(\vek v\) (lemma 1.79).
  2. In lemma 4.50 we take \(\alpha\,\{\eta\}\) as the second strain. The mixed term is \(\alpha \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The last term is \(w(\alpha\,\{\eta\}) = \tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}}\sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,(\alpha\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}})(\alpha\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}}) = \alpha^2\,w(\{\eta\})\), because every term of the energy density has two strain factors. The lemma does not ask \(\alpha\,\{\eta\}\) and \(\{\varepsilon\} + \alpha\,\{\eta\}\) to be small strains, and for a large \(\alpha\) they are not. Then we compute \(w\), and with it \(\Pi(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v)\), with the polynomial from the lemma.
  3. We integrate and add the potential energy of the loads as in the proof of theorem 4.51:
    \[\Pi(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v) = \Pi(\vek u) + \alpha\,B(\vek v) + \alpha^2\,U(\vek v) , \tag{4.36}\]
    where \(B(\vek v) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}A\) is the internal virtual work of the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) on the virtual displacement \(\vek v\) minus the external virtual work (section 4.4).

Along every direction \(\vek v\) the energy is thus a polynomial of degree two in the number \(\alpha\), a parabola (figure 4.49). Its derivative with respect to \(\alpha\) at \(\alpha = 0\) is \(B(\vek v)\), by the rules of differentiation. If \(\vek u\) is the true field, then \(B(\vek v) = 0\) for every admissible virtual displacement by the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.42), and all the parabolas have a horizontal tangent at \(\alpha = 0\). The converse holds too. If \(B(\vek v) = 0\) for every admissible virtual displacement and the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) are continuously differentiable, the virtual work equation holds for every such displacement, and by the converse of the principle of virtual displacements in section 4.4 the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) satisfy the equilibrium equations and the condition \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). An admissible field is therefore the true one exactly when the derivative of the total potential energy in every admissible direction is zero at it. Such a point is called a stationary point (stacionarna točka) of the energy, and the condition stationarity (SADD §6.6, PDF p. 139). The expression \(\alpha\,B(\vek v)\), the part of the change of the energy proportional to \(\alpha\), is called the first variation (prva variacija) in the books and written \(\delta\Pi\) (EP (4.3.2), p. 180, CM (7.6.1), PDF p. 344).

For the bracket \(U(\vek w)\) is \(3{,}7044\) J for \(\vek w = 1\ \text{mm}\ \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(0{,}7056\) J for \(\vek w = 1\ \text{mm}\ \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), which are the numbers in front of \(u^2\) and \(v^2\) in equation (4.35), converted to millimetres. Along the horizontal line through the lowest point, therefore, \(\Pi = -53{,}57\ \text{J} + 3{,}7044\ \text{J} \cdot \alpha^2\), and along the vertical one \(-53{,}57\ \text{J} + 0{,}7056\ \text{J} \cdot \alpha^2\), with \(\alpha\) in millimetres (figure 4.49). The derivatives along the directions \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) at the lowest point are the partial derivatives from the previous subsection, and both are zero.

Stationarity is weaker than a smallest value. It says only that the tangent along every line is horizontal, not that the energy is larger elsewhere. For our material the parabola (4.36) opens upward, because \(U(\vek v) \ge 0\), and the stationary point is therefore the lowest point. Stationarity, however, also holds for a nonlinear elastic material, where lemma 4.50 does not hold: EP shows that \(\delta\Pi = 0\) follows from the principle of virtual displacements for every material whose stresses are partial derivatives of an energy density (EP (4.3.2), p. 180). That the stationary point is also the lowest one must then be checked separately, and for a beam that can bend sideways it is not always so (EP Example 4.3.1, pp. 184-187).

4.5.7 Castigliano's first theorem

For the bar with a load the strain energy is \(U(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2\) and its derivative \(k\,e\). At the equilibrium elongation this is \(k\,\Delta L = F\), the weight of the load (figure 4.50). For the bracket the energy \(U(u, v)\) is equation (4.35) without its last term. We differentiate by the rules of differentiation: the derivative of the term \(3{,}7044 \cdot 10^6\,u^2\) with respect to \(u\) is \(7{,}4088 \cdot 10^6\,u\), the derivative of the term \(0{,}7056 \cdot 10^6\,v^2\) with respect to \(v\) is \(1{,}4112 \cdot 10^6\,v\), and the mixed term gives \(-1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\) times the other variable for each variable. With numbers the partial derivatives are

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial U}{\partial u} &= 7{,}4088 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u - 1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v , \\ \frac{\partial U}{\partial v} &= -1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u + 1{,}4112 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v . \end{aligned}\]

At \(u = -2{,}721\) mm and \(v = -10{,}71\) mm the first derivative is \(0\) and the second \(-10\,000\) N, which we checked with SymPy. These are the \(x\) and \(y\) components of the load \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\). The derivative of the strain energy with respect to a displacement is thus the component of the force that acts at the point and in the direction of this displacement.

Theorem 4.52 Castigliano's first theorem (prvi Castiglianov izrek)

Let the state of a structure made of a linear elastic material be fixed by \(n\) numbers \(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}\), components of displacements of chosen points in chosen directions, so that every choice of the numbers gives a state that respects the supports. Let the strain energy be a function \(U(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}})\) that has partial derivatives with respect to all variables. Let only forces independent of the deformation act on the structure, such that the component of the force at the point and in the direction of the displacement \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\) has the value \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the potential energy of the loads is \(-\sum_{\ix{i}} F_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\). If the total potential energy

\[\Pi(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}) = U(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}) - \sum_{\ix{i}} F_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\]

has its smallest value among all choices of the numbers at the equilibrium values of the displacements, then at these values, for every \(\ix{i}\),

\[F_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{\partial U}{\partial \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}} . \tag{4.37}\]
Proof

We have to show that the partial derivative of the total potential energy with respect to each displacement is zero in equilibrium, and compute this derivative.

  1. We denote the equilibrium values by \(\Delta_1^0, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}^0\). Choose \(\ix{i}\), and for every number \(t\) let \(g(t)\) be the value of \(\Pi\) when the \(\ix{i}\)-th displacement equals \(t\) and all others equal their equilibrium values.
  2. Every choice of the number \(t\) gives a state that respects the supports, and \(\Pi\) has its smallest value at the equilibrium values among all states, so also among these. The function \(g\) therefore has its smallest value on the interval \([\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0 - 1, \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0 + 1]\) at the interior point \(t = \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0\).
  3. The derivative of \(g\) at \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0\) is the partial derivative of \(\Pi\) with respect to \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\) at the equilibrium values, since we vary only one variable and hold the others fixed (definition 1.23, in the same way for \(n\) variables). It exists because \(U\) has it by assumption and the linear term has it by the rules of differentiation.
  4. By lemma 1.80 on the derivative at an interior extremum, \(g'(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0) = 0\).
  5. When only \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\) varies, the term \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a linear function with derivative \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the other terms of the sum \(\sum F_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{j}}\) are constant and have derivative zero (lemma 1.79). Therefore \(g'(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0) = \partial U/\partial\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} - F_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  6. Steps 4 and 5 give \(\partial U/\partial\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = F_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: EP §4.3.2, (4.3.22), (4.3.23) (pp. 188-189), where the theorem is derived from stationarity and holds also for nonlinear elastic materials, and EP Example 4.3.2 (pp. 189-190) for a truss of two bars.

When does \(\Pi\) really have its smallest value at the equilibrium values? For the bar with a load we showed it with equation (4.29), for the bracket with the computation in subsection 4.5.5, and for a body, when the true displacement field is among the fields described by the numbers \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\), by theorem 4.51. In a truss the state is always fixed by the displacements of the joints, because every bar carries a constant axial force and stretches evenly, and the computation of subsection 4.5.5 repeats with more bars and joints. EP derives the theorem from stationarity and therefore states it also for nonlinear elastic materials (EP, p. 188).

What does the theorem say? If we know the strain energy as a function of the displacements, differentiation gives the forces these displacements require. For the bracket the theorem gives two equations that are linear in the displacements:

\[\begin{aligned} 7{,}4088 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u - 1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v &= 0 , \\ -1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u + 1{,}4112 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v &= -10\,000\ \text{N} . \end{aligned}\]

Their solution is again \(u = -2{,}721\) mm and \(v = -10{,}71\) mm. The four numbers on the left say how much force is needed for every metre of displacement in each direction. Arranged in a matrix they are the stiffness matrix (togostna matrika) of the bracket (EP Example 4.3.3, p. 191). The matrix is symmetric, because the numbers off the diagonal are the mixed derivatives of the energy, \(\partial^2 U/\partial u\,\partial v\) and \(\partial^2 U/\partial v\,\partial u\), which are equal by theorem 1.121 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives. This is how the finite element method, which we will meet in chapter 7, sets up its equations, with the energy written in terms of the displacements of the joints. We did not compute the bracket with the geometry of intersecting bars but with derivatives of one single function, and this is the route a computer takes too.

4.5.8 Trial fields for the hanging bar

For the bracket the state was described by finitely many numbers. For a body, or for a bar with a load along its length, the displacement is a function, and we often cannot compute the true field. The principle of minimum energy offers a way out. We choose a family of simple fields that respect the supports and depend on a few numbers, write the energy as a function of these numbers and look for the smallest value. We get the best field in the family. Let us try it on the hanging bar, where we know the true field and can compare the approximation with it.

The model is the bar from section 4.3: a bar of length \(L\), fixed at \(x = 0\), with Young's modulus \(E\) and cross-section area \(A\), loaded by a distributed axial load \(q\), a force per unit length, and by a force \(F\) at the end \(x = L\). Every cross section moves only along the axis, by \(u(x)\), the axial force is \(N = EA\,u'\), and the energy per unit length is \(\tfrac12\,EA\,u'^2\) (section 4.1). The model is not a special case of a body with \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), since in the bar the cross sections may thin freely. So we state the principle for it separately, with a proof that is the proof of theorem 4.51 carried over to integrals along the length.

Corollary 4.53 Minimum total potential energy of a bar (najmanjša potencialna energija palice)

Let a bar lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and be fixed at \(x = 0\). Let its Young's modulus \(E\) and its cross-section area \(A\) be positive numbers. Let a distributed axial load \(q\), continuous on \([0, L]\), act on it, and at the end \(x = L\) a force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), both independent of the deformation. For every function \(u\) that is continuously differentiable on an open interval containing \([0, L]\) and satisfies \(u(0) = 0\), let

\[\Pi(u) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,u'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q(x)\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x - F\,u(L) . \tag{4.38}\]

Let \(u\) be such a function that the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, L)\), \(N'(x) + q(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in (0, L)\) and \(N(L) = F\). Then for every function \(\tilde u\) that is continuously differentiable on an open interval containing \([0, L]\) and satisfies \(\tilde u(0) = 0\)

\[\Pi(\tilde u) - \Pi(u) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,\big(\tilde u'(x) - u'(x)\big)^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0 ,\]

with equality only for \(\tilde u = u\).

Proof

We have to show the same splitting as for a body, and then that the integral of a square is zero only for the zero function.

  1. Let \(v = \tilde u - u\). The function \(v\) is continuously differentiable and \(v(0) = 0\).
  2. We expand the square: \(\tilde u'^2 = (u' + v')^2 = u'^2 + 2\,u'\,v' + v'^2\). Therefore \(\tfrac12\,EA\,\tilde u'^2 = \tfrac12\,EA\,u'^2 + N\,v' + \tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\), because \(EA\,u' = N\).
  3. We integrate and use the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.38, item 1). In the same way we split \(\int_0^L q\,\tilde u\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,u\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L q\,v\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(F\,\tilde u(L) = F\,u(L) + F\,v(L)\). We get
    \[\Pi(\tilde u) = \Pi(u) + \Big[ \int_0^L N\,v'\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q\,v\,\mathrm{d}x - F\,v(L) \Big] + \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  4. By the principle of virtual displacements for a bar (theorem 4.36) with the virtual displacement \(\delta u = v\), the expression in square brackets is zero. We may do this because \(N\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), since \(u'\) is continuous, and satisfies the equilibrium of the bar, while \(v\) is differentiable on an open interval containing \([0, L]\), with a continuous derivative and \(v(0) = 0\).
  5. The function \(\tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\) is not negative, so by the monotonicity of the integral (lemma 3.38, item 4) its integral is not negative either.
  6. Let the integral of step 5 be zero, and suppose that \(v'(x_0) \ne 0\) at some point \(x_0\) of the interval \([0, L]\). The function \(f = \tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\) is continuous and \(f(x_0) > 0\). By the definition of continuity 1.56 with the allowed error \(f(x_0)/2\) there is a closed interval \([c, d] \subseteq [0, L]\) with \(c < d\) that contains \(x_0\) and on which \(f > f(x_0)/2\).
  7. By additivity (lemma 3.38, item 2) the integral over \([0, L]\) is the sum of the integrals over \([0, c]\), \([c, d]\) and \([d, L]\). The first and the last are not negative by step 5, and the middle one is not smaller than \(\tfrac12\,f(x_0)\,(d - c) > 0\) by item 3 of the same lemma. The integral is therefore positive, which contradicts the assumption. So \(v' = 0\) on \([0, L]\).
  8. By corollary 1.83 on a function with zero derivative, \(v(x) = v(0) = 0\) for every \(x \in [0, L]\), so \(\tilde u = u\).

Source: EP (3.3.3), (3.3.4) (p. 124) for the total potential energy of bars and beams, EP §4.3.1 (pp. 179-183) for the principle. The step-by-step proof is not from the sources.

The hanging bar is steel, with length \(L = 10\) m, cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and Young's modulus \(E = 196\) GPa, so \(EA = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N. The top cross section is fixed, \(u(0) = 0\), the axis \(x\) points down, the only load is the weight \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m per unit length, and there is no force at the lower end, \(F = 0\). The true field is \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (section 3.1). Its axial force is \(N = EA \cdot 2a\,(L - x) = \rho g A\,(L - x)\), because \(2aE = \rho g\), and it satisfies \(N' + q = -\rho g A + \rho g A = 0\) and \(N(L) = 0 = F\). By corollary 4.53 the true field therefore has the smallest energy. By Clapeyron's theorem this energy is \(-U = -391{,}03\) µJ, since the work of the weight over the whole displacement is \(2U\).

First trial field: a straight line. Take the fields \(\tilde u(x) = c\,x\) with a free number \(c\). All of them respect the fixing, \(\tilde u(0) = 0\).

  1. The derivative is \(\tilde u' = c\), so the strain energy is \(\int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,c^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,EA\,c^2 L\) by item 3 of lemma 3.38.
  2. The function \(x^2/2\) has the derivative \(x\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus the potential energy of the weight is \(-\int_0^L q\,c\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\tfrac12\,q\,c\,L^2\).
  3. The total potential energy is \(\Pi(c) = \tfrac12\,EA\,L\,c^2 - \tfrac12\,q\,L^2\,c\), a parabola in \(c\).
  4. Its derivative is \(EA\,L\,c - \tfrac12\,q\,L^2\). At the lowest point it is zero by lemma 1.80, so \(c = q\,L/(2EA)\). Since \(q = \rho g A\), this is \(c = \rho g L/(2E) = a\,L = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\).

The best straight line is therefore \(\tilde u(x) = a L\,x\). For it \(\Pi = \tfrac12\,EA\,L\,(aL)^2 - \tfrac12\,\rho g A\,L^2\,aL = \tfrac12\,EA\,a^2 L^3 - EA\,a^2 L^3 = -\tfrac12\,EA\,a^2 L^3 = -293{,}27\) µJ, where we used \(\rho g = 2aE\) again. The true field has \(-\tfrac23\,EA\,a^2 L^3 = -391{,}03\) µJ, less, as the principle requires. The difference is \(97{,}76\) µJ.

How good is the approximation? Figure 4.51 shows two remarkable things. At the lower end the displacement of the line is \(aL \cdot L = aL^2 = 19{,}52\) µm, exactly the true displacement \(u(L) = a\,(2L^2 - L^2) = aL^2\). At the middle, however, the line gives \(9{,}760\) µm instead of \(14{,}64\) µm, a third too little. Why is the displacement of the end exact? The strain of the line is \(aL\) everywhere, while the strain of the true field falls from \(2aL\) at the top to zero at the bottom, and its average is \(aL\), because \(\int_0^L 2a\,(L - x)\,\mathrm{d}x = aL^2\). So the best line has the average strain of the true field. The displacement of the end is the integral of the strain along the length, so it agrees. This is no coincidence. Step 4 requires \(\int_0^L EA\,c\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,x\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the principle of virtual displacements for a bar with the virtual displacement \(\delta u = x\) says that the right side equals \(\int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x\), where \(N\) is the true axial force. Hence \(EA\,c\,L = \int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x\), and \(c\) is the average of the true strain \(N/(EA)\). The line is the chord of the parabola from figure 1.100.

The difference of energies, \(97{,}76\) µJ, has a precise meaning. By corollary 4.53 it equals the strain energy of the error, the difference between the trial field and the true field. The error is \(a\,(2Lx - x^2) - aL\,x = a\,(Lx - x^2)\), with the derivative \(a\,(L - 2x)\), and its energy is \(\int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,a^2\,(L - 2x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac16\,EA\,a^2 L^3 = 97{,}76\) µJ, which we computed with the function \((2x - L)^3/6\), whose derivative is \((2x - L)^2\). Looking for the smallest energy in a family of fields thus picks the field whose error has the smallest strain energy. The error in energy, \(97{,}76\) µJ out of \(391{,}03\) µJ, is a quarter, the error in the displacement at the middle a third, and the error in the displacement of the end zero. The energy measure is an average over the whole bar, and single points may be better or worse than it.

Second trial field: a parabola. Take the fields \(\tilde u(x) = c_1\,x + c_2\,x^2\) with two free numbers.

  1. The derivative is \(\tilde u' = c_1 + 2c_2\,x\), its square \(c_1^2 + 4c_1 c_2\,x + 4c_2^2\,x^2\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus with the functions \(x\), \(x^2/2\) and \(x^3/3\) the strain energy is \(\tfrac12\,EA\,\big(c_1^2 L + 2c_1 c_2 L^2 + \tfrac43\,c_2^2 L^3\big)\).
  2. The potential energy of the weight is \(-q\,\big(\tfrac12\,c_1 L^2 + \tfrac13\,c_2 L^3\big)\).
  3. The partial derivatives of the total potential energy with respect to \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are zero at the lowest point, as for the bracket:
    \[EA\,(c_1 L + c_2 L^2) - \tfrac12\,q\,L^2 = 0 , \qquad EA\,\big(c_1 L^2 + \tfrac43\,c_2 L^3\big) - \tfrac13\,q\,L^3 = 0 .\]
  4. We divide the first equation by \(EA\,L\) and the second by \(EA\,L^2\), and use \(q/(EA) = \rho g/E = 2a\): \(c_1 + c_2 L = aL\) and \(c_1 + \tfrac43\,c_2 L = \tfrac23\,aL\).
  5. We subtract the first from the second: \(\tfrac13\,c_2 L = -\tfrac13\,aL\), so \(c_2 = -a\). The first then gives \(c_1 = aL + aL = 2aL\).

The best parabola is \(2aL\,x - a\,x^2 = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), exactly the true field, and its energy is \(-391{,}03\) µJ. Why exactly? The family contains the true field, since we get it for \(c_1 = 2aL\) and \(c_2 = -a\). By corollary 4.53 the true field has a smaller energy than all other admissible fields, so also than all other parabolas, and the search for the smallest value in the family finds it. We checked with SymPy that the system of step 3 gives exactly these two numbers.

The example shows the idea that we will develop into the Ritz method in chapter 6. Every family of trial fields gives an energy that is not smaller than the true one, so every trial computation is an estimate of the true energy from above (CM, PDF p. 343). A richer family that contains a poorer one gives an estimate at least as good, since it searches among more fields. The finite element method of chapter 7 cuts the bar into pieces and takes a straight line on each piece, which is a family that we can make as rich as we like by a finer division.

With this we have answered the question from the start of the section. For a body made of an ideal elastic and linear elastic material with loads independent of the deformation, the total potential energy of the true displacement field is the smallest among all kinematically admissible fields. We proved this by splitting the energy of any admissible field into the energy of the true field, the work of the stresses on the difference, which the principle of virtual displacements cancels against the potential energy of the loads, and the strain energy of the difference, which is not negative. Clapeyron's theorem, from the principle of virtual displacements with the true field in place of a virtual one, gave \(2U\) as the work of the full loads, and so confirmed that the work of slow loading is stored completely. For the bracket, the search for the smallest value of a function of two displacements gave the displacement of the joint, 2,721 mm to the left and 10,71 mm down, and the derivatives of the energy gave the equilibrium of the joint and Castigliano's first theorem. For the hanging bar the two trial fields showed how the principle picks the best approximation. The principle searches among displacement fields that respect the supports and gets the equilibrium as the condition for the smallest value. In the next section we swap the roles: we will search among stresses that are in equilibrium, and the condition will be that the strains fit the displacements and the supports. For this we will need the complementary strain energy density from section 3.6.

4.6 Virtual forces and complementary energy

In sections 4.3 and 4.4 we wrote equilibrium with work. We imagined small displacements that the supports allow, and we left the forces as they really are. The work of the true forces on the imagined displacements gave the principle of virtual displacements (4.27), which holds exactly when the body is in equilibrium. The imagined displacements were a tool with which we expressed equilibrium. In this section we swap the roles. We imagine forces that are in equilibrium among themselves, and we leave the displacements true. Imagined forces of this kind are called virtual forces (virtualne sile) (EP §3.4.2, p. 131). We will see that the work of virtual forces on the true displacements gives an equation that does not speak about equilibrium but about geometry: about the strains coming from a single displacement field that respects the supports, that is, about the strains being compatible (definition 1.119).

The goal of the section is twofold. First, we want to compute the displacement of a chosen point of a structure without knowing all its displacements. So far we got the displacement of the joint \(C\) of the bracket by solving two equations for both components at once, in section 4.3 from the changes of the lengths of the bars, in section 4.5 from the smallest value of the energy. Virtual forces give each part of the displacement separately, with a single sum over the bars. Second, we want a new principle of a smallest value. The principle of section 4.5 compares displacement fields that respect the supports and picks from them the one in which the body is in equilibrium. The new principle will compare stress fields that satisfy equilibrium and pick from them the one whose strains fit together. With it we will compute the forces in a truss for which equilibrium alone does not determine them.

The model is the same as in sections 4.4 and 4.5. Let us list the assumptions and for each say where we use it.

  1. Strains and displacements are small. We compute all quantities on the shape of the body before loading, and the strain with the small strain tensor (definition 1.113). For a truss it follows that the change of length of a bar is the projection of the displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar. We use this in all proofs of the section.
  2. The truss is idealized as in definition 4.4: frictionless pins, forces only at the joints and negligible weight of the bars. Each bar therefore carries only an axial force, which is constant along the bar (lemma 4.5). As in section 4.1, we do not treat buckling of compressed bars.
  3. For the work of virtual forces we need no property of the material. So the first two subsections hold for every material, except where we compute the changes of length of the bars from the axial forces. From subsection 4.6.3 on, however, the material is ideal elastic (definition 3.42) and linear elastic, with a strain energy density that is positive for every small strain that is not zero, as in section 4.5. We also assume that the stresses determine the strains uniquely, as Hooke's law (3.12) determines them for an isotropic material. For a bar of such a material the length changes by \(\Delta L = N L/(EA)\).
  4. The displacement and stress fields are continuously differentiable (definition 1.88) on an open set that contains the body together with its surface. The body is a box or made of boxes, and the parts of the surface with supports and with prescribed forces are made of whole rectangles on the faces of these boxes, as in section 4.4. We have proved the divergence theorem for such bodies and for bodies cut into pieces between graphs (section 4.2.10), for which the proofs hold with the same changes as for the principle of virtual displacements (end of section 4.4.4). For other bodies with a curved surface everything we derive holds if we accept the divergence theorem, which for them we only stated with a source (section 4.2.6).

The route is as follows. First, on the bracket of two bars, we show what virtual forces are and what their work on the true displacements gives. From this we get a simple formula for the displacement of a joint in a chosen direction and with it both parts of the displacement of the joint \(C\). Then we write the same for a body of any shape. Next comes an energy that we build from the complementary strain energy density, and the principle of its smallest value. From it we derive how a displacement is obtained as a derivative of energy with respect to a force. At the end we add a third bar to the bracket, so that the forces in the bars can no longer be computed from equilibrium, and we find them from the smallest value of the energy.

4.6.1 Virtual forces on a truss

Let us return to the bracket of section 4.1 and repeat its setting (figure 4.52, left). The bracket lies in a vertical plane. The axis \(x\) points horizontally to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up, and the origin is at the joint \(C = (0, 0, 0)\). The horizontal bar \(AC\) of length \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m is pinned to the wall at \(A = (-4, 0, 0)\) m, and the inclined bar \(BC\) of length \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m at \(B = (-4, 3, 0)\) m. A load hangs at the joint \(C\) and acts on it with the force \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\), \(F = 10\) kN. Both bars are of steel, with Young's modulus \(E = 196\) GPa and cross-section area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\). The unit vectors along the bars from the wall toward the joint are \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\). From the equilibrium of the pin \(C\) we got the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN (tension) and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN (compression), and from them the changes of length

\[\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,L_{\mathrm{BC}}}{E\,A_{\mathrm{BC}}} = 4{,}252\ \text{mm} , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,L_{\mathrm{AC}}}{E\,A_{\mathrm{AC}}} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} .\]

We denote the displacement of the joint \(C\) by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\), as in sections 4.3 and 4.5: \(u\) is the horizontal part, positive to the right, and \(v\) the vertical part, positive upward. How is the displacement related to the two changes of length? In section 4.3 we derived for a virtual displacement of the joint that the elongation of a bar is, to first approximation, the projection of the displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar. The derivation used only that the displacement is small and that the fixed end does not move, so there we used it for the true displacement as well:

\[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} .\]

We have left out the term \(\big(|\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2 - (\vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})^2\big)/(2L)\), the square of the part of the displacement perpendicular to the bar divided by \(2L\), where \(\vek n\) is the unit vector and \(L\) the length of the bar. For our bracket, whose joint moves by a good centimetre, this term is \(0{,}014\) mm for the bar \(AC\) and \(0{,}010\) mm for the bar \(BC\), less than a hundredth of the change of length of the bar. These are two equations for the two unknown components of the displacement in the plane, and in section 4.3 we solved them. We look, however, for a route that we can repeat for a body of any shape and that picks out of all the displacements only the one we are interested in.

Let us imagine that instead of the load another force, \(\delta\vek F\), of any size and direction, acts on the same bracket at \(C\) (figure 4.52, right). This force does not really exist, so it is a virtual force. The sign \(\delta\) in front of a quantity means a virtual quantity, as in section 4.3. We denote the axial forces that would balance the pin \(C\) under this force by \(\delta N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\delta N_{\mathrm{BC}}\). We write the equilibrium of the pin as for the load. A bar with axial force \(\delta N\) acts on the pin with the force \(-\delta N\,\vek n\), where \(\vek n\) is its unit vector from the wall toward \(C\) (section 4.1), so (figure 4.53)

\[\delta\vek F - \delta N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} - \delta N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek 0 .\]

The virtual state is just a set of forces that are in equilibrium. It says nothing about displacements, and no material needs to actually produce it. Now we have two states of the same bracket: the true one, in which we know the changes of length of the bars, and the virtual one, in which we know the forces. What do we get if we multiply the forces of the virtual state by the displacements of the true one?

Let us write the answer for a joint at which any number of bars meet, since a bracket with three bars also awaits us. We number the bars \(k = 1, \dots, m\).

Lemma 4.54 Virtual forces on a truss (virtualne sile na paličju)

Let \(m\) bars of a truss meet at the joint \(C\), with their other ends pinned to fixed supports, and let \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the unit vector along the bar \(k\) from the support toward \(C\), for \(k = 1, \dots, m\). Let the joint move by a small displacement \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), and let the bar \(k\) lengthen by \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). Let \(\delta N_1, \dots, \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\) be numbers and \(\delta\vek F\) a vector such that

\[\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \delta\vek F .\]

Then

\[\Delta L_1\,\delta N_1 + \dots + \Delta L_{\mathrm{m}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{m}} = \delta\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} . \tag{4.39}\]
Proof

We have to show that the scalar product of the virtual force with the true displacement splits into the products of the virtual axial forces with the true changes of length. We use only the equilibrium of the virtual forces and the properties of the scalar product.

  1. The vectors on the two sides of the equality in the assumption are equal, so their scalar products with \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) are equal too: \((\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}})\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \delta\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\).
  2. The scalar product of a sum with a vector is the sum of the scalar products, and a number can be taken out of a scalar product (lemma 2.12). The left side is therefore \(\delta N_1\,(\vek n_1\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}) + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{m}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})\).
  3. By assumption \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every \(k\). Inserting this gives (4.39).

Source: EP §4.4.2, example 4.4.1 (pp. 198-199), where the equality is written for a truss of two bars. The lemma and the proof are not from the source.

The proof is short, but it says something important. We multiplied the forces of one state by the displacements of another. We used only two things: that the virtual forces are in equilibrium and that the changes of length of the bars come from a single displacement of the joint. We did not use the material. EP calls the left side of (4.39) the internal complementary virtual work (notranje komplementarno virtualno delo), and the right side with the opposite sign the external complementary virtual work, so that their sum is zero (EP (4.4.3)-(4.4.5), pp. 196-197). Let us compare with the principle of virtual displacements for the truss of section 4.3, where we multiplied the true axial forces by the virtual elongations. There we took the scalar product of the equilibrium of the true forces with a virtual displacement, here of the equilibrium of the virtual forces with the true displacement. The computation is the same, the roles are swapped.

How do we use the lemma for a displacement? We choose the virtual force so that the component of the displacement we are looking for remains on the right. If \(\delta\vek F\) points in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek d\), the right side is the size of the force times the component of the displacement in the direction \(\vek d\). The left side contains only the changes of length, which we know from the true axial forces, and the virtual axial forces, which we get from equilibrium.

Theorem 4.55 Unit dummy load method (metoda enotske sile)

Let the truss be as in lemma 4.54 on virtual forces on a truss, with bars of a linear elastic material. Let the bar \(k\) have length \(L_{\mathrm{k}}\), cross-section area \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and Young's modulus \(E_{\mathrm{k}}\), and under the true load of the joint the axial force \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\), which makes it lengthen by \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\). Let the joint move by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) in this, so that \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) for every \(k\). Let \(\vek d\) be a unit vector and let \(\hat N_1, \dots, \hat N_{\mathrm{m}}\) be numbers such that

\[\hat N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \hat N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek d .\]

Then the component of the displacement of the joint \(C\) in the direction \(\vek d\) is

\[\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{E_{\mathrm{k}}\,A_{\mathrm{k}}} . \tag{4.40}\]
Proof

We have to show that the equality of lemma 4.54, for a suitably chosen virtual force, is (4.40).

  1. Let \(\delta F > 0\) be any number with the unit newton. We take the virtual force \(\delta\vek F = \delta F\,\vek d\) and the virtual axial forces \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} = \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta F\). Multiplying the equality in the assumption by \(\delta F\) gives \(\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \delta\vek F\), the equilibrium the lemma requires.
  2. By lemma 4.54 therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta F = \delta F\,(\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})\).
  3. The number \(\delta F\) is not zero, so we divide both sides by it and get \(\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. We insert \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\) and get (4.40).

Source: EP (4.4.11), (4.4.12) (p. 198), where the method is written for a body, and example 4.4.1 (pp. 198-199) for a truss of two bars.

What are the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\)? Let us multiply their equation by \(1\) N. It then says that the axial forces \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}} \cdot 1\ \text{N}\) balance a force of \(1\) N in the direction \(\vek d\). When equilibrium alone determines the axial forces, as for the bracket of two bars, the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the axial forces that a force of size \(1\) N in the direction \(\vek d\) would cause in the bars, divided by \(1\) N, and they have no unit. The theorem, however, asks of them only that they balance the unit force, which we shall use in subsection 4.6.5. Hence the name of the method: the virtual force has size one. The hat over the letter \(N\) reminds us of this unit force. The formula (4.40) says that each bar contributes to the displacement its change of length, multiplied by how strongly a unit force in the direction of the displacement sought would load it. For the bracket of two bars we get the true axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) from equilibrium alone, so we need nothing else for the displacement. In the proof we used the linearity of the material only in step 4. The equality of step 3, \(\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\), holds for bars of any material, only the changes of length must then be computed by the law of that material, as EP does for bars with a nonlinear relation between stress and strain (EP example 4.4.1, pp. 199-200). For large displacements, however, the equation \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) no longer holds, and with it the method fails.

Let us apply the method to our bracket (figure 4.54).

  1. The horizontal part of the displacement. We take \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 0)\). The equation for the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) reads \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) + \hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) = (1, 0, 0)\). The component \(y\) gives \(-\tfrac35\,\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), and the component \(x\) gives \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\). By (4.40)
    \[u = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 1 \cdot \Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} + 0 \cdot \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} .\]
    The joint moves \(2{,}721\) mm to the left.
  2. The vertical part of the displacement. We take \(\vek d = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, -1, 0)\), in the direction of the load. The component \(y\) of the equation gives \(-\tfrac35\,\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -1\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53\), and the component \(x\) gives \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} + \tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac53 = 0\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43\). By (4.40)
    \[\begin{aligned} -v &= -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -\tfrac43 \cdot (-2{,}721\ \text{mm}) + \tfrac53 \cdot 4{,}252\ \text{mm} \\ &= 3{,}628\ \text{mm} + 7{,}086\ \text{mm} = 10{,}71\ \text{mm} . \end{aligned}\]
    The joint drops by \(10{,}71\) mm.

The displacement of the joint is therefore \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (-2721, -10\,714, 0)\) µm. The component \(v\) equals \(-2U/F = -10{,}71\) mm of section 4.1. There we got it by assuming that all the work of the load is stored in the bars, here from equilibrium, geometry and the material law, with which we computed the two changes of length. The agreement is no accident. For \(\vek d\) in the direction of the load the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the true axial forces divided by \(F\), and the right side of (4.40) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}/F\), which by section 4.1 is twice the energy \(U = 53{,}57\) J divided by \(F\).

There are two patterns in the numbers, which we explain. Why does the horizontal part of the displacement depend only on the bar \(AC\)? A horizontal force at \(C\) loads only the bar \(AC\), because the bar \(BC\) cannot give a horizontal force without also giving a vertical one, and nothing balances that. Geometrically the same is even more direct: the bar \(AC\) is horizontal, so by the equation \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) its change of length is just the horizontal part of the displacement. And where do the contributions \(3{,}628\) mm and \(7{,}086\) mm to the vertical part come from, and why with the factors \(\tfrac43\) and \(\tfrac53\)? Let us split the displacement into two parts, as in figure 4.55.

  1. Let only the bar \(AC\) shorten, while the bar \(BC\) keeps its length. Then the joint moves perpendicular to the bar \(BC\), because \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), and horizontally by \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = -2{,}721\) mm. Perpendicular to \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\) is the direction \((3, 4, 0)\), in which the vertical part is \(\tfrac43\) times the horizontal one. The joint therefore drops by \(\tfrac43 \cdot 2{,}721\) mm \(= 3{,}628\) mm. When the bar \(AC\) shortens, it pulls the joint toward the wall, and the bar \(BC\) turns it about \(B\) downward as it does.
  2. Let only the bar \(BC\) lengthen, while the bar \(AC\) keeps its length. Then the joint moves perpendicular to the bar \(AC\), that is, vertically. The elongation of the bar \(BC\) is the projection of this displacement onto \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\), whose vertical component is \(-\tfrac35\), so the vertical displacement is \(\tfrac53\) times the elongation, \(\tfrac53 \cdot 4{,}252\) mm \(= 7{,}086\) mm down.

To first approximation the two changes of length are linear functions of the displacement, so the displacements of the two parts add up to the true displacement, \((-2721, -3628, 0) + (0, -7086, 0) = (-2721, -10\,714, 0)\) in micrometres. The factors \(\tfrac43\) and \(\tfrac53\) are exactly the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) in size. The unit dummy load method thus does by itself the geometric computation that we would otherwise have to draw.

The same displacement of the joint, \(u = -2{,}721\) mm and \(v = -10{,}71\) mm, we obtained in section 4.3 from the changes of the lengths of the bars, and in section 4.5 as the lowest point of the total potential energy, a function of the two components of the displacement. Both times we solved two equations for both components at once, here each component of the displacement is a sum of two terms. The advantage shows in large structures. We proved the lemma and the theorem only for a truss with one free joint. For a truss with several free joints we write the equilibrium of each joint separately, take its scalar product with the displacement of that joint and add the equalities. Each bar appears twice in the sum, once at each end and with opposite unit vectors, and together it gives the product of its virtual axial force and its change of length. We do not write this computation out here, and EP states the unit dummy load method for every elastic structure (EP §4.4.2, p. 198). If we want the displacement of one point of a truss with a hundred bars, the unit dummy load method needs only the axial forces due to the load and due to one unit force, while the search for the smallest value needs all displacements of all joints at once. When equilibrium does not determine the axial forces, the true axial forces must be found first, which we show in subsection 4.6.5.

4.6.2 Virtual forces on a body

Now let us write the same for a body of any shape. We repeat the setting of section 4.4. Before loading the body occupies the set of points \(V\) with the surface \(S\). On the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface there are supports that prescribe the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\). On the remaining part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) with which the surroundings act on the body is prescribed, and a body force with density \(\vek b\) acts on the matter. In the truss the virtual forces were axial forces in the bars that balanced the pin. In a body the role of the axial forces is taken by a virtual stress field, and the role of the equilibrium of the pin by the equilibrium equations. Which fields do we allow?

Definition 4.56 Statically admissible virtual stress field (statično dopustno virtualno polje napetosti)

Let the body occupy the set of points \(V\) before loading, and let its surface be divided into the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), where the displacement is prescribed, and the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where the force per unit area is prescribed. A virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\), which assigns to every point of the body a matrix of nine numbers \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), is statically admissible (statično dopustno) if:

  1. the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuously differentiable (definition 1.88) on an open set that contains the body together with its surface,
  2. at every point of the body the field is symmetric, \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\),
  3. at every point of the body it satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force,
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = 0 ,\]
    and the same with the second index \(y\) and \(z\) instead of \(x\),
  4. at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal.

Source: EP (4.4.1), (4.4.2) (p. 196), where a statically admissible field also allows a virtual body force, SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139).

The word statically says that the conditions speak only about forces, not about displacements, just as the word kinematically in an admissible virtual displacement spoke only about displacements. We explain each condition by what we will use it for. Symmetry and the equilibrium equations are the two conditions of equilibrium from chapter 2, written for the virtual field. In the proof they will remove the volume integral with the derivatives of the stress. There is no body force because we will multiply the virtual field by the true displacement and we do not want the true displacement at every point of the body to appear in the equation. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the virtual traction vector is zero, which means that there are no virtual loads there. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), however, the virtual traction vector \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) may be anything. These are the virtual forces of the supports, and their work on the prescribed displacements will remain in the equation. Continuous differentiability is needed for the divergence theorem.

A simple example is a steel bar welded with both ends between two walls, as in figure 4.56. The faces at the walls are \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the mantle is \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). Let the axis \(x\) point along the bar. The field in which \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the same number everywhere and all other components are zero is statically admissible. The components are constant, so they are continuously differentiable and all their derivatives are zero, which satisfies the equilibrium equations. The field is symmetric. On the mantle the normal has the component \(x\) equal to zero, so \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = (\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0) = \vek 0\). On the faces at the walls the virtual traction vectors are \(\pm\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), virtual forces of the walls that pull the bar apart.

In the truss the work of the virtual forces on the true displacements was the sum of the products of the virtual axial forces and the true changes of length. In a body the strain of a small piece of the body takes the place of the change of length of a bar, and an integral over the body the place of the sum over the bars. The proof will be short, because we did all the analysis in section 4.4. Lemma 4.41 on internal virtual work through the surface does not speak about the physical meaning of its fields. It holds for every symmetric continuously differentiable field of nine numbers and every continuously differentiable vector field. There we used it with the true stress and a virtual displacement, here we use it with a virtual stress and the true displacement.

Theorem 4.57 Principle of virtual forces (načelo virtualnih sil)

Let the body before loading occupy the set of points \(V\), which is a box or made of boxes, and let its surface be divided into the parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), which do not overlap and are made of whole rectangles on the faces of these boxes. Let \(\vek u\) be a displacement field that is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface and equals the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and let

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\]

be the components of its small strain tensor, where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) and \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). Then for every statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) (definition 4.56)

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.41}\]

where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface.

Proof

We have to show that the integral on the left turns into the work of the virtual forces of the supports on the prescribed displacements. We use lemma 4.41 with the roles of the fields swapped, then the conditions of the definition of a statically admissible field and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\).

  1. The components of the field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) are by definition 4.56, items 1 and 2, continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface, and symmetric at every point. The components of the field \(\vek u\) are by assumption continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface. The intersection of the two sets is an open set containing the body with its surface. By lemma 4.41, in which we take \(\delta\ten\sigma\) in place of the stress and \(\vek u\) in place of the virtual displacement, therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\,u_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
    The numbers that the lemma calls the virtual strain are here the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\), because we compute them with the same formula from the same partial derivatives. The traction vector of the lemma is here \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\).
  2. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) for \(j = x\) equals \(\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x + \partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial y + \partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}/\partial z\), which by definition 4.56, item 3, is zero at every point of the body. The same for \(j = y\) and \(j = z\). The function under the second volume integral is therefore zero at every point, and this integral is zero.
  3. The surface is made of the rectangles of the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and the rectangles of the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), which do not overlap, so the surface integral is the sum of the integrals over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) (section 4.2).
  4. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\) by definition 4.56, item 4, so there \((\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek u = 0\), and the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero.
  5. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) we have \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) by assumption, so the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equals \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  6. The order of the factors in the product \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) does not matter. Inserting steps 2 to 5 into step 1 gives (4.41).

Source: EP (4.4.5)-(4.4.8) (p. 197), SADD (6.6.1), (6.6.2) (PDF p. 139). The sources state the theorem for a general body, with a virtual body force and with virtual forces on the whole surface. The proof with lemma 4.41 is not from the sources.

The proof showed where the equation comes from. The lemma moved the derivative from the true displacement to the virtual stress. The equilibrium equations of the virtual field cancelled the volume integral with the derivatives of the stress, and on the surface the work of the virtual forces of the supports on the prescribed displacements remained. The lemma needed the symmetry of the virtual field to write the strain instead of the partial derivatives of the displacement.

What is not in the theorem? There is no relation between stress and strain. The virtual stress only has to be in equilibrium, and the strains have to come from one displacement field that equals the prescribed one on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The theorem therefore holds for every material, also for one that deforms permanently, and for strains that are not caused by stress, such as the strains caused by temperature of section 3.3. It does not hold, however, for large strains, where we may not identify the shapes before and after loading and may not compute the strains with the small strain tensor. The principle is a statement about geometry. EP writes that the strains and displacements are compatible and consistent with the supports exactly when the equation holds for every statically admissible field (EP (4.4.5), p. 197). We proved the direction we will need: the equation follows from compatibility. EP derives the converse by obtaining from the equation the conditions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) in the body and \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (EP (4.4.9), (4.4.10), p. 198). We prove the first part of the converse for a body in subsection 4.6.8: if the equation holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field, the strains satisfy the compatibility equations of section 1.18, and in a body in which every point can be joined to one chosen point by a segment that does not leave the body, a box for instance, we also get a displacement field from them. The condition on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is only cited there. How the equation demands compatibility, however, we will see on a truss in subsection 4.6.5.

How is the theorem related to the lemma on virtual forces on a truss? Take a bar of length \(L\) and cross-section area \(A\) in which the virtual stress \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \delta N/A\) is constant and the true strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \Delta L/L\) is constant too, while the other components are zero. The integral on the left side of (4.41) is then the product of the two numbers and the volume of the bar,

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \frac{\Delta L}{L} \cdot \frac{\delta N}{A} \cdot A L = \Delta L\,\delta N ,\]

which is the term of the bar in (4.39). In the truss the virtual force \(\delta\vek F\) acted at the joint where the true load acts too. For a body we get such a case if on a part of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), instead of \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\), we require the virtual traction vector to equal a chosen virtual force per unit area \(\delta\bar{\vek t}\). Then only step 4 of the proof changes. The integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is no longer zero but \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \delta\bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\), and the equation becomes

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \delta\bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]

as SADD (6.6.2) (PDF p. 139) writes it. If the virtual force is spread over a small patch of the surface and has the total size \(1\) N in a chosen direction, the first term on the right is approximately the component of the displacement of the patch in this direction, multiplied by \(1\) N, and we get the unit dummy load method for a body (EP (4.4.12), p. 198). We will use it for beams in chapter 5.

4.6.3 Complementary energy

We obtained the principle of minimum total potential energy of section 4.5 by taking as the virtual displacement the difference of two admissible displacement fields. We do the same with virtual forces: as the virtual stress field we take the difference of two stress fields that satisfy equilibrium. For this we need an energy written with forces, not with displacements.

We met the complementary strain energy density \(w^*\) in section 3.6 (definition 3.48). In a uniaxial state it is the area between the curve of stress against strain and the stress axis, and for an ideal elastic material it depends only on the final state. For a linear elastic material it equals the strain energy density in value, \(w^* = w = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (section 3.6), but we write it as a function of the stresses. For an isotropic material we express it with Hooke's law.

  1. In the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) there are three terms with equal indices. We insert into them the strains of the left column of (3.12): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 2\nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})\big)/E\). Each product of two different normal stresses appears twice, once from each of the two rows, hence the factor \(2\nu\).
  2. The six terms with different indices form three pairs, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\). By the symmetry of stress and strain and by the right column of (3.12) this pair is \(2\,(1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2/E\).
  3. We add and divide by \(2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} w^* &= \frac{1}{2E}\Big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 2\nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}) \\ &\qquad + 2\,(1 + \nu)\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}^2)\Big) . \end{aligned}\]

This is how EP (3.2.23) (p. 108) writes it. In a bar only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A\) is not zero, so \(w^* = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2/(2E) = N^2/(2EA^2)\), the same as the strain energy density.

Definition 4.58 Complementary energy (komplementarna energija)

Let the body be of an ideal elastic material whose complementary strain energy density \(w^*\) at every point is a function of the components of stress at that point, and let the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) be prescribed on the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface. For a stress field \(\ten\sigma\) in the body the complementary energy (komplementarna energija) of the body is the number

\[U^*(\ten\sigma) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} w^*\,\mathrm{d}V ,\]

where \(w^*\) at every point is computed from the components of the field \(\ten\sigma\) at that point, and the total complementary energy (celotna komplementarna energija) is the number

\[\Pi^*(\ten\sigma) = U^*(\ten\sigma) - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.42}\]

where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface.

Source: EP (3.2.10) (p. 106) for \(U^*\) and (4.5.3) (p. 204) for \(\Pi^*\), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 140).

What kind of object is \(\Pi^*\)? Like the total potential energy, it is a function whose input is a whole field and whose output is one number in joules, except that the input here is a stress field, not a displacement field. The first term is the complementary energy the body would have with the field \(\ten\sigma\). The second term is the work that the forces of the supports \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) would do on the prescribed displacements if they were constant all the time, with a minus sign. In the total potential energy the second term had known forces on unknown displacements, here it has the known displacements of the supports on the unknown forces of the supports. For fixed supports, \(\bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\), the second term is zero, and \(\Pi^* = U^*\).

In a truss the stress in each bar is constant, so the complementary energy of the bar \(k\) is the product of the density and the volume, \(A_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}} \cdot N_{\mathrm{k}}^2/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}^2) = N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\). The complementary energy of the truss is the sum over the bars. For our bracket with the fixed pins \(A\) and \(B\)

\[\Pi^* = U^* = \frac{N_{\mathrm{AC}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2E\,A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \frac{N_{\mathrm{BC}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{BC}}}{2E\,A_{\mathrm{BC}}} = 18{,}14\ \text{J} + 35{,}43\ \text{J} = 53{,}57\ \text{J} ,\]

equal to the strain energy \(U\) of section 4.1. They are equal because the material is linear. The difference lies in what the input is: \(U^*\) is written with the axial forces, while the energy for a displacement field we wrote with the displacements in section 4.5 (EP, p. 107).

Which stress fields will we compare? Those that could be the true one if we look only at equilibrium.

Definition 4.59 Statically admissible stress field (statično dopustno polje napetosti)

Let the body be as in definition 4.56, with the prescribed force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the body force with density \(\vek b\). A stress field \(\ten\sigma\) is statically admissible (statično dopustno) if its components are continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface, if at every point of the body it is symmetric and satisfies the equilibrium equations (2.31) with the body force \(\vek b\), and if at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) it gives \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\).

Source: EP (4.4.1), (4.4.2) (p. 196) and p. 205, SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139).

A statically admissible field fulfils all conditions of equilibrium, but not necessarily those of geometry. The strains that the material law would assign to it need not come from any displacement field. The difference of two statically admissible fields, however, is a statically admissible virtual stress field. When we subtract the equilibrium equations of the two fields, the body force cancels, and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the difference of the traction vectors is \(\bar{\vek t} - \bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). We will need this in the proof.

Theorem 4.60 Principle of minimum complementary energy (načelo najmanjše komplementarne energije)

Let the body be as in theorem 4.57 on the principle of virtual forces, of an ideal elastic and linear elastic material whose strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero, and in which the stresses determine the strains uniquely. Let \(\vek u\) be a displacement field that is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface and equals the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and let the stress field \(\ten\sigma\) that the material law assigns to the strains of the field \(\vek u\) be statically admissible.
