Then for every statically admissible stress field \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}\) to which the material law assigns small strains:

  1. the difference of the total complementary energies is the complementary energy of the difference of the fields,
    \[\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) - \Pi^*(\ten\sigma) = U^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma) \ge 0 , \tag{4.43}\]
  2. equality \(\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = \Pi^*(\ten\sigma)\) holds only if \(\tilde{\ten\sigma} = \ten\sigma\) at every point of the body.

The strain that the material law assigns to the difference \(\tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma\) need not be small, so we compute \(U^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma)\) with the density \(w^*\) that at every point is the value of the polynomial \(w\) from lemma 4.50 at this strain.

Proof

We have to show that the difference of the energies splits into an expression from the principle of virtual forces, which is zero, and the complementary energy of the difference of the fields, which is not negative. We follow the proof of theorem 4.51 on the principle of minimum total potential energy with the roles swapped.

1. The difference of the energies.

  1. Let \(\ten\tau = \tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma\). The components of both fields are continuously differentiable on open sets containing the body with its surface, so the components of the field \(\ten\tau\) are continuously differentiable on their intersection. Both fields are symmetric, so \(\ten\tau\) is symmetric too. When we subtract the equilibrium equations of the field \(\ten\sigma\) from those of the field \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}\), \(\vek b\) cancels, and since the partial derivative of a difference is the difference of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.79), the field \(\ten\tau\) satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\ten\tau\,\vek n = \tilde{\ten\sigma}\,\vek n - \ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t} - \bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\) (lemma 1.95). The field \(\ten\tau\) is therefore a statically admissible virtual stress field.
  2. At every point of the body let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the strains of the field \(\vek u\), which by assumption belong to the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the strains that the material law assigns to the stresses \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The material law is linear, so the stresses \(\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} + \tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) have the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are small by assumption 1 at the start of the section, the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) by the assumption of the theorem. Their difference \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) need not be small, since two components below the bound in absolute value can differ by almost twice the bound. Lemma 4.50 does not need smallness, because it only expands the polynomial \(w\).
  3. For a linear elastic and ideal elastic material the complementary strain energy density equals in value the strain energy density in the same state (section 3.6), \(w^* = w\). Therefore at every point \(w^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\})\), \(w^*(\ten\sigma) = w(\{\varepsilon\})\) and \(w^*(\ten\tau) = w(\{\eta\})\), where the braces, as in section 4.5, denote the Voigt column of the six strain components. When \(\{\eta\}\) is not a small strain, the last equality is the definition of the density \(w^*(\ten\tau)\) from the theorem.
  4. By lemma 4.50 on the energy density of a sum of strains, \(w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = w(\{\varepsilon\}) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\eta\})\).
  5. We use the same lemma with the two strains swapped, \(\{\eta\}\) in the first place and \(\{\varepsilon\}\) in the second. The stresses belonging to \(\{\eta\}\) are \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so \(w(\{\eta\} + \{\varepsilon\}) = w(\{\eta\}) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\varepsilon\})\). The left sides of steps 4 and 5 are equal, because the sum of the strains is the same, so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  6. From steps 3, 4 and 5, at every point
    \[w^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = w^*(\ten\sigma) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}} + w^*(\ten\tau) .\]
  7. We integrate over the body and use the linearity of the integral over a body (section 4.2):
    \[U^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = U^*(\ten\sigma) + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V + U^*(\ten\tau) .\]
  8. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) we have \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}\,\vek n = \ten\sigma\,\vek n + \ten\tau\,\vek n\) (lemma 1.95), the scalar product is distributive (lemma 2.12), and by linearity the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) in (4.42) splits into an integral with \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) and an integral with \(\ten\tau\,\vek n\).
  9. We insert steps 7 and 8 into equation (4.42), which defines the total complementary energy, and arrange the terms:
    \[\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = \Pi^*(\ten\sigma) + \Big[ \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\ten\tau\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A \Big] + U^*(\ten\tau) .\]
  10. The field \(\vek u\) satisfies the assumptions of theorem 4.57, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the components of its small strain tensor, and \(\ten\tau\) is by step 1 a statically admissible virtual stress field. By the principle of virtual forces the expression in square brackets is therefore zero, and \(\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) - \Pi^*(\ten\sigma) = U^*(\ten\tau)\).
  11. By step 8 of item 1 of the proof of theorem 4.51 the polynomial \(w\) is zero at the zero column and positive at every other column, also when that column is not a small strain. There we used only the positivity of the energy density at small strains, which this theorem assumes too. So \(w^*(\ten\tau) = w(\{\eta\}) \ge 0\) at every point. The integral of a non-negative function is not negative (section 4.2), so \(U^*(\ten\tau) \ge 0\).

2. Equality.

  1. Let \(\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = \Pi^*(\ten\sigma)\). By item 1 then \(U^*(\ten\tau) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), where \(g = w(\{\eta\})\) at every point of the body.
  2. The function \(g\) is continuous and non-negative. The components \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuous, the strains \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are by the linear material law sums of their multiples, and \(g\) is a sum of products of the components \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with constant numbers, so it is continuous by corollary 1.67 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space. It is non-negative by step 11 of item 1.
  3. A continuous non-negative function whose integral over the body is zero is zero at every point of the body. We showed this in steps 3 to 7 of item 2 of the proof of theorem 4.51: if it were positive at some interior point, it would be positive on a small cube around it and the integral would be positive, and on the surface it is zero by continuity. Therefore \(g = 0\) at every point of the body.
  4. By step 11 of item 1 the polynomial \(w\) is positive at every column that is not zero, so \(\{\eta\}\) is the zero strain at every point. The stresses are linear functions of the strains, so the stress \(\ten\tau\) belonging to zero strain is zero, and \(\tilde{\ten\sigma} = \ten\sigma\) at every point.

Source: EP §4.5.1, (4.5.2)-(4.5.12) (pp. 204-205), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 140), which states the principle and leaves the proof to other books. EP proves the minimum with the compliance coefficients and their symmetry. The proof with lemma 4.50 and item 2 are not from the sources.

What does the theorem say? Among all stress fields that fulfil equilibrium and the prescribed forces, the true field has the smallest total complementary energy. Every other field has a larger one, larger by exactly the complementary energy of the difference. The proof showed where this comes from. The mixed term of the expanded energy, the work of the difference of stresses on the true strains, cancels against the work of the difference of the forces of the supports on the prescribed displacements, because the true strains are compatible and the difference is a statically admissible virtual field. Only the energy of the difference remains, and it is not negative because the material is stable.

Let us compare the two principles of a smallest value. The principle of minimum total potential energy searches among displacement fields that respect the supports, that is, among fields that fulfil the conditions of geometry, and picks from them the one that fulfils equilibrium as well. The principle of minimum complementary energy searches among stress fields that fulfil equilibrium and picks from them the one that fulfils the conditions of geometry as well, that is, whose strains come from a displacement field that equals the prescribed one on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). For the true state all three sets of equations must hold: equilibrium, geometry and the material law. Each principle requires two of them in advance and finds the third as the condition for the smallest value.

Where does the theorem stop holding? We used the linearity of the material in steps 2 to 5, where we added strains and used lemma 4.50. SADD states the principle also for nonlinear elastic materials (SADD, PDF p. 140), but the proof needs more about the shape of the function \(w^*\) than we have developed. For large strains the principle of virtual forces does not hold in this form, because we may not compute the strains with the small strain tensor. Item 2 says moreover that the true stress field is unique. For displacement fields we got less in section 4.5: the true displacement field is unique only up to a difference without strain, for example a rigid motion, which does not change the stresses.

For a truss with fixed supports we translate the theorem directly. The proof is shorter, because sums over the bars take the place of integrals.

Corollary 4.61 Minimum complementary energy of a truss (najmanjša komplementarna energija paličja)

Let the truss be as in lemma 4.54 on virtual forces on a truss, with the joint \(C\) on which the force \(\vek P\) acts, and with bars of a linear elastic material with lengths \(L_{\mathrm{k}}\), cross-section areas \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and Young's moduli \(E_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\). Let \(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}}\) be the true axial forces, that is, forces that balance the joint, \(N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek P\), and whose changes of length \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\) come from one displacement of the joint, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). Let \(N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) be any axial forces that also balance the joint. Then

\[U^*(N_1 + \delta N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}) - U^*(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} \ge 0 ,\]

where \(U^*(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\), and equality holds only if all \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are zero.

Proof

We have to show that the mixed terms of the expanded squares cancel. For this we use the lemma on virtual forces on a truss with zero virtual force.

  1. Subtracting the equilibrium of the true forces from the equilibrium of the other ones gives \(\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek P - \vek P = \vek 0\). The numbers \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are therefore virtual axial forces in equilibrium with the virtual force \(\delta\vek F = \vek 0\).
  2. We expand the square of the sum as the product \((N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}})(N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}) = N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + 2N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). The difference of the energies is therefore
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{2N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} ,\]
    where in the first sum we used \(N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}) = \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. By lemma 4.54 with \(\delta\vek F = \vek 0\) we have \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\).
  4. The second sum remains. Each of its terms is a square times the positive number \(L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\), so it is not negative and is zero only for \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). The sum is therefore non-negative and is zero only if all \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are zero.

Source: EP §4.5.1 (pp. 204-205) for a body and example 4.5.1 (p. 207) for a truss of two bars. The corollary and the proof are not from the source.

For the bracket of two bars the corollary says nothing new. The equilibrium of the joint is two equations for two axial forces, so \(\delta N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \delta N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) is the only solution of the equation of step 1, and there are no other axial forces that would balance the joint. There is nothing to compare. The corollary becomes important for a truss with more bars than equilibrium can determine. Before we treat one, let us derive from the complementary energy a formula for a displacement.

4.6.4 Displacement as a derivative of the complementary energy

In section 4.5 we got a force from the strain energy written with displacements, as the derivative of the energy with respect to a displacement. The complementary energy is written with the axial forces, which depend on the load. What is its derivative with respect to a force? For a single bar with the force \(F\) at its end \(U^* = F^2 L/(2EA)\), and its derivative with respect to \(F\) is \(F L/(EA)\), the elongation of the bar, the displacement of the end in the direction of the force. For a truss the same holds.

Theorem 4.62 Castigliano's second theorem (drugi Castiglianov izrek)

Let the truss be as in theorem 4.55 on the unit dummy load method. Let the force \(F_1\,\vek d_1 + F_2\,\vek d_2\) act on the joint \(C\), where \(\vek d_1\) and \(\vek d_2\) are unit vectors of two chosen directions and \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) are numbers with the unit newton. Let the axial forces be written as functions \(N_{\mathrm{k}}(F_1, F_2)\), each of which is the sum of a constant number and multiples of the numbers \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). For all values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) let them balance the joint,

\[N_1(F_1, F_2)\,\vek n_1 + \dots + N_{\mathrm{m}}(F_1, F_2)\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = F_1\,\vek d_1 + F_2\,\vek d_2 ,\]

and for the actual values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) let them equal the true axial forces. Let

\[U^*(F_1, F_2) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}(F_1, F_2)^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} .\]

Then for the actual values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) the component of the displacement of the joint in the direction \(\vek d_1\) is

\[\vek d_1\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \frac{\partial U^*}{\partial F_1} , \tag{4.44}\]

and likewise \(\vek d_2\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \partial U^*/\partial F_2\).

Proof

We have to show that the derivative of the energy with respect to \(F_1\) is the right side of the formula (4.40) for suitably chosen numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\). For this we obtain the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) as the derivatives of the axial forces with respect to \(F_1\).

  1. Let \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}} = \partial N_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial F_1\). The function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the sum of a constant number and multiples of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a number that does not depend on \(F_1\) and \(F_2\): a multiple of \(F_1\) has its factor as derivative, and the other terms are constant for constant \(F_2\) and have derivative zero (lemma 1.79).
  2. The equilibrium equation holds for all \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). Each of its components is therefore an equality of two functions of the variable \(F_1\) for constant \(F_2\), and the derivatives of the two sides are equal. By the rules for differentiating a sum and a multiple, the derivative of the left side is \(\hat N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \hat N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}}\), that of the right side \(\vek d_1\). The numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) therefore satisfy the equation of theorem 4.55 with the direction \(\vek d = \vek d_1\).
  3. By the product rule (lemma 1.79) the derivative of the square \(N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) with respect to \(F_1\) is \(2\,N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\). Therefore
    \[\frac{\partial U^*}{\partial F_1} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{2\,N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} .\]
  4. For the actual values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) the \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the true axial forces, so by theorem 4.55 the right side of step 3 equals \(\vek d_1\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). This proves (4.44). For \(F_2\) we repeat steps 1 to 4 with derivatives with respect to \(F_2\).

Source: EP §4.5.2, (4.5.13) (p. 206), where the theorem is derived from the principle of minimum complementary energy for every elastic structure, and example 4.5.1 (p. 207) for a truss of two bars. The proof with the unit dummy load method is not from the source.

Why does the derivative of energy with respect to a force give a displacement? Figure 4.57 shows the mechanism for a structure with a single force \(F\) whose point of application moves by \(\Delta\) in the direction of the force. The complementary energy is the area between the line of force against displacement and the force axis. When we raise the force by a small number \(h\), the area grows by a strip whose height is \(h\) and whose width is the displacement \(\Delta\), and by a small triangle at the end of the strip. The increase of energy is therefore almost \(h\,\Delta\), and when we send the quotient of the increase of energy and the increase of force \(h\) toward zero, we get \(\Delta\). The theorem holds also for nonlinear elastic structures, where the line becomes a curve (EP, p. 206), but we proved it only for linear bars.

Let us apply the theorem to the bracket of two bars. The load points down, so we take \(\vek d_1 = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(F_1 = F\). For the horizontal part of the displacement we also need a force in the horizontal direction, which does not really exist. We add it in our minds, with \(\vek d_2 = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and size \(F_2 = Q\). After differentiating we set \(Q = 0\). Books call such a force a fictitious load (navidezna sila) (EP, p. 206). Why do we need it? The energy written only with \(F\) does not tell how it would change if we added a horizontal force, and by the theorem that is exactly the horizontal displacement.

  1. The equilibrium of the joint under the force \((Q, -F, 0)\) reads \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) = (Q, -F, 0)\). The component \(y\) gives \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F\), the component \(x\) gives \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = Q - \tfrac43 F\). Both are sums of multiples of \(F\) and \(Q\), as the theorem requires.
  2. The complementary energy is
    \[U^*(F, Q) = \frac{(Q - \tfrac43 F)^2 \cdot 4\ \text{m} + (\tfrac53 F)^2 \cdot 5\ \text{m}}{2EA} ,\]
    where \(EA = 196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N.
  3. The derivative with respect to \(F\) at \(Q = 0\) is
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial U^*}{\partial F} &= \frac{2\,(-\tfrac43 F)(-\tfrac43) \cdot 4\ \text{m} + 2\,(\tfrac53 F)\,\tfrac53 \cdot 5\ \text{m}}{2EA} = \frac{(\tfrac{64}{9} + \tfrac{125}{9})\,F \cdot 1\ \text{m}}{EA} \\ &= \frac{21\ \text{m} \cdot F}{EA} = 10{,}71\ \text{mm} . \end{aligned}\]
  4. The derivative with respect to \(Q\) at \(Q = 0\) is
    \[\frac{\partial U^*}{\partial Q} = \frac{2\,(-\tfrac43 F) \cdot 4\ \text{m}}{2EA} = -\frac{16\ \text{m} \cdot F}{3EA} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} .\]

The joint drops by \(10{,}71\) mm and moves \(2{,}721\) mm to the left, as we got with the unit dummy load method. The numbers \(\tfrac{64}{9}\) and \(\tfrac{125}{9}\) in step 3 are the contributions of the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\), \(\tfrac43 \cdot \tfrac43 \cdot 4\) and \(\tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac53 \cdot 5\), which we saw in figure 4.55 as \(3{,}628\) mm and \(7{,}086\) mm. The unit dummy load method and Castigliano's second theorem are the same computation written in two ways. The derivative \(\partial N_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial F_1\) is exactly the axial force due to a unit force in the direction \(\vek d_1\), divided by \(1\) N.

Let us compare with Castigliano's first theorem of section 4.5. There a force was the derivative of the strain energy, written with displacements, with respect to a displacement. Here a displacement is the derivative of the complementary energy, written with forces, with respect to a force. For a linear material the two energies are equal in value, but since they are written with different variables, they have different derivatives (EP, p. 206).

4.6.5 A statically indeterminate truss

Let us add a third bar to the bracket (figure 4.58). Below the joint \(C\) we place a vertical bar \(CD\) standing on the floor, with the pin \(D = (0, -3, 0)\) m. It has length \(L_{\mathrm{CD}} = 3\) m, is of steel with the same cross section \(A_{\mathrm{CD}} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\), and its unit vector from the floor toward the joint is \(\vek n_{\mathrm{CD}} = (0, 1, 0)\). Everything else stays: the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\), the pins on the wall and the load \(F = 10\) kN at \(C\). Here too we do not treat buckling.

The equilibrium of the pin \(C\) is now

\[N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) + N_{\mathrm{CD}}\,(0, 1, 0) = (0, -F, 0) .\]

These are two equations, for the components \(x\) and \(y\), for three unknown axial forces. Equilibrium does not determine them. Such a truss is called a statically indeterminate truss (statično nedoločeno paličje). EP calls a structure indeterminate when there are more unknown forces than equations of equilibrium (EP, p. 116), and FELIPPA calls a truss whose forces follow from equilibrium statically determinate (FELIPPA, PDF p. 54). The word statically says that we do not get the forces from statics, from the conditions of equilibrium alone. The truss of two bars was statically determinate. Let us choose the axial force in the post as the unknown and denote it by \(X = N_{\mathrm{CD}}\). For a chosen \(X\) the two equations give the other two forces.

  1. Component \(y\): \(-\tfrac35\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} + X = -F\), so \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53\,(F + X)\).
  2. Component \(x\): \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} + \tfrac45\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43\,(F + X)\).

Every number \(X\) thus gives axial forces that balance the joint. For \(X = 0\) the post carries nothing, and the forces in the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\) are the same as for the bracket with two bars. For \(X = -F\) the post carries the whole load and the bars on the wall carry nothing. Which number \(X\) is the true one? Equilibrium cannot tell. Geometry must tell: the changes of length of all three bars must come from one displacement of the joint.

By corollary 4.61 the true force in the post has the smallest complementary energy of all, because every other choice of \(X\) gives axial forces that also balance the joint and are therefore of the form \(N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the corollary. Let us write the energy as a function of \(X\) and find its smallest value.

  1. We insert the axial forces into the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2EA)\) and factor out \((F + X)^2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} U^*(X) &= \frac{\tfrac{16}{9}\,(F + X)^2 \cdot 4\ \text{m} + \tfrac{25}{9}\,(F + X)^2 \cdot 5\ \text{m} + X^2 \cdot 3\ \text{m}}{2EA} \\ &= \frac{21\ \text{m} \cdot (F + X)^2 + 3\ \text{m} \cdot X^2}{2EA} , \end{aligned}\]
    where we added \(\tfrac{64}{9} + \tfrac{125}{9} = \tfrac{189}{9} = 21\).
  2. We expand the square \((F + X)^2\) as the product \((F + X)(F + X) = F^2 + 2FX + X^2\) and order the numerator by powers of \(X\): \(21\,(F + X)^2 + 3X^2 = 24X^2 + 42FX + 21F^2\), where each term is multiplied by 1 m.
  3. We complete the square, as for the bar with a load in section 4.5. The expanded square \(24\,(X + \tfrac78 F)^2\) is \(24X^2 + 42FX + \tfrac{147}{8}F^2\), because \(2 \cdot 24 \cdot \tfrac78 = 42\) and \(24 \cdot \tfrac{49}{64} = \tfrac{147}{8}\). Therefore \(24X^2 + 42FX + 21F^2 = 24\,(X + \tfrac78 F)^2 + \tfrac{21}{8}F^2\), and
    \[U^*(X) = \frac{24\ \text{m} \cdot \big(X + \tfrac78 F\big)^2 + \tfrac{21}{8}\ \text{m} \cdot F^2}{2EA} .\]
  4. The first term of the numerator is never negative and is zero only at \(X = -\tfrac78 F\). The second term does not depend on \(X\). The energy is therefore smallest at \(X = -\tfrac78 F = -8{,}75\) kN and only there (figure 4.59), and its smallest value is \(\tfrac{21}{16}\ \text{m} \cdot F^2/(EA) = 6{,}696\) J. At \(X = 0\) it would be \(53{,}57\) J.
  5. The true force in the post is therefore \(N_{\mathrm{CD}} = -8{,}75\) kN, the post is compressed. The other two axial forces are \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac18\,F = 2{,}083\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 \cdot \tfrac18\,F = -1{,}667\) kN.

The post carries seven eighths of the load, the bars on the wall only one eighth. Why so unequally? Let us look at the two paths along which the load reaches the supports as two springs that the joint \(C\) connects (figure 4.60). The bracket of two bars drops under a vertical force \(P\) at \(C\) by \(21\ \text{m} \cdot P/(EA)\), as we computed above, and the post shortens under the force \(P\) by \(3\ \text{m} \cdot P/(EA)\). Under the same force the post therefore moves seven times less, or for the same displacement it needs a seven times larger force. The ratio of a force to the displacement it causes is called the stiffness (togost), and the stiffness of the post \(EA/(3\ \text{m})\) is seven times the stiffness of the bracket \(EA/(21\ \text{m})\). The two paths must have the same vertical displacement at \(C\), because they meet at the same joint. The post acts on the joint only vertically, because it carries only an axial force along its axis (lemma 4.5), and it does not resist a horizontal displacement of the joint, because the length of the vertical bar does not change, to first approximation, under a small horizontal displacement. Let the bracket carry the vertical force \(P_1\) and the post \(P_2\). The displacements of the two paths are \(21\ \text{m} \cdot P_1/(EA)\) and \(3\ \text{m} \cdot P_2/(EA)\). Then \(P_1 + P_2 = F\) and \(21\,P_1 = 3\,P_2\), so \(P_2 = 7\,P_1\), \(P_1 = F/8\) and \(P_2 = 7F/8\). The load divides in the ratio of the stiffnesses: the stiffer path carries more.

What does it mean that the energy is smallest? At the lowest point of the parabola the derivative of \(U^*\) with respect to \(X\) is zero. From the form in step 3 this derivative is \(48\ \text{m} \cdot (X + \tfrac78 F)/(2EA)\), which is indeed zero at \(X = -\tfrac78 F\). Let us write the same derivative with the changes of length. By the product rule (lemma 1.79) the derivative of the term of the bar \(k\) is \((N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(EA))\,\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{k}}/\mathrm{d}X = \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{k}}/\mathrm{d}X\), and the derivatives of the axial forces from the formulas above are \(\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{AC}}/\mathrm{d}X = -\tfrac43\), \(\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{BC}}/\mathrm{d}X = \tfrac53\) and \(\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{CD}}/\mathrm{d}X = 1\). The condition that the derivative is zero therefore reads

\[-\tfrac43\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} + \tfrac53\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} + \Delta L_{\mathrm{CD}} = 0 .\]

The numbers \(-\tfrac43\), \(\tfrac53\) and \(1\) are virtual axial forces that balance the joint without any force at it, since \(-\tfrac43\,(1, 0, 0) + \tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) + (0, 1, 0) = (0, 0, 0)\). Such axial forces are called self-equilibrating (samouravnotežene) (EP, p. 196). The condition is therefore the equation (4.39) with zero virtual force.

What does the condition say? By the unit dummy load method the first two terms are the downward vertical displacement of the joint that the bars on the wall allow, since \(-\tfrac43\) and \(\tfrac53\) are the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) of subsection 4.6.1. The third term is the change of length of the post, which is negative when it shortens, and is therefore the downward vertical displacement of the joint that the post allows, with the opposite sign. The condition thus demands that the two paths give the joint the same vertical displacement. At \(X = 0\) we do not fulfil it: the bars on the wall would let the joint drop by \(10{,}71\) mm, while the unloaded post would leave it in place. If the changes of length come from one displacement of the joint, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), the condition holds for every displacement: with \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\) the left side is \(-\tfrac43\,u + \tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac15\,(4u - 3v) + v = -\tfrac43\,u + \tfrac43\,u - v + v = 0\). With two bars the ends can always meet again when the bars turn about the pins (figure 4.11). A third bar, however, adds a third requirement for the same two components of the displacement. Three changes of length come from two components of the displacement, so they must satisfy one equation. This is the compatibility condition of the truss, just as the compatibility equations of section 1.18 are the condition that six strains come from three components of the displacement. The principle of minimum complementary energy picked from all distributions of forces in equilibrium the one whose changes of length fit together.

Let us check the result in another way too, by searching for the smallest total potential energy of section 4.5, where the unknowns are displacements. Let the displacement of the joint be \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\). The changes of length of the bars are \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u\), \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4u - 3v)\) and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{CD}} = v\), the energy of a bar with the change of length \(\Delta L\) is \(EA\,\Delta L^2/(2L)\), and the work of the load is \(\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -F v\). The total potential energy is therefore

\[\Pi(u, v) = \frac{EA}{2}\Big(\frac{u^2}{4\ \text{m}} + \frac{(4u - 3v)^2}{25 \cdot 5\ \text{m}} + \frac{v^2}{3\ \text{m}}\Big) + F v .\]

By section 4.5 the true displacement is the lowest point of the function \(\Pi\), so its partial derivatives with respect to \(u\) and \(v\) are zero there (lemma 1.80, applied to each variable separately). The solution of these two equations, computed with SymPy, is \(u = -\tfrac23 \cdot 1\ \text{m} \cdot F/(EA) = -0{,}3401\) mm and \(v = -\tfrac{21}{8} \cdot 1\ \text{m} \cdot F/(EA) = -1{,}339\) mm. From it the changes of length are \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = -0{,}3401\) mm, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0{,}5315\) mm and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{CD}} = -1{,}339\) mm, and the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{k}} = EA\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}/L_{\mathrm{k}}\) are \(-1{,}667\) kN, \(2{,}083\) kN and \(-8{,}75\) kN, the same as with the minimum complementary energy. The check also shows that axial forces that balance the joint and whose changes of length come from one displacement really exist, which corollary 4.61 assumed. The joint drops by only \(1{,}339\) mm, eight times less than without the post, because the bracket with the post is eight times stiffer than the bracket without it: the stiffnesses \(EA/(21\ \text{m})\) and \(EA/(3\ \text{m})\) add up to \(8\,EA/(21\ \text{m})\).

Finally, one more peculiarity of the unit dummy load method. Theorem 4.55 asks of the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) only that they balance the unit force, not that they be the axial forces that the unit force would really cause. In a statically indeterminate truss there are many such sets of numbers, and each gives the same displacement. For the vertical displacement let us simply take the numbers of the bracket without the post, \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43\), \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{CD}} = 0\), which balance the downward unit force without the post carrying anything. With the true changes of length (4.40) gives

\[\begin{aligned} -v &= -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -\tfrac43 \cdot (-0{,}3401\ \text{mm}) + \tfrac53 \cdot 0{,}5315\ \text{mm} + 0 \cdot (-1{,}339\ \text{mm}) \\ &= 0{,}4535\ \text{mm} + 0{,}8858\ \text{mm} = 1{,}339\ \text{mm} , \end{aligned}\]

which is the true displacement. The numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) only have to balance the unit force, but the changes of length have to be the true ones. In a statically indeterminate truss we get the true changes of length only once we know the true axial forces, which was the task of the minimum complementary energy.

4.6.6 Mathematics: a field from its partial derivatives

For the bracket with the post of subsection 4.6.5, the equation of virtual forces demanded that the changes of length of all three bars come from one single displacement of the joint. For a body the same demand takes the form of the six compatibility equations (1.66) of section 1.18. There we proved that the strains of every displacement field with continuous partial derivatives up to third order satisfy them (theorem 1.123). The converse, that in a simply connected body the equations imply that a displacement field exists, we only stated, as theorem 1.133. We postponed it because it needs the summation of small changes of the displacement along a path through the body, for which we had no integral then. Now we have it. In this subsection and the next we prove the theorem for bodies in which every point can be joined to one chosen point by a straight segment that does not leave the body. All the bodies we have computed with so far are of this kind: the box, the strip and the round bar. For general simply connected bodies the theorem stays stated with a source.

How we will find the displacement we described in words already in section 1.18.5. We choose a point \(P_0\) and the displacement zero there. The displacement at another point \(P\) we get by walking from \(P_0\) to \(P\) in short steps and adding up the changes of the displacement. By theorem 1.86 on the change of a field over a short step, the change of the component \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) over a short step is almost exactly the sum of the products of the partial derivatives \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the components of the step. The strains, however, do not give us all partial derivatives of the displacement, only the symmetric part of the displacement gradient. The antisymmetric part, the rotation of the material (definition 1.114), we must first find ourselves, and in the same way, because by lemma 1.124 its partial derivatives are determined by the derivatives of the strains. Both times we solve the same problem. Three functions of three variables are given, \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\), and we look for a function \(\varphi\) whose partial derivatives are exactly these three functions:

\[\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x} = w_{\mathrm{x}} , \qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y} = w_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z} = w_{\mathrm{z}} .\]

This subsection solves the problem. First we name the sets in which we can add up along segments from one point, then we show how a function changes along a segment, and finally we write down the solution.

We will add up along straight segments that all start at the same point \(P_0\). Each such segment must lie in the body entirely, otherwise the summation would need strains at points where there is no material. We write the points of the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) with one single number. Let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). The point \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) is the point \(P_0\) at \(t = 0\), the point \(P\) at \(t = 1\), the midpoint of the segment at \(t = \tfrac12\), and as \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\), the point runs through the whole segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\).

Definition 4.63 Star-shaped set (zvezdasta množica)

Let \(D\) be a set of points of space and \(P_0\) a point of \(D\). The set \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\) (zvezdasta glede na točko \(P_0\)) if for every point \(P\) of \(D\) the whole segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) lies in \(D\), that is, if the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is in \(D\) for every number \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). A set is star-shaped (zvezdasta) if it is star-shaped with respect to at least one of its points. A set that is star-shaped with respect to every one of its points is convex (konveksna).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 9.3.5 (PDF p. 86), for open sets in \(\mathbb R^n\). Convex set: LEBL2 §8.1.4 (PDF p. 16).

The definition is written for the points of our space. In a space with \(n\) coordinates it reads the same (LEBL2, PDF p. 86). The name says what such a set looks like: from the point \(P_0\) we see every one of its points, as from the centre of a star we see all its arms. Figure 4.61 shows four bodies drawn as plane shapes, as if they were thin plates.

  1. The box \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) is convex. Let \(P_0\) and \(P\) be two of its points. The coordinate \(x\) of the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{P}} - x_{\mathrm{P}_0}) = (1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + t\,x_{\mathrm{P}}\). Let \(m\) be the smaller and \(M\) the larger of the numbers \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\). For \(0 \le t \le 1\) the factors \(1 - t\) and \(t\) are not negative, so the number \((1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + t\,x_{\mathrm{P}}\) lies between \((1 - t)\,m + t\,m = m\) and \((1 - t)\,M + t\,M = M\), hence in \([a_1, b_1]\). The same holds for the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The same computation with strict inequalities shows that the set of interior points of a box is convex too.
  2. The ball with centre \(C\) and radius \(R\), the set of points \(Q\) with \(|CQ| < R\), is convex by lemma 1.125 on the distance to the points of a segment, item 3: if \(P_0\) and \(P\) are at a distance less than \(R\) from \(C\), then for \(0 \le t \le 1\) the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is also at a distance less than \(R\) from \(C\). A cylinder is convex too, for example a round bar with axis \(x\), radius \(r\) and length \(L\). The coordinate \(x\) stays between \(0\) and \(L\) as for the box, and the distance from the axis stays below \(r\) by the same lemma, used on the points \((0, y_{\mathrm{P}_0}, z_{\mathrm{P}_0})\), \((0, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(C = O\). We used both already in section 1.18.4, when we checked which bodies are connected.
  3. The L-shaped bracket (figure 4.61, top right) is made of two boxes, a horizontal and a vertical leg, which overlap in the corner square. Let \(P_0\) be a point of the corner square and \(P\) any point of the bracket. The point \(P\) lies in one of the legs, and \(P_0\) lies in the same leg too. The leg is a box, so by item 1 the whole segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) lies in that leg. The bracket is therefore star-shaped with respect to every point of the corner square. It is not convex, however: the segment from the point \(P_1\) at the end of the horizontal leg to the top of the vertical leg passes the corner and leaves the bracket.
  4. The ring with centre \(O\) is not star-shaped (figure 4.61, bottom left). Let \(P_0\) be any point of the ring and \(P\) the point with \(\overrightarrow{OP} = -\overrightarrow{OP_0}\), which is as far from \(O\) as \(P_0\) and therefore also in the ring. The midpoint of the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) has the vector from \(O\) equal to \(\overrightarrow{OP_0} + \tfrac12\,(\overrightarrow{OP} - \overrightarrow{OP_0}) = \tfrac12\,(\overrightarrow{OP_0} + \overrightarrow{OP}) = \vek 0\), so the midpoint is the point \(O\), which is in the hole. From no point of the ring do we see all its points. The same holds for the cut ring of section 1.18.5 (figure 4.61, bottom right). If the point \(P\) falls on the cut, we take a point right next to it, and the segment passes right next to \(O\), still through the hole.

The cut ring shows that a star-shaped set is a special case of a simply connected one (definition 1.132). Every star-shaped set is simply connected. We shrink a closed curve in it to the point \(P_0\) by moving every one of its points \(Q\) at the same time to the point \(P_0 + (1 - \lambda)\,\overrightarrow{P_0 Q}\), as the number \(\lambda\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\). These points lie on the segment from \(P_0\) to \(Q\), which is entirely in the set, the curve does not tear on the way, and at \(\lambda = 1\) it is gathered entirely at \(P_0\). This reasoning is as precise as the definition of simple connectedness, which does not write the continuous shrinking with formulas. The converse does not hold, because the cut ring is simply connected (section 1.18.5) but not star-shaped. LEBL2 chooses star-shaped sets for the same reason as we do: the proof is simpler, and it writes the function sought with one single formula (LEBL2, PDF p. 86).

For the summation along a segment we will need two properties of continuously differentiable functions (definition 1.88). The first is that they are continuous, that is, without jumps (lemma 1.89 of section 1.15.6).

The second property tells how fast the function changes as we move along a segment. We proved it in lemma 1.128 on the derivative along a segment. If \(f\) is continuously differentiable on an open set \(D\) and the point \(P + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), then the function \(g(t) = f(P + t\,\vek d)\) is differentiable at \(t\) with the derivative \(g'(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\), and this derivative is continuous at \(t\). A step \(h\,\vek d\) along the segment therefore changes the function by almost \(h\) times the sum of the products of the partial derivatives with the components of the vector \(\vek d\).

Now let us write the solution of the problem from the start of the subsection. Suppose for a moment that a function \(\varphi\) with the partial derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) exists and that \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\). Then \(\varphi(P)\) is the change of the function from \(P_0\) to \(P\). We cut the segment into short pieces. On the piece from \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) to \(P_0 + (t + \Delta t)\,\vek d\) the step is \(\Delta t\,\vek d\) with the components \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta t\), and by the theorem on the change of a field \(\varphi\) changes on it by about \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta t\) (figure 4.62). The sum of these changes is a Riemann sum of the function \(t \mapsto \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\) on the interval \([0, 1]\), and as the pieces shrink, it approaches the integral. So we propose

\[\varphi(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t , \qquad \vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P} .\]

The notation \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}}\) means the sum over \(k = x, y, z\), and the numbers \(d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the components of the vector \(\vek d\). This reasoning is only the idea, since it assumed that \(\varphi\) exists. The theorem will show that the function given by this formula really has the required derivatives when the three given functions agree with each other.

What must the agreement be? If \(\varphi\) has continuous second partial derivatives and \(\partial\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = w_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every \(k\), then by theorem 1.121 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives

\[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\]

for every two indices \(k\) and \(l\). Three functions that do not satisfy this are not the partial derivatives of any function with continuous second partial derivatives. Take for example \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = x\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), where \(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = 0\) and \(\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 1\). The formula still gives some function. With \(P_0 = O\) we have \(\vek d = (x, y, z)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{y}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d) = t\,x\), so \(\varphi(P) = \int_0^1 t\,x\,y\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12\,x\,y\). Its partial derivatives, however, are \(\tfrac12\,y\), \(\tfrac12\,x\) and \(0\), not \(0\), \(x\) and \(0\). The theorem says that the condition is also sufficient when the set is star-shaped.

Theorem 4.64 A field from its partial derivatives (polje iz parcialnih odvodov)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points that is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\) (definition 4.63), and let \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions that are continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.88) and satisfy at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} \quad \text{for all } \ix{k}, \ix{l} \in \{x, y, z\} , \tag{4.45}\]

where \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). For a point \(P\) of \(D\) let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) with the components \(d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\) and

\[\varphi(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{4.46}\]

Then \(\varphi\) is defined at every point of \(D\), \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\), and at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = w_{\mathrm{l}} \quad \text{for } \ix{l} = x, y, z .\]

The function \(\varphi\) is therefore continuously differentiable on \(D\).

Proof

We must show that the integral exists and that its partial derivative with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{l}}\) equals \(w_{\mathrm{l}}\). We will differentiate under the integral sign. The condition (4.45) will turn the integrand into the derivative of a function of the variable \(t\), and the fundamental theorem of calculus will give the value of the integral.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\) and \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). Since \(D\) is open, there are numbers \(r_0 > 0\) and \(r > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(r_0\) from \(P_0\) and all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(P\) are in \(D\). Let \(\vek d \neq \vek 0\). The point \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\) for every \(t\) of the open interval \(I = (-r_0/|\vek d|,\ 1 + r/|\vek d|)\), which contains \([0, 1]\). For \(0 \le t \le 1\) this holds because \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to \(P_0\). For \(t < 0\) the point is at the distance \(|t|\,|\vek d| < r_0\) from \(P_0\). For \(t > 1\) we have \(P_0 + t\,\vek d = P + (t - 1)\,\vek d\), and the point is at the distance \((t - 1)\,|\vek d| < r\) from \(P\). If \(\vek d = \vek 0\), then \(P = P_0\), all points \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) are \(P_0\), and we take for \(I\) the set of all numbers.
  2. By lemma 1.128 on the derivative along a segment, item 1, every function \(t \mapsto w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) is differentiable at every point of \(I\), so by lemma 1.77 it is continuous on \([0, 1]\). The integrand in (4.46) is a sum of such functions multiplied by the numbers \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\), so it is continuous on \([0, 1]\) (corollary 1.62) and by theorem 3.37 integrable. The number \(\varphi(P)\) therefore exists. At \(P = P_0\) we have \(\vek d = \vek 0\), the integrand is zero, and \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\).
  3. Let us choose an index \(l\). For a number \(s\) with \(|s| < r\) the point \(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\) is at the distance \(|s| < r\) from \(P\), so it is in \(D\). Its vector from \(P_0\) is \(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\). Its component \(l\) is \(d_{\mathrm{l}} + s\), the other two equal the components of the vector \(\vek d\). We write the component \(k\) of this vector as \((\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})_{\mathrm{k}}\). By (4.46)
    \[\varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}) = \int_0^1 f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t , \qquad f(t, s) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}\big(Q(t, s)\big)\,\big(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\big)_{\mathrm{k}} ,\]
    where \(Q(t, s) = P_0 + t\,(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\) is a point of the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\). Since \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to \(P_0\), the point \(Q(t, s)\) is in \(D\) for all \(t \in [0, 1]\) and \(|s| < r\) (figure 4.62).
  4. For a fixed \(t\) we have \(Q(t, s) = (P_0 + t\,\vek d) + s\,(t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\). By lemma 1.128, item 1, with the point \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) and the vector \(t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\), which we may use at every \(s\) with \(|s| < r\), because there the point \(Q(t, s)\) is in \(D\), the derivative of the function \(s \mapsto w_{\mathrm{k}}(Q(t, s))\) is the sum of the products of the partial derivatives with the components of the vector \(t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\). Only its component \(l\), equal to \(t\), can differ from zero, so this derivative is \(t\,\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,(Q(t, s))\). The factor \((\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})_{\mathrm{k}}\) has the derivative \(1\) with respect to \(s\) when \(\ix{k} = \ix{l}\) and \(0\) otherwise. By the product rule (lemma 1.79) therefore
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) = t \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}}\big(Q(t, s)\big)\,\big(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\big)_{\mathrm{k}} + w_{\mathrm{l}}\big(Q(t, s)\big) .\]
  5. The functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) are continuous on the rectangle \([0, 1] \times [-r/2, r/2]\), whose point \((t, s)\) we treat as the point \((t, s, 0)\) of the plane \(z = 0\), as the rectangles of section 4.2.2. Let a sequence of points \((t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) of the rectangle converge to \((t, s)\). By lemma 1.64 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(t_{\mathrm{n}}\) then converges to \(t\) and \(s_{\mathrm{n}}\) to \(s\). The coordinates of the points \(Q(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) are sums and products of the numbers \(t_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{n}}\) and constants, so by lemma 1.58 on limit laws for sequences they converge to the coordinates of the point \(Q(t, s)\), and by the same lemma on convergence coordinate by coordinate the points \(Q(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to \(Q(t, s)\). The function \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuous at \(Q(t, s)\) by lemma 1.89, and its partial derivative \(\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) by assumption. By lemma 1.66 on continuity through sequences of points, the values of both at the points \(Q(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to the values at \(Q(t, s)\). By the lemma on limit laws for sequences, \(f(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) therefore tends to \(f(t, s)\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\,(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) to \(\partial f/\partial s\,(t, s)\), and by lemma 1.66 the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) are continuous.
  6. We use lemma 4.19 on differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter, item 1, on the rectangle \([0, 1] \times [-r/2, r/2]\). Its hypotheses hold: the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial s\) exists at every point of the rectangle by step 4, since there \(|s| \le r/2 < r\), and the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) are continuous on the rectangle by step 5. The function \(G(s) = \int_0^1 f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\) of the lemma equals \(\varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\) by step 3, and the number \(0\) lies in \((-r/2, r/2)\). By the lemma, the function \(s \mapsto \varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\) is therefore differentiable at \(s = 0\), with the derivative \(\int_0^1 \partial f/\partial s\,(t, 0)\,\mathrm{d}t\). This derivative is the limit of the quotient \((\varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}) - \varphi(P))/s\), so by the definition of the partial derivative 1.23 it is the partial derivative \(\partial\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,(P)\).
  7. At \(s = 0\) we have \(Q(t, 0) = P_0 + t\,\vek d\) and \((\vek d + 0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})_{\mathrm{k}} = d_{\mathrm{k}}\). By step 4 and by the condition (4.45), which replaces \(\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) by \(\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\),
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, 0) = t \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}} + w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d) .\]
  8. Let \(h(t) = t\,w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) for \(t \in I\). By lemma 1.128, items 1 and 2, the function \(t \mapsto w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) has the derivative \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial w_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is continuous on \(I\). By the product rule, \(h'(t)\) is exactly the right side of step 7. The function \(h'\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\) as a sum of products of continuous functions (corollary 1.62), and \(h\) is continuous because it is differentiable.
  9. By step 6 and by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39, item 1, with the function \(h\) on the interval \([0, 1]\),
    \[\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}}(P) = \int_0^1 h'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = h(1) - h(0) = 1 \cdot w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + \vek d) - 0 = w_{\mathrm{l}}(P) .\]
  10. The functions \(w_{\mathrm{l}}\) are continuous at every point of \(D\) by lemma 1.89. The partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) therefore exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\), and \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\).

Source: LEBL2 Thm. 9.3.6 (Poincaré lemma, PDF p. 87), for star-shaped domains in \(\mathbb R^n\), with the same formula and with differentiation under the integral sign. Steps 1, 3 to 5 and 8, which check the hypotheses of the differentiation under the integral and of the fundamental theorem of calculus, are not from the source.

The proof has shown why the formula works. The derivative with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{l}}\) under the integral gave two terms: the change of the values \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) when the segment moves together with its end \(P\), and the change of the component \(d_{\mathrm{l}}\). The condition (4.45) combined both terms into the derivative of the function \(t\,w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) with respect to \(t\), and the fundamental theorem of calculus turned the integral of this derivative into the difference of the values at the ends, \(w_{\mathrm{l}}(P) - 0\). Without the condition, step 7 would have left another integral, which for the example with \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = x\) above gave not \(0\) but \(\tfrac12\,y\). We will use the theorem twice in the next subsection.

Let us test the formula on the hanging bar, where we know the answer. The component \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) of the field (1.18) has, by the first row of the table in section 1.7.2, the partial derivatives

\[w_{\mathrm{x}} = 2a\,(L - x) , \qquad w_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,y , \qquad w_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}6\,a\,z .\]

Let us forget \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) for a moment and ask which function has these three partial derivatives. The condition (4.45) holds, since all mixed derivatives are zero: \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) not on \(x\) and \(z\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) not on \(x\) and \(y\). The functions are polynomials, defined in all of space, and space is convex, since the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is always in space. Let us take \(P_0 = O\). Then \(\vek d = (x, y, z)\) and \(P_0 + t\,\vek d = (t\,x, t\,y, t\,z)\), so the integrand of (4.46) is

\[2a\,(L - t\,x)\,x - 0{,}6\,a\,t\,y \cdot y - 0{,}6\,a\,t\,z \cdot z = 2aLx - \big(2a\,x^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,y^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,z^2\big)\,t .\]

The function \(G(t) = 2aLx\,t - \big(2a\,x^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,y^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,z^2\big)\,t^2/2\) has this integrand as its derivative by the rules of differentiation, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus

\[\varphi(P) = G(1) - G(0) = 2aLx - a\,x^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) = u_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

The formula returned exactly \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), because \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(O) = 0\), just as \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\). At the point \(P = (5\ \text{m}, 4\ \text{mm}, 0)\) this is \(1{,}464 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, the displacement of section 1.7.1.

What does the formula mean? If we think of the functions \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) as the components of a force that depends on the position of the point, then \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta t\) is the work of this force over the short step \(\Delta t\,\vek d\) (definition 4.1, item 1), and \(\varphi(P)\) is the sum of such works along the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\). The condition (4.45) then tells when the work of a force does not depend on the path along which we move the point, but only on the initial and final positions. We will need this in chapter 8. Books call the theorem the Poincaré lemma (Poincaréjeva lema) (LEBL2, PDF p. 87). It also holds in simply connected sets that are not star-shaped, but the proof then needs integrals along curves and their continuous deformation (LEBL2, PDF p. 86). KREYSZIG proves it for integrals along curves with Stokes's theorem (KREYSZIG §10.2, Theorem 3, PDF p. 449, and §10.9, PDF pp. 489-492).

4.6.7 Displacements from strains

Now let us prove the theorem on the sufficiency of the compatibility equations for star-shaped bodies. First we state the problem precisely. An open set of points \(D\) is given, for example the set of interior points of a body, which is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\). In it six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are given, which we complete to nine with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Their partial derivatives of first and second order shall exist and be continuous at every point of \(D\), and the compatibility equations (1.66) shall hold at every point of \(D\). Where the functions come from does not matter. They can be strains prescribed by uneven heating, or strains from the equation of virtual forces. We assume nothing about the material or the forces, the problem is purely geometric. We look for a continuously differentiable displacement field whose small strain tensor (definition 1.113) has the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

The route has two steps. First we find the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By lemma 1.124 on the derivatives of the rotation from the derivatives of the strains, item 1, its partial derivatives must be

\[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]

For chosen \(i\) and \(j\) the right sides for \(k = x, y, z\) are three given functions, and we get \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with theorem 4.64 if the condition (4.45) holds for them. Then we find the displacement. The displacement gradient is the sum of the small strain tensor and the small rotation tensor, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (section 1.17.5), so for every \(i\) we know all three partial derivatives of \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\), and we get \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) with the same theorem.

What does the condition demand in the first step? For chosen \(i\) and \(j\) and indices \(k\) and \(l\) it reads

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}}\Big(\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\Big(\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) .\]

This is an equation with second derivatives of the strains and four indices, which can be arbitrary. The equations (1.66) are only six special cases. We must show that all of them follow from these six.

Lemma 4.65 Compatibility equations for all indices (enačbe kompatibilnosti za vse indekse)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\), where the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), be functions whose partial derivatives of first and second order exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\). For indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\), \(l\) let

\[Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} . \tag{4.47}\]

If the compatibility equations (1.66) hold at a point \(P\) of \(D\), then at \(P\) the number \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) is zero for all \(3^4 = 81\) choices of the indices.

Proof

Each of the six equations (1.66) has the form left side equals right side. We must show that each of the 81 numbers \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) is zero, or equals the difference of the left and right sides of one of the six equations, or the opposite of this difference. We use three symmetries of the expression (4.47).

  1. Swapping \(i\) and \(j\). When we swap the indices \(i\) and \(j\) in (4.47), we get
    \[Z_{\mathrm{jikl}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} .\]
    These are the same four terms as in \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\), each with the opposite sign, so \(Z_{\mathrm{jikl}} = -Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\).
  2. Swapping \(k\) and \(l\). In the same way we get \(Z_{\mathrm{ijlk}} = \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} - \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} - \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = -Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\).
  3. Swapping the pairs. When we swap the pair \(i\), \(j\) with the pair \(k\), \(l\), we get
    \[Z_{\mathrm{klij}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ki}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{li}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} .\]
    The functions are symmetric, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ki}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}\), and by theorem 1.121 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives the order of differentiation does not matter. So the first term equals the first term of \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\), the second the second, the third the fourth and the fourth the third, and \(Z_{\mathrm{klij}} = Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\).
  4. If \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\), step 1 gives \(Z_{\mathrm{iikl}} = -Z_{\mathrm{iikl}}\), so \(Z_{\mathrm{iikl}} = 0\). In the same way step 2 gives \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkk}} = 0\). There are \(3 \cdot 9 = 27\) choices with \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\), likewise \(27\) choices with \(\ix{k} = \ix{l}\), and \(9\) choices with both, so there are \(27 + 27 - 9 = 45\) choices for which \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) is zero by the very structure of the expression.
  5. There remain \(81 - 45 = 36\) choices with \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k} \neq \ix{l}\). Without regard to order, the pair of different indices \(i\), \(j\) is one of three, \(x\) and \(y\), \(y\) and \(z\), or \(z\) and \(x\), and likewise the pair \(k\), \(l\). By steps 1 and 2, \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) only changes into the opposite number when we swap the order within a pair. Each of the 36 numbers therefore equals one of nine numbers, one for each choice of two pairs, or the opposite of this number.
  6. By step 3 the two numbers in which the pairs are swapped are equal. Of the nine, six remain: \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}}\), \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyz}}\) and \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzx}}\), where the same pair appears twice, and \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}}\), \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyx}}\) and \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzy}}\), where the pairs differ.
  7. Let us compute the first and the fourth. By (4.47), the symmetry \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the theorem on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives,
    \[\begin{aligned} Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}} &= \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y\,\partial x} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} , \\ Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}} &= \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} . \end{aligned}\]
    These are the differences of the left and right sides of the first and the fourth equation (1.66).
  8. When we rename the axes as in the proof of theorem 1.123, \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\), \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}}\) turns into \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyz}}\) and then into \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzx}}\), and \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}}\) into \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyx}}\) and then into \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzy}}\). In the same way the first equation turns into the second and the third, and the fourth into the fifth and the sixth. The six numbers of step 6 are therefore the differences of the left and right sides of the six equations (1.66).
  9. If the equations hold at \(P\), all six numbers of step 6 are zero. By steps 4 to 6 all 81 numbers \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) are therefore zero.

Source: SADD (2.6.1) (PDF p. 51), CM (3.7.10) (PDF p. 151). SADD says that the general form would give 81 equations, which are mostly identities or repetitions, and only six are meaningful, and CM that of the 81 equations only six are different. Neither derives the count. The proof is not from the sources.

Figure 4.63 shows all 81 numbers as the lemma gives them. The row gives the pair \(i\), \(j\), the column the pair \(k\), \(l\), and the number in the cell which of the six equations the expression \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) repeats and with which sign. The equations 1 to 3 appear four times each, once for each choice of the order within both pairs, and the equations 4 to 6 eight times each, because the swap of the pairs comes on top: \(3 \cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 8 = 36\). We checked all 81 cells with SymPy. SADD writes the same expression with differently named indices as the general form of the compatibility equations and obtains the six equations from it by choosing the indices (SADD (2.6.1), (2.6.2), PDF p. 51).

Theorem 4.66 Sufficiency of the compatibility equations in a star-shaped body (zadostnost enačb kompatibilnosti v zvezdastem telesu)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points that is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\) (definition 4.63), and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\), where the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), be functions whose partial derivatives of first and second order exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\) and which satisfy the compatibility equations (1.66) at every point of \(D\). For a point \(P\) of \(D\) let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) with the components \(d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\) and

\[\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Big(\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{4.48}\]
\[u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\big)(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{4.49}\]

Then the displacement field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), its components also have continuous second partial derivatives at every point of \(D\), and at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} \quad \text{for all } \ix{i}, \ix{j} .\]

If \(D\) is the set of interior points of a body, the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are therefore compatible strains (definition 1.119).

Proof

We must show that the integrals exist, that the displacements have continuous first and second partial derivatives, and that the symmetric part of their gradient is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). We use theorem 4.64 twice, once for the rotation and once for the displacement.

1. The rotation.

  1. Let us choose indices \(i\) and \(j\) and write \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) for \(k = x, y, z\). The partial derivatives of the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are differences of second partial derivatives of the functions \(\varepsilon\), which exist and are continuous by assumption, so the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(D\).
  2. The condition (4.45) for the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) demands that \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} - \partial\psi_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) for every \(k\) and \(l\). Written out,
    \[\frac{\partial\psi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} - \frac{\partial\psi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
    By theorem 1.121 the order of differentiation does not matter, so the right side is exactly \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) of (4.47), which is zero by lemma 4.65.
  3. By theorem 4.64 with the functions \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}\), the function \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of (4.48) is defined and continuously differentiable on \(D\), with the derivatives
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} \quad \text{for } \ix{k} = x, y, z .\]
  4. When we swap \(i\) and \(j\), the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) change sign. By the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.38, item 1) therefore \(\omega_{\mathrm{ji}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point of \(D\). For \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) the integrand is zero, so \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\).

2. The displacement.

  1. Let us choose an index \(i\) and write \(w_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for \(j = x, y, z\). The partial derivatives \(\partial w_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} + \partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) exist and are continuous: the first term by assumption, the second because by step 3 it is the difference of two first partial derivatives of the functions \(\varepsilon\). The functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\) are therefore continuously differentiable on \(D\).
  2. The condition (4.45) holds for the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\). By step 3
    \[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} - \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = 0 ,\]
    because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}\).
  3. By theorem 4.64 with the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\), the function \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) of (4.49) is defined and continuously differentiable on \(D\), with the derivatives
    \[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} \quad \text{for } \ix{j} = x, y, z .\]
  4. The second partial derivatives of the function \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) are the partial derivatives of the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\), which exist and are continuous by step 5.

3. The strain.

  1. By step 7, step 4 and the symmetry \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), at every point of \(D\)
    \[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \frac12\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ji}}\big) = \frac12\,\big(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} - \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\big) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

Source: SADD §2.6, (2.6.3)-(2.6.7) (PDF pp. 52-53). SADD writes the displacement as an integral along an arbitrary curve from \(P_0\) to \(P\), the rotation by the derivatives of the strains as in lemma 1.124, and shows with Stokes's theorem that in a simply connected body the result does not depend on the curve. BARBER (PDF p. 46) calls such integrals Cesàro integrals (Cesàrovi integrali). The proof along straight segments with the Poincaré lemma (LEBL2 Thm. 9.3.6, PDF p. 87) is not from the sources.

The proof has shown where the compatibility equations do their work. They are needed in the first step: with them the partial derivatives of the rotation that the derivatives of the strains prescribe agree with each other, and the rotation exists. In the second step the condition held by itself, because the rotation is exactly as lemma 1.124 demands. The functions \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) really are the small rotation tensor of the field obtained (definition 1.114), since by steps 7 and 4

\[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \frac12\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} - \omega_{\mathrm{ji}}\big) = \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

Since the vector \(\vek d\) is zero at \(P = P_0\), we have \(\vek u(P_0) = \vek 0\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P_0) = 0\): the field obtained leaves the point \(P_0\) in place and does not turn the material next to it. The set \(D\) is connected (definition 1.126), since any two of its points \(P\) and \(Q\) are joined by the broken line with the points \(P\), \(P_0\) and \(Q\), whose two segments lie in \(D\) because \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to \(P_0\). By corollary 1.131, every other continuously differentiable field with the same strains therefore differs from the one obtained by a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) with a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\). With such a displacement we fit the field to the supports of the body.

Let us test the theorem on the corrected strip of section 1.18.3 (figure 4.64). A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The axis \(x\) points along the strip, and the origin is at the middle of the left end. The thickness of the strip in the direction of the axis \(z\) does not matter for the computation, because no function depends on \(z\). The prescribed strains are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \qquad k = -10\ \text{m}^{-2} ,\]

and the other three components are zero. In section 1.18.3 we checked that they satisfy the compatibility equations, and said that the number \(k\) is strongly exaggerated. At the right end \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}4\), far beyond the bound of small strains. All computations are linear in \(k\), so with a realistic \(k\) they hold in the same way, only the numbers are smaller. The interior points of the strip make up the interior of a box, which is convex, so it is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. For \(P_0\) we take the centre of the strip, \(P_0 = (x_0, 0, 0)\) with \(x_0 = 100\) mm.

  1. The rotation. For the pair \(x\), \(y\) the functions of the proof are \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial x = 2k\,y\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}/\partial x = 2k\,x\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The condition holds, \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = 2k = \partial\psi_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\). For the pairs with the index \(z\) all functions are zero, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are zero and no strain depends on \(z\), so \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. For the point \(P = (x, y, z)\) we have \(\vek d = (x - x_0, y, z)\) and \(P_0 + t\,\vek d = (x_0 + t\,(x - x_0),\ t\,y,\ t\,z)\), so by (4.48)
