    \[\begin{aligned} \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(P) &= \int_0^1 \Big(2k\,t\,y\,(x - x_0) + 2k\,\big(x_0 + t\,(x - x_0)\big)\,y\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= k\,y\,(x - x_0) + 2k\,x_0\,y + k\,y\,(x - x_0) = 2k\,x\,y . \end{aligned}\]
    We computed the integral with the fundamental theorem of calculus: a term with the factor \(t\) has an antiderivative with the factor \(t^2/2\), which equals \(\tfrac12\) at \(t = 1\).
  2. The displacement. For \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xj}} + \omega_{\mathrm{xj}}\) are \(k\,y^2\), \(2k\,x\,y\) and \(0\), and for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) they are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} + \omega_{\mathrm{yx}} = -2k\,x\,y\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \omega_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\) and \(0\), because \(\omega_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\). For \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) all three are zero. The two integrals (4.49), computed with SymPy, are
    \[u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2 , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

This is exactly the field we guessed in section 1.18.3. Exactly, not only up to a rigid displacement, because that field has zero displacement at \(P_0\), where \(y = 0\), and the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2k\,x_0 \cdot 0 = 0\). At the point \(P = (10\ \text{mm}, 5\ \text{mm}, 0)\) near the left end the rotation is \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2 \cdot (-10\ \text{m}^{-2}) \cdot 0{,}01\ \text{m} \cdot 0{,}005\ \text{m} = -0{,}001\), and the displacement has the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -2{,}5\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 5\ \mu\text{m}\). In figure 4.64 the bands of the strip, deformed by the field obtained, fit together without gaps, since one single field moves all points. Had we chosen the point \((100\ \text{mm}, 5\ \text{mm}, 0)\) for \(P_0\), the formulas would have given a field with zero displacement and zero rotation at that point. By SymPy it differs from ours by \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\), where \(a_{\mathrm{x}} = -25\ \mu\text{m}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}} = 500\ \mu\text{m}\), \(a_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -W_{\mathrm{yx}} = 0{,}01\), and the other entries of the matrix \(\mat W\) are zero. This is a small rigid displacement of corollary 1.131.

And the strip with the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), which does not satisfy the first equation? The proof stops already in the first step. For the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the functions are \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}} = 2k\,y\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and the condition fails, since \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = 2k = -20\ \text{m}^{-2}\) and \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 0\). The rotation would have to change along the strip at the rate \(2k\,y\), which differs at different heights, while it would not be allowed to change with height. In section 1.18.3 we saw this as bands that curve differently (figure 1.132, right). The formula (4.48) still gives some function, for \(P_0 = (x_0, 0, 0)\) the function \(k\,y\,(x - x_0)\), but its derivative with respect to \(x\) is \(k\,y\), not \(2k\,y\).

Why does the theorem not help with the ring of section 1.18.5? The ring is not star-shaped (figure 4.61): the segment from a point \(P_0\) to the opposite point passes through the hole, where there is no material and the strains are not defined. The formulas (4.48) and (4.49) need the strains and their derivatives at every point of the segment, so for such points we cannot write them down. That this is not merely a shortcoming of the proof we saw in section 1.18.5: the strains of the ring satisfy the compatibility equations, but there is no displacement field. The cut ring has a displacement field although it is not star-shaped. Our theorem does not show this, but theorem 1.133 for simply connected bodies, which the book only states, does. In a general simply connected body we add up along curves that avoid the holes, and Stokes's theorem shows that the result does not depend on the choice of the curve (SADD, PDF p. 53, KREYSZIG §10.2, Theorem 3, PDF p. 449). For the bodies we compute with, our theorem is enough, since the box, the strip, the round bar and the ball are convex. In the next subsection we will use it for the question whether the equation of virtual forces also demands compatibility.

4.6.8 Converse of the principle of virtual forces

In subsection 4.6.2 we proved the principle of virtual forces (theorem 4.57). Let us repeat the setting. Before loading the body occupies the set of points \(V\), which is a box or made of boxes. On the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) is prescribed, on the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the force per unit area. If \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the components of the small strain tensor of a displacement field \(\vek u\) that equals \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), then for every statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) the equation (4.41) holds,

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

A field is statically admissible if it is symmetric and continuously differentiable, satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force and has zero traction vector on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) (definition 4.56). For the statically indeterminate truss in subsection 4.6.5 the same equation with self-equilibrating virtual axial forces gave the condition that the changes of length of the bars fit together. Now let us ask the converse for a body. Let six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be given, of which we do not know whether they come from some displacement field, as for the strips of section 1.18.1. If the equation above holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field, are the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) compatible strains, that is, is there a displacement field from which we get them?

EP answers yes: the strains and displacements are compatible and consistent with the supports exactly when the equation holds for every statically admissible field (EP (4.4.5), p. 197). In the derivation EP assumes that a displacement field \(\vek u\) already exists, turns the equation into an integral of the difference \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} - \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) multiplied by \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and concludes that the difference is zero because \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is arbitrary in the body (EP (4.4.9), (4.4.10), p. 198). The virtual field is not arbitrary, however, because it has to satisfy the equilibrium equations. How strong this restriction is, the following argument shows. Let \(\varphi\) be a function that is positive in the interior of a small box in the interior of the body and zero outside it, of the kind we built in subsection 4.4.5. If we were allowed to take the virtual field \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varphi\) with all other components zero, the right side of the equation would be zero, because the field does not reach the surface. By the fundamental lemma for boxes (lemma 4.43, item 2) the equation would then give \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at every interior point, and we would get the same for every other component. The equation would demand that all strains are zero, while for true displacement fields, for instance in the hanging bar, the strains are not zero. Such a field is not in equilibrium. The first equilibrium equation reads \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = 0\) for it, and the bump is not constant along the axis \(x\). The equilibrium equations therefore restrict the admissible fields strongly, and so the equation demands less than \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\). We will show that it demands exactly the compatibility equations (1.66).

The goal of the subsection is a theorem that says this precisely, and a test on the strip with numbers. The model is the same as in theorem 4.57, with one difference: we do not compute the strains from a displacement field, but six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are given, where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) means the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}}\) the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}}\) the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Let us list the assumptions and say for each where we use it.

  1. The strains are small, as in the whole section, so the principle of virtual forces holds in the form above. We need no material law, because none enters the equation.
  2. The functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body together with its surface. We need the second derivatives because the compatibility equations contain second derivatives of the strains and because we will move two derivatives from the virtual field to the strains. Theorem 1.133 has the same assumption.
  3. The body is a box or made of boxes, as in theorem 4.57, because we proved the principle only for such bodies. For the existence of a displacement field we will also need the set of interior points of the body to be star-shaped (definition 4.63): it contains a point \(P_0\) such that for every point \(P\) of the set the whole segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) lies in the set.

The route is the same as for the converse of the principle of virtual displacements in subsection 4.4.5. We take virtual fields that are nonzero only in a small box in the interior of the body. Such a field does not reach the surface, so the right side of the equation is zero, and the left side is an integral over the box. With integration by parts we move the derivatives from the virtual field to the strains and use the fundamental lemma. Two steps are new. First, we need fields in equilibrium that are zero outside the box. We will get them from a single function, through its second derivatives. Second, these fields contain second derivatives of the bump, so we need a bump that is smoother than the bump of subsection 4.4.5.

How do we get a field in equilibrium that is zero outside the box? It helps to start from the goal. Let \(\varphi\) be a function that is zero outside the box \(K\), and such that its first partial derivatives are zero on the faces of the box too. Integration by parts (corollary 3.40) moves a derivative from one function to the other, and in doing so it adds a minus sign and a term at the end points, which is zero here, because the function from which we moved the derivative is zero there. Integration by parts twice therefore moves two derivatives without changing the sign, for example

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2}\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

We will prove this below. The first compatibility equation (1.66) reads

\[\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} = 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} .\]

We want the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), after the derivatives are moved, to equal the left side of this equation minus the right side, multiplied by \(\varphi\). So we read the components of the virtual field straight off the equation. Next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) there must stand \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\), next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) there must stand \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\). The component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) appears twice in the double sum, as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), so we must have \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\). Let the other components be zero. Is this field in equilibrium? The first equilibrium equation gives

\[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y^2} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x\,\partial y} + 0 = 0 ,\]

because both third derivatives differentiate once with respect to \(x\) and twice with respect to \(y\), and by corollary 1.122 the order of differentiation does not matter. In the same way the left side of the second equilibrium equation is zero, and in the third all terms are zero. The field, which we chose only so that it would give a compatibility equation, is in equilibrium.

This is no coincidence. We chose the field so that its work on the strains of every displacement field with continuous derivatives up to third order is zero, since by theorem 1.123 such strains satisfy the compatibility equations. A stress field that does no work on any admissible virtual displacement, however, is in equilibrium without body force by the converse of the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.44). This argument is not a proof, because the converse requires the equation for all admissible virtual displacements, also for those without third derivatives. But it tells us why equilibrium and compatibility belong together. The equation of virtual work connects forces with displacements, and the condition that one side imposes on stress fields, the other side imposes on strains. For the proof the computation with derivatives above is enough.

We proceed in the same way with the fourth compatibility equation,

\[\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} .\]

Here \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) appears once in the double sum, and each of the three shear components twice. To avoid halves, we look for a field whose sum, after the derivatives are moved, gives twice the left side minus the right side. Next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) there must therefore stand \(2\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial y\,\partial z\), next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}}\) the derivative \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\), next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}}\) the derivative \(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\), and next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) the derivative \(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial z\). This field is in equilibrium too.

Lemma 4.67 Virtual stress fields from one function (virtualna polja napetosti iz ene funkcije)

Let \(\varphi\) be a function of three variables that has continuous partial derivatives of first, second and third order in all of space.

  1. The field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) with the components
    \[\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2} , \qquad \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} , \qquad \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} \tag{4.50}\]
    and the other components zero is symmetric at every point, its components are continuously differentiable in all of space, and it satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force at every point.
  2. The same holds for the field with the components
    \[\begin{aligned} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial z} , & \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} , \\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = -\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} , & \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial z} \end{aligned} \tag{4.51}\]
    and the other components zero.
  3. The same holds for the fields we get from the fields of items 1 and 2 when we rename the axes once or twice, \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\).
Proof

We must show that the two fields are symmetric, continuously differentiable and in equilibrium. We check equilibrium by differentiation, in which the third derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) cancel, because the order of differentiation does not matter.

1. The first field.

  1. By its definition \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), and the other off-diagonal components are zero, so the field is symmetric.
  2. The components of the field are second partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) or zero. Their first partial derivatives are therefore third partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) or zero, which by hypothesis exist and are continuous in all of space. The components are therefore continuously differentiable (definition 1.88).
  3. Every point of space is an interior point of space, so by corollary 1.122 on the independence of the order of differentiation the third partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) do not depend on the order of differentiation at any point.
  4. The equilibrium equation with second index \(x\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y^2} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x\,\partial y} + 0 = 0 ,\]
    because the two third derivatives are equal by step 3.
  5. The equilibrium equation with second index \(y\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x^2} + 0 = 0 ,\]
    because both derivatives differentiate twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\).
  6. The equilibrium equation with second index \(z\) contains only the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), which are zero, so its left side is zero.

2. The second field.

  1. Symmetry and continuous differentiability follow as in steps 1 and 2 of the first part.
  2. The equilibrium equation with second index \(x\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = 2\,\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y\,\partial z} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x\,\partial z} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial z\,\partial x\,\partial y} = 0 ,\]
    because all three third derivatives differentiate with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) and are equal by step 3 of the first part.
  3. The equilibrium equation with second index \(y\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial x\,\partial z} + 0 + \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial z\,\partial x^2} = 0 ,\]
    because both third derivatives differentiate twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(z\).
  4. The equilibrium equation with second index \(z\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x^2} + 0 = 0 ,\]
    because both third derivatives differentiate twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\).

3. Renamed axes.

  1. When the axes are renamed, the equilibrium equations turn into one another, the equation with second index \(x\) into the equation with second index \(y\), this one into the equation with \(z\) and this one into the equation with \(x\). Symmetry and continuous differentiability do not change, and neither does the hypothesis on the function \(\varphi\). The steps of the first and second parts therefore hold with renamed axes.

Source: SADD (13.6.4), (13.6.10), (13.6.12) (PDF pp. 421-423), where the stress field is written with second derivatives of a symmetric matrix of functions. The field of item 1 is the case of (13.6.10) with a single nonzero function on the diagonal, the field of item 2 the case of (13.6.12) with a single function off the diagonal, with the opposite sign. SADD shows equilibrium for the general form (PDF p. 421). The proof by components is not from the source.

The lemma gives six families of virtual fields, one for each compatibility equation. Renaming the axes \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\) turns the first equation (1.66) into the second, the second into the third, the fourth into the fifth and the fifth into the sixth, as we saw in the proof of theorem 1.123. From the field (4.50) we get in this way for the second equation the field with the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial z^2\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial y\,\partial z\), and from the field (4.51) for the sixth equation the field with the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 2\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial z^2\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial z\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial y\,\partial z\).

The function \(\varphi\) is called a stress function (napetostna funkcija). The field (4.50) with a function that depends only on \(x\) and \(y\) was introduced for plane problems by Airy in 1862, and such a function is called the Airy stress function (Airyjeva napetostna funkcija) (BARBER (4.6), PDF p. 63, SADD (7.5.3), PDF p. 158). With it we will look for the stresses in plane bodies in chapter 11. SADD writes a more general formula, in which the stress field is obtained through second derivatives from a symmetric matrix of six functions (SADD (13.6.4), PDF p. 421). When only the functions on the diagonal are nonzero, they are called Maxwell stress functions, when only the functions off the diagonal, Morera stress functions (SADD (13.6.9)-(13.6.12), PDF pp. 422-423). SADD also states that it has been shown that every solution of an elasticity problem can be written in this form (SADD, PDF p. 421). We need less, only enough fields in equilibrium that are zero outside a small box.

Now we need the function \(\varphi\). The bump \(p_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (t - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - t)^2\) of subsection 4.4.5 is not smooth enough. Its first derivative is continuous, but its second derivative jumps at the points \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (figure 4.65, top). To the left of \(\alpha\) the second derivative is zero. To the right of \(\alpha\) it is the second derivative of the polynomial \((t - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - t)^2\), which near \(\alpha\) approaches the value \(2\,(\beta - \alpha)^2\): when we differentiate the first derivative \(2\,(t - \alpha)\,(\beta - t)\,(\alpha + \beta - 2t)\) once more and put \(t = \alpha\), only the term in which we differentiated the factor \(t - \alpha\) remains, which is \(2\,(\beta - \alpha)\,(\beta - \alpha)\). The field (4.50) with a bump made of the functions \(p_{\alpha\beta}\) would therefore jump on the faces of the box and would not be continuously differentiable, as definition 4.56, item 1, requires. Fourth powers help. Each additional factor \(t - \alpha\) gives one more derivative that is zero at \(\alpha\). The bump \((t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\) therefore has continuous derivatives up to third order (figure 4.65, bottom), and the field (4.50) made with it has continuous first partial derivatives, because these are third partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\).

Lemma 4.68 Fundamental lemma with smooth bumps (osnovna lema z gladkimi grbinami)

For numbers \(\alpha < \beta\) let \(q_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\) for \(\alpha \le t \le \beta\) and \(q_{\alpha\beta}(t) = 0\) for other \(t\).

  1. The function \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) has a first, second and third derivative at every real number. All three are continuous and equal to zero at the points \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).
  2. For a box \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) let \(\varphi(x, y, z) = q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\). The function \(\varphi\) has continuous partial derivatives of first, second and third order in all of space. The function \(\varphi\) and all these partial derivatives are zero at every point that does not lie in the interior of the box \(K\), that is, on its faces and outside it.
  3. Let \(g\) be a function of three variables, continuous on an open set \(D\). If for every box \(K\) that lies in \(D\), with the function \(\varphi\) of item 2,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 ,\]
    then \(g = 0\) at every point of \(D\).
Proof

We must show three items. In the first we follow the derivatives of the polynomial \((t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\) and show that they have zeros at the end points of the interval that are enough for three derivatives. We get the second from the first as for the bump in a box, the third as in lemma 4.43.

1. Derivatives of the bump.

  1. The function \(t - \alpha\) has the derivative \(1\), and the function \(\beta - t\) the derivative \(-1\) (lemma 1.79, items 1, 2 and 4). By the product rule and by induction on the natural number \(m\), \((t - \alpha)^m\) has the derivative \(m\,(t - \alpha)^{m-1}\): from \((t - \alpha)^{m+1} = (t - \alpha)\,(t - \alpha)^m\) we get the derivative \((t - \alpha)^m + (t - \alpha)\,m\,(t - \alpha)^{m-1} = (m + 1)\,(t - \alpha)^m\). Likewise \((\beta - t)^m\) has the derivative \(-m\,(\beta - t)^{m-1}\).
  2. Let \(r(t) = (t - \alpha)^m\,(\beta - t)^m\,s(t)\), where \(m \ge 1\) is a natural number and \(s\) a polynomial. By the product rule and by step 1,
    \[r'(t) = (t - \alpha)^{m-1}\,(\beta - t)^{m-1}\,\big(m\,(\beta - t)\,s(t) - m\,(t - \alpha)\,s(t) + (t - \alpha)\,(\beta - t)\,s'(t)\big) ,\]
    again a product of \((t - \alpha)^{m-1}\,(\beta - t)^{m-1}\) and a polynomial.
  3. Let \(r_0(t) = (t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\), and let \(r_1\), \(r_2\), \(r_3\) be its first, second and third derivatives. By step 2, used three times, \(r_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = (t - \alpha)^{4-k}\,(\beta - t)^{4-k}\,s_{\mathrm{k}}(t)\) with a polynomial \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\). Each \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) is therefore zero at \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), because the exponent \(4 - k\) is at least \(1\).
  4. For \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\) let \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = r_{\mathrm{k}}(t)\) for \(\alpha < t < \beta\) and \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = 0\) for other \(t\). Then \(q_0 = q_{\alpha\beta}\), since \(r_0(\alpha) = r_0(\beta) = 0\) too. Let us show that for \(k = 0, 1, 2\) the function \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is differentiable at every number \(t\) with the derivative \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}(t)\).
  5. Outside the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is constantly zero on an open interval around \(t\), so its derivative is zero there, like \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). On the interval \((\alpha, \beta)\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals the polynomial \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\), so its derivative is \(r_{\mathrm{k}+1}(t) = q_{\mathrm{k}+1}(t)\).
  6. At the point \(\alpha\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha) = 0\). For \(h < 0\) the difference quotient \(\big(q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha + h) - q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha)\big)/h\) is zero. For \(0 < h < \beta - \alpha\) it equals by step 3
    \[\frac{r_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha + h)}{h} = h^{3-k}\,(\beta - \alpha - h)^{4-k}\,s_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha + h) ,\]
    which is a polynomial in \(h\) that is zero at \(h = 0\), because \(3 - k \ge 1\). A polynomial is continuous (corollary 1.62, item 2), so for every \(\eta > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\), which we take at most \(\beta - \alpha\), such that the absolute value of the quotient is less than \(\eta\) for \(0 < |h| < \delta\). By definitions 1.5 and 1.8, \(q_{\mathrm{k}}'(\alpha) = 0 = q_{\mathrm{k}+1}(\alpha)\). Likewise at the point \(\beta\), with the factor \((\beta - t)^{4-k}\) in place of \((t - \alpha)^{4-k}\).
  7. The functions \(q_1\), \(q_2\) and \(q_3\) are therefore the first, second and third derivatives of the function \(q_{\alpha\beta}\), and by step 3 they are zero at \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). They are continuous at every point. Outside \([\alpha, \beta]\) they are constantly zero on an open interval around the point, on \((\alpha, \beta)\) they equal polynomials, which are continuous. At the point \(\alpha\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha) = 0 = r_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha)\) for \(k = 1, 2, 3\). For a given \(\eta > 0\) the continuity of the polynomial \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) at \(\alpha\) therefore gives \(\delta > 0\), which we take at most \(\beta - \alpha\), such that \(|q_{\mathrm{k}}(t)| = |r_{\mathrm{k}}(t)| < \eta\) for \(\alpha \le t < \alpha + \delta\), while to the left of \(\alpha\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = 0\). Likewise at the point \(\beta\).

2. Bump in a box.

  1. In differentiating with respect to \(x\) the factors depending on \(y\) and \(z\) are constant (lemma 1.79, item 2), so \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}'(x)\,q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\), and likewise for the other variables. Using this rule several times, every partial derivative of the function \(\varphi\) up to third order is a product of three factors, a derivative of the function \(q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}\) with respect to \(x\), a derivative of the function \(q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}\) with respect to \(y\) and a derivative of the function \(q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}\) with respect to \(z\), each of order at most \(3\). By item 1 these derivatives exist.
  2. Each factor is a continuous function of one coordinate and therefore a continuous function of the point, as in step 2 of item 1 of the proof of lemma 4.43. By corollary 1.67, item 1, all partial derivatives up to third order are therefore continuous in all of space.
  3. A point that does not lie in the interior of the box has at least one coordinate outside the open interval, for instance \(x \le \alpha_1\) or \(x \ge \beta_1\). There \(q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}\) and its derivatives up to third order are zero by item 1, so every product of step 1 is zero.

3. Fundamental lemma.

  1. We repeat steps 1 to 8 of item 2 of the proof of lemma 4.43, with the functions \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) in place of \(p_{\alpha\beta}\). The steps use only that the bump is nowhere negative and that the integral of the bump over its interval is positive. The first holds because both factors \((t - \alpha)^4\) and \((\beta - t)^4\) are powers with an even exponent.
  2. Only step 7 changes. Let \(\ell = \beta - \alpha\). On the middle half of the interval both factors \(t - \alpha\) and \(\beta - t\) are at least \(\ell/4\), so there \(q_{\alpha\beta}(t) \ge (\ell/4)^8\), and by additivity and the bound of the integral (lemma 3.38, items 2 and 3), \(\int_\alpha^\beta q_{\alpha\beta}\,\mathrm{d}t \ge \tfrac{\ell}{2}\,(\ell/4)^8 > 0\). The exact value is \(\ell^9/630\).

Source: EP Lemma 3.1 (pp. 140-141) for functions of one variable, with a different proof. The bumps with fourth powers and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma repeated lemma 4.43 with a smoother bump. The proof of item 3 was the same, because it needed only that the bump is not negative and has a positive integral. Item 2 will ensure that the virtual field made from the bump is continuously differentiable and that it is zero on the faces of the box and outside it, together with the first derivatives of the bump that integration by parts will need.

What remains is moving the derivatives. For the bar we used integration by parts on an interval. In a box we use it along every segment parallel to the chosen axis, and then we integrate over the other two coordinates.

Lemma 4.69 Integration by parts twice with a smooth bump (dvakratna integracija po delih z gladko grbino)

Let \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) be a box, \(\varphi\) the product of its three bumps from lemma 4.68, item 2, and \(g\) a function of three variables with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set \(D\) containing \(K\). Then for any two variables \(a\) and \(b\), each of them \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\), possibly equal,

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial a\,\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial a\,\partial b}\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.52}\]
Proof

We must show that each move of one derivative produces only a minus sign, because the terms on the faces of the box are zero. Two moves give two minus signs, so a plus.

  1. One move. Let \(f\) be a function continuous on \(D\) whose partial derivative with respect to \(a\) exists and is continuous on \(D\), and \(\psi\) a function continuously differentiable in all of space that is zero on both faces of the box perpendicular to the axis \(a\). Let us show that
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial a}\,\mathrm{d}V = -\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial a}\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
    Let \(a = x\). Both functions under the integrals are continuous on \(K\) as products of continuous functions (corollary 1.67, item 1). By theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, item 2, the integral over \(K\) equals the iterated integral in which we integrate over \(x\) first.
  2. Let \(y\) and \(z\) be fixed, with \(\alpha_2 \le y \le \beta_2\) and \(\alpha_3 \le z \le \beta_3\). The segment from \((\alpha_1, y, z)\) to \((\beta_1, y, z)\) lies in \(K\), hence in \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, the points on the same line a little beyond the end points of the segment are in \(D\) too, so the functions \(x \mapsto f(x, y, z)\) and \(x \mapsto \psi(x, y, z)\) are differentiable on an open interval containing \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), and their derivatives are the partial derivatives with respect to \(x\) and are continuous. By integration by parts (corollary 3.40)
    \[\int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} f\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x = f(\beta_1, y, z)\,\psi(\beta_1, y, z) - f(\alpha_1, y, z)\,\psi(\alpha_1, y, z) - \int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
    The points \((\alpha_1, y, z)\) and \((\beta_1, y, z)\) lie on the faces \(x = \alpha_1\) and \(x = \beta_1\), where \(\psi = 0\), so the term at the end points drops out.
  3. The inner integrals on the two sides are equal for every \(y\) and \(z\), so the iterated integrals over \(y\) and \(z\) are equal too. By theorem 4.9 these are the integrals over \(K\) of step 1. For \(a = y\) and \(a = z\) the steps are the same, with the roles of the coordinates swapped.
  4. The first move. Take \(f = g\) and \(\psi = \partial\varphi/\partial b\). By hypothesis the function \(g\) has continuous partial derivatives on \(D\). The function \(\psi\) is continuously differentiable in all of space, because by lemma 4.68, item 2, \(\varphi\) has continuous partial derivatives of second order, and by the same item it is zero on all faces of the box. By steps 1 to 3,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial a\,\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V = -\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial g}{\partial a}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  5. The second move. Take \(f = \partial g/\partial a\), move the derivative with respect to \(b\), and take \(\psi = \varphi\). The function \(f\) is continuous on \(D\), and its partial derivative with respect to \(b\), the second partial derivative \(\partial^2 g/\partial b\,\partial a\), is continuous on \(D\). The function \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable in all of space and zero on the faces of the box. By steps 1 to 3,
    \[-\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial g}{\partial a}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial b\,\partial a}\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  6. The set \(D\) is open, and the second partial derivatives of the function \(g\) are continuous on it, so by theorem 1.121 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives the derivative \(\partial^2 g/\partial b\,\partial a\) equals \(\partial^2 g/\partial a\,\partial b\) at every point of \(K\). For \(a = b\) this is not needed. Combining steps 4 and 5 we get (4.52).

Source: EP (4.4.8) (p. 197) moves one derivative with the Green-Gauss theorem, in a body of any shape. The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma says that two derivatives move from the bump to another function without a change of sign. Each move gives a minus sign, and two minus signs give a plus. The terms at the end points dropped out because the bump and its first partial derivatives are zero on the faces of the box. Now we have everything for the theorem.

Theorem 4.70 Converse of the principle of virtual forces (obrat načela virtualnih sil)

Let the body \(V\), the parts of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) be as in theorem 4.57. Let six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body together with its surface, and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). If for every statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) (definition 4.56)

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]

where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface, then:

  1. the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) satisfy the compatibility equations (1.66) at every interior point of the body,
  2. if the set of interior points of the body is star-shaped (definition 4.63), there is a displacement field \(\vek u\), defined at the interior points of the body, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order, whose small strain components equal \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point.
Proof

We must show two items. For the first we take virtual fields from lemma 4.67 with a bump in a small box that does not reach the surface, and move the derivatives to the strains. The second follows from the first and theorem 4.66.

1. Compatibility equations.

  1. Let \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) be a box that lies in the set of interior points of the body, and \(\varphi\) the product of its three bumps from lemma 4.68, item 2. By the same item \(\varphi\) has continuous partial derivatives up to third order in all of space. Let \(\delta\ten\sigma\) be the field (4.50) with this function. By lemma 4.67, item 1, it is symmetric, continuously differentiable in all of space, and satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force at every point.
  2. The components of the field are second partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) or zero, so by lemma 4.68, item 2, they are zero at every point that does not lie in the interior of the box \(K\). The points of the box \(K\) are interior points of the body, so no point of the surface lies in \(K\), and at every point of the surface all components of the field are zero. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) therefore \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\). The field satisfies all four conditions of definition 4.56 and is a statically admissible virtual stress field.
  3. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) too \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\), so the right side of the equation of the hypothesis is zero, and
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
  4. We add the planes \(x = \alpha_1\), \(x = \beta_1\), \(y = \alpha_2\), \(y = \beta_2\), \(z = \alpha_3\) and \(z = \beta_3\) to the grid of the body. By lemma 4.12 the integral over the body does not change, and the box \(K\) is a union of cells of the new grid. On the cells outside \(K\) the virtual field is zero, so the integrals over them are zero, and the integrals over the cells in \(K\) add up to the integral over \(K\) by lemma 4.10, item 3. Therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).
  5. In the double sum only the terms with the pairs \((x, x)\), \((y, y)\), \((x, y)\) and \((y, x)\) are nonzero. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), at every point
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} .\]
  6. The functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body, hence also \(K\). The integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals (lemma 4.10, item 1). We use lemma 4.69 on each of the three terms, with \(g = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(a = b = y\), with \(g = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(a = b = x\), and with \(g = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(a = x\) and \(b = y\). By steps 4 and 5,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \Big( \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} \Big)\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
  7. Let \(c_1\) be the function in the brackets, the left side of the first equation (1.66) minus the right side. As a sum of multiples of continuous functions it is continuous on the set of interior points of the body (corollary 1.67, item 1), and this set is open (section 1.15). Step 6 holds for every box that lies in it, so by lemma 4.68, item 3, \(c_1 = 0\) at every interior point of the body. This is the first compatibility equation.
  8. We repeat steps 1 to 7 with the two fields we get from the field (4.50) when we rename the axes once or twice (lemma 4.67, item 3). The renaming turns the first compatibility equation into the second and the second into the third, as in the second part of the proof of theorem 1.123. The second and third equations therefore hold at every interior point.
  9. For the fourth equation we take the field (4.51) with the function \(\varphi\) of step 1. Steps 1 to 4 stay the same, by lemma 4.67, item 2. The nonzero terms of the double sum are those with the pairs \((x, x)\), \((y, z)\), \((z, y)\), \((x, z)\), \((z, x)\), \((x, y)\) and \((y, x)\), so at every point
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial z} + 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} - 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial z} .\]
  10. With lemma 4.69, used on each of the four terms, we get as in step 6
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} 2\,\Big( \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} \Big)\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
    The expression in the brackets is the left side of the fourth equation (1.66) minus the right side. As in step 7, with twice this expression in place of \(c_1\), the expression is zero at every interior point, and the fourth equation holds.
  11. We get the fifth and sixth equations as in step 8, with the two fields we get from the field (4.51) by renaming the axes.

2. Displacement field.

  1. The set of interior points of the body is open (section 1.15) and star-shaped by hypothesis. The functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on it, because they have them on an open set containing the body, and by item 1 they satisfy the compatibility equations on it. By theorem 4.66 on the sufficiency of the compatibility equations in a star-shaped body there is therefore a displacement field on it with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order whose small strain components are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Source: EP (4.4.5), (4.4.9), (4.4.10) (pp. 197-198), where the converse follows from the arbitrariness of the virtual stresses, with a displacement field assumed. Stress functions: SADD (13.6.10), (13.6.12) (PDF pp. 422-423). The proof with stress functions and smooth bumps is not from the sources.

The proof showed how the equation of virtual forces demands compatibility. A virtual field made from a stress function is in equilibrium and is zero outside a small box, so the right side of the equation drops out for it. Integration by parts twice moved the derivatives from the field to the strains, and the work of the field on the strains became the integral of the left side of a compatibility equation minus the right side, multiplied by the bump. Since this integral is zero for every box, the difference is zero at every interior point by the fundamental lemma. The same three steps, a field that does not reach the surface, moving the derivatives and the fundamental lemma, gave the converse of the principle of virtual displacements in subsection 4.4.5. There one move of a derivative gave the equilibrium equations, here two moves gave the compatibility equations.

What does the theorem not say? EP gets from the equation also that the displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equals the prescribed one, \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) (EP (4.4.10), p. 198). Our virtual fields are zero near the whole surface, so they say nothing about \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). For this part we would need statically admissible virtual fields with support forces \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) chosen in advance, that is, solutions of the equilibrium equations with prescribed forces on the surface. We do not solve such boundary value problems in this chapter, chapter 11 deals with them. We therefore only cite this part of the converse. In words it says the following. The displacement field of item 2 is determined by the strains only up to a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) (corollary 1.131, subsection 4.6.7), and the equation demands that it can be chosen so that it fits the supports on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). Item 2 also needs a star-shaped body, because we get it from theorem 4.66. For the ring of section 1.18.5 the compatibility equations hold at every point, but there is no displacement field. Our virtual fields are nonzero only in a small box and do not go around the hole, so for the ring they do not tell whether the equation demands anything more than the compatibility equations.

Let us test the theorem with numbers on the strip of section 1.18.1 (figure 4.67). We repeat the setting. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The axis \(x\) points along the strip, the origin \(O\) is at the middle of the left end, so the strip reaches from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 200\) mm and from \(y = -10\) mm to \(y = 10\) mm. For a computation in space let us give it a thickness of 2 mm, from \(z = -1\) mm to \(z = 1\) mm. No force acts on it and no support holds it, so \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty and the right side of the equation is zero for every virtual field. The prescribed strains are (1.62), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) with \(k = -10\) m⁻², the other components are zero. In section 1.18.3 we saw that the first compatibility equation does not hold for them, since the left side is \(2k = -20\) m⁻² and the right side zero. By the theorem there must therefore be a statically admissible virtual field for which the equation does not hold. Let us find it.

  1. Let the box \(K\) with edges 10 mm, 10 mm and 1 mm have its centre at the point with coordinates \(x = 100\) mm, \(y = 0\) and \(z = 0\). So it reaches from \(x = 95\) mm to \(x = 105\) mm, from \(y = -5\) mm to \(y = 5\) mm and from \(z = -0{,}5\) mm to \(z = 0{,}5\) mm and lies in the middle of the strip. It is 5 mm from the upper and lower edges of the strip and \(0{,}5\) mm from both faces of the strip, so all its points are interior points of the strip.
  2. As the stress function we take
    \[\varphi = \Phi_0\,\frac{q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)}{h_1^8}\,\frac{q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)}{h_2^8}\,\frac{q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)}{h_3^8} ,\]
    where \(h_1 = h_2 = 5\) mm and \(h_3 = 0{,}5\) mm are the halves of the edges of the box. Each of the three quotients has the value \(h^4 \cdot h^4/h^8 = 1\) at the centre of its interval. Since \(\varphi\) is a constant multiple of the product of three bumps from lemma 4.68, the field (4.50) with this function is statically admissible, as in steps 1 and 2 of the proof of the theorem. The number \(\Phi_0\) has the unit newton, so that the second derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) have the unit pascal.
  3. At the centre of the box the second derivative of the quotient with respect to \(y\) is \(-8/h_2^2\), which we compute with SymPy, so there \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -8\,\Phi_0/h_2^2\). Let us choose \(\Phi_0 = 3{,}125\) N, so that \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -8 \cdot 3{,}125\ \text{N}/(25 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2) = -1\) MPa. Figure 4.66 shows the signs of all three components of the field in the box.
  4. The only nonzero strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so the left side of the equation, computed with SymPy directly, without moving derivatives, is
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} k\,y^2\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2}\,\mathrm{d}V = -4{,}194 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{J} .\]
    The right side is zero, so the equation does not hold for this statically admissible virtual field, as the theorem demands for strains that are not compatible.
  5. Let us check the number with lemma 4.69. Since \(\partial^2(k\,y^2)/\partial y^2 = 2k\), the left side equals \(2k \int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V\). The integral of the function \(\varphi\) is the product of the number \(\Phi_0\) and three integrals along the edges, each of which is \(\tfrac{128}{315}\) of the length of the edge, which we compute with SymPy. Therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 3{,}125\ \text{N} \cdot \big(\tfrac{128}{315}\big)^3 \cdot 10\ \text{mm} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} \cdot 1\ \text{mm} = 2{,}097 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{N}\,\text{m}^3\) and \(2k \int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = -20\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot 2{,}097 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{N}\,\text{m}^3 = -4{,}194 \cdot 10^{-7}\) J, the same as in step 4.
  6. For the corrected strip of section 1.18.3 there is also \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\), and the left side gets the term \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} (-k\,x^2)\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\,\mathrm{d}V = 4{,}194 \cdot 10^{-7}\) J, with SymPy. The sum is zero, as it must be, since we get these strains from the displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).
  7. For the strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), \(R = 10\) m, which we bend into an arc, the left side is \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} (y/R)\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), with SymPy.

Why is the work zero for the strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), but not for the strip with \(k\,y^2\)? Figure 4.67 shows the component \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) along the transverse segment through the centre of the box, at \(x = 100\) mm and \(z = 0\). In the middle there is compression of \(1\) MPa, between \(1{,}89\) mm and \(5\) mm from the middle there is tension, which is largest, \(0{,}653\) MPa, at \(3{,}27\) mm and fades to zero at the edge of the box. The area under the curve is zero, because the integral of the second derivative is the difference of the first derivatives at the end points, \(\int_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = \partial\varphi/\partial y\,(h_2) - \partial\varphi/\partial y\,(-h_2) = 0\). The virtual forces on a transverse cut of the box therefore add up to zero. Their moment about the middle is zero too. By integration by parts

\[\int_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} y\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2}\,\mathrm{d}y = \Big[ y\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y} \Big]_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} - \int_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y = 0 - \big(\varphi(h_2) - \varphi(-h_2)\big) = 0 ,\]

where for \(\varphi\) and its derivative we wrote only the coordinate \(y\). A strain that is a linear function of \(y\) along the segment, like \(y/R\), therefore does no work on this field. The parabola \(k\,y^2\), however, is not linear. In the bands with tension, between \(1{,}89\) mm and \(5\) mm from the middle, the shortening is from \(3{,}6 \cdot 10^{-5}\) to \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), in the compressed band in the middle at most \(3{,}6 \cdot 10^{-5}\), so the contributions of the bands do not cancel. The contribution of the bands with tension, where the shortening is larger, prevails, and since there the product of a positive virtual stress and a negative strain is negative, the left side in step 4 is negative. The corrected strip makes up for this difference with the transverse fibres. The term with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\) on the field \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), which has the same picture turned by a right angle, gives exactly the opposite number.

Let us compare with the bracket with the post of subsection 4.6.5. There the numbers \(-\tfrac43\), \(\tfrac53\) and \(1\) were self-equilibrating virtual axial forces that balance the joint without any external force, and the equation (4.39) with them was the condition that the three changes of length come from one displacement of the joint. Three unknown axial forces and two equations of equilibrium give one such set of numbers, up to a multiple, and one compatibility condition. In a body the role of these numbers is played by the virtual fields made from stress functions. They are self-equilibrating too, since no virtual force acts on them, neither on the surface nor in the body. There are infinitely many such fields, six for every box in the body, and they give the six compatibility equations at every interior point.

The section has shown the following. Virtual forces are forces that we imagine in equilibrium, and their work on the true displacements is, for a truss, the sum of the products of the virtual axial forces and the true changes of length, and for a body the integral of the products of the virtual stresses and the true strains. We proved this by taking the scalar product of the equilibrium of the virtual forces with the true displacement, and for a body with the lemma on internal virtual work through the surface, used with the roles swapped. Since only equilibrium and geometry enter, it holds for every material. With a unit virtual force we got both parts of the displacement of the joint, \(2{,}721\) mm to the left and \(10{,}71\) mm down. For linear elastic materials we got from the principle that the true stress field has the smallest total complementary energy among all fields in equilibrium, and from this that a displacement is the derivative of the complementary energy with respect to a force. For the bracket with the post the smallest energy gave forces that equilibrium could not, and its condition was the condition that the changes of length of the bars fit together. Finally we showed that the converse holds too. If the equation of virtual forces holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field, the strains satisfy the compatibility equations, and in a star-shaped body we get a displacement field from them. For this, self-equilibrating virtual fields made from stress functions that are nonzero only in a small box were enough. In all computations of this section we multiplied the forces of one state by the displacements of another. In section 4.7 we take as the two states two true loadings of the same body and show that the work of the first loading on the displacements of the second equals the work of the second on the displacements of the first.

4.7 Reciprocity: Betti's and Maxwell's theorems

So far we have loaded every body with a single load. The bracket of two bars from the beginning of the chapter carried a load at the joint \(C\), the hanging bar its own weight. We computed the displacement of the joint \(C\) under the load in several ways, from the changes of the lengths of the bars in section 4.3, with the minimum of the total potential energy in section 4.5 and with virtual forces in section 4.6. Structures, however, usually carry several loads at once, and the loads change. Besides the load, the wind pushes on the bracket, and a lorry drives across a bridge, now here, now there. Do we have to compute everything again for every new combination of loads? And is there any connection between what one load causes and what another load causes?

The goal of the section is to obtain three results that answer these questions for bodies of a linear elastic material with small displacements. The first says that the effects of loads add up: the displacements and stresses caused by two loads together are the sum of the displacements and stresses that each causes alone. The second compares the work of two loads. The work that the first load would do on the displacements caused by the second equals the work that the second load would do on the displacements caused by the first. The third is a special case of the second for two forces, each of magnitude 1 N. The displacement of the point of application of the first force in its direction, caused by the second force, equals the displacement of the point of application of the second force in its direction, caused by the first force. The second result is named after Betti (1823-1892), the third after Maxwell (1831-1879) (EP §4.6.4 and §4.6.5, pp. 227 and 230). The property that the roles of two loads may be exchanged is called reciprocity (vzajemnost).

The route is as follows. First we compute the displacement of the joint \(C\) of the bracket under an arbitrary force at the joint. In the result we notice both phenomena: the displacement is a sum of contributions of the two components of the force, and the horizontal displacement caused by a vertical force equals the vertical displacement caused by an equally large horizontal force. We prove the first phenomenon for every body. The second we first explain with the work the two forces do when we put them on the bracket in different orders, and then we prove it for every body, from the principle of virtual displacements and the symmetry of the elastic constants. At the end we obtain the third result from it, test it on the bracket and on the hanging bar, and show how it is used in measurement.

The physical model is the same as in section 4.5. Let us list the assumptions and say for each where we use it.

  1. Small displacements. The strains are small. Equilibrium and strains are computed on the shape of the body before loading, the strain with the small strain tensor (definition 1.113). In the bracket the strains of the bars are smaller than one thousandth (section 4.1.4). Therefore all equations that determine the displacements are linear, which we use when adding loads, and the principle of virtual displacements holds (theorem 4.42), on which the proofs of both theorems of the section rest.
  2. Linear and ideal elastic material. The stresses are below the yield stress, as in the steel bars of the bracket (section 4.1.4). The stress components are linear functions of the strain components, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\) (definition 3.16), and the material stores the work it receives and returns it on unloading (definition 3.42). Therefore \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\) (theorem 3.46 on the symmetry of the elastic constants). We use the linearity when adding loads and the symmetry of the constants in the proof of the relation between the works of two loads.
  3. Stable material. The strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero (section 3.6.6). We use it when we show that a load determines the displacements uniquely.
  4. Loads independent of the deformation. The magnitude and direction of the loads do not change with the deformation (section 4.5.3). Therefore the work of a load on displacements is the work of a constant force, as in Clapeyron's theorem.
  5. Fixed supports. On a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface the body is held, and the displacement there is zero, for all the loads we compare. The supports shall prevent every small rigid displacement of the body, that is, a translation and a small rotation of the body as a whole, in which the distances between its points do not change. We use the first in both theorems, the second for uniqueness.
  6. Slow loading. The forces grow so slowly that the velocities of the points are negligible, as in section 4.1. We need it only in the explanation with the order of loading. The proofs do not need it, because they speak only about final states.

4.7.1 The bracket with two forces

Let us restate the setting of the bracket from section 4.1.4 (figure 4.68). The bracket lies in a vertical plane. The axis \(x\) points horizontally to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up, and the origin is at the joint \(C\). The horizontal bar \(AC\) has the length \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m, the inclined bar \(BC\) the length \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m. The pins \(A = (-4, 0, 0)\) m and \(B = (-4, 3, 0)\) m are fixed to the wall. Both bars are of steel, with \(E = 196\) GPa, and have the same cross section with the area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\). We therefore simply write \(EA = E\,A_{\mathrm{AC}} = E\,A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N. The truss model (definition 4.4) assumes pins without friction, forces only at the joints and bars without weight, and as in section 4.1.4 we assume that compressed bars stay straight, without buckling. Instead of the load, however, let an arbitrary force in the plane of the bracket act at the joint \(C\), \(\vek F = (F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\). The load from the beginning of the chapter is the case \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -10\) kN.

We denote the displacement of the joint \(C\) by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\), as in sections 4.3.9 and 4.5.5: \(u\) is the horizontal displacement, positive to the right, \(v\) the vertical displacement, positive upwards. Let us compute them in five steps.

  1. Equilibrium of the pin \(C\). A bar with the axial force \(N\) acts on the pin with the force \(-N\,\vek n\), where \(\vek n\) is the unit vector along the bar from the wall towards \(C\), \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\) (section 4.1.4). The sum of the three forces on the pin is zero:
    \[(F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0) - N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) = (0, 0, 0) .\]
  2. The forces in the bars. The \(y\) component of the equation gives \(F_{\mathrm{y}} + \tfrac35\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\). The \(x\) component gives \(F_{\mathrm{x}} - N_{\mathrm{AC}} - \tfrac45\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = F_{\mathrm{x}} - \tfrac45\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F_{\mathrm{x}} + \tfrac43\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\). For the load, \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -10\) kN, we get \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}67\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}33\) kN, as in section 4.1.4.
  3. The elongations of the bars. A bar with a constant axial force \(N\) gets longer by \(\Delta L = N L/(EA)\) (section 4.1.4). For our two bars \(L_{\mathrm{AC}}/(EA) = 4\ \text{m}/(EA)\) and \(L_{\mathrm{BC}}/(EA) = 5\ \text{m}/(EA)\), so
    \[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \frac{4\ \text{m}}{EA}\,\Big(F_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac43\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\Big) , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{5\ \text{m}}{EA}\,\Big({-\frac53}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\Big) .\]
  4. The elongations from the displacement. For small displacements the change of length of a bar is the projection of the displacement of the joint \(C\) onto the direction of the bar. We showed this for a virtual displacement in equation (4.24), and since the derivation used only that the displacement is small, in section 4.3.9 we used the same for the actual displacement, \(\Delta L = \vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). Therefore
    \[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac45\,u - \tfrac35\,v .\]
  5. The displacement. From the first equation of step 4, \(u = \Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}\), from the second \(v = \tfrac43\,u - \tfrac53\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}\). We insert the elongations from step 3:
    \[u = \frac{4\ \text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{16}{3}\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad v = \frac{16}{3}\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + 21\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} . \tag{4.53}\]
    The number \(\tfrac{16}{3}\) in the expression for \(u\) is \(4 \cdot \tfrac43\) from the elongation of the bar \(AC\). In the expression for \(v\), \(\tfrac{16}{3}\) is the number \(\tfrac43 \cdot 4\) from the term \(\tfrac43\,u\). The number 21 at \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) in the expression for \(v\) is the sum of two contributions, \(\tfrac43 \cdot \tfrac{16}{3} = \tfrac{64}{9}\) from the term \(\tfrac43\,u\) and \(\tfrac53 \cdot 5 \cdot \tfrac53 = \tfrac{125}{9}\) from the term \(-\tfrac53\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}\), together \(\tfrac{189}{9} = 21\).

Let us check with the load. For \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -10^4\) N

\[u = \frac{16}{3} \cdot \frac{1\ \text{m} \cdot (-10^4\ \text{N})}{1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\ \text{N}} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} , \qquad v = 21 \cdot \frac{1\ \text{m} \cdot (-10^4\ \text{N})}{1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\ \text{N}} = -10{,}71\ \text{mm} .\]

Under the load the joint moves by 2,721 mm towards the wall and by 10,71 mm down, as we computed in sections 4.3, 4.5 and 4.6. The horizontal displacement is exactly the shortening of the compressed bar \(AC\), because this bar is horizontal.

The result (4.53) shows two things. The first is that each component of the displacement is a sum of two terms, one proportional to \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the other proportional to \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\). The force \((F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) therefore causes the sum of the displacements that the forces \((F_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\) and \((0, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) would cause each alone, and a force twice as large causes a displacement twice as large. Why? In each of the five steps we only multiplied numbers by constant numbers and added them. We wrote the equilibrium on the shape before loading, so the directions \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\) do not depend on the force. The elongation of a bar is proportional to its force, and the projection is a sum of products of components with constant numbers.

Let us name the four numbers in front of the forces in (4.53):

\[u = D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad v = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} .\]

The first index gives the direction of the displacement, the second the direction of the force. Each number is a displacement per newton of force. The number \(D_{\mathrm{yx}}\), for example, is the vertical displacement of the joint caused by a horizontal force of 1 N. For our bracket

\[\begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{4\ \text{m}}{EA} = 204{,}1\ \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} , \\ D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}} &= \frac{16}{3}\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA} = 272{,}1\ \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} , \\ D_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{21\ \text{m}}{EA} = 1071{,}4\ \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} , \end{aligned}\]

where we wrote the displacements in micrometres per kilonewton of force. The second thing the result shows is exactly the equality \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\). A horizontal force of 1 kN to the right moves the joint by 272,1 µm up, and a vertical force of 1 kN upwards moves it by 272,1 µm to the right (figure 4.69).

Let us look at how each of the two displacements arises. For the horizontal force \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) kN, step 2 gives the forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\). The bar \(AC\) gets longer by \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot D_{\mathrm{xx}} = 204{,}1\) µm, while the bar \(BC\) keeps its length. The joint must therefore stay 5 m from the pin \(B\) and moves along the circle about \(B\), for a small displacement perpendicular to the bar \(BC\) (figure 4.69, left). The second equation of step 4 with \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) gives \(v = \tfrac43\,u = \tfrac43 \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} = 272{,}1\) µm. Here the factor \(\tfrac43\) comes from geometry: the direction perpendicular to the bar \(BC\) goes 4 units up for every 3 units sideways. We made the same argument in section 4.6 for the displacement under the load (figure 4.55). For the vertical force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN upwards, step 2 gives the forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac43\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) kN. The horizontal displacement is the elongation of the bar \(AC\), \(\tfrac43\ \text{kN} \cdot 4\ \text{m}/(EA) = 272{,}1\) µm (figure 4.69, right). Here the factor \(\tfrac43\) comes from equilibrium: this many kilonewtons must be carried by the horizontal bar when the inclined bar balances the vertical force of 1 kN. The same triangle with the sides 3, 4 and 5, two different routes, the same number. Is this a coincidence of this bracket? It is not. In the next two subsections we will see that the equality holds for every elastic body, and that its reason is the work the two forces do.

4.7.2 Adding loads

The first observation holds for every body that satisfies the assumptions from the beginning of the section. To state it precisely, we must first say which displacement field the body takes under a given load. Let the body be as in theorem 4.42 on the principle of virtual displacements: before loading it occupies the set of points \(V\) with the surface \(S\). On a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface it is held, and on the remaining part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) a prescribed traction vector \(\bar{\vek t}\) acts on it, the force per unit area with which the surroundings act on the body. A body force \(\vek b\) acts in the body (definition 2.25). The displacement field that the body takes in equilibrium must meet three requirements, which combine what we learned in the first three chapters: strains from displacements, the relation between stresses and strains, and equilibrium.

Definition 4.71 Solution for a load (rešitev za obremenitev)

Let the body \(V\) and the division of its surface into the parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) be as in theorem 4.42 on the principle of virtual displacements, and let the displacement \(\vek 0\) be prescribed on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). Let the material be linear elastic, with the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\) (definition 3.16). A load on the body is a pair \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\): a body force \(\vek b\), continuous on \(V\), and a prescribed traction vector \(\bar{\vek t}\), continuous on each outer face of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). A displacement field \(\vek u\) is a solution for the load \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\) if:

  1. \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable (definition 1.88) on an open set that contains the body together with its surface, and is equal to \(\vek 0\) at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\),
  2. the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), computed from the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\), are continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface, and satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.31) at every interior point of the body,
  3. Cauchy's formula \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) holds at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface.

Source: EP §4.6.1, (4.6.1)-(4.6.4) (p. 218), SADD §6.2 (PDF p. 133), BOWER §5.8.1 (PDF p. 379).

The first requirement says that the field respects the supports and has a small strain tensor at every point. The second says that the stresses are as the material requires, and that every small piece of the body is in equilibrium (theorem 2.27). The third says that the stresses at the surface carry the prescribed forces. All three requirements are written on the shape of the body before loading, as assumption 1 requires. The stresses of a solution are symmetric, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\), because the elastic constants are symmetric in the first pair of indices, \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{jikl}}\) (lemma 3.17, item 2). A solution therefore satisfies the assumptions that the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.42) makes about the stresses, and the assumptions that the principle of minimum total potential energy (theorem 4.51) makes about the true displacement field. Can one load have two different solutions? If it could, we could not speak of the displacement that the load causes, because there would be two of them. It cannot.

Lemma 4.72 Uniqueness of the solution (enoličnost rešitve)

Let the body be as in definition 4.71, of an ideal elastic material whose strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero. Let the body be in one piece: its interior points form a connected open set (definition 1.126), and every point of the body is the limit of a sequence of its interior points, so that the body has no parts without an interior, such as a sheet without thickness. Let \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be solutions for the same load \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\), both with small strains. Then:

  1. the strains and stresses of the two solutions are equal at every point of the body,
  2. the difference \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is a small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). If the supports prevent every small rigid displacement of the body, then \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\).
Proof

We must show that the difference of the two solutions has no strain, and draw from this the conclusions about the stresses and the displacements. We use the principle of minimum total potential energy, once for each solution.

  1. By requirement 1 of definition 4.71 both fields are continuously differentiable and equal to \(\vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so they are kinematically admissible displacement fields with the prescribed displacement \(\vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (definition 4.48).
  2. By requirements 2 and 3 the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) are continuously differentiable and satisfy the equilibrium equations and, on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), Cauchy's formula. The load \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\) is given and does not change with the deformation, as the theorem requires. By theorem 4.51 on the principle of minimum total potential energy, item 1, applied with the other admissible field \(\tilde{\vek u}\), therefore \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) - \Pi(\vek u) \ge 0\).
  3. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is a solution too, so we may exchange the roles, and the same theorem gives \(\Pi(\vek u) - \Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) \ge 0\).
  4. A number that is not negative and whose opposite is not negative either is zero, so \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u)\). By item 2 of the same theorem the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is zero at every point of the body.
  5. A partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.79), so the strain of the field \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u + \vek v\) is the sum of the strains of the fields \(\vek u\) and \(\vek v\), and thus equal to the strain of the field \(\vek u\). The stresses are computed from the strains (definition 3.16), so they are equal too. This is item 1.
  6. The field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable, since the fields \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) are (lemma 1.79, corollary 1.67, item 1), and by step 4 it has a zero small strain tensor at every point of the body. The interior points of the body form a connected open set. So by theorem 1.130 on a displacement field without strain there are a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that \(\vek v(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) at every interior point \(P\). A continuously differentiable field is continuous (section 1.15.6), and the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) is a polynomial in the coordinates and therefore continuous (corollary 1.67, item 2). Let \(P\) be a point of the surface and \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) a sequence of interior points that converges to \(P\). By lemma 1.66, used for each component, the sequence \(\vek v(P_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(\vek v(P)\), and the sequence \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP_{\mathrm{n}}}\) to \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\). The two sequences are equal term by term, so by lemma 1.39 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence their limits are equal too, and the equality holds at the points of the surface as well. By (2.32), \(\mat W\,\vek r = \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r\) for \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = (W_{\mathrm{zy}}, W_{\mathrm{xz}}, W_{\mathrm{yx}})\), which we check component by component, for the component \(x\) for example \(W_{\mathrm{xx}}\,x + W_{\mathrm{xy}}\,y + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z = W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z - W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,y\), because \(W_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) (lemma 1.101, item 3) and \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -W_{\mathrm{yx}}\). So the field \(\vek v\) is a small rigid displacement of lemma 4.32 with \(\delta\vek a = \vek a\). On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(\vek v = \vek 0 - \vek 0 = \vek 0\).
