  7. If the supports prevent every small rigid displacement, the only small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the field \(\vek 0\). Therefore \(\vek v = \vek 0\) and \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\). This is item 2.

Source: SADD §6.2, (6.2.1)-(6.2.5) (PDF p. 133), EP §4.6.3, (4.6.14)-(4.6.21) (pp. 225-226), CM (7.3.45) (PDF p. 314). The sources insert the difference of the two solutions directly into the strain energy. The proof with the principle of minimum total potential energy is not from the sources. The statement in step 6, that a field without strain is a small rigid displacement, SADD states without proof (PDF p. 133), and in this book it is proved by theorem 1.130 on a displacement field without strain.

The proof showed why there is only one solution. Two solutions would have the same smallest total potential energy, while a difference with a strain that is not zero would increase the energy. The difference therefore has no strain and can only be a rigid displacement, which the supports do not allow. What if they allow it? The hanging bar of chapter 1 is held only at the centre \(O\) of its top face. A fixed point prevents a translation, but not a rotation of the bar about \(O\), so CM adds the condition that the material at the point \(O\) does not rotate (CM, PDF p. 306). Without this condition the stresses would still be determined uniquely, the displacements only up to a small rotation. In the bracket of two bars the pins \(A\) and \(B\) are enough. The two elongations determined the displacement of the joint \(C\) uniquely in step 4, since we computed it from them. Step 6 uses the two assumptions on a body in one piece. Without the first, theorem 1.130 on a displacement field without strain fails, as the two separate cubes of figure 1.138 show, each of which moves rigidly in its own way. The second carries the equality \(\vek v = \vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) from the interior points to the surface, where the supports are. Only because of it does the condition \(\vek v = \vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) restrict the rigid displacement. For a body made of boxes the second assumption holds by itself, as we saw in step 3 of the proof of theorem 4.42.

Now we can state the first observation for every body.

Lemma 4.73 Principle of superposition (načelo superpozicije)

Let the body be as in definition 4.71, let \(\vek u^{(1)}\) be a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)})\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)})\), with the strains \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the stresses \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be numbers. Then the field \(\alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) is a solution for the load

\[\big(\alpha\,\vek b^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek b^{(2)},\ \alpha\,\bar{\vek t}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\big) ,\]

its strains are \(\alpha\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and its stresses \(\alpha\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Proof

For the field \(\vek u = \alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) we must check the three requirements of definition 4.71. Each follows from the requirement being linear.

  1. A partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives, and a partial derivative of a multiple is the multiple of the partial derivative (lemma 1.79). A sum of continuous functions of a point and a multiple of a continuous function are continuous functions (corollary 1.67, item 1). Therefore \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(\vek u = \alpha\,\vek 0 + \beta\,\vek 0 = \vek 0\). This is requirement 1.
  2. By the same rule for derivatives, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \alpha\,\partial u^{(1)}_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \beta\,\partial u^{(2)}_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). The component of the small strain tensor \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) is therefore \(\alpha\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  3. By definition 3.16 the stresses are
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\big(\alpha\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}} + \beta\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\big) = \alpha \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}} + \beta \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}} = \alpha\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} ,\]
    because a finite sum may be split into two sums and the constant numbers \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) taken out. By step 1, applied to the stresses, they are continuously differentiable.
  4. We insert the stresses from step 3 and the body force \(\alpha\,\vek b^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek b^{(2)}\) into the first equilibrium equation (2.31) and use the rule for derivatives from step 1:
    \[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\,\Big(\frac{\partial\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b^{(1)}_{\mathrm{x}}\Big) + \beta\,\Big(\frac{\partial\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b^{(2)}_{\mathrm{x}}\Big) .\]
    Both brackets are zero, because \(\vek u^{(1)}\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) are solutions, so the left side is \(\alpha \cdot 0 + \beta \cdot 0 = 0\). The same holds for the second and third equilibrium equations. This is requirement 2.
  5. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the component \(i\) of the column \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) is, by (1.38),
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \big(\alpha\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\big)\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \alpha \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} + \beta \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} ,\]
    where we split the finite sum and took out the numbers as in step 3. On the right are the components \(i\) of the columns \(\ten\sigma^{(1)}\vek n = \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\) and \(\ten\sigma^{(2)}\vek n = \bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\), so \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \alpha\,\bar{\vek t}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\). This is requirement 3.

Source: EP §4.6.1, (4.6.1)-(4.6.4) (pp. 217-218), CM §7.4.1 (PDF p. 314). EP states the principle for all problems that are linear geometrically and in the material, but does not write a proof. The proof in steps is not from the sources.

The lemma together with lemma 4.72 on the uniqueness of the solution says what we saw in the computation for the bracket. If the supports prevent rigid displacements, \(\alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) is the only solution for the combined load. We may therefore compute the displacements and stresses of two loads separately and add them, and a load increased by the factor \(\alpha\) causes \(\alpha\) times larger displacements and stresses. It is therefore enough to compute the effect of each load on a structure once, and the combinations follow by adding. The same holds for the bracket, which is not a body in the sense of the definition but a model of bars. There the linearity was shown by the computation (4.53).

When does adding fail? Each of the linearities we used can fail. For large displacements we may no longer write the equilibrium on the shape before loading, and the directions of the bars of the bracket would depend on the displacement, as they would for a rope that sags under a load. A material above the yield stress (definition 2.7) or rubber is not linear elastic. A load that changes with the deformation, like water pressure on a wall that tilts (section 4.5.3), does not allow adding, because the force is no longer determined by the load alone. Adding also fails for a support that can only push the body and cannot pull it, for example for a body lying on a table. Under one load the body touches the table, under another it lifts off, and the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is not the same for both. EP states the principle for problems that are linear geometrically and in the material (EP, p. 218).

Displacements and stresses add up, but energy does not. Take the bracket with a horizontal force \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) kN and a vertical force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN upwards at the joint \(C\). By step 2 the force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) alone gives the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) alone \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac43\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) kN, and both together the sums, \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac73\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) kN. The strain energy of the bracket is \(U = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}^2 L_{\mathrm{i}}/(2EA)\) by (4.5), and with SymPy we get

\[U(F_{\mathrm{x}}) = 0{,}1020\ \text{J} , \qquad U(F_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0{,}5357\ \text{J} , \qquad U(F_{\mathrm{x}}\ \text{and}\ F_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0{,}9099\ \text{J} .\]

The sum of the first two is only \(0{,}6378\) J, \(0{,}2721\) J less than the energy with both forces. The reason is the square in the formula for the energy. With both forces the force in a bar is the sum \(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} + N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\) of the forces caused by each force alone, and

\[\big(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} + N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\big)^2 = \big(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)}\big)^2 + 2\,N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)} + \big(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\big)^2 .\]

The first and last terms give the energies of each force alone, and the middle term adds the mixed energy \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)} L_{\mathrm{i}}/(EA)\). For the bracket this is \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot \tfrac43\ \text{kN} \cdot 4\ \text{m}/(EA) + 0 \cdot \big({-\tfrac53}\ \text{kN}\big) \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 0{,}2721\) J. EP and CM say this explicitly: energy does not add up, because it is a quadratic function of the displacements or forces (EP, p. 220, CM §7.4.1, PDF p. 314). The mixed energy is exactly \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\ \text{µm} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 0{,}2721\) J. The next subsection shows that this is no coincidence.

4.7.3 The order of loading

Let us load the bracket slowly with the forces \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) kN to the right and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN upwards, first with the first and then with the second, and count the work the two forces do (figure 4.70, top). We need the work of a force that grows in proportion to the displacement of its point of application. Let us compute it in three steps.

  1. Let the point of application move along a straight segment by \(\Delta\vek u = \ell\,\vek d\), where \(\ell\) is the length of the segment and \(\vek d\) the unit vector of its direction, and let the force grow in proportion to the distance travelled \(s\), from zero to \(\vek F\). At the distance \(s\) the force is \((s/\ell)\,\vek F\), and its projection onto the direction of motion is \((s/\ell)\,\vek F\cdot\vek d\).
  2. By item 2 of definition 4.1 the work is \(\int_0^\ell (s/\ell)\,\vek F\cdot\vek d\ \mathrm{d}s\). The function \(s^2/(2\ell)\) has the derivative \(s/\ell\) (lemma 1.79), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.39 the work equals \(\tfrac12\,\ell\,\vek F\cdot\vek d\).
  3. Since \(\ell\,\vek d = \Delta\vek u\), this is \(\tfrac12\,\vek F\cdot\Delta\vek u\), half the work that the constant force \(\vek F\) would do on the same displacement (item 1 of definition 4.1).

For a bar we got the same in theorem 4.3 on the work and energy of a bar. Now let us count.

  1. The force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) grows slowly from zero to 1 kN, the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) is not there yet. By (4.53) the joint moves along a straight segment, in proportion to the force, and at the end \(u = D_{\mathrm{xx}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 204{,}1\) µm and \(v = D_{\mathrm{yx}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\) µm. The force \((F_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\) counts only the horizontal part of the displacement, since its scalar product with the displacement is \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\,u\). By the computation above it does the work \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} = 0{,}1020\) J, the area of the grey triangle at the top left of the figure.
  2. The force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) grows slowly from zero to 1 kN, while the force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) stays 1 kN. The joint moves further by \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\) µm to the right and by \(D_{\mathrm{yy}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 1071{,}4\) µm up. The force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) does \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 1071{,}4\ \text{µm} = 0{,}5357\) J, the grey triangle at the top right. The force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the same throughout this stage and its point of application moves by 272,1 µm in its direction, so it does the work of a constant force, \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot 272{,}1\ \text{µm} = 0{,}2721\) J, the blue rectangle at the top left. There is no half here, because the force does not grow from zero, it is already fully present.
  3. The total work is \(0{,}1020 + 0{,}5357 + 0{,}2721 = 0{,}9099\) J. This is exactly the strain energy of the bracket with both forces, which we computed in subsection 4.7.2, as it must be for slow loading (section 4.1).

Now we apply the two forces in the opposite order (figure 4.70, bottom). First \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) grows and does \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 1071{,}4\ \text{µm} = 0{,}5357\) J, and the joint also moves by 272,1 µm to the right. Then \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) grows and does \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} = 0{,}1020\) J, while the joint moves further by \(D_{\mathrm{yx}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\) µm up, and on this displacement the constant force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) does \(0{,}2721\) J. Together again \(0{,}9099\) J. We have now recognized the mixed energy of subsection 4.7.2. It is the work done by a force that is already fully present when the other force moves its point of application.

Let us write the same with letters, for forces \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) of any magnitude. With the order first \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), then \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), the work is

\[W_{\mathrm{I}} = \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + F_{\mathrm{x}}\,D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} ,\]

and with the opposite order

\[W_{\mathrm{II}} = \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + F_{\mathrm{y}}\,D_{\mathrm{yx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

The Roman numerals in the index give the order, they are not forces or directions. In both cases the final state is the same: by adding loads, the final forces in the bars and the final displacement of the joint with both forces are the same, regardless of which force came first. For the bracket we computed that the work in both cases equals the strain energy of the final state. In general we expect this for every ideal elastic body. The work the material receives depends only on the final strain, not on the path (definition 3.42, item 2), and in slow loading the work of the forces is stored entirely in the material (section 4.1). If this is so, \(W_{\mathrm{I}} = W_{\mathrm{II}}\). The first two terms are the same in both expressions, so the last ones must be equal too, \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\,D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} = F_{\mathrm{y}}\,D_{\mathrm{yx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\), and for forces that are not zero \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

What would it mean if \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} \ne D_{\mathrm{yx}}\)? We would load the bracket in the first order and unload it in the reverse of the second order, first reducing \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and then \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\). When unloading along the same path backwards, the forces act in every state as in loading, but the displacements have the opposite sign, so the bracket gives back the work \(W_{\mathrm{II}}\). After such a cycle the bracket would be in the same state as at the start, but the forces would have done on it the work \(W_{\mathrm{I}} - W_{\mathrm{II}} = F_{\mathrm{x}} F_{\mathrm{y}}\,(D_{\mathrm{xy}} - D_{\mathrm{yx}})\), which is not zero. The cycle in the opposite direction would give the work \(W_{\mathrm{II}} - W_{\mathrm{I}}\). One of the two numbers would be negative, and in that cycle the bracket would give out work from nothing. This is forbidden by the same argument that we used for a small piece of material in section 3.6.3. The equality \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\) is therefore a consequence of the fact that an elastic body returns the work it receives.

This explanation is the explanation of EP and CM (EP §4.6.4, (4.6.22)-(4.6.24), pp. 226-227, CM §7.4.2, (7.4.11)-(7.4.13), PDF pp. 317-318). It uses, however, a conclusion that we have not proved for a body: that the work of the external forces in slow loading depends only on the final state, also when the ratio between the loads changes during loading, as in our two orders. For a bar we proved it in theorem 4.3. For a body we proved it only for loads that all grow in proportion at the same time (corollary 4.47 on the work of the loads and the strain energy). A precise proof that does not need the loading path at all follows in the next subsection.

4.7.4 Betti's theorem

Take a body with supports on a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of its surface and two loads (figure 4.71). The first, \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)})\), causes the displacement field \(\vek u^{(1)}\), the second, \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)})\), the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\). The work that the forces of the first load would do if they stayed the same while their points of application move by \(\vek u^{(2)}\) is, by definition 4.1 summed over the pieces of the body and of the surface as for the potential energy of the loads in section 4.5.3, equal to

\[W_{12} = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

The first index says which load works, the second on whose displacements. The letter \(W\) with two indices is a work, not the weight of the hanging bar. For the bracket this work was the blue rectangle in figure 4.70, the work of the first force on the displacement caused by the second.

Theorem 4.74 Betti's reciprocal theorem (Bettijev izrek)

Let the body be as in definition 4.71, of an ideal elastic material. Let \(\vek u^{(1)}\) be a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)})\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)})\). Then

\[\begin{aligned} &\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ &\qquad = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}A . \end{aligned} \tag{4.54}\]
Proof

We must show that both sides equal the same integral of stresses and strains. We get each side from the principle of virtual displacements, taking as the virtual displacement the solution for the other load, and the equality of the two integrals from the symmetry of the elastic constants.

  1. By requirement 1 of definition 4.71 the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body with its surface, and equal to \(\vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so it is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.39). The definition does not require the virtual displacement to be small. The components of the small strain tensor of the field \(\delta\vek u = \vek u^{(2)}\) are the strains \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the solution, because they are computed from the same partial derivatives.
  2. By requirements 2 and 3 the stresses \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuously differentiable, satisfy the equilibrium equations with the body force \(\vek b^{(1)}\) and, on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), Cauchy's formula with \(\bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\). They are symmetric, because \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{jikl}}\) (lemma 3.17, item 2). These are the assumptions of the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.42), which with the virtual displacement \(\vek u^{(2)}\) gives
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
    The right side is the left side of equation (4.54).
  3. In the same way, with the roles of the two loads exchanged, the principle with the virtual displacement \(\vek u^{(1)}\) gives
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    and the right side is the right side of equation (4.54). It remains to show that the left sides of steps 2 and 3 are equal.
  4. At every point of the body \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\) by definition 3.16, so
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]
  5. The material is ideal elastic and linear elastic, so by theorem 3.46 on the symmetry of the elastic constants, item 1, \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\) for all indices. We insert this:
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \Big( \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{klij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} \Big)\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}} ,\]
    where we exchanged the order of the finite sums and took \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\) out of the sum over \(i\) and \(j\).
  6. By definition 3.16, written for the pair of indices \(kl\) instead of \(ij\), the expression in the bracket is the stress \(\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\) of the second solution. The right side of step 5 is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\). When we rename the indices, \(k\) to \(i\) and \(l\) to \(j\), this is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  7. The integrands on the left sides of steps 2 and 3 are therefore equal at every point, so the integrals are equal too. The right sides of steps 2 and 3 are therefore equal, which is (4.54).

Source: EP theorem 4.6.2, (4.6.25)-(4.6.27) (pp. 227-228), SADD §6.4.2, (6.4.2), (6.4.3) (PDF pp. 135-136), CM §7.4.2, (7.4.14)-(7.4.18) (PDF pp. 318-319), BOWER §5.8.1 (PDF pp. 379-380). In steps 2 and 3 the sources use the divergence theorem directly, which in our case the principle of virtual displacements has already used.

This is Betti's reciprocal theorem. The work \(W_{12}\) of the first load on the displacements of the second equals the work \(W_{21}\) of the second load on the displacements of the first. The proof showed which properties of the body are needed for this. The principle of virtual displacements knows nothing about the material and holds for every body in equilibrium. The material enters only in steps 4 to 6, and there only with the symmetry \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\), which we derived in section 3.6 from the requirement that the material returns the work it receives. This is the precise form of the explanation with the order of loading.

For an isotropic material the symmetry is directly visible. By Hooke's law (3.13), \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) when \(i = j\), and \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) when \(i \ne j\), where \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants (definition 3.10). The sum in step 2 is therefore

\[\begin{aligned} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} &= \lambda\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}}\,\big(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{zz}}\big) + 2\mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} \\ &= \lambda\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} , \end{aligned}\]

an expression that does not change if we exchange the labels (1) and (2). And what if, for example, \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}} \ne C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\)? Take a first strain whose only nonzero component is \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and a second whose only nonzero component is \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\). In the sum of step 4 only the term with \(i = j = y\) and \(k = l = x\) remains, that is \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and with the roles exchanged only \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The two sums would differ, and the theorem would not hold. Such a material would give out work in a cycle, like the imagined material with \(C_{16} \ne C_{61}\) in section 3.6.3. SADD mentions that Truesdell proved the theorem to be even a necessary and sufficient condition for an elastic material to have a strain energy density (SADD, PDF p. 136).

When does the theorem fail? First, when the supports prescribe displacements that are not zero. Then the support forces on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) do work, and in the proof the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\) is not a kinematically admissible virtual displacement. SADD therefore integrates the traction vector over the whole surface \(S\) in the theorem, where on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) it is the force of the support (SADD (6.4.2), PDF p. 135). For fixed supports these terms are zero, because the displacement there is zero, and we get (4.54). Second, for a material without symmetric elastic constants, as we have just seen. Third, when adding loads fails: for large displacements, for a nonlinear material and for loads that change with the deformation, since there the principle of virtual displacements or Hooke's law in the form we used does not hold.

Let us test the theorem on the bracket. The bracket is not a body but a model of bars, and the same statement holds for it with the same proof. Instead of the principle of virtual displacements for a body we use the principle for the truss (4.25), \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\delta e_{\mathrm{AC}} + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\delta e_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek F\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), where \(\delta e = \vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the virtual elongation of a bar (equation (4.24)). For the first load, the force \(\vek F^{(1)}\) at the joint, we take as the virtual displacement of the joint its actual displacement under the second load, \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)}\). The virtual elongations are then the actual elongations \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\) of the bars under the second load (step 4), and by step 3 the axial forces are \(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} = EA\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)}/L_{\mathrm{i}}\). Therefore

\[\frac{EA}{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(1)}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(2)} + \frac{EA}{L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}^{(1)}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}^{(2)} = \vek F^{(1)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)} .\]

The left side does not change if we exchange the labels (1) and (2), so \(\vek F^{(1)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)} = \vek F^{(2)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(1)}\). The role of the symmetric elastic constants is played here by the numbers \(EA/L_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(EA/L_{\mathrm{BC}}\), by which each force in a bar is connected only with the elongation of the same bar.

Let us check with numbers. For the first load take the load from the beginning of the chapter, \(\vek F^{(1)} = (0, -10, 0)\) kN, for the second a horizontal force \(\vek F^{(2)} = (1, 0, 0)\) kN. By (4.53) the displacement of the joint has under the first load the components \(u^{(1)} = -2721\) µm and \(v^{(1)} = -10\,714\) µm, and under the second \(u^{(2)} = 204{,}1\) µm and \(v^{(2)} = 272{,}1\) µm. The two works are

\[\begin{aligned} W_{12} &= \vek F^{(1)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)} = (-10\ \text{kN}) \cdot 272{,}1\ \text{µm} = -2{,}721\ \text{J} , \\ W_{21} &= \vek F^{(2)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(1)} = 1\ \text{kN} \cdot (-2721\ \text{µm}) = -2{,}721\ \text{J} . \end{aligned}\]

Both works are negative. The horizontal force lifts the joint, against the load that pulls down. The load in turn pushes the joint towards the wall, against the horizontal force that pulls to the right. The works are equal, although they are products of very different numbers, a large force of 10 kN with a small rise of 272,1 µm and a small force of 1 kN with a large displacement of 2721 µm.

Let us also test it on loads that do not act at a point (figure 4.72). Let the steel bar of chapter 1, of length \(L = 10\) m, with the cross-sectional area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and Young's modulus \(E = 196\) GPa, be held at its top cross section, and let the axis \(x\) point down from it. We describe it with the bar model of section 4.3, in which the whole cross section at \(x\) moves down by \(u(x)\), as in section 4.5.2. The first load is the weight of the bar, per unit length \(q = \rho g A\), with \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ and \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s². We know the displacement it causes from chapter 1, \(u^{(1)}(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (section 3.1.5). The second load is a force \(F\) at the lower end, without the weight. Then every cross section carries the force \(F\), the strain is \(F/(EA)\) everywhere, and the displacement is \(u^{(2)}(x) = F x/(EA)\).

The work of the weight on the displacements of the second load is the sum of the works of the weights of the small pieces, \(q\,\Delta x\), on the displacement \(u^{(2)}(x)\), in the limit an integral. The work of the force \(F\) on the displacements of the first load is \(F\) times the displacement of the lower end, \(u^{(1)}(L)\):

\[\begin{aligned} W_{12} &= \int_0^L \rho g A \cdot \frac{F x}{EA}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\rho g F}{E}\cdot\frac{L^2}{2} , \\ W_{21} &= F\,u^{(1)}(L) = F\,a\,(2L \cdot L - L^2) = F\,\frac{\rho g}{2E}\,L^2 . \end{aligned}\]

We computed the first integral with the fundamental theorem of calculus, since \(x^2/2\) has the derivative \(x\). Both works are \(\rho g F L^2/(2E)\), for \(F = 1\) kN this is \(0{,}01952\) J. Here too the theorem holds with the same proof as for a body. In the principle of virtual displacements for a bar (theorem 4.36), \(\int_0^L N\,\delta u'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,\delta u\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L)\), we take \(\delta u = u^{(2)}\) for the first load and \(\delta u = u^{(1)}\) for the second. Both fields are polynomials, so they have a continuous derivative, as the theorem requires, and both are zero at \(x = 0\). The axial force of a linear elastic bar is \(N = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} A = E A\,u'\) (definition 3.1), so the left side for the first load is \(\int_0^L EA\,(u^{(1)})'\,(u^{(2)})'\,\mathrm{d}x\), and for the second \(\int_0^L EA\,(u^{(2)})'\,(u^{(1)})'\,\mathrm{d}x\), the same integral. The role of the elastic constants is played here by the single number \(EA\), and the product does not change if we exchange the labels (1) and (2).

What does the theorem give us here? Suppose we knew only the simple field \(u^{(2)}\) of the end force, but not the displacement due to the weight. The theorem would give us the displacement of the lower end due to the weight without solving the problem with the weight:

\[u^{(1)}(L) = \frac{W_{12}}{F} = \int_0^L \rho g A\,\frac{x}{EA}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\rho g L^2}{2E} = \frac{7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 10^2}{2 \cdot 196 \cdot 10^9}\ \text{m} = 19{,}52\ \text{µm} ,\]

which is \(a L^2\), as in chapter 1. This is how EP uses the theorem for the bending of beams, which we will meet in chapter 5: the displacement of the end due to a force at the end is known, and the displacement of the end due to a distributed load is sought (EP example 4.6.5, p. 229). EP and CM also check the theorem on the same pair of loads (EP example 4.6.4, pp. 228-229, CM example 7.4.4, PDF pp. 319-320).

4.7.5 Maxwell's theorem

Betti's theorem compares the works of whole loads. The simplest load is a single force, and for the bracket we got \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\) for two such loads. How do we state this for a body? A force at a single point of a body is an idealization that does not work well in a body. SADD writes the displacement of an unbounded isotropic body due to a force at one point, and at the distance \(r\) from the point it is proportional to \(1/r\) (SADD (6.4.5), PDF p. 136). As \(r\) approaches zero it grows beyond all bounds, and the displacement of the point itself is not a finite number. We therefore spread the force evenly over a small patch of the surface, and as the displacement we take the average displacement of the patch in the direction of the force. For the bracket and for the bar, where the forces act at joints and on cross sections, this is not necessary, and there the displacement of the point of application is a finite number.

Definition 4.75 Flexibility matrix (podajnostna matrika)

Let the body be as in definition 4.71, and let patches \(\Delta S_1, \dots, \Delta S_{\mathrm{m}}\) of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) with the areas \(\Delta A_1, \dots, \Delta A_{\mathrm{m}}\) and unit vectors \(\vek d_1, \dots, \vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\) be chosen. The force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the load without a body force, with the traction vector \((F_{\mathrm{j}}/\Delta A_{\mathrm{j}})\,\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\) on \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\vek 0\) elsewhere on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). The displacement of the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{i}}\) for a displacement field \(\vek u\) is the number

\[\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{1}{\Delta A_{\mathrm{i}}} \int_{\Delta \mathrm{S}_\mathrm{i}} \vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

The flexibility coefficient \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the displacement \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the solution for the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\), divided by \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\). The matrix \(\mat D\) with \(m\) rows and \(m\) columns and the elements \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the flexibility matrix of the chosen patches and directions.

Source: EP §4.6.5 (p. 230), CM §7.4.3 (PDF p. 320), BARBER (1.18) (PDF p. 27), where the coefficients are called influence coefficients. Patches instead of points are not from the sources.

The force on a patch drops to zero at the edge of the patch. A solution with continuously differentiable stresses as in definition 4.71 does not allow this, as we said at assumption 3 in section 4.4.1. This force is therefore an idealization, like the loads on part of a face in the figures of this chapter. An exact treatment would replace it by a force that falls continuously to zero at the edge of the patch, and compute the displacement of the patch as an average weighted with the same distribution. We also assume that a solution exists for every such force that falls continuously to zero at the edge of the patch. We do not prove existence in this book. EP remarks that the existence of solutions is difficult to establish, while their uniqueness is easy to prove (EP p. 225).

The displacement \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the average of the component of the displacement in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\) over the patch. Since the solution for each load is unique (lemma 4.72), \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is a definite number. The name says that \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) measures how flexible the body is: how far the patch \(i\) moves per newton of force acting on the patch \(j\). Its unit is metre per newton. For the bracket we need no patches. Force 1 acts horizontally at the joint \(C\), force 2 vertically at the same joint, displacement 1 is the horizontal displacement of the joint, displacement 2 the vertical one. The matrix

\[\mat D = \begin{bmatrix} D_{\mathrm{xx}} & D_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ D_{\mathrm{yx}} & D_{\mathrm{yy}} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1\ \text{m}}{EA}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 16/3 \\ 16/3 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\]

is the flexibility matrix of the bracket for these two forces. The same patch or the same joint may appear several times, with different directions, as here. The quotient depends only on the patches and directions, not on the magnitude of the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\). By the principle of superposition and the uniqueness of the solution, the solution for the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \((F_{\mathrm{j}}/1\ \text{N})\) times the solution for the force 1 N, and the average \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is linear in the field \(\vek u\), since the integral of a sum splits into the sum of the integrals. For the same reason the displacement under several forces at once is the sum of the contributions,

\[\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{m} D_{\mathrm{ij}}\,F_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad \text{that is} \qquad \begin{bmatrix} \Delta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \Delta_{\mathrm{m}} \end{bmatrix} = \mat D \begin{bmatrix} F_1 \\ \vdots \\ F_{\mathrm{m}} \end{bmatrix} ,\]

where on the right is the product of a matrix and a vector (definition 1.94). For the bracket this is exactly (4.53).

Theorem 4.76 Maxwell's reciprocal theorem (Maxwellov izrek)

Let the body be as in definition 4.71, of an ideal elastic material, and let \(\mat D\) be the flexibility matrix of the chosen patches \(\Delta S_1, \dots, \Delta S_{\mathrm{m}}\) and directions \(\vek d_1, \dots, \vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\). Then \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = D_{\mathrm{ji}}\) for all \(i\) and \(j\) from \(1\) to \(m\): the flexibility matrix is symmetric.

Proof

We must show that the displacement of the patch \(i\) due to a force of 1 N on the patch \(j\) equals the displacement of the patch \(j\) due to a force of 1 N on the patch \(i\). This is Betti's theorem for two loads that are single forces.

  1. Let \(\vek u^{(1)}\) be the solution for the force \(F_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) N on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) the solution for the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\) N on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\). By definition 4.75 the displacement of the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\) equals \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} \cdot 1\) N, and the displacement of the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\) for the field \(\vek u^{(1)}\) equals \(D_{\mathrm{ji}} \cdot 1\) N.
  2. The first load has no body force, its traction vector is \((1\ \text{N}/\Delta A_{\mathrm{i}})\,\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\) on \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek 0\) elsewhere on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). The left side of equation (4.54) is therefore
    \[\int_{\Delta \mathrm{S}_\mathrm{i}} \frac{1\ \text{N}}{\Delta A_{\mathrm{i}}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A = 1\ \text{N} \cdot \frac{1}{\Delta A_{\mathrm{i}}}\int_{\Delta \mathrm{S}_\mathrm{i}} \vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A = 1\ \text{N} \cdot D_{\mathrm{ij}} \cdot 1\ \text{N} ,\]
    where we took the constant number out of the integral and used step 1.
  3. In the same way the right side of equation (4.54) equals \(1\ \text{N} \cdot D_{\mathrm{ji}} \cdot 1\ \text{N}\).
  4. By Betti's theorem 4.74 the two sides are equal, so \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = D_{\mathrm{ji}}\).

Source: EP §4.6.5, (4.6.28) (p. 230), CM §7.4.3, (7.4.19), (7.4.20) (PDF p. 320). The sources take the two forces at two different points. The proof does not need this, so the theorem holds also for the same point and two directions, as for the bracket.

Maxwell's theorem is older than Betti's. Maxwell presented it in 1864, Betti his in 1872, so one says that Betti generalized Maxwell's theorem (EP, p. 230, CM, PDF p. 320). For the bracket we saw the symmetry of the flexibility matrix in the computation and proved it in subsection 4.7.4 with the principle of virtual displacements for the truss. For a truss, however, the symmetry is also visible in a formula. Let \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{b}}\) be the directions of two forces at the joint \(C\). Let \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(a)}\) be the axial forces in the bars due to a force of 1 N in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\), divided by 1 N, as in the unit dummy load method (theorem 4.55), and likewise \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(b)}\) for the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{b}}\). Under an actual force of 1 N in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{b}}\) the axial force of the bar \(k\) is \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(b)} \cdot 1\) N. The unit dummy load method with a unit force in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) gives the component of the displacement in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\), and dividing it by 1 N we get

\[D_{\mathrm{ab}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(a)}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(b)}\,\frac{L_{\mathrm{k}}}{E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} .\]

Exchanging \(a\) and \(b\) does not change the formula. For our bracket, \(\hat N^{(x)}_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\) and \(\hat N^{(x)}_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) for the horizontal force, and \(\hat N^{(y)}_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac43\) and \(\hat N^{(y)}_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) for the vertical force upwards (step 2), so \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1 \cdot \tfrac43 \cdot 4\ \text{m}/(EA) + 0 \cdot \big({-\tfrac53}\big) \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = \tfrac{16}{3}\ \text{m}/(EA)\), as in (4.53).

Now we also see why the factor \(\tfrac43\) appeared twice in subsection 4.7.1. The same unit vectors \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\) tell, in the equilibrium of the pin, how the forces in the bars make up the force on the pin (step 1), and, in the elongations, how the displacement of the pin changes the lengths of the bars (step 4). This connection between equilibrium and geometry is expressed by the principle of virtual displacements for the truss, which we obtained precisely by taking the scalar product of the equilibrium of the pin with the displacement of the pin (section 4.3.9).

For the bracket both forces were at the same joint. Let us also look at two forces at different points (figure 4.73). Take again the steel bar of length 10 m with the cross section \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), held at its top cross section, in the bar model, and this time leave out its weight. By the principle of superposition the displacement due to the weight is simply added to the displacements we compute. The product of Young's modulus and the cross-sectional area is \(EA = 196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 78{,}54 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N. Force 1 acts downwards on the cross section at the depth \(x_1 = 5\) m, force 2 downwards at the lower end, at the depth \(x_2 = 10\) m.

  1. A force \(F_1 = 1\) kN at the depth 5 m. The upper half of the bar carries 1 kN and gets longer by \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 324{,}8\) µm. The lower half carries nothing, does not get longer and only moves together with the middle cross section. The lower end therefore moves by 324,8 µm, and \(D_{21} = 324{,}8\) µm/kN.
  2. A force \(F_2 = 1\) kN at the lower end. The whole bar carries 1 kN. The middle cross section moves by the elongation of the upper half, again \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 324{,}8\) µm, and \(D_{12} = 324{,}8\) µm/kN.

Here the mechanism is visible. In both cases the displacement of the other point is the elongation of the part of the bar above the higher of the two points, which carries 1 kN in both cases. In general, for forces at the depths \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) the flexibility coefficient is \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = \min(x_{\mathrm{i}}, x_{\mathrm{j}})/(EA)\), where \(\min(x_{\mathrm{i}}, x_{\mathrm{j}})\) is the smaller of the two numbers, and exchanging \(i\) and \(j\) does not change it. For the same point \(D_{11} = 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 324{,}8\) µm/kN and \(D_{22} = 10\ \text{m}/(EA) = 649{,}6\) µm/kN, so

\[\mat D = \begin{bmatrix} 324{,}8 & 324{,}8 \\ 324{,}8 & 649{,}6 \end{bmatrix} \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} .\]

That \(D_{11} = D_{12}\) is a peculiarity of the bar: the middle cross section moves by the elongation of the upper half, which carries 1 kN, no matter where below the middle the force acts.

What is the theorem good for in measurement? Take a light footbridge with three marked points \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) on the walking surface, and suppose that the bridge behaves linearly elastically (figure 4.74). We load the bridge with a test load of 10 kN at the point \(B\) and measure the vertical displacements downwards: 2,8 mm at \(A\), 5,0 mm at \(B\) and 4,0 mm at \(C\). The numbers are made up for the example. With this we know the column \(B\) of the flexibility matrix, the displacements of all three points per kilonewton of force at \(B\): \(D_{\mathrm{AB}} = 0{,}28\) mm/kN, \(D_{\mathrm{BB}} = 0{,}50\) mm/kN and \(D_{\mathrm{CB}} = 0{,}40\) mm/kN. By Maxwell's theorem we thereby also know the row \(B\): \(D_{\mathrm{BA}} = D_{\mathrm{AB}} = 0{,}28\) mm/kN and \(D_{\mathrm{BC}} = D_{\mathrm{CB}} = 0{,}40\) mm/kN. How far does the point \(B\) go down when 6 kN stand at \(A\) and 4 kN at \(C\)? By adding loads

\[\begin{aligned} \Delta_{\mathrm{B}} &= D_{\mathrm{BA}} \cdot 6\ \text{kN} + D_{\mathrm{BC}} \cdot 4\ \text{kN} = 0{,}28 \cdot 6\ \text{mm} + 0{,}40 \cdot 4\ \text{mm} \\ &= 1{,}68\ \text{mm} + 1{,}60\ \text{mm} = 3{,}28\ \text{mm} . \end{aligned}\]

Without the theorem we would need two tests, with the load at \(A\) and with the load at \(C\), and would measure the displacement at \(B\) each time. With the theorem one test with the load at \(B\) is enough. EP and CM give such an example (EP example 4.6.7, p. 231, CM example 7.4.4, PDF pp. 319-320). If we measured the displacement at many points, one test with the load at \(B\) would tell how far \(B\) goes down when the load stands at any one of them.

The flexibility matrix gives displacements from forces. The reverse, forces from displacements, is given by the stiffness matrix of the bracket, which we obtained in section 4.5.7 from the derivatives of the strain energy with respect to the displacements. It is the inverse matrix of the flexibility matrix (definition 1.105). For the bracket we checked with SymPy that

\[\begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{bmatrix} 10^6\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} \cdot \frac{1\ \text{m}}{EA}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 16/3 \\ 16/3 & 21 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The stiffness matrix is symmetric too. In section 4.5.7 we saw this from the equality of the mixed derivatives of the energy, and COOK proves the symmetry of the stiffness matrix precisely with Betti's theorem (COOK (2.6-1)-(2.6-3), PDF p. 51). The stiffness matrix is the basis of the finite element method, which we will meet in chapter 7.

With this we have reached the end of the chapter. We started with the work of a force and the energy a bar stores. Then we wrote equilibrium as the equality of the work of the external forces and the work of the stresses for every admissible virtual displacement, derived from this form the principle of minimum total potential energy, and with the roles of forces and displacements exchanged the principle of virtual forces. In this section we obtained from the same principle of virtual displacements, used twice, and from the symmetry of the elastic constants that the roles of two loads may be exchanged. All results of the chapter hold for small displacements and for a linear elastic material that returns the work it receives.

4.8 Connections

The subject abbreviations are the same as in section 1.19.

  • The principle of virtual displacements: the weak form of the boundary value problem and the Ritz and Galerkin methods (AK, MK, DSK, chapter 6), the finite element equations of bars (AK, MK, chapter 7), virtual work for a beam with an axial force, a shear force and a bending moment (VT 8, MK, chapter 5), virtual work for mechanisms in generalized coordinates and d'Alembert's principle (VD 1, DSK 2, chapter 8).
  • The principle of minimum total potential energy: the stiffness matrix from the second derivatives of the energy (AK, chapter 7), Dirichlet's condition for the stability of an equilibrium (VD, chapter 8), Rayleigh's method for natural frequencies (DSK, chapter 13), structural optimization with minimum compliance (MK, chapter 29).
  • Virtual forces, the unit dummy load method and Castigliano's theorems: displacements and statically indeterminate structures made of beams and frames (MK, VT, chapter 5).
  • Betti's and Maxwell's theorems: the symmetry of the stiffness and flexibility matrices (AK, chapter 7), influence coefficients and influence lines (VD, DSK, chapter 10).
  • Integrals over a body and the divergence theorem: the equilibrium of a finite part of a body and the boundary value problem (VT, chapter 11), the weak form (chapter 6), heat conduction (AK, VT, chapter 14).
